entries.review_note: Lesson plan reviewed 17 Sep 2026 13:41 CEST, posted Talk rev 8613. Status at review: 'Lesson plan: review'. REVISION REQUESTED (major). Plan-only review (SharePoint folder empty): major revision. The plan never says how it relates to the unclaimed sibling LEs H-049/H-051/H-052/H-053/H-055; LO3 mixes up accidental shift and overconfidence with adversarial vulnerability; LO2 mixes taxonomy levels; indirect prompt injection is missing; LO5 has no student activity and no running example is named; most author fields are empty and show 'None.' even though the plan assumes ML prerequisites. 6 must-fix item(s).

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed the H-050 lesson plan on the wiki as of 17 September 2026 (revision 8449; your last content edit was revision 7167 on 1 July 2026). The SharePoint folder 4.1 Horizontal/H-050 is empty and the Talk page had no earlier comments, so this is a plan-only review, and our verdict is major revision.

Reviewer expertise: familiar with the topic (industry practitioner in ML deployment and LLM security review).

What works

The first paragraph of the instructions sets the right register for a Horizontal audience: "a reliability and safety problem in machine learning, not as a practical hacking tutorial", plus "Keep examples conceptual and avoid step-by-step attack recipes". Keep both sentences.
The central point is correct: "a model can perform well on ordinary test data and still be fragile when inputs are chosen by an adaptive adversary", and adversarial settings are harder "because the data-generating process reacts to the deployed system". That is how Dalvi et al. first framed spam and fraud detection (Adversarial classification, KDD 2004).
The 10-20 minute block asks four threat-model questions: "who can attack, what they can observe, what they can change, and what they want to achieve". These map onto attacker goals, capabilities and knowledge in NIST AI 100-2e2025 section 2.1, so the material can build on a published reference without changing the plan.
The 20-30 minute block names feedback loops as an attack surface and says attacks reach "text, tabular data, signals, recommender systems, and operational workflows". Keep this: it stops students treating adversarial ML as an image-only problem.
The 50-60 minute block says defences are partial and "may trade off with accuracy, usability, cost, or fairness". This matches NIST AI 100-2e2025 section 4.1.1.
Six 10-minute blocks add up to the declared 60 minutes, and every outcome carries a level tag.
Must fix

The plan does not say whether H-050 is the overview for the sibling security LEs or the evasion LE, and it names none of them. (learningOutcomes 2 and 5; instructions, first paragraph; 20-30 and 50-60 minute blocks)
The Horizontal master list has H-049 Prompt injection and Jailbreaking Attacks, H-051 Data Poisoning Attacks, H-052 Privacy Attacks (Membership Inference and Model Inversion) and H-053 Defensive Strategies and Robust AI, all 60-minute lectures, plus H-055 Privacy-preserving machine learning (BME and TUD). On 17 September 2026 all five have no named author and "!Missing status!" in the master list, and their SharePoint folders are empty. Outcome 2 asks students to differentiate "evasion attacks, poisoning attacks, model extraction, privacy attacks, and prompt or input manipulation" and outcome 5 asks them to evaluate defences, which is the ground those siblings are titled for. Evasion and model extraction are the two classes no sibling title covers. Evasion is the plan's unstated default (the 0-10 examples of a manipulated image classifier, a spam filter bypass and fraud detection are all evasion), but its core concepts never appear: white-box and black-box access, transferability, physical-world attacks. Elsewhere in the track adversarial topics appear on one or two slides per deck, for example HC-164 Intro to agentic AI.pdf page 38 ("Security & Prompt Injection"), HC-170 Limitations & Risks2.pdf pages 9 and 10 ("Direct and indirect prompt injection", "Tool-Use Hijacking") and HC-168 Limitations & Risks1.pdf page 42 (agent-level: "Sensor spoofing", "Policy manipulation", "Reward exploitation"). You are second author on all three.
Fix: Pick one scope and write it into the first paragraph of the instructions. (a) H-050 is the overview and entry LE for H-049 to H-053 and H-055: each attack class gets a definition, one case from the running example and a pointer to the LE that covers it in depth, and evasion gets real time because no sibling owns it. (b) H-050 is the evasion LE: adversarial examples, white-box and black-box attacks, transferability, physical-world attacks, why models are vulnerable, adversarial training and certified defences at concept level, with the other classes named and pointed to. The plan as written is closer to (a). Keep (a) only if WP4 confirms the siblings will be authored. If they will not, H-050 is the only dedicated adversarial ML event in the Horizontal track and 60 minutes may not be enough. Please raise it with the WP4 lead, who decides whether H-050 and the siblings all stay. Put the map of related LEs in the instructions: the reviewer guidelines say "References to other LEs belong in the lesson plan, not in the slides."
Outcome 3 lists accidental distribution shift and overconfidence as reasons for adversarial vulnerability, which blurs the distinction your own instructions ask for. (learningOutcomes 3: "Describe why adversarial vulnerability can arise from high-dimensional data, learned shortcuts, distribution shift, excessive confidence, and mismatch between training data and real-world use."; repeated in the 30-40 minute block)
The instructions say "Make the difference between accidental distribution shift and adversarial manipulation explicit." The outcome then gives shift and train/deployment mismatch as causes of adversarial vulnerability. Adversarial examples do not need a shift: Szegedy et al. (Intriguing properties of neural networks, ICLR 2014) found imperceptible perturbations of ordinary test images that change the network's output. NIST AI 100-2e2025 section 4.1.2 allows both cases: adversarial examples "may come from the same data distribution on which the model was trained and to which it expects the inputs to belong or may be OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION (OOD) inputs". So the inputs can overlap, but the cause and the threat model differ: nobody chooses an accidental shift, while an attacker searches for the inputs that fail. Overconfidence explains why confidence thresholds miss adversarial inputs (Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy, ICLR 2015, describe them as misclassified with high confidence), but it is not one of the standard explanations for why such inputs exist.
Fix: Rewrite outcome 3 as: "Describe the main explanations for why models that perform well on test data can be changed by small or targeted input modifications (near-linear behaviour in high-dimensional input spaces, reliance on non-robust or shortcut features), and distinguish adversarial manipulation from accidental distribution shift. (knowledge, intermediate level)". In the 30-40 block say the cause is still debated and name the accounts: Goodfellow et al. 2015 (linearity); Ilyas et al., Adversarial examples are not bugs, they are features, NeurIPS 2019 (non-robust features); Geirhos et al., Shortcut learning in deep neural networks, Nature Machine Intelligence 2(11):665-673, 2020. Move overconfidence to the defence block as the reason monitoring on confidence scores fails.
Outcome 2 mixes levels of the attack taxonomy. (learningOutcomes 2; 20-30 minute block: "evasion at inference time, data poisoning during training, model extraction, membership or privacy inference, and prompt or input manipulation in AI systems")
NIST AI 100-2e2025 places model extraction at 2.4.4 inside 2.4 Privacy Attacks, next to membership inference at 2.4.2, so outcome 2 lists a parent class ("privacy attacks") beside one of its own members ("model extraction"). "Input manipulation" at inference time is evasion under another name. As written, students are asked to differentiate labels that overlap.
Fix: Use two of the NIST classification dimensions, which your 10-20 block already half-teaches. Stage of learning: training time (data and model poisoning, backdoors) or deployment time (evasion; privacy attacks, including membership inference and model extraction; direct prompting and indirect prompt injection). Attacker objective: availability, integrity, privacy, and for generative AI misuse enablement. Rewrite outcome 2 as: "Classify a described attack by lifecycle stage and attacker objective using the NIST AI 100-2e2025 categories. (cognitive skill, intermediate level)", give it a short classification activity (see the re-timing below), and cite the NIST report in the plan.
The LLM content covers only a user typing a malicious prompt. Indirect prompt injection is missing. (instructions paragraph 2: "a user prompt designed to make an AI assistant ignore instructions"; 0-10 block: "a malicious prompt to an AI assistant"; outcome 4: "large language model use")
With a direct prompt the attacker is the user. In LLM systems that read external content (email, web pages, shared documents, tool outputs) the attacker can be a third party and the user the victim. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 ranks prompt injection, direct and indirect, first (LLM01), and NIST AI 100-2e2025 treats direct prompting (3.3) and indirect prompt injection (3.4) as separate classes. Greshake et al., Not what you've signed up for, AISec 2023, set out the indirect case. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, disclosed by Aim Security in June 2025) was a zero-click case in Microsoft 365 Copilot where one crafted email could lead to data exfiltration; Microsoft fixed it server-side. The UK NCSC blog of 8 December 2025, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), argues it may never be fully mitigated the way SQL injection was and advises limiting impact through system design. This changes the threat model students build in your 10-20 block, so it belongs in H-050 under either scope, with the depth left to H-049.
Fix: In the 0-10 block replace "a malicious prompt to an AI assistant" with a contrast pair: a user trying to make a chatbot break its rules (jailbreak, attacker is the user) and an email assistant that reads a message with hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection, attacker is a third party). Add indirect prompt injection to outcome 2 and the 20-30 block. Add least privilege for tool and data access, and human confirmation before consequential actions, to the 50-60 defence list, since input filtering alone does not stop it. Point to H-049 for depth.
Outcome 5 is a competence-level "Evaluate" with no student activity behind it, and the one exercise (40-50 block) is untimed and has no scenario or answer key. (learningOutcomes 5; 40-50 block: "Ask students to identify the attacker, attack surface, and likely harm in one running example"; 50-60 block)
The 50-60 block is three lecturer-led bullets, so outcome 5 cannot be observed; the reviewer checklist item on professional judgement asks where students could "make, justify or evaluate decisions". The one exercise shares its 10 minutes with two content bullets, and the running example is never chosen: the plan offers an image classifier, a spam filter, fraud detection and a malicious prompt as alternatives. Your H-128 and H-129 plans both tell the teacher to "Use one running example throughout"; H-050 mentions a running example only in the 40-50 block and never introduces one. The format checklist for lecture slides asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements, so schedule them in the plan now. The 20-30 block is also overloaded: six lifecycle attack surfaces, five attack types and five kinds of target in 10 minutes.
Fix: Name one running example in the instructions. One that suits a mixed audience and both predictive and generative AI: a bank's card-fraud screening model plus an LLM assistant that drafts replies to customer dispute emails. It carries evasion (fraudsters shape transactions to pass), poisoning (false fraud reports that flow back as training labels), probing (many small test transactions to learn what gets approved) and indirect prompt injection (a dispute email with hidden instructions), and it has people on both sides of an error: customers wrongly blocked and fraud victims. Then re-time, for example:
0-8: opening poll with four short cases, including the jailbreak and indirect-injection pair; students vote "ordinary error, noise, distribution shift or attack?" (outcome 1).
8-18: threat model on the running example, using the NIST objective names (outcome 2).
18-30: attack classes by stage and objective, closing with a four-minute check where students classify three short attack descriptions (outcome 2).
30-38: why models are vulnerable, with one poll question that separates shift from attack (outcome 3).
38-50: pair exercise on the running example: the attacker, what they can see and change, the attack surface, who is harmed and who carries the residual risk (outcome 4).
50-60: students judge five proposed controls: which threat each addresses, how it was tested and what risk remains (outcome 5).
Write the case texts and an expected-answer outline for each activity into the instructions. This timing has no slack, so keep the additions from this review small: most are one sentence in a block, a line in an answer key or a reading in recommTePrep, and depth goes to the sibling LEs, HC-195, HC-205, H-128 and H-129.
Most author-owned wiki fields are empty, and the live page tells students that no preparation or prior LE is needed. (expectedLEs, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx and origContrib are empty in the wikitext; keywords holds only "adversarial attack")
The template renders empty preparation fields and an empty expectedLEs as "None.", so the page currently says students need no prior LE and no background. The plan assumes decision boundaries, gradients and test-set accuracy (instructions, paragraph beginning "Keep the mathematical and algorithmic details light": "perturbations, decision boundaries, gradients, and high-dimensional spaces"). The blank Expected preparation rendering is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally, but the fields are yours to fill. The page also contains no reading or reference. A different teacher and the students work from the wiki page, so we treat an empty or one-line field as a must-fix.
Fix: Decide prerequisites with one rule that holds for either scope. Either list H-108 Fundamentals of Machine Learning (decision boundaries, 60-75 and 110-120 minute blocks) and H-122 Model Training, Evaluation and Generalization (loss and gradient descent, 15-35 minutes; model evaluation, 105-115 minutes) in expectedLEs and set Self-standing to No, or keep Self-standing Yes, add a short intuition segment on decision boundaries and gradients to the 30-38 block, and list H-108 and H-122 in backgrStPrep. Then fill the other fields as set out under Wiki page completeness below.
Should fix

Defences are listed without the test that makes them credible: an evaluation by someone trying to break that specific defence. (50-60 block: "adversarial testing, monitoring"; learningOutcomes 5)
NIST AI 100-2e2025 section 4.1.3 says "new mitigations should be tested adversarially, with the researchers proposing the mitigation also trying to break it." Athalye, Carlini and Wagner (Obfuscated gradients give a false sense of security, ICML 2018) found 7 of 9 ICLR 2018 white-box defences relied on obfuscated gradients and circumvented 6 fully and 1 partially. Tramèr, Carlini, Brendel and Madry (On adaptive attacks to adversarial example defenses, NeurIPS 2020) circumvented 13 more. Detection does not avoid the problem: NIST 4.1.2 cites Tramèr (Detecting adversarial examples is (nearly) as hard as classifying them, ICML 2022). Students who later read a vendor's "adversarially tested" claim need to know this.
Fix: Add one bullet to the 50-60 block: a defence counts only if someone who knew about it tried to break it. Put three questions into the controls exercise: who tested it, against which threat model, with what access. Add that detectors and filters can be attacked too.
"Adversarial robustness cannot usually be guaranteed absolutely" needs the qualifier that bounded guarantees exist. (instructions, last paragraph before "Suggested lesson structure")
Certified defences give guarantees inside a stated perturbation budget. Cohen, Rosenfeld and Kolter (Certified adversarial robustness via randomized smoothing, ICML 2019) certified an ImageNet classifier against small L2 perturbations, with the certificate holding at a stated high probability. The guarantee covers only that threat model and says nothing about stickers, poisoning or prompt injection. That gap is what "careful communication of residual risk" in outcome 5 has to explain.
Fix: Replace the sentence with: "Guarantees exist only for narrow, formally defined threat models. Outside them robustness cannot be guaranteed, so residual risk has to be stated against a named threat model."
No link to the AI Act, to the LEs that already teach it, or to the tools practitioners use. (instructions; keywords)
Article 15(5) of the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, requires the technical solutions of high-risk AI systems to include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. These are the attack classes this lecture covers. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, the Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028. The track already teaches the legal and governance side: HC-205 EU AI Act Basics slide 17 has the row "Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity | Stable and secure operation | Protection against attacks | Article 15"; HC-204 slide 30 covers Article 55 ("Conduct adversarial testing") for general-purpose models with systemic risk; HC-195 Model Risk Management names "adversarial vulnerabilities" among deployed-model failure modes (slide 2) and requires at its pre-deployment gate that the "Model behaves correctly on edge cases and adversarial inputs" (slide 15). In practice teams also work from the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning) and MITRE ATLAS.
Fix: In the 50-60 block add one sentence that this is a legal requirement for high-risk systems in the EU, with Article 15(5) and the dates above, and say who asks for the evidence in an organisation: security, model risk or compliance, and procurement when buying a vendor model. Refer to HC-205 and HC-195 rather than teaching the Act or the stage gate here. Put OWASP and MITRE ATLAS in optionStPrep or recommTePrep. Recheck the dates when the material is finalised.
The 30-40 block goes over ground from your H-128 and H-129 without naming them. (30-40 block: "overconfidence", "mismatch between training and deployment", "Connect adversarial vulnerability to the broader themes of robustness, validation, and uncertainty")
H-128 teaches overconfident probabilities and calibration (55-70 minute block) and H-129 teaches distribution shift (68-80) and perturbation and stress tests (80-90). H-129's stress tests check plausible data shifts, not inputs chosen by an attacker, and students will conflate the two unless H-050 says so.
Fix: List H-128 and H-129 in backgrStPrep, refer to them in the 30-40 block instead of re-teaching shift and calibration, and add one sentence that a stress test under plausible shift is not an adversarial test. Name H-049, H-051, H-052, H-053 and H-055 as follow-on LEs in the instructions, so a teacher sees them whatever the template does with successor links.
No second author. (authorOrg2 and authorPers2 empty)
Nobody is assigned to do the didactic second-author review before the material is built.
Fix: Ask the WP4 lead to assign one. Ioannis Patias (SU), first author of HC-164, HC-168 and HC-170, is one option and would help settle where prompt injection is taught.
The examples in the plan are not traceable, so the material and a different teacher may use different ones. (instructions paragraph 2 and 0-10 block: "a slightly modified image that fools a classifier", "a spam email rewritten to bypass detection"; 40-50 block: "medical decision support")
Each has a standard, citable source. Image perturbations: Szegedy et al., ICLR 2014, and Goodfellow et al., ICLR 2015. Physical world: Eykholt et al., Robust physical-world attacks on deep learning visual classification, CVPR 2018 (stickers on a real stop sign, misclassified in 84.8% of video frames taken from a moving vehicle). Spam and fraud: Dalvi et al., KDD 2004. Medical: Finlayson et al., Adversarial attacks on medical machine learning, Science 363(6433):1287-1289, 2019, which also explains the billing and insurance incentives behind attacks and is short enough for non-technical students. Model extraction: Carlini et al., Stealing part of a production language model, ICML 2024 (the embedding projection matrix of OpenAI's Ada and Babbage models recovered through the API for under 20 USD).
Fix: Name these next to the blocks that use them and add them to recommTePrep.
The harm side stays abstract for a human-centred programme. (40-50 block: "likely harm"; 50-60 block: "may trade off with accuracy, usability, cost, or fairness")
The plan never asks who is harmed by an attack or by a defence. The fairness trade-off can be made concrete: Xu et al., To be robust or to be fair, ICML 2021, found adversarial training on CIFAR-10 left the "automobile" class at 67% adversarial accuracy and the "cat" class at 17%. That is a result across image classes, but the same mechanism can leave subgroups of people less protected.
Fix: Add "who is harmed, and who carries the residual risk" to the 40-50 exercise (38-50 in the re-timing above), and use the Xu et al. result, labelled as a class-level finding, in the answer key for the controls exercise.
Plan the material now so a different teacher can run it. (instructions; lessonMaterials)
The guidelines ask for slides that "contain lecturer notes that make the slides usable for a lecturer who was not involved in developing the material", sample solutions or model answers where relevant, and "clear naming and availability of all required files". BME's H-132, H-147 and HC-040 decks have notes on every slide. The H-128 and H-129 decks are PDFs without speaker notes, and they and the H-130 notebook carry no licence, funding or acknowledgement statement, although they do carry reference lists. The standard adversarial-example figures (the panda from Goodfellow et al. 2015, the stop-sign photos from Eykholt et al. 2018) belong to their authors.
Fix: Deliver H-050 as .pptx with per-slide lecturer notes, the exercise case texts and model answers in the notes, and timing markers that match the plan blocks. Keep a references slide as in H-128 and H-129, and add the licence, funding and acknowledgement back matter; the funding wording is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally, so use the corrected slide once WP4 issues it. Credit reused figures in origContrib and check their licences against CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, or redraw them.
Smaller things

Outcome 1 says "deliberately constructed inputs or conditions". Poisoning manipulates training data, not inputs, and "conditions" is vague. Use "inputs, training data or content the system retrieves".
Outcome 4 names six domains ("computer vision, spam filtering, fraud detection, medical AI, cybersecurity, and large language model use"), while the exercise uses one running example. Trim it to the running example plus one contrast domain so the outcome matches what students practise.
The 10-20 block lists "causing denial of service" among attacker goals. Use the NIST objective names (availability, integrity, privacy, misuse enablement) so the terms match outcome 2.
The 0-10 block lists "a spam filter bypass" and "fraud detection" among its opening scenarios. Say that adversarial ML started there (Dalvi et al. 2004), so students do not assume it began with image attacks on deep networks. Biggio and Roli, Wild patterns: Ten years after the rise of adversarial machine learning, Pattern Recognition 84:317-331, 2018, gives the history.
If a poisoning example stays in the overview (instructions paragraph 2: "poisoned training examples"), use a current one and state its limit. Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute reported in October 2025 that about 250 poisoned documents planted a backdoor in models from 600M to 13B parameters regardless of training data size; the backdoor was narrow (gibberish output after a trigger phrase). Carlini et al., Poisoning web-scale training datasets is practical, IEEE S&P 2024, showed 0.01% of LAION-400M or COYO-700M could have been poisoned for 60 USD. Put these in the teacher notes; depth belongs in H-051.
The timing table in the instructions was pasted from a document: bullet lines start with spaces and "•", and "When?" and "What?" are plain lines. MediaWiki can render lines that start with a space as preformatted boxes. Check the rendered page; if that happens, remove the leading spaces and use one <p> block per time slot, as H-108 and H-122 do.
Wiki page completeness

keywords: thin, one term ("adversarial attack"). Add, $-separated as on H-128 and H-129: adversarial example$evasion attack$data poisoning$backdoor$model extraction$membership inference$prompt injection$indirect prompt injection$jailbreak$threat model$attack surface$transferability$adversarial training$certified robustness$red teaming$AI Act Article 15
expectedLEs: empty, renders "None.". Apply the rule under Must fix: H-108 and H-122 here with Self-standing set to No, or keep Yes and put them in backgrStPrep.
obligStPrep: empty, renders "None.". Confirm that is intended, or set Finlayson et al. 2019 (three pages, non-technical).
optionStPrep: empty, renders "None.". Suggested: NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), 8 December 2025; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, entries LLM01 and LLM04.
backgrStPrep: empty, renders "None.". H-128 and H-129; H-014 Introduction to LLMs for the LLM part; H-108 and H-122 if Self-standing stays Yes.
recommTePrep: empty, renders "None.". Vassilev, Oprea, Fordyce, Anderson, Davies and Hamin, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, NIST AI 100-2e2025, March 2025, doi:10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025, sections 2.1, 2.4, 3.1 to 3.4 and 4.1; Biggio and Roli 2018; Athalye et al. 2018; Greshake et al. 2023; MITRE ATLAS; plus the example sources listed under Should fix.
ackThx: empty. Fill it now with the people or sources you want to thank, or write "None". The funding sentence the page shows (Connecting Europe Facility, grant "???", where PANORAIMA is Digital Europe grant 101189994) is template text and a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally; no action for you on that sentence.
origContrib: empty. Write "None" or credit reused figures and examples.
lessonMaterials: empty, and there is no material yet. When you upload, list each file by name with its SharePoint location. The stub the section shows now is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally.
authorOrg2 / authorPers2: empty. See Should fix.
learningOutcomes: filled, but outcomes 2, 3 and 5 need the rewrites under Must fix.
instructions: filled and substantial, but a different teacher cannot yet run the session without a named running example, exercise texts with expected answers, sources and links to related LEs.
We will re-review the plan once it is revised and back in review, and review the material separately when it reaches SharePoint.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST

action_summary.text:
Hi András, this is the short, actionable version of our review of 17 September 2026; the full text stays above as the record. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: major revision. Keep the reliability framing and the four threat-model questions.

Please do next:
# State your scope in the first instructions paragraph: overview for H-049, H-051, H-052, H-053 and H-055, or the evasion LE.
# Rewrite learning outcome 3 and the 30-40 block so shift and overconfidence are not causes of vulnerability; move overconfidence to the 50-60 block.
# Rewrite learning outcome 2 as classifying an attack by lifecycle stage and attacker objective (NIST AI 100-2e2025), with a short classification activity.
# Add indirect prompt injection to the 0-10 block, outcome 2 and the 20-30 block, and add least privilege and human confirmation to the 50-60 block.
# Name one running example in the instructions; give outcome 5 a timed student activity with case texts and an answer outline.
# List H-108 and H-122 in expectedLEs and set Self-standing to No, or keep Yes and add a short decision-boundary and gradient segment.
# Add to the 50-60 block that a defence counts only if someone who knew it tried to break it; reword "cannot usually be guaranteed".

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):
* expectedLEs, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep: all render "None."
* keywords: one term only
* ackThx, origContrib, Lesson materials link, Author Person 2: empty or template text

A short summary is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off.

When the items are done, tell us on this Discussion page and email the review inbox so we can re-review.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 14 October 2026, 20:51 CEST

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan and material, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed revision 8606 of the H-108 wiki page (Kristina Arnaoudova, 16 September 2026, 08:35 UTC) and "Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf" in the H-108 SharePoint folder (37 pages, dated 16 September 2026). Both need major revision: the status reads "Lesson plan: review", but the deck is already in the folder, so we reviewed plan and deck together and the deck comments below are part of this review.

Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert (machine learning in industry practice). Slide numbers below are the numbers printed on the slides; the PDF has 37 pages because number 18 is missing. There is no Talk page yet and the PDF carries no comments, so there were no earlier remarks to reconcile. The PDF was exported at 15:06 CEST, about four and a half hours after revision 8606, so some of the plan-deck mismatches below may come from that order. They still need aligning.

What works

Slide 3 gives three paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), which matches the taxonomy RealAI recommended at programme level after finding four different taxonomies across the Horizontal ML introductions. Slide 11 adds a useful step on top of that: it separates the learning paradigm ("the information or feedback available during training") from the modelling approach ("discriminative or generative modeling"). Keep both slides.
Slide 26 puts the confusion matrix and the accuracy, precision, recall and F1 formulas together, with correct cell placement (rows actual, columns predicted). Our 9 September cross-series check found no definition of the confusion matrix in the 25 events it covered. Elsewhere in the 4.1 Horizontal SharePoint folder, only BME's HC-030 shows one, as a large table of rates used to define group fairness (pages 11, 12 and 15), plus a third-party Orange tutorial in HC-183. Slide 26 is the clearer introduction, and HC-030 can build on it.
Slides 22 and 24 state the validation and test roles the way practitioners need them: "The validation set is not used for training and is not the final performance estimate" and "The test set is used only once after model selection to estimate generalization performance". Reusing the test set during tuning is one of the commonest mistakes in real projects. Keep both lines as written.
One flower example runs through the deck: roses and sunflowers from data collection on slide 14 to classification, k-NN and clustering on slides 19, 20, 21 and 31, roses alone for regression on slide 17, and a wider flower set on slides 34 and 35. Students compare methods on the same kind of picture. Several of the figures need fixing (below), but keep the design.
Slide 16 gives the training loop with the empirical risk, R(w) = (1/N) Σ L(y_i, f_w(x_i)). The formula is correct and the notation level suits a first machine learning lecture.
Plan against deck, block by block

0-15 min (paradigms, example problems): slides 3 and 4, as planned.
15-30 min (workflow, data quality, features, "numerical representation"): slides 6 to 9.
30-45 min (supervised learning, classification and regression tasks): slides 11, 13, 14 and 15.
45-60 min (training, validation, tuning, test, evaluation, inference): slide 16, then slides 22, 24, 25 and 26, which sit after the model slides. The block says "evaluation" but names no metric.
60-75 min (classification, linear and nonlinear boundaries): slides 19 and 20.
75-90 min (regression, residuals): slide 17 only, placed before the classification slides.
90-100 min (k-NN, "choice of k"): slide 21 only.
100-110 min (clustering, "k-means", centroids): slides 29 to 31.
110-120 min (discriminative and generative): slides 33 to 36.
In no block: slide 23 (model complexity) and slide 27 (applications).
Must fix

The Instructions for teachers is a topic list another lecturer cannot run, and the deck has no lecturer notes. (Wiki field instructions, all nine blocks, for example "90–100 min: k-nearest neighbors, similarity, distance, nearest examples, choice of k, majority voting.")
None of the nine blocks says which slides to use, what the lecturer explains or asks, what students do, or what answer to expect. There is no break in 120 minutes. The block order differs from the deck in two places (see the mapping above): a lecturer following the wiki clock at minute 45 needs slides 22 to 26, which sit after the model slides 17 to 21, and regression comes after classification on the wiki but before it in the deck. The deck is a PDF with no lecturer notes, while the guidelines ask for notes "that make the slides usable for a lecturer who was not involved in developing the material".
Fix: Rewrite each block as minutes, slide numbers, what the lecturer explains or asks, what students do, the expected answer, and the transition to the next block. H-132's Instructions for teachers shows the level of detail we mean. Schedule a 10-minute break around minute 60; none of the 120-minute plans we reviewed on 9 September schedules one and we have raised that with WP4, but please add it here. Reorder the wiki blocks or the slides so they match. Upload the .pptx source next to the PDF, with notes on every slide, including the answer keys asked for below. Without an editable source the Adapt right on slide 38 is also hard to use in practice.
Ten PanoLessonPlan fields are empty. (Revision 8606: keywords, expectedLEs, self-standing, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx, origContrib, lessonMaterials)
Lecturers at other institutions choose and prepare from these fields.
Fix: What to put in each one is under Wiki page completeness below. Please fill them all before the next round.
About 65 of the 120 minutes cover topics that H-114a and H-122, which you also author, schedule again, and much of the rest overlaps HC-019, HC-021 and HC-022. (Wiki instructions blocks 45-60, 60-75, 75-90, 90-100 and 110-120, and learning outcome 5, against the H-114a and H-122 wiki pages)
H-114a lists H-108 as its prerequisite, then schedules discriminative and generative models (0-10 min), linear classification and regression (10-30), residuals (30-45), linear against nonlinear relationships (90-100) and "100–108 min: KNN, similarity, nearest neighbors, k distance, majority voting", which is your 90-100 block almost word for word.
H-122 schedules data splitting and tuning (35-60 minutes), "generalization, unseen data, underfitting, overfitting, model complexity" (60-80) and "confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score" (105-115). Its outcome "Select and interpret appropriate evaluation metrics for classification and regression" contains H-108 outcome 5.
Across partners, H-108 outcomes 1 and 3 restate HC-019's "describe the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning" and "give examples of tasks that can be solved using classification, regression and clustering", the 45-60 block repeats HC-022's workflow block, and the k-means block repeats HC-021's clustering section. RealAI's cross-series analysis counted four ML introductions in the Horizontal track; H-108 would be the fifth.
Slide 4 item 3, "Learn to play chess by maximizing wins", expects reinforcement learning. HC-022 slide 4 (checked 9 September) uses a child told "good move" or "bad move" at chess as its first example of supervised learning. A student taking both events gets two answers.
Fix: Decide the split across H-108, H-114a and H-122 and record it on the wiki. Our suggestion, the same one we make in today's H-114a and H-122 reviews: H-108 already has the slides, so it keeps the introduction to these topics, and H-114a and H-122 replace their repeated blocks with a short recap of H-108 and go further (logistic regression, kernels and trees in H-114a; gradient descent, leakage, bias-variance and ROC curves in H-122). For H-108 that means keeping each topic at introduction depth and saying in the instructions where H-114a and H-122 take it further. Add H-108 to H-122's expectedLEs. For the cross-partner overlap, Béla Pataki is second author here, first author of HC-021 and HC-022 and second author of HC-019, so please agree with him and the WP4 lead which event owns the ML introduction, and settle the chess example between the two decks.
The learning outcomes, slide 2 and the timed blocks do not match, and outcomes 4 and 5 are not delivered. (Wiki learningOutcomes; slides 2, 3, 23, 26, 29 to 31)
Outcome 4 lists "overfitting"; the word does not appear anywhere in the deck. Slide 23 shows the curves under "High Bias", "Good Balance" and "High Variance" and never says overfitting or underfitting.
Outcome 5 asks students to "Select appropriate basic evaluation metrics for common supervised learning tasks". Slide 26 defines four classification metrics but gives no basis for choosing between them, such as class imbalance or the cost of a false negative against a false positive. There is no regression metric, although slide 17 teaches regression.
The 100-110 block promises "k-means". Slide 31, titled "Clustering Training", only assigns a new point to the nearer of two existing centroids. That is the inference step; nothing shows how the centroids were found.
In the other direction, k-NN (90-100) and discriminative against generative (110-120) have time but no outcome. Reinforcement learning is taught on slides 3 and 4, but outcome 1 names only supervised and unsupervised learning. Dimensionality reduction (slide 29) has neither a block nor an outcome. Slide 2 gives a third list: "Distinguish discriminative from generative models", "Explain the basic training process", "Interpret how models make predictions", and no metrics objective.
The outcomes carry no type or level. HC-020, HC-021 and HC-022 tag every outcome, for example "Explain (knowledge, intermediate level)"; HC-021 and HC-022 are first-authored by your second author, Béla Pataki. Outcome 4, "Explain the concepts of features, labels, training data, test data, overfitting, and generalization", is six outcomes in one sentence and cannot be assessed as one.
Fix: Make the wiki outcomes and slide 2 one list, give every outcome a block and slides, and give every block an outcome. Tag each outcome with type and level. Split outcome 4 into data concepts (features, labels, training and test data) and generalization (overfitting, generalization). Add reinforcement learning to outcome 1. Give dimensionality reduction a block and an outcome, or cut it from slide 29. Name overfitting and underfitting on slide 23. Add MAE and RMSE for regression and one slide on choosing a metric, using the screening example below. Add two or three slides on the k-means algorithm (choose k, initialise centroids, assign, recompute, repeat until assignments stop changing) and retitle slide 31 "Assigning a new example to a cluster". If you reuse slide 31's figure for the recompute step, move the Cluster 1 centroid onto the mean of its four roses; it sits visibly to the right of it.
Slide 21's k-NN figure links two of the wrong neighbours, so the majority vote it teaches is not what the plot shows. (Slide 21: "The model finds the k = 3 nearest examples", "Majority vote 2 sunflowers, 1 rose")
We measured centre-to-centre distances on a 2000-pixel-wide render of the slide. From the new flower, the three nearest training points are all sunflowers, at about 170, 180 and 183 px (lower-left sunflower, upper-right sunflower, blue-background sunflower below). The dotted links go to the third nearest (183 px), the fifth (the right-hand sunflower, about 217 px) and the sixth (the orange rose, about 250 px). On the slide's own geometry, k = 3 gives three sunflowers and no rose. The x-axis also has no label, so students cannot tell what horizontal distance means.
Fix: Move the orange rose closer to the new flower than two of the sunflowers, or move sunflowers away, and redraw the links to the true three nearest. Label the x-axis. The plan promises "choice of k": show k = 1 and k = 5 on the same points so students see the prediction change.
Slide 20 draws a nonlinear boundary for data a straight line already separates, and its Prediction bullets repeat the Training bullets. (Slide 20: "A flexible model can learn a curved boundary when the classes are not separated by a straight line")
All four roses sit left of all four sunflowers with a wide gap between them. A straight line separates the classes perfectly (even a vertical one would), and slide 19 draws a straight boundary on an almost identical layout. The curve also assigns the whole lower-left region, where there is no training data, to sunflowers. Students see a complex boundary where a simple one fits, which is what slide 23 calls high variance. Under "Prediction" the slide repeats "Labeled examples are represented in the same feature space" and "The model learns a curved boundary between the classes", which are training statements.
Fix: Move two roses into the sunflower side, or two sunflowers into the rose side, so no straight line separates the classes, then draw the curve around them. Keep only the prediction step under Prediction. One line pointing to slide 23 (a flexible boundary can also fit noise) turns this into the overfitting example outcome 4 needs.
One interactive element in 120 minutes, and it has no answer key. (Slide 4, "Activity: Which type of learning?"; nothing interactive on slides 5 to 36)
The guidelines ask for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements. RealAI has asked WP4 to scale that with duration, which would mean at least 4 here, but even the current wording needs 2. Slide 4 gives the lecturer no answers. Item 5, "Detect unusual transactions without labels", gives its answer away. Item 6, "Train a robot to navigate a maze", can also be solved by imitation learning from labelled demonstrations, which is supervised.
Fix: Put an answer key in the slide 4 notes (1 supervised, 2 unsupervised, 3 reinforcement, 4 supervised regression, 5 unsupervised anomaly detection, 6 reinforcement, with the imitation-learning caveat). Reword item 5 as "Detect fraudulent transactions" and ask what data would make it supervised (confirmed fraud cases, chargebacks), so students reason about available data instead of spotting a keyword. Add at least three activities with answers: k-NN on a printed grid of eight points with k = 1 and k = 5 after slide 21; two k-means iterations by hand on six points after slide 31; and a screening confusion matrix after slide 26 (10,000 patients, 100 with the disease, TP 60, FN 40, FP 300, TN 9,600: accuracy 96.6 percent, precision 16.7 percent, recall 60 percent, F1 about 26 percent, while predicting "healthy" for everyone scores 99 percent accuracy).
The deck never says how these models affect people. (Slide 7 step "Decision"; slide 8 "Representative examples from the target domain"; slide 26 "FN (false negative) Missed positive"; slide 27 "Cancer screening", "Clinical decision support", "Pedestrian detection in autonomous driving")
The reviewer checklist asks about "risks, limitations, trade-offs, uncertainty, implementation barriers or ethical issues", and the second-author checklist asks that students understand "how AI in this context impacts people". The deck names high-stakes uses on slide 27 and defines a missed positive on slide 26, but never says what a missed positive costs a person, who sets the threshold, or what happens when the training data under-represents a group. Slide 8 lists "Data quality and diversity as key factors in model performance", but only as a performance point. Slide 7's last step, "Decision", has no explanation. The only occurrence of "human" in the PDF is inside the RAISE-U acknowledgement.
Fix: Add one slide and a short discussion after slide 27. Use the screening numbers above: what a false negative and a false positive mean for the patient, and who decides the trade-off. Tie slide 8's "Representative examples" to a documented case: Daneshjou et al., "Disparities in dermatology AI performance on a diverse, curated clinical image set", Science Advances 8, eabq6147 (2022), where state-of-the-art dermatology models lost 27 to 36 percent of their ROC-AUC on a diverse, pathology-confirmed image set compared with their original results and performed worse on dark skin tones. Give "Decision" on slide 7 one line: a prediction becomes a decision made by a person or a system, and that is where accountability sits. In the instructions, name HC-030 (BME) as a follow-up: it builds a confusion matrix per group to define equal opportunity and equalized odds.
There is no references slide, and the image rights are not cleared for release under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. (Whole deck; image credit line on slides 19, 20, 21 and 31 only; photographs with no credit on slides 14, 17, 34 and 35)
The deck cites nothing except the flower images. That citation is correct (Nilsback and Zisserman, ICVGIP 2008), but the VGG dataset page states no licence for the images, so they cannot go under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 until the rights are confirmed. Slides 14, 17, 34 and 35 show photographs with no source line at all, and not all of them can come from Oxford 102: slide 34 shows a tulip, and Oxford 102 has no tulip class (only "siam tulip", a different plant). The missing references slide is also a template gap RealAI raised centrally, but this deck should not be released until it has one.
Fix: Add a references slide before the acknowledgements. Confirm the redistribution status of the Oxford 102 images with the dataset owners, or replace them with images under a stated open licence, and credit every image, including those on slides 14, 17, 34 and 35. Point the standard material (complexity curve, empirical risk, discriminative against generative) to a source students can read, for example James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, "An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python" (Springer, 2023, free PDF at statlearning.com).
Should fix

Nothing in the deck covers what goes wrong in practice, and students are never asked to judge whether machine learning fits a problem. (Slides 6 and 7, workflows ending at "Prediction on new data" and "Decision"; slides 22 and 24)
The workflow stops at prediction: no deployment, monitoring, drift or retraining. Slides 22 and 24 say nothing about data leakage, for example fitting preprocessing on all the data before the split. A text search of the PDF finds no "limit", "leak", "deploy", "monitor", "drift", "noise" or "imbalance", and "risk" appears only as "empirical risk". HC-022's plan gives a block to "overfitting, noisy or incorrect labels, poor feature representation, class imbalance, and dataset bias"; H-108 has nothing equivalent. The reviewer checklist also asks whether students "develop professional judgement, rather than only learn definitions", and after slide 4 the deck is definitions and worked pictures.
Fix: Add one slide on common failure modes (leakage, label noise, class imbalance, distribution shift after deployment) with one example each, extend the workflow on slides 6 and 7 with deployment and monitoring, and add one short discussion where students decide whether machine learning is the right tool for two or three problems and say what data they would need. Deeper treatment can sit in H-122 and HC-020; say so in the instructions.
Slides 33 to 36 use "generative" in two senses without saying so, and slide 36 names methods the deck never explains. (Slide 34 "p(x ∣ y = rose)"; slide 35 "Learns the distribution and generates a new rose example"; slide 36 row "Unsupervised/Self-supervised" and "Triplet learning")
Slides 33 and 34 describe a generative classifier: model p(x | y) and p(y), then classify with Bayes' rule, as naive Bayes and LDA do (Ng and Jordan, NIPS 14, 2001, pp. 841-848). Slide 35 shows something different: noise in, a rose out, which is sampling from a deep generative model, and nothing in the picture tells the model to produce a rose rather than any flower. Students who hear "generative AI" every day will merge the two.
Slide 36 uses "Self-supervised" in a row header and nothing defines it, although RealAI's programme-level recommendation was to define self-supervised learning once, where generative models are introduced. Autoregressive language models, the generative models students use, are absent. "Triplet learning" sits under unsupervised, but triplet loss as introduced in FaceNet (Schroff, Kalenichenko and Philbin, CVPR 2015) builds its triplets from identity labels, which is supervised. The table also names SVM, LDA, GMM, VAE, GAN, diffusion models and contrastive learning, none of which the deck explains, and slide 35 draws a neural network that is never introduced.
Fix: On slide 35 add one sentence for each sense: a generative classifier uses p(x | y)p(y) to get p(y | x); deep generative models sample new data, and to get a rose you condition on the class or train only on roses. Show the conditioning in the figure. On slide 36 add "autoregressive language models (GPT-style transformers)" to the generative column, define self-supervised in one line (the labels come from the data itself, for example predicting the next word), and rename "Triplet learning" to "metric learning with triplet loss (usually supervised)". Say in the notes that the table is for orientation and which event teaches each method (H-114a for SVM and naive Bayes, for example).
Colour is plotted as a continuous axis with no encoding, the feature numbering changes between slides, and feature scaling is never mentioned. (Slide 19 x-axis "Feature 1 color"; slide 20 "color"; slide 21 y-axis "(Feature 1) Petal width" with no x-axis label; slide 31 "(Feature 1) Color" and "(Feature 2)Petal width")
Slide 9 says features may be "numerical, categorical, or derived from raw data" and the 15-30 block promises "numerical representation", but no slide shows how a colour becomes a number. One-hot encoded colour names cannot sit on one axis; a mean hue value can. k-NN on slide 21 and centroid distance on slide 31 then combine that colour value with a width in centimetres, where whichever feature has the larger numeric range dominates the distance.
Fix: Add one line on slide 9 or 15 giving the encoding you intend (for example "colour = mean hue of the flower pixels, 0 to 360 degrees"). Use the same feature numbers on every plot. Before slide 21, add one bullet: distance-based methods need features on comparable scales, so standardise first, and name the distance (Euclidean).
Slide 17's regression line does not fit the points drawn, and the prediction is an extrapolation. (Slide 17: "The model fits a line to the training examples", "New input: petal length = 4.8 cm")
The residuals are correctly drawn as vertical segments. The line itself is too steep: the two left-most points sit well above it and the two right-most well below it, so the residuals run from positive to negative across the plot. A least-squares line through the six plotted points is about a third as steep as the drawn one. The new input is placed left of every training point, so the example predicts outside the training range, where a linear model is least reliable. The axes carry no scale, so "4.8 cm" cannot be read off the plot. Oxford 102 is an image dataset with no petal measurements, so the plotted values are invented; slide 19 says "Illustrative two-feature example", but slides 17, 20, 21 and 31 do not.
Fix: Replot from real data. The Iris dataset (Fisher 1936, UCI Machine Learning Repository, DOI 10.24432/C56C76, CC BY 4.0) has measured petal length and width in centimetres. Fit the line with a library, place the new input inside the data range, and print the predicted width. Where you keep the flower pictures, label every plot "illustrative".
The deck gives three different workflows and never explains its last step. (Slide 6, seven steps from "Data collection and preparation" to "Prediction on new data"; slide 7, seven steps ending "Inference", "Decision"; wiki outcome 2, five stages)
Slide 6 includes feature selection and model selection; slide 7 drops both and adds "Decision"; outcome 2 lists "data collection, data preparation, model training, evaluation, and inference". A student asked to "Describe the main stages" has three answers to choose from. On slide 7 the number badges sit at the right-hand end of each step, so badge 1 reads as the label for "Data preprocessing" and badge 7 seems to have no step.
Fix: Pick one list, use it on slides 6 and 7 and in outcome 2, and explain "Decision" as suggested above. Put each badge on its own step.
Slides 14 and 15 repeat slides 8 and 9. (Slide 9 "For a flower, features may include color, size, petal shape, and sepal shape" and "Each example is represented by a feature vector"; slide 15 "Examples include color, size, petal shape, and sepal shape" and "Each example is represented by a feature vector")
Fix: Merge them, or give 14 and 15 new work: three rows of an actual feature table for roses and sunflowers with their label column. That makes the "features, labels" part of outcome 4 concrete and frees a few minutes for the activities above.
Slide 23 shows only the classical U-shaped curve. (Slide 23, "Model complexity and generalization")
Very large models can show "double descent": test error falls again once capacity passes the point where training error reaches zero (Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, PNAS 116(32): 15849-15854, 2019, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1903070116). Students who later train large neural networks will think the slide is wrong.
Fix: Add one line and the reference, or leave it to H-122 (our H-122 review asks for it there) and say so in the instructions.
Slide 29's definitions are circular or hard to parse, and slide 31 suggests clusters are classes. (Slide 29: "Dimensionality reduction is a technique for reducing the dimension of input data"; "Clustering is used to determine groups of similar objects, which allows using a small number of representatives in different tasks that can describe the diversity of a larger set of data")
The dimensionality reduction line defines the term with itself. On slide 31, Cluster 1 holds exactly the roses and Cluster 2 exactly the sunflowers, which suggests clustering recovers the labels.
Fix: "Dimensionality reduction maps each example to fewer features while keeping as much useful structure as possible, for visualisation or preprocessing (for example PCA)." "Clustering groups examples so that examples in the same group are more similar to each other than to examples in other groups." Add a bullet on slide 31: clusters need not match any class; here they happen to.
Machine learning is never defined. (Slides 2 to 4; wiki block "0–15 min: introduction to machine learning")
Slide 3 goes straight to "Types of Machine Learning".
Fix: Add one line before slide 3: a model whose behaviour is fitted from data rather than written as rules, with one contrast (a hand-written spam rule against a learned spam filter).
Smaller things

Slide numbering jumps from 17 to 19. If slide 18 is hidden, check whether it was meant to be taught; if it was deleted, renumber.
Slide 1 credits only "Kristina Arnaoudova(SU)", while the wiki lists Béla Pataki (BME) as Author Person 2. Under CC BY-NC-SA users copy the credit from the title slide, so add him or correct the wiki. Add the space before "(SU)". The PDF metadata author reads "Arnaudova".
Slide 16: the "M" in "Update Model" is a Cyrillic capital Em (U+041C), which breaks search and screen readers. "Update Parameters" and "Update Model" are the same step drawn twice in the cycle. "L is the loss on example i" should read "L is the loss function; L(y_i, f_w(x_i)) is the loss on example i". The slide has the model predict "for all training examples" each iteration; in practice training uses mini-batches, and one sentence in the notes is enough. The RAISE-U corner mark sits at top centre instead of bottom right, and the slide number sits inside the cycle diagram.
Slide 22 says "previously unseen images" while slides 19 to 21 and 31 work on two measured features. Say "examples", and state once how an image becomes the feature vector.
Slide 26: add Positive and Negative headers to the rows and columns; at present only the "actual positive" and "predicted positive" call-outs identify them. The F1 label is typeset as "F1 − score", which reads as F1 minus score. Slide 24 names ROC-AUC and nothing defines it; define it or say in the notes that H-122 does.
Slide 34 asks "Is this a rose, a daisy, a sunflower, or a tulip?" but also shows dandelions, which the question does not name. On the generative panel the rose photographs sit outside the density ellipses they are meant to illustrate.
The drop shadows under the flower images on slides 17, 21 and 31 export as grey smudges in the PDF. Remove the effect or export again.
No second-author review is recorded yet, either on the Talk page or as comments in the SharePoint file. The guidelines accept either place. Its distinctiveness and connections checks matter most for this event.
Following the guidelines' next steps, the status moves to "Learning materials: under revision" now that this review is posted. The problems are major, so please ask us to check the revision when it is done.
Wiki page completeness

Known template issues RealAI raised centrally on 9 to 13 September, not of your making: the acknowledgement on the wiki and on slide 37 credits the "Connecting Europe Facility", although call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU is Digital Europe (grant agreement 101189994 on slide 37 is correct), and the wiki reads "Grant № ???"; the Expected preparation fields start blank; and Lesson materials names no file. Swap slide 37 when the corrected template arrives, and fill your own fields below.
self-standing: empty. Enter Yes or No; Yes if H-108 opens the SU machine learning sequence and assumes no earlier event.
keywords: empty. Suggested: supervised learning $ unsupervised learning $ reinforcement learning $ features and feature vectors $ training, validation and test sets $ classification $ regression $ k-nearest neighbours $ clustering $ overfitting $ generalization $ confusion matrix $ precision and recall $ discriminative and generative models. Adjust to the agreed split.
expectedLEs: empty. Write "None" explicitly, or name the event the programme decides H-108 follows. H-114a already lists H-108; H-122 should as well.
obligStPrep: empty. State "None" or set a short pre-reading, for example Chapter 2 (Statistical Learning) of An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (2023, free PDF).
optionStPrep: empty. Point to the same book's unsupervised learning chapter for k-means and its classification chapter for logistic regression against generative classifiers.
backgrStPrep: empty. State the intended level and the assumed background (vectors, the notation P(y | x), means and sums), and give one refresher link. The formal content is the feature vector on slide 9, the empirical risk on slide 16 and the metric formulas on slide 26, which fits a first machine learning lecture for master's students from mixed backgrounds; say that here so a lecturer knows the level.
recommTePrep: empty. For the lecturer: Ng and Jordan (2001) for discriminative against generative, Daneshjou et al. (2022) for the human-centred example, and the answer keys for every activity once written.
ackThx: empty. The funding sentence is template text (first line above), but the field is yours: thank the Oxford Visual Geometry Group for the 102 Flowers dataset and credit any other contributors and image sources.
origContrib: empty. Credit the Oxford 102 Flowers images (Nilsback and Zisserman 2008) with their licence status, the sources of the other photographs, and any figure adapted from a textbook.
lessonMaterials: empty. Name each file ("Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf", and the .pptx once uploaded), link the SharePoint folder, and give a licence line per file.
learningOutcomes: filled but not aligned with the deck or slide 2, with no type or level. See the outcomes must-fix.
instructions: filled but a topic list with no slide mapping, activities or break. See the first must-fix.
mandatory: blank here and on every RealAI Horizontal page we hold, so we take it as a programme-level field.
jobrole ("any") and status are set.
Settle the split with H-114a and H-122 first, because it decides how deep each topic goes in this deck.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST

Verdict: major revision still stands. Several figures and definitions are fixed; the lesson itself is not yet teachable by someone else.

Closed since our review:
* Slide 3 now defines machine learning.
* Slide 22 links the right nearest neighbours; slide 19 now keeps the regression line inside the data and says it is illustrative.
* The outcomes and slide 2 now match (the overfitting and metric-choice outcomes were dropped), and k-means has its own slide.
