entries.title: H-110a Data Types and Representations
entries.author: SU · Kristina Arnaoudova
entries.review_note: H-110a is an empty stub. Its outcomes, keywords and instructions are identical to HC-176's (entered on H-110a first, the same day, by the same account), and despite the title no block covers how data becomes model input. It needs owners, a decision on the HC-176 overlap, every field filled, and material before UNINA's planned first use in October 2026.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): lesson plan not yet reviewable, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review: we read the H-110a wiki page as pulled on 17 September 2026 (last content edit revision 5924, 19 May 2026) and the SharePoint folders 4.1 Horizontal/H-110a and H-110b, which are both empty, and there is no Talk page yet. The page is a stub whose learning outcomes, keywords and instructions are identical to HC-176's, so before a formal review it needs named authors, a decision on how H-110a relates to HC-176, a filled lesson plan and the status set to "Lesson plan: review".

Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert, AI industry practice.

What works

The plan puts the programming view of a data type ("Primitive data types, examples & Composite data types, examples") next to the statistical view ("quantitative and qualitative data, NOIR") in one session. Many common data errors come from mixing the two: a patient ID or postcode stored as an integer and then averaged, a 1 to 5 satisfaction score fed to a model as a continuous number, a date stored as text in dd/mm/yyyy form and sorted alphabetically. Whatever H-110a becomes, keep that link.
Must fix

No author is named and the status is blank. (Author Person 1 and Author Person 2 are empty, with SU and BME as organisations. Status renders "!Missing status!", also on the Master List.)
The page was created on 24 April 2026 by Bajor Péter with the title already set. The outcomes, keywords and instructions were added on 19 May 2026 by KalinkaKaloyanova2 ("Keywords, learning outcomes, instruction added"). HC-176, which carries the same text, names Kalinka Kaloyanova (SU) and András Gézsi (BME). By sort order (630) H-110a sits between H-108 (620) and H-114a (650), whose first author is Kristina Arnaoudova (SU), with Béla Pataki (BME) as second author on H-108. This is urgent: in "Merged Planned Learning Events July 2026.xlsx" the UNINA tab lists H-110a and H-110b as "yes" with first use "Oct 26", and the SU tab lists both as "yes", "later".
Fix: Kalinka Kaloyanova and Kristina Arnaoudova to agree who owns H-110a and whether it belongs to the H-108 to H-114a sequence. Then fill both author names, or remove BME if nobody there works on it, so the second-author review has someone to go to. Set Status to "Lesson plan: development" now.
The learning outcomes, keywords and instructions are identical to HC-176. (Learning Outcomes, Keywords, Instructions for teachers.)
The four outcomes match those of HC-176 "Introduction to Data Types and Data Formats (Part 1)" apart from bullet characters, tabs, line breaks and full stops. The keywords ("definition of data type, common data types") and the 319-character instructions ("Introducing data types (in computer science, in data science)-10 min, ...") are character for character the same, and so are the organisations and the duration. The other fields differ: HC-176 fills the author names, Self-standing, Learning Events to be completed before and Status, and H-110a leaves them blank. The same account entered the text on H-110a at 15:25 UTC on 19 May 2026 and on HC-176 at 18:09 UTC the same day.
Fix: first confirm whether this text was meant for HC-176 and went onto H-110a by mistake. If it was, replace it with H-110a's own plan. If H-110a and HC-176 are the same event, retire one code or reduce H-110a to a pointer to HC-176. Either way, do not build H-110a from HC-176's timing line or deck as they stand. We reviewed HC-176 on 12 September 2026 and found no slides behind its composite types, image/audio/video and wrap-up blocks, an ordinal scale defined as having "no logical order" (slide 12), ≠ listed as not permitted for nominal data (slide 10), no interval slide, Gender {male, female} as the example of a symmetric binary variable (slide 11), and the Tan, Steinbach and Kumar operations table with no credit (slide 14).
No block covers how data becomes model input, although the title says "Representations". (Title "Data Types and Representations" against Instructions for teachers.)
H-108 introduces features and feature vectors ("Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf", 16 September 2026, slides 6, 9 and 15; slide 9: "Features may be numerical, categorical, or derived from raw data"), and its plan lists "numerical representation" in the 15 to 30 minute block. No slide shows how a categorical attribute becomes a number: slides 19, 20 and 31 plot flower colour on a numeric axis without saying how colour is encoded. "HC 178 Data-2 v1.pdf" gives it one line ("Text data is typically processed as sequences of tokens, images as pixel matrices", pages 10 and 18). H-114a's lesson plan assumes the features already exist ("feature-based decisions, feature-space partitions"). No event in this sequence teaches encoding. The current H-110a plan instead spends 40 minutes on "Primitive data types, examples & Composite data types, examples", which is first-year programming content and too basic for a master's programme, and another 40 minutes on NOIR, which HC-176 and HC-172 already cover.
Fix: the title was set when the page was created, so one option is to change it at programme level. If H-110a stays a separate event under this title, build it around encoding and representation and point to HC-176 and HC-172 for types and NOIR. One workable 120-minute structure, to adapt freely:
0-10: recap of storage types and NOIR levels, with a pointer to HC-176 and HC-172.
10-30: numbers and missing values. Floating point (0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, so money is stored as decimal or integer cents). Nullable types (a pandas integer column with one missing value becomes float64 unless the nullable Int64 type is used). Interactive element: students find the type errors in a small schema.
30-55: categorical data and dates. One-hot encoding for nominal attributes, ordinal encoding for ordinal ones, target encoding and its leakage risk (scikit-learn's TargetEncoder, added in version 1.3, cross-fits inside fit_transform for that reason), dates and times as features.
55-65: break.
65-90: unstructured data as numbers. Text as tokens and embeddings (the current "image, audio, video data" block leaves text out), images as arrays of height, width and colour channels (H×W×C in NumPy and TensorFlow, C×H×W in PyTorch), audio as amplitudes sampled at a fixed rate, video as frame sequences. Interactive element: choose a representation for a stated task and say what it loses.
90-105: personal data in a dataset (see Should fix).
105-120: interactive element on a small real table (a loan or admissions dataset works): students classify each column, choose an encoding, justify it and compare against the answer key.
The learning outcomes cannot be assessed and do not match the timing line. (Learning Outcomes.)
"Students can understand" in outcome 1 is not assessable. Outcome 1 also promises "major data sources", which no H-110a block covers and which HC-178 already schedules ("Structured and unstructured data: definitions, examples, sources"). Outcome 3, "analyze datasets using programming and data science (statistical) perspectives", and outcome 4, "apply data types concepts to practical scenarios", need a dataset and a student activity. The plan names no dataset, no programming environment and no exercise, only "wrap up, common use cases - 10 min".
Fix: rewrite each outcome with an assessable verb, map each one to a timed block, and leave data sources to HC-178. Suggested wording if H-110a follows the structure above:
(a) Identify type errors in a given schema (an identifier stored as an integer, money stored as a float, an ordinal score treated as continuous) and state what goes wrong downstream.
(b) Choose and justify an encoding for nominal, ordinal and date attributes and for missing values, and explain the leakage risk of target encoding.
(c) Choose a numerical representation for text, image and audio data for a stated ML task, and explain what it keeps and what it loses.
(d) Identify personal data and GDPR Article 9 special categories in a dataset, and explain how a representation choice affects the people it describes.
If some of these are practised in H-110b rather than in the lecture, say so on both pages.
Instructions for teachers only lists topics and minutes. (Instructions for teachers, 319 characters on two lines.)
A teacher who did not write this cannot run 120 minutes from "Primitive data types, examples & Composite data types, examples - 40 min". The five blocks fill all 120 minutes with no break and no time for interaction.
Fix: write one paragraph per block with the start and end minute, what the teacher explains, the examples or dataset used, what students do and for how long, which slides or files belong to the block, and the expected answers to every question put to the room. Schedule a break and place 2 to 4 interactive elements in the timeline, each with an answer key.
Every other lesson plan field is empty or one line. (Self-standing, Learning Events to be completed before, Keywords, the four Expected preparation fields, Acknowledgements, origContrib, Lesson materials.)
Fix: fill all of them before asking for the formal review. What to put in each is in the Wiki page completeness list below.
There is no material, and first use is planned for October 2026. (SharePoint folders H-110a and H-110b: empty.)
Our 9 September cross-series analysis found that the 14 SU events we reviewed ship as PDF, which cannot carry lecturer notes, and that 16 of 25 events have no reference list.
Fix: deliver the slides as PowerPoint in the RAISE-U template, with speaker notes on every slide that a different teacher can teach from, the answer to each interactive element in the notes, and a references slide. For H-110b, provide the named dataset, the notebook or tool setup, and model solutions.
Should fix

Overlaps with four other Horizontal events are not declared. (Learning Events to be completed before: empty, renders "None.")
HC-176 carries the same plan (above). "HC 178 Data-2 v1.pdf" already has MULTIMODAL DATA slides ("text, audio, video, image, sensory data", pages 10 and 18) and a BINARY FORMATS slide ("JPEG, PNG, TIFF", "MP3, WAV, FLAC", page 27), which is what H-110a's 20-minute "image, audio, video data" block would teach. "Presentation HC-172.pdf" page 10 defines nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio. H-108 introduces features and feature vectors (slides 6, 9 and 15).
Fix: state on the page which of these H-110a builds on and which topics it leaves to them. List H-108 in Learning Events to be completed before, and HC-176 as well if the recap depends on it.
Nothing about the people the data describes. (Learning Outcomes and Instructions for teachers: no mention of personal data.)
Deciding a column's type is also when a practitioner decides whether it holds personal data. The programme guidelines ask every event to show how its topic affects people (Human-centered orientation). Our 9 September cross-series analysis found none of "privacy", "consent", "GDPR" or "personal data" in HC-176, HC-178 and HC-180.
Fix: add a 15-minute block (90-105 in the structure above) on personal data and the GDPR Article 9 special categories (for example health data or ethnic origin), with one worked example of a representation choice that affects people: a gender field fixed to two values, as on HC-176 slide 11, or ethnicity one-hot encoded as a model feature. Teach Article 9 as currently in force. The GDPR amendments in the Digital Omnibus (the "Data Omnibus" part) were still under negotiation in September 2026, so check the text again before the pilot.
Name the language and the tools. (Instructions for teachers, "Primitive data types, examples".)
"Primitive" means different things per language: Java has eight primitive types, while in Python every value is an object. For data work the types that matter are the ones the tool enforces: NumPy and pandas dtypes, SQL column types, Arrow or Parquet schemas.
Fix: say which language and library the examples use, and use the same ones in H-110b.
H-110b has no author, reviewer or status. (Master List: no author organisation, no author, no reviewer, "!Missing status!". SharePoint folder H-110b: empty.)
The H-110a outcomes that need practice have nowhere to go. H-114b is in the same state.
Fix (WP4 lead): assign an author and a reviewer to H-110b. Fix (authors): once it has an author, plan H-110a and H-110b together and state which outcomes H-110b practises, with the dataset and tool students will use.
Smaller things

The learning outcomes were pasted from Word: each line starts with a "•" bullet character and a tab. H-108 and H-114a separate outcomes with "$". Use the same separator so the list renders like the rest of the series.
Wiki page completeness

Status: empty. Set "Lesson plan: development" now.
Author Person 1 and Author Person 2: empty. Name both (see Must fix).
Self-standing: empty. Say Yes or No. If H-110a depends on H-108 or only works together with H-110b, it is No.
Learning Outcomes: four present, not assessable and identical to HC-176. Rewrite as above.
Learning Events to be completed before: empty (renders "None."). List H-108, and HC-176 if the recap depends on it, or state that nothing is required.
Keywords: two terms. Add, for example: levels of measurement, NOIR, categorical encoding, one-hot encoding, target encoding, missing values, feature representation, embeddings, unstructured data, multimodal data, personal data.
Obligatory for students: empty. Give a short real task (a named reading, or installing Python with pandas if H-110b needs it), or write "None" as a deliberate choice.
Optional for students: empty. For example the scikit-learn user guide section "Encoding categorical features".
References and background for students: empty. For example Stevens, S. S. (1946), "On the Theory of Scales of Measurement", Science 103(2684): 677-680, doi:10.1126/science.103.2684.677; and Tan, P.-N., Steinbach, M., Karpatne, A. and Kumar, V. (2019), Introduction to Data Mining, 2nd ed., Pearson, Chapter 2 "Data".
Recommended for teachers: empty. For example Gebru, T. et al. (2021), "Datasheets for Datasets", Communications of the ACM 64(12): 86-92, doi:10.1145/3458723, which supports the personal-data block.
Acknowledgements, thanks: empty. Add the thanks and credits that belong to this event.
origContrib: empty. If any content comes from HC-176 or from a textbook, record the source here and on the slides.
Lesson materials: empty. Once files exist, list each file by name with its link and the block that uses it.
Instructions for teachers: 319 characters. Needs the block-by-block detail described above.
Known template issue we have raised with WP4, not your doing: the acknowledgement text credits the Connecting Europe Facility and reads "Grant № ???" (PANORAIMA is Digital Europe Programme grant 101189994). The preparation and Lesson materials fields are still yours to fill.
When the fields above are filled and the HC-176 question is settled, set the status to "Lesson plan: review" and we will do the formal review.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST

action_summary.text:
Kristina and Béla, this is the short version of our early feedback of 17 September 2026; the full text above stays as the record. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: early feedback only, not yet a formal review.

Since our review:
* Done: both authors are named and the status is set (wiki edit of 13 October).
* Done: the new deck (13 October) teaches encoding (slides 20-23), scaling (24-28), similarity (29-43), text (46-54) and images (56-58).
* Still open: Learning Outcomes, Keywords and Instructions for teachers are unchanged, identical to HC-176. They list primitive and composite types, which the deck does not teach, and a 40-minute NOIR block against slides 10 and 12.

Please do next:
# Rewrite Learning Outcomes with assessable verbs that match the deck: encoding, scaling, similarity, text and image representation.
# Rewrite Instructions for teachers per block: minutes, examples, student activity, expected answers; drop the primitive and composite types block.
# Add 2 to 4 timed exercises with answer keys on a named dataset, name the language and library, and schedule a break.
# Add a slide on personal data and GDPR Article 9, with one worked example of a representation choice that affects people.
# Correct slide 46 (five glossary words, four vector entries), slide 48 ("Reverse" to "Inverse", "scarce" to "sparse") and slide 23 (stray bullet, garbled example).
# Deliver the deck as PowerPoint with speaker notes and add a references slide.

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):
* Self-standing empty; Keywords two terms; Expected preparation all "None".
* Learning Events to be completed before: still "None"; name H-108 and say what you leave to HC-176 and HC-172.
* Lesson materials: add the file link.

A short summary is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off.

When the items are done, tell us on this Discussion page and email the review inbox, and we will re-review.

entries.review_note: Lesson plan reviewed 17 Sep 2026 13:41 CEST, posted Talk rev 8614. Status at review: 'Lesson plan: review'. REVISION REQUESTED (major). long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed the H-114a lesson plan at wiki revision 8593 (Kristina Arnaoudova, 13 September 2026) against the H-108 wiki plan and deck (Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf, SharePoint, 16 September 2026); on 17 September 2026 the H-114a SharePoint folder was empty and there was no lesson-plan document and no Talk page, so there is no material to review. Our verdict is major revision: a lecturer who did not write this plan cannot run the session from it, and four of its blocks largely overlap H-108, the plan's own prerequisite.

Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert, industry machine learning practice.

What works

The ten timing blocks are contiguous and add up to exactly 120 minutes, and each of the seven learning outcomes has a block whose topics match it.
The model set covers the standard supervised families for a Horizontal lecture: linear models, SVM, Naive Bayes, KNN, decision trees and an MLP. The terms listed per block are accurate apart from one ambiguous item noted under Smaller things, for example 75–90 min "prior, likelihood, posterior, conditional independence" and 45–60 min "margin, support vectors".
Outcome 4, "Explain how classification scores can be transformed into probabilities", is a good practitioner choice. Teams often read raw classifier scores as probabilities, and introductory courses rarely cover the difference. Keep the outcome; the Should fix section asks for it to be taught differently.
"Learning Events to be completed before" names H-108, so a planner can see where this event sits.
Must fix

Teacher instructions are keyword lists with no teacher actions, student activities or slide mapping. (Field instructions, all ten blocks)
Every block is a string of keywords, for example "0–10 min: machine learning models, model definition, model families, discriminative and generative models." and "108–114 min: decision trees, feature-based decisions, tree structure, feature-space partitions." No block names an example or dataset, says what the teacher shows or asks, says what students do, or points to slides. The field holds about 975 characters of text for 120 minutes, roughly 8 per minute. H-128 and H-132 in the same track run at about 45 per minute and read as scripts. RealAI has raised thin lesson plans for long events with WP4, but this page still needs the rewrite.
Fix: For each block write three to five lines: the running example, what the teacher shows or derives, the question put to students, what students produce, and the one sentence they should leave the block with. H-108 uses an illustrative rose/sunflower example (flower images from the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset), and reusing that example gives students continuity. Add slide numbers once the deck exists. The "Suggested lesson structure" in H-128's instructions, also a lecture, shows the level of detail we mean.
Four blocks totalling 43 minutes largely overlap H-108, which this plan declares as its prerequisite. (Field instructions, blocks 0–10, 30–45, 90–100 and 100–108, against the H-108 wiki plan and deck)
Slide numbers here and below are the numbers printed on the H-108 slides. The PDF has no slide 18, so from slide 19 onward the PDF page is one lower.
0–10 "discriminative and generative models" repeats H-108 110–120 "discriminative and generative models, decision boundaries, class probabilities, class-conditional feature distributions" and H-108 slides 33 to 36, where the slide 36 table already sorts logistic regression, SVM, Naive Bayes and LDA into the two groups. Your outcome 2, "Distinguish between discriminative and generative models.", is already a learning objective on H-108 slide 2: "Distinguish discriminative from generative models". 30–45 "linear regression, slope, intercept, residuals" overlaps H-108 75–90 ("regression models ... residuals") and, more directly, H-108 slide 17, which already fits a linear regression line and defines Residual = y − ŷ. 90–100 "linear vs. nonlinear relationships" repeats H-108 60–75 "linear boundaries, nonlinear boundaries" and slides 19 and 20. 100–108 "KNN, similarity, nearest neighbors, k distance, majority voting" repeats H-108 90–100 almost term for term, and H-108 slide 21 already works a k = 3 majority vote ("2 sunflowers, 1 rose"). The 10–30 block ("linear classification, linear score, decision boundary") also overlaps H-108 slide 19, which draws a learned linear decision boundary, so 43 minutes is the lower bound.
Fix: Replace the repeated parts with a short recap that names H-108 and its slides, and spend the recovered time where H-108 stops: logistic regression and the sigmoid, soft margins and kernels, how a tree chooses a split, ensembles. If H-114a must also work for students who skipped H-108, say so in Self-standing and in the recap block instead of repeating four blocks.
The last 20 minutes carry three model families plus the recap, and tree ensembles are missing. (Field instructions, blocks 100–108, 108–114 and 114–120; learning outcomes 6 and 7)
KNN gets 8 minutes, decision trees 6, and "MLP and recap" share the final 6. Outcome 6 asks students to "Explain the principles of SVM, Naive Bayes, KNN, and decision trees" and outcome 7 to "Explain how multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) model nonlinear relationships". Six minutes is too short for split criteria and overfitting, and the MLP gets whatever the recap leaves of the last six. Random forests and gradient boosting appear nowhere in the plan, although gradient-boosted trees are still the usual production baseline for tabular data: Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (NeurIPS 2022, Datasets and Benchmarks track) found tree-based models ahead of deep learning on medium-sized tabular data across 45 datasets. Later in the track, H-130 Statistics in practice asks students to "Fit or load a simple probabilistic model, such as logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, or gradient boosting model", and no other plan we have read teaches the last two.
Fix: Re-budget, and add random forests and gradient boosting to the trees block. To make room, merge the two linear regression blocks, replace the H-108 repeats with a recap, and cut the MLP to a short introduction that shows why one hidden layer gives a nonlinear boundary. H-118a Neural Network Architectures, also yours, is the likely owner of the MLP. It is at Lesson plan: review but is not assigned to us and we have not read its plan, so state in both plans which event teaches the MLP. If it moves to H-118a, reword outcome 7 to match or move the outcome as well.
One workable 120-minute structure, to adapt freely:
0–8: recap of H-108 (slides 17, 19 to 21, 33 to 36) and a map of supervised model families: linear, probabilistic, instance-based, tree-based, neural
8–30: linear and logistic regression: linear score, sigmoid, softmax for more than two classes; interactive element 1
30–45: SVM: margin, support vectors, soft margin and one RBF kernel example on a non-separable 2D dataset, which introduces linear versus nonlinear boundaries
45–55: break
55–70: Naive Bayes with a spam example, then discriminative versus generative with logistic regression and Naive Bayes as the pair; interactive element 2
70–78: KNN: distance metric, choice of k, feature scaling
78–92: decision trees (split criterion, depth, overfitting), random forests, gradient boosting; interactive element 3
92–100: short MLP introduction, pointing to H-118a
100–112: model-choice case exercise; interactive element 4
112–120: recap: where each family is used today, what H-114b practises, what H-118a, H-122 and H-130 pick up
The plan has no interactive element, no answer key and no break. (Field instructions, whole session)
None of the ten blocks contains a student activity. The consortium checklist asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements, and a 120-minute session with no student activity and no break is too long to hold attention. RealAI has asked WP4 to scale the interactivity rule with duration and to require break placement in long sessions. For this plan we ask for at least four elements, about one every half hour.
Fix: Schedule at least four, each with a model answer in the plan or in the speaker notes, and put the break in the plan with a time. Suggestions: (1) Score to probability by hand: a logistic regression gives a score of 2.0; what is the predicted probability, and what does a score of 0 mean? Answer: σ(2.0) ≈ 0.88; a score of 0 gives 0.5, the usual default threshold, which is a choice and not a rule. (2) A four-email Naive Bayes spam table where students compute the posterior for one new email, which also makes the conditional independence assumption visible. (3) Gini impurity for one split: a node with 5 spam and 5 ham emails splits into (4 spam, 1 ham) and (1 spam, 4 ham). Answer: parent 0.5, each child 0.32, so the split reduces impurity by 0.18. (4) The model-choice exercise in the next point.
Nothing asks students to choose between models, and the plan never mentions the people affected by a model's output. (Field learningOutcomes, all seven; field instructions)
All seven outcomes are define, distinguish or explain. The plan never asks when a practitioner would pick logistic regression over an MLP, or a tree ensemble over KNN, and on what grounds: data size, feature types, need for probability estimates, prediction cost, and whether a decision has to be explained to the person it affects. The words interpretability, explanation, fairness and bias do not occur in the plan. The reviewer checklist asks for professional judgement, and the programme is human-centred. The choice of model decides whether a person affected by a prediction can get a reason for it, so it belongs in this lecture.
Fix: Add an outcome such as "Select a suitable model family for a given problem and justify the choice in terms of data size, feature types, need for calibrated probabilities, cost, and explainability to the people affected." Back it with a 12-minute case exercise in small groups, one case per group: (a) loan pre-screening on 5,000 rows of tabular data, where turned-down applicants ask for reasons; (b) a spam filter retrained daily on cheap hardware; (c) a hospital readmission risk score where clinicians act on the probability itself. The answer key should list defensible options and their trade-offs, not one right model. Point to HC-040 for explainability and to H-128 for calibration instead of teaching either here.
Most PanoLessonPlan fields are empty. (Fields keywords, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx, self-standing, authorPers2)
The four preparation fields show the template default "None.". That default is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally, but this lecture assumes H-108 and needs its own entries. With Self-standing and Author Person 2 also blank, a planner cannot tell whether the event can run on its own or who does the second-author review.
Fix: Fill every field in the Wiki page completeness block below before the plan comes back for review. Only the Lesson materials file list can wait until the deck exists.
Should fix

Outcome 4 sits after SVM, and the plan never mentions logistic regression, softmax or calibration. (Field instructions, 60–75 min "from scores to probabilities, linear score, class decision, probability, sigmoid function"; learning outcome 4)
Logistic regression does not appear in the plan, although the sigmoid belongs to it and it is the standard linear classifier in practice. Placed straight after the 45–60 SVM block, the 60–75 block invites a teacher to put SVM scores through a sigmoid and call the result a probability. SVM decision values are not probabilities; they need a separately fitted mapping such as Platt scaling (Platt, in Smola et al. (eds.), Advances in Large Margin Classifiers, MIT Press, 2000, pp. 61–74). Naive Bayes, taught next, is known to push probabilities toward 0 and 1 (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, ICML 2005). For H-114b: scikit-learn 1.9 deprecated SVC(probability=True) and recommends CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(), ensemble=False) instead.
Fix: Teach the sigmoid inside the linear models block as part of logistic regression, add softmax for more than two classes, and add two sentences: scores from other models need calibration before anyone reads them as probabilities, and calibration has to be checked on data, not assumed. Link H-128 (Statistics: uncertainty & calibration), which teaches reliability diagrams, and H-130, where students build a calibration curve. Reword outcome 4 to match.
The plan never says what any model is fitted to minimise. (Field instructions, all model blocks)
None of loss, objective, least squares, log loss, hinge loss, impurity or backpropagation occurs in the plan. H-108 slide 16 already defines the empirical risk R(w) as the average loss over the training set, and H-122, which comes after this event, teaches gradient descent. Without the objective, students cannot see what the models have in common or why they behave differently, which falls short of the rigour a master's lecture needs.
Fix: One line per model block on what is fitted: least squares for linear regression, log loss for logistic regression, hinge loss and the maximum margin for the SVM, class and feature frequencies for Naive Bayes, impurity reduction for trees, nothing for KNN (it stores the training data), and for the MLP a pointer to H-122 for how the loss is minimised.
The SVM block names neither the soft margin nor kernels. (Field instructions, 45–60 min "support vector machines (SVM), decision boundary, margin, support vectors")
Real data is rarely linearly separable. The soft margin (Cortes and Vapnik, Machine Learning 20(3), 273–297, 1995) and the kernel trick (Boser, Guyon and Vapnik, COLT 1992) are what made SVMs practical. Without kernels, the 90–100 block on nonlinear relationships arrives 30 minutes after the model that shows the step from linear to nonlinear boundaries most clearly.
Fix: Add the C parameter (the soft-margin trade-off) and one RBF kernel example to the SVM block, and introduce linear versus nonlinear relationships there.
Discriminative versus generative opens the lecture, before students have met any of its models. (Field instructions, 0–10 min; learning outcome 2)
Students have seen the labels on H-108 slide 36 but have not yet met SVM or Naive Bayes as models, so the distinction stays abstract until both are on the board. It is easier to teach with the classic pair side by side: logistic regression models P(y|x) directly, while Naive Bayes models P(x|y) and P(y) and applies Bayes' rule. Ng and Jordan (NIPS 2001) is the standard reference for that comparison, including the result that the generative classifier can approach its (higher) asymptotic error with fewer training examples.
Fix: Move outcome 2 to directly after Naive Bayes and teach it through that pair, with a one-line reference back to H-108 slides 33 to 36.
Feature scaling is missing, and several of the models depend on it. (Field instructions, KNN, SVM and MLP blocks)
KNN works on raw distances, and SVMs, MLPs and regularised logistic regression (scikit-learn's LogisticRegression applies an L2 penalty by default) are sensitive to feature ranges; trees and Naive Bayes are not. Unscaled features are a common reason a KNN or SVM baseline looks worse than it is.
Fix: One slide in the KNN block with a two-feature example (income in euros, age in years), and one sentence that the scaler is fitted on training data only, with a pointer to H-122, which teaches data leakage.
The plan does not say how it connects to the events around it. (Field expectedLEs; field instructions, 114–120 recap)
H-114b "Machine Learning Models" is a 120-minute tutorial with no authors, no status and an empty SharePoint folder, so nobody can tell which outcomes the lecture leaves for practice. H-122 "Model Training, Evaluation and Generalization" teaches gradient descent, and its own prerequisite field is empty although it should list H-114a. H-130 fits the models this lecture introduces. Two other events cover related topics: HC-022 (30–40 min) plans to "Briefly mention model families such as linear models, decision trees, and neural networks, without going into technical depth", and HC-158 schedules 30 minutes on artificial neural networks, forward propagation and backpropagation. The wiki template has no successor field; RealAI has raised that centrally.
Fix: In the recap block, name what H-114b practises and what H-118a, H-122 and H-130 pick up. Add H-114a to H-122's prerequisite field in the same edit, and agree the H-114b scope with whoever is assigned to it. Ask Béla Pataki, who wrote HC-022 and is second author on H-108 and H-122, whether HC-022 can point here for the technical treatment of model families, and agree with the HC-158 authors which event owns neural network basics.
The plan does not say where these models are used today. (Field instructions, 0–10 "model families" and 114–120 recap)
Students in a Horizontal track will ask why they cannot use a large pretrained model instead. For tabular data, gradient-boosted trees remain the usual production baseline, and pretrained tabular models are now competitive: TabPFN (Hollmann et al., Nature 637, 319–326, 2025) beat tuned baselines on datasets of up to 10,000 samples, and its successor TabPFN-2.5 (Grinsztajn et al., arXiv 2511.08667, 2025) reports beating tuned tree-based models on tables of up to 50,000 rows. Both results come from the developers' own benchmarks. For text and images, practitioners usually start from a pretrained model and train a simple classifier, often logistic regression, on its embeddings.
Fix: One recap slide on where each family is used today, with those two examples.
No second-author review exists yet. (Field authorPers2; Talk page)
Author Organisation 2 is BME but Author Person 2 is blank, while H-108 and H-122 name Béla Pataki. The Talk page did not exist on 17 September, so the didactic review the guidelines give to the second author has not happened. Missing second-author reviews across the track are already with WP4 from our 9 September cross-series analysis.
Fix: Name the BME second author and ask for their Talk page review before the next round.
Smaller things

Instructions 100–108 min: "k distance" reads like the k-distance used in DBSCAN and LOF. Your H-108 plan writes "distance, nearest examples, choice of k", so this is probably a missing comma. Write "choice of k, distance metric".
Instructions 108–114 min: name the split criterion (Gini impurity or entropy) and tree depth. "Feature-based decisions" does not tell a lecturer what to explain.
The instructions repeat terms across blocks: "linear regression" in both 10–30 and 30–45, "linear score" in 10–30 and 60–75, "decision boundary" in 10–30 and 45–60. Merging the two linear regression blocks alone frees time.
KNN, decision trees and MLPs also do regression (mean of the neighbours, mean of the leaf, linear output unit). One line prevents students reading outcome 6 as classification only.
The title and outcome 1 say "machine learning models" and "model families", but every model in the plan is supervised. Write "supervised" into outcome 1, or point to H-108 slides 30, 31 and 36 for clustering and Gaussian mixture models.
Outcome 2 uses "generative" in the classical sense (Naive Bayes, LDA). H-108 slide 36 lists VAEs, GANs and diffusion models in the same column, and the track also has H-077 Generative Modeling Foundations and HC-154 Introduction to Generative AI. Add one sentence that separates a generative classifier from generative AI.
The learningOutcomes field ends with " $" after the last outcome, which will probably render as an empty eighth item. Remove the trailing separator and the spaces before several "$" marks.
Outcome 6 bundles four models into one sentence. Split it so each part can be assessed, and consider tagging each outcome with type and level as the BME plans do, for example HC-021 "Explain (knowledge, intermediate level)".
expectedLEs reads "H-108". BME pages use the full page name, for example HC-021 "HC-020_Designing_a_machine_learning_system". Check that "H-108" resolves; if not, use "H-108_Fundamentals_of_Machine_Learning".
H-110a Data Types and Representations (sort number 630) sits between H-108 and this event. The proposed model-choice outcome and the scaling slide depend on feature types, so decide whether H-110a belongs in expectedLEs as well.
Job role is "any". Say in the plan how much mathematics students are expected to follow, for example sigmoid and Bayes' rule written out, kernels shown as pictures without derivation, so every lecturer pitches the session at the same level.
When you build the deck, deliver it as .pptx with speaker notes and slide numbers, and end it with a references slide. Your H-108 deck is a PDF, which cannot carry speaker notes, and a second lecturer needs them.
Wiki page completeness

The "None." entries under Expected preparation, the Lesson materials section that names no file, and the acknowledgement crediting the Connecting Europe Facility with "Grant № ???" are known template issues RealAI has raised centrally. They are not your doing, but the fields below are still yours to fill.
keywords: empty. Suggested: machine learning model$supervised learning$linear regression$logistic regression$sigmoid$softmax$support vector machine$soft margin$kernel$Naive Bayes$k-nearest neighbours$feature scaling$decision tree$random forest$gradient boosting$multilayer perceptron$discriminative model$generative model$probability calibration
learningOutcomes: filled but thin. Add the model-choice outcome, reword outcome 4, split outcome 6, adjust outcome 7 if the MLP moves to H-118a, and remove the trailing "$".
expectedLEs: H-108 is correct. Check the link format and whether H-110a belongs here (see Smaller things).
obligStPrep: empty. State that H-108 is required, or at minimum H-108 slides 16, 17, 19 to 21 and 33 to 36 for students who missed it.
optionStPrep: empty. Suggested: James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (Springer, 2023), free PDF at statlearning.com: section 2.2.3 for KNN, and chapters 3 (Linear Regression), 4 (Classification), 8 (Tree-Based Methods), 9 (Support Vector Machines) and 10 (Deep Learning, sections 10.1 and 10.2 on single-layer and multilayer networks).
backgrStPrep: empty. entries.title: H-122 Model Training, Evaluation and Generalization
entries.author: SU · Kristina Arnaoudova
entries.review_note: Lesson plan reviewed 17 Sep 2026 13:41 CEST, posted Talk rev 8615. Status at review: 'Lesson plan: review'. REVISION REQUESTED (major). Review of the plan only, because the SharePoint folder is empty. The topics and their order are sound, but the teacher instructions are keyword lists. Evaluation gets 10 minutes with no thresholds, ROC or AUROC, and five of its eight items are already on slide 26 of the author's H-108 deck. There are no exercises and no break, and the preparation, keyword and acknowledgement fields are empty. 7 must-fix item(s).

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed the H-122 lesson plan at wiki revision 8594 (Kristina Arnaoudova, 13 September 2026); the SharePoint folder 4.1 Horizontal/H-122 is empty and there is no lesson-plan document, so this is a formal review of the plan only, by a subject-matter expert reviewer (AI practitioners, industry). Our verdict is major revision: the topics and their order are sound, but a teacher who did not write the plan could not run the session from it, and the evaluation part that later events depend on is too short and incomplete.

What works

Every outcome has a block that names its content, from "Explain the model training process" (0–15) to "Explain the purpose of cross-validation in model evaluation" (115–120), so a second author can check coverage outcome by outcome.
Data leakage sits in the 35–60 block with data splitting and hyperparameter tuning, which is where students need it. It is a common failure in published work: Kapoor and Narayanan (Patterns 4(9), 100804, 2023) compiled published reports of leakage from 17 scientific fields, affecting 294 papers.
The keywords come in a sensible order: parameters and hyperparameters (0–15), tuning on the validation set (35–60), and the "final test set" at the end (115–120). The last block is the right place to state the rule that the test set is used once.
Learning curves are in the generalization block (60–80). Reading training and validation curves is how practitioners spot underfitting and overfitting, and it makes a good in-class exercise.
H-122 is the only Horizontal plan we have read whose schedule names the confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1, so it is the obvious event to teach model evaluation in the track.
Must fix

Do items 1 to 4 first. They change the schedule, and the other items fit into the new one.

1. The evaluation block is 10 minutes and does not cover thresholds, TPR and FPR, the ROC curve or AUROC. (Field instructions, block 105–115; learningOutcomes 6.)
The whole block is "105–115 minutes: model evaluation, regression metrics, confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, class imbalance." That is too little time for outcome 6, "Select and interpret appropriate evaluation metrics for classification and regression", and it comes in the last quarter of the session with no exercise. The plan does not mention decision thresholds, true or false positive rates, specificity, the ROC curve, AUROC or the precision-recall curve. Later events need them. H-128 and H-129 use AUROC without defining it, and the only definition we found in the track is in the H-130 notebook, which comes after both. The equal opportunity and equalized odds criteria in HC-030 are defined on true and false positive rates (Hardt, Price and Srebro, NeurIPS 2016).
Five of the eight items in the block are already in the H-108 deck (Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf, SharePoint H-108 folder, 16 September 2026): slide 26 defines the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and F1, and slide 24 names "ROC-AUC" without defining it. Regression metrics and class imbalance are not in that deck. H-108 slide numbers in this review are the numbers printed on the slides. The PDF has no slide 18, so from slide 19 on the PDF page is one lower (slide 26 is PDF page 25).
Fix: give evaluation 20 minutes (schedule in item 3). Recap H-108 slide 26 in two minutes, then teach the decision threshold, TPR, FPR and specificity, the ROC curve, AUROC with its ranking reading (the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative), the precision-recall curve, and MAE, RMSE and R² for regression. On class imbalance, teach both curves and have students choose by what the decision needs. Many courses still teach "use AUPRC when classes are imbalanced", but McDermott et al., "A Closer Look at AUROC and AUPRC under Class Imbalance" (NeurIPS 2024), show that AUPRC is not generally the better metric under imbalance. Leave cost-based threshold choice to H-130 (82–98) and subgroup evaluation to H-129 (68–80), and say so in the plan. Once the material exists we will propose to WP4 that H-122 becomes a prerequisite of H-128 and H-129, which now read Self-standing: Yes with no prerequisites; the sort numbers already put H-122 (690) before them (720, 730).
2. The Instructions for teachers are keyword lists that another teacher could not run. (Field instructions, all eight blocks.)
The field is about 1,000 characters for 120 minutes. Each block is a comma-separated list, for example "15–35 minutes: gradient descent, loss function, derivative, local slope, gradient direction, learning rate, parameter updates." The plan does not say what the teacher shows or asks, which example runs through the session, what students do, or which slides belong to which block.
Fix: for each block, write a few sentences on what the teacher explains and with which example, what students do (a question, a calculation or a discussion) and what they should be able to do afterwards. Add slide numbers once the deck exists. The H-128 and H-132 plans show this level of detail, and each uses one running example for the whole session. For H-122 one binary scoring task can carry every block, from loss and gradient descent to the confusion matrix and ROC curve. Pick one where each error type falls on named people, for example a screening model where a false negative is a missed patient and a false positive is an unnecessary follow-up test, so the evaluation block can ask who carries each error.
3. The schedule is front-loaded, and the two evaluation outcomes get the last 15 minutes. (Field instructions, blocks 0–15, 35–60, 105–115 and 115–120; learningOutcomes 6 and 7.)
"115–120 minutes: cross-validation and recap, k-fold cross-validation, model development cycle, final test set" puts four topics into five minutes, and cross-validation is also listed in 95–105. Meanwhile 0–15 repeats the training loop on H-108 slide 16, and 35–60 gives 25 minutes to validation, tuning and the test set, which H-108 already schedules at 45–60 ("training data, validation data, hyperparameter tuning, test data") and covers on slides 22 and 24.
Fix: rebalance. One possible split, with a 10-minute break and the four exercises from item 4:
0–10: recap of H-108; training as minimising a loss; the loss that is optimised against the metric that is reported
10–30: gradient descent, learning rate, mini-batches and epochs; exercise (a)
30–45: training, validation and test sets, tuning, two forms of leakage; exercise (b)
45–55: underfitting, overfitting, learning curves; exercise (c)
55–65: break
65–77: bias-variance decomposition; one slide on double descent
77–87: regularization, early stopping, more data
87–107: evaluation as in item 1; exercise (d)
107–117: k-fold and stratified cross-validation; the final test set, used once
117–120: recap and what H-128, H-129 and H-130 build on
This is still full. If it does not fit, cut regression metrics to one slide or move the bias-variance derivation to teacher reading, and keep the threshold, ROC and AUROC part. If it still does not fit, the guidelines say to split the event; moving the practice into a tutorial is the other option (see Should fix on H-122b).
4. There are no interactive elements and no break in 120 minutes. (Field instructions, whole field.)
The plan never asks the teacher to stop and give students something to do. The programme guidelines ask for a design that keeps learners actively engaged throughout, and the slide checklist asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements; the lesson plan is where their place and timing are set. Missing breaks in long plans are a known issue RealAI has raised centrally, but this plan still needs one.
Fix: add at least four activities, with answer keys in the lecturer notes once the deck exists, and a 10-minute break at the midpoint. Four that fit the blocks: (a) one gradient descent step by hand on a one-parameter squared loss, then predict what happens with a learning rate ten times larger; (b) three short pipeline descriptions, two with a leak (a scaler fitted on all data before the split; the same patient in training and test data) and one without, where students find the leaks and explain them; (c) three pairs of training and validation curves, where students label each underfit, overfit or fine and propose one remedy; (d) 1,000 screening cases with 10 positives, where students compute accuracy and recall for a model that always predicts negative, then read TPR and FPR at two thresholds from a small score table. The full leakage checklist and the cost-based threshold choice belong to H-129 (40–55) and H-130 (82–98).
5. No prerequisites are declared, Self-standing is blank, and the plan overlaps with H-108 (same author). (Fields expectedLEs and self-standing.)
H-108's wiki outcomes include "Explain the concepts of features, labels, training data, test data, overfitting, and generalization" and "Select appropriate basic evaluation metrics for common supervised learning tasks", which cover the same ground as H-122 outcomes 3, 4 and 6. Besides the slides named in items 1 and 3, the H-108 deck already has the training and validation error curve against complexity, labelled "High Bias" and "High Variance" (slide 23). H-114a declares H-108 as its prerequisite, but H-122 declares no prerequisites. The H-108 wiki plan has no metrics block, although its outcome 5 asks students to select metrics, so at the moment the metrics exist only in the H-108 deck.
Fix: set expectedLEs to H-108_Fundamentals_of_Machine_Learning$H-114a_Machine_Learning_Models, set Self-standing to No, and say in the opening block which H-108 slides are recapped and what H-122 adds. Decide in both plans which event teaches the basic metrics. Also check the order of the SU machine learning chain. H-114a ends on MLPs and names no training method, and in that chain H-122 is the first plan we have read that names gradient descent. We have not read the H-118a (Neural Network Architectures) plan. If it trains networks by backpropagation, gradient descent is taught here after it is needed, and either the block moves earlier in the chain or H-118a says where it is taught.
6. Outcome 1 is too vague to assess, and no outcome asks students to justify a choice for a use context. (Field learningOutcomes.)
Five of the seven outcomes start with "Explain", one with "Distinguish" and one with "Select and interpret". "Explain the model training process" overlaps outcome 2 and does not say what a student has to show. The reviewer checklist asks whether the material builds professional judgement, and outcome 6 stops at selecting a metric without asking students to justify the choice for a given use.
Fix: merge outcomes 1 and 2, and rewrite outcome 6, for example as "Choose and justify an evaluation metric for a given classification or regression use case, taking class imbalance and the cost of each error type into account (competence, intermediate level)". A second outcome fits the learning-curve block: "Diagnose underfitting or overfitting from training and validation curves and propose a remedy (cognitive skill, intermediate level)". We also recommend tagging every outcome with type and level, as H-129 does ("... (knowledge, intermediate level)"), so the second author and WP4 can see the level the event is pitched at.
7. The keyword, preparation and acknowledgement fields are empty. (Fields keywords, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx.)
With these empty, the page shows the template defaults: "None." for preparation, and an acknowledgement that names the wrong EU programme with "Grant № ???". Both defaults are known template issues RealAI has raised centrally, but these fields are yours to fill, and at the moment a teacher preparing this session has nothing to read.
Fix: see Wiki page completeness below for what to put in each field.
Should fix

The bias-variance block puts two different error decompositions into 15 minutes and uses non-standard terms. (Field instructions: "80–95 minutes: bias and variance, bias–variance intuition, hypothesis class, approximation gap, estimation gap, error decomposition.")
The bias-variance decomposition splits expected squared error into squared bias, variance and irreducible noise. Approximation error and estimation error form a second decomposition, of the error of a learner that picks from a fixed hypothesis class (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning, Cambridge University Press 2014, chapter 5, "The Bias-Complexity Tradeoff"). The block lists both and does not say they differ. The textbook terms are approximation error and estimation error; "approximation gap" is used for something else in the variational inference literature (Cremer, Li and Duvenaud, ICML 2018). The noise term is not listed.
Fix: name both decompositions and keep them on separate slides, add irreducible error, and use "approximation error" and "estimation error". With 12 minutes in the new schedule, keep bias-variance in class and move approximation and estimation error to teacher reading.
Overlap with H-129, H-130, HC-022 and HC-020 is not declared. (Opening and closing blocks, expectedLEs; none of these pages links to another.)
H-129 covers split design and "why the final test set should be touched only once" (25–40), a leakage list with "duplicated patients, preprocessing before splitting, target leakage, hyperparameter tuning on the test set" plus a leakage-detection checklist (40–55), and "AUROC, accuracy, sensitivity/specificity" with class imbalance and asymmetric costs (55–68). H-130 (82–98) has students choose a threshold and discuss how it "depends on the cost of mistakes". HC-022 (Béla Pataki, Stefano Marrone) covers "training, validation, testing, and generalization to unseen data" (outcome 3) and overfitting and class imbalance (40–50). HC-020 (András Gézsi, Ahmad Khalidi) covers train/validation/test splitting and "the importance of preventing leakage" (20–30). These sit in different chains, although Béla Pataki is on both H-122 and HC-022.
Fix: agree a split before the deck is built. One option: H-122 teaches the concepts and mechanics (definitions, curves, k-fold), H-129 teaches validation design and the leakage checklist, and H-130 teaches cost-based thresholds and subgroup checks. Name H-129 and H-130 in the closing block of H-122 with one line on what each adds. Béla Pataki (second author here, first author of HC-022) and András Gézsi (H-129, H-130, HC-020) are the people to agree it with. The final distinctiveness call is made at programme level.
Training is presented through gradient descent only. (learningOutcomes 1 and 2; blocks 0–15 and 15–35.)
"Explain the model training process" is followed directly by the gradient descent block, yet most of the models students met in H-114a are not fitted that way.
Fix: one slide in the opening block. Training usually means fitting parameters to minimise a loss on training data. Logistic regression and neural networks use iterative gradient-based methods; linear regression is usually solved in closed form by least squares, with gradient descent used at scale; SVMs are fitted by convex quadratic optimisation; decision trees are grown by greedy splitting; Naive Bayes estimates class priors and class-conditional distributions; k-NN stores the training data.
The gradient descent block names no mini-batch or stochastic gradient descent, batch size, epochs or optimiser. (Block 15–35.)
Neural networks are trained on mini-batches, and students need epochs to read the loss curves in the learning-curve block.
Fix: add mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, batch size and epochs, and name Adam as the usual default optimiser. Teacher reference: Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press 2016, free at deeplearningbook.org), section 5.9 and chapter 8.
Cross-validation is listed as a way to improve generalization, and only k-fold is named. (Blocks 95–105 and 115–120.)
"95–105 minutes: improving generalization, ... regularization, early stopping, cross-validation" puts cross-validation among the remedies. Cross-validation estimates how well a model generalizes and helps choose hyperparameters; it does not by itself make a model generalize better. Outcome 7 places it correctly ("in model evaluation"). Two practice points are also missing: tuning and reporting on the same cross-validation gives an optimistic estimate (Varma and Simon, BMC Bioinformatics 7:91, 2006), and plain k-fold gives wrong answers when rows are grouped (several records per patient) or ordered in time.
Fix: take cross-validation out of the remedies block. Teach k-fold and stratified k-fold, add one sentence on nested cross-validation or a separate test set, and one sentence that grouped and time-ordered splits are covered in H-129 (25–40).
Data leakage is named but not described. (Block 35–60.)
The block says only "data leakage".
Fix: in H-122, show two forms with a worked example: preprocessing fitted on the full dataset before splitting (the Data leakage section of the scikit-learn page "Common pitfalls and recommended practices" has an example to reuse), and the same person on both sides of the split. Add one sentence on a current form: for pretrained models, test data that was already in the pretraining data. Leave the full list to H-129 (40–55).
Nothing beyond the classical U-shaped complexity curve is planned. (Blocks 60–80 and 80–95.)
H-108 slide 23 shows validation error falling and then rising with complexity, and the H-122 blocks ("model complexity, learning curves", "bias–variance intuition") do not go beyond it. For heavily overparameterised models, test error can fall again past the point where the model fits the training data exactly (Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, PNAS 116(32):15849-15854, 2019). Nakkiran et al. (ICLR 2020) found the same pattern over training epochs, which matters for how early stopping is presented.
Fix: one slide after the bias-variance part with the double descent curve and one sentence on when the classical picture applies. Section 10.8, "Interpolation and Double Descent", of An Introduction to Statistical Learning covers it at student level.
Nothing in the plan links evaluation to the people affected by model errors. (Whole plan.)
The guidelines ask that students understand how AI in this context affects people, and evaluation is an easy place to do it. A model with high overall accuracy can have much lower recall for one subgroup.
Fix: besides the running example with named error costs (Must fix item 2), show one confusion matrix split by subgroup and point forward to HC-030 and H-129 (68–80). Add one line on practice: Article 15(3) of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) says "The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use". After Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 this applies from 2 December 2027 to Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 to high-risk AI in Annex I products.
There is no H-122b tutorial. (Horizontal master list; SharePoint folders.)
H-110a, H-114a, H-118a and H-124a each have a paired tutorial; H-108 and H-122 do not. None of the SU chain plans we have read has students plot learning curves, compute a ROC curve or run cross-validation in code.
Fix: say in the plan whether hands-on work for this content is planned (in H-118b, H-124b or a new H-122b), or whether the in-class exercises are the only practice. If a tutorial is needed, raise it with WP4.
Plan the H-122 deck so it avoids the gaps in the H-108 deck. (For the material stage.)
The H-108 deck is a PDF with no lecturer notes and no reference list (its only source line is the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset credit), and its acknowledgement slide credits the Connecting Europe Facility. PDF delivery without notes is a known issue RealAI has raised centrally.
Fix: deliver the H-122 deck as a PowerPoint file in the RAISE-U template with lecturer notes on every slide, mark the interactive slides and put the answer keys in the notes, add a reference slide, give a source for each standard figure (U-curve, ROC curve, double descent), and use the corrected acknowledgement sentence under ackThx below.
Smaller things

"60–80 minutes: ... learning curves": say which curve. Loss against epochs and performance against training-set size are both called learning curves, and they diagnose different problems.
"0–15 minutes: ... loss/error": separate the loss the optimiser minimises (for example cross-entropy) from the metric that gets reported (for example recall). Students often assume they are the same number.
"105–115 minutes: ... regression metrics" names none. Name MAE, RMSE and R², with one line on when each misleads: RMSE is dominated by large errors, and R² depends on the spread of the target, so it cannot be compared across datasets.
Outcome 3, "Distinguish the roles of training, validation, and test data and recognize data leakage", holds two outcomes. Split it, or keep it and assess both halves.
"class imbalance" appears only among the metrics. Add one line on remedies (class weights, resampling, moving the threshold) and on the trap that oversampling before the split is itself leakage. Exercise (d) is also the place to state that a model should be compared with a trivial baseline such as always predicting the majority class.
"hyperparameter tuning" (35–60) gives no method. One sentence on grid search and random search inside the validation scheme is enough.
There is no second-author review on record for H-122. Please ask Béla Pataki to post his didactic review on this Talk page, as the guidelines ask.
Wiki page completeness

keywords: empty. Suggested: model training$loss function$gradient descent$stochastic gradient descent$learning rate$training, validation and test sets$data leakage$generalization$underfitting$overfitting$bias-variance trade-off$regularization$early stopping$cross-validation$confusion matrix$precision and recall$decision threshold$ROC curve and AUROC$class imbalance$regression metrics
expectedLEs: empty. H-108_Fundamentals_of_Machine_Learning$H-114a_Machine_Learning_Models, plus H-118a_Neural_Network_Architectures if it is meant to come before H-122.
self-standing: empty. No, once the prerequisites are declared.
mandatory: empty. Ask WP4 whether this event is mandatory, then enter Yes or No.
obligStPrep: empty. Either slides 16 and 22 to 26 of the H-108 deck, or three pages of the Classification module in Google's Machine Learning Crash Course (free, about 40 minutes): "Thresholds and the confusion matrix", "Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics" and "ROC and AUC". The ROC page says precision-recall curves "may offer a better comparative visualization" on imbalanced data; McDermott et al. (2024) show this does not hold in general, so flag that sentence to students.
optionStPrep: empty. James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (Springer 2023, free PDF at statlearning.com), section 2.2 on assessing model accuracy and the bias-variance trade-off, and section 5.1 on cross-validation.
backgrStPrep: empty. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (2016), sections 5.2 to 5.4 and 5.9; Kapoor and Narayanan, "Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science", Patterns 4(9), 100804 (2023).
recommTePrep: empty. Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014) chapter 5 for the error decomposition; Belkin et al. (2019) for double descent; Varma and Simon (2006) for nested cross-validation; McDermott et al. (2024) for AUROC against AUPRC; the scikit-learn page "Common pitfalls and recommended practices" for leakage; and the H-108 deck plus the H-128, H-129 and H-130 plans, so the teacher knows what students have seen and what comes next.

Until WP4 issues corrected wording, enter: "The PANORAIMA programme is co-financed by the Digital Europe Programme of the European Union under grant agreement No 101189994." Use the same sentence on the deck's acknowledgement slide.

While you revise, please set the status to Lesson plan: development, and back to Lesson plan: review with a note on this page when the revised plan is up; we will review it again, together with the deck if it exists by then.

entries.title: H-128 Statistics: uncertainty & calibration
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (signed off with minor fixes). A well-built, accurate 90-minute lecture on uncertainty and calibration with a fully verified bibliography and a strong running case; three small edits are needed before teaching (one confidence interval that contradicts the deck's own standard error, on-slide credit for the Van Calster calibration hierarchy, and a definition of AUROC), after which we would close the review without a second round. 3 must-fix item(s); 20 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8543.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
A well-built, accurate 90-minute lecture on uncertainty and calibration with a fully verified bibliography and a strong running case; three small edits are needed before teaching (one confidence interval that contradicts the deck's own standard error, on-slide credit for the Van Calster calibration hierarchy, and a definition of AUROC), after which we would close the review without a second round.

What works

Every one of the ten bibliography entries on slide 51 checks out exactly. Brier (1950) Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3; Murphy (1973) J Applied Meteorology 12(4):595-600; Gneiting & Raftery (2007) JASA 102(477):359-378; Greenland et al. (2016) Eur J Epidemiol 31:337-350; Wasserstein & Lazar (2016) Am Stat 70(2):129-133; Van Calster et al. (2016) J Clin Epidemiol 74:167-176; Guo et al. (2017) PMLR 70:1321-1330; Van.
The eight custom figures are numerically consistent where they can be checked. Slide 15's site-mix arithmetic is exactly right (0.50x5 + 0.30x9 + 0.20x15 = 8.2%, and 0.20x5 + 0.30x9 + 0.50x15 = 11.2%). Slide 31's threshold table is internally consistent across all three rows: 12 total failures at every threshold (9+3, 7+5, 4+8). Slide 11's SE of about 3 points is the correct binomial SE for p=11% at n=100 (3.13)..
Slide 43, 'Selective deployment: model-guided intervention changes which failures are observed.' This is the intervention feedback loop, and it is the most common way calibration dies quietly in a deployed system. Most courses at this level skip it. Keeping it in one line, in the right place, is good judgement.
Slide 30 carries a footnote distinguishing pump 417's individual predicted p from the population rate p used on slides 9 to 22, and notes that a calibrated model's individual probabilities should average to the subgroup rate. This is exactly the collision a careful student would hit, and the author saw it coming.
Slide 44's fourth row, 'Decision-region check: is calibration adequate near the threshold where action changes?' That is the question a practitioner actually asks, and the paired message ('global averages can look acceptable while calibration is poor near the decision threshold') is the right warning. It goes beyond the standard textbook treatment.
What to fix before this is taught

The 95% confidence interval on slide 22 contradicts the standard error the deck established on slides 11 and 21. (Slide 22 (question and answer overlay), against slides 11 and 21)
Slide 11 fixes the running numbers: n=100, population rate 11%, 1 SE of about 3 points. Slide 21's figure then draws repeated 95% intervals spanning roughly 4% to 18%, which is right. Slide 22 then states 'the estimated 30-day failure rate is 11%, with a 95% confidence interval of 8%-14%'. That is 11% plus or minus 1 SE, which is about a 68% interval, not 95%. At n=100 the 95% Wald interval is 4.9% to 17.1% and the Wilson interval is 6.3% to 18.6%. You would need n of about 418 to get 8%-14%. This is the deck's.
Fix: Either change slide 22 to '11%, 95% CI 5%-17%' so it follows from slide 11, or keep 8%-14% and state on the slide that this interval comes from the larger validation sample rather than the n=100 illustration. One line either way.
Slide 44 reproduces the Van Calster calibration hierarchy without naming it on the slide. (Slide 44, 'Calibration can fail in level, spread or local shape')
The first three rows (calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, flexible calibration curve) are levels 1 to 3 of the calibration hierarchy defined in Van Calster B, Nieboer D, Vergouwe Y, De Cock B, Pencina M, Steyerberg E (2016), J Clin Epidemiol 74:167-176, in that order, with the fourth row substituted for their 'strong calibration'. The paper is in the bibliography on slide 51, so the credit exists, but it is not on the slide that uses the framework. These decks ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and slides get.
Fix: Add 'Hierarchy adapted from Van Calster et al. (2016), J Clin Epidemiol 74:167-176' as a footline on slide 44. Optionally note that the paper's fourth level is 'strong calibration' and that the decision-region check is the author's own practical addition, which is a good addition and worth claiming.
AUROC is load-bearing from slide 25 onwards but is never defined, while the wiki declares the LE self-standing with no prerequisites and job role 'any'. (Slides 25, 35, 36, 47 and 48; wiki 'Learning Events to be completed before: None' and 'Self-standing: Yes')
AUROC first appears as a bare number on slide 25 ('AUROC = 0.82'), then carries the whole discrimination-versus-calibration argument on slides 35 and 36, and both closing exercises on slides 47 and 48 turn on 'AUROC 0.84'. The glossary on slide 50 defines discrimination, not AUROC itself. Sensitivity and specificity appear in slide 31's message with no definition either. For a horizontal lecture declared self-standing with no prerequisite LE and open to any job role, a lecturer facing a mixed cohort will have to.
Fix: Add one backup slide (or two lines on slide 35) giving the one-sentence operational definition of AUROC (the probability that a randomly chosen failure receives a higher score than a randomly chosen non-failure) plus one line each for sensitivity and specificity. Alternatively, name the prerequisite LE on the wiki and drop 'Self-standing: Yes'. The backup slide is the cheaper.
Also noted on the second pass

The root defect behind must_fix 1, which the review does not name: 11% does triple duty in the running case. It is sample B's estimate on slides 9 and 10, the fixed population parameter p on slides 11 and 21, and the observed estimate again on slides 19 and 22. Slide 19 exists specifically to separate estimand from estimator from estimate, so using one number for both the target and the observation is the.
AUROC drifts from 0.82 on slide 25 to 0.84 on slide 48 with no explanation, in a deck whose selling point is one running case followed end to end. Slide 25's is a validation figure and slide 48's is 'externally', so it may be deliberate, but nothing on the slides says so. One clause on slide 48 ('externally, against the 0.82 seen in validation') closes it.
Site D appears exactly once, on slide 47, and is never introduced. Slide 15 defines Sites A, B and C, slide 32 says the model was 'Developed on Sites A-C', and slide 48 says 'the new site' without naming it. A lecturer who did not build the deck will be asked what Site D is. One word on slide 32 or 48 fixes it.
No licence line and no EU or PANORAIMA funder acknowledgement appears anywhere in the deck text. I grepped for CC BY, PANORAIMA, RAISE, Connecting Europe and co-financed: zero hits across all 55 pages, including the title slide. The wiki states the materials ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This is exactly the redistribution scenario the review invokes to justify its slide 44 finding, so it is inconsistent to raise that.
Smaller fixes

Slide 45, recalibration table: add temperature scaling. Guo et al. (2017) is already in the bibliography and temperature scaling is that paper's headline recommendation, a single-parameter variant of Platt scaling. It is what practitioners reach for first on a neural network, and its absence from a.
Slide 41: add expected calibration error (ECE) to the 'use summary measures' column, with the one-line caveat that it depends on the binning choice and is not a proper scoring rule. Students will meet ECE in every ML calibration paper and in most tooling, and the caveat is exactly the professional.
Slides 8 and 49: name the aleatoric and epistemic pair. Slide 8 teaches precisely that distinction (variability belongs to the world, uncertainty belongs to our knowledge) and Hullermeier & Waegeman (2021) is already cited, but the two words never appear. Adding them to the glossary costs nothing.
Slides 27 and 28: two sentences on conformal prediction. This is the deck's main currency gap for an AI programme in 2026. The deck presents prediction intervals only through the classical regression band on slide 27, while distribution-free conformal methods are now the standard way practitioners.
Slide 39: the formula shown is the binary Brier score, which ranges 0 to 1. Brier's 1950 definition sums over both categories and ranges 0 to 2. A one-line footnote avoids the mismatch a student hits on opening the cited paper.
Slide 30: state the assumption that inspection removes the failure. As written, the threshold p > 0.10 follows only if a preventive inspection prevents the failure with certainty. If inspection is only partly effective the threshold rises. One clause fixes it, and it reinforces the slide's own.
Slide 46: one sentence tying monitoring and recalibration to the regulatory record would sharpen the practice link for a horizontal LE. Article 15(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires that levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk systems be declared in the instructions.
Slide 48 model answer: it refers to 'the 12% validation rate', but the stem describes 14 failures in 120 pumps at a new site, not a validation set. 14/120 is 11.7%, so the number is right and the label is not. Change to 'the observed new-site rate (14/120, about 12%)'.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 20 items in total. The notable results:

Brier, G. W. (1950), 'Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability', Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3. Verified via AMS journals and ADS. DOI 10.1175/1520-0493(1950)078<0001:VOFEIT>2.0.CO;2. Correct as cited.
Murphy, A. H. (1973), 'A new vector partition of the probability score', Journal of Applied Meteorology 12(4):595-600. Verified via AMS journals and ADS. Correct as cited. The three-term partition (uncertainty, reliability, resolution) is what supports slide 39's claim that both probability accuracy and ranking affect.
Gneiting, T. & Raftery, A. E. (2007), 'Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation', JASA 102(477):359-378. Verified via Taylor & Francis and the UW Statistics technical report. Correct as cited, and it supports slide 41's framing of Brier and log loss as proper scores.
Greenland, S. et al. (2016), 'Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations', European Journal of Epidemiology 31(4):337-350, DOI 10.1007/s10654-016-0149-3. Verified via PubMed (PMID 27209009). Correct as cited. Full author list is Greenland, Senn, Rothman, Carlin, Poole,.
Wasserstein, R. L. & Lazar, N. A. (2016), 'The ASA's statement on p-values: context, process, and purpose', The American Statistician 70(2):129-133, DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108. Verified via Taylor & Francis. Correct as cited.
Van Calster, B. et al. (2016), 'A calibration hierarchy for risk models was defined: from utopia to empirical data', Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 74:167-176, DOI 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2015.12.005. Verified via PubMed (PMID 26772608) and the KU Leuven Lirias record. Authors are Van Calster, Nieboer, Vergouwe, De Cock,.
Plan against material
["They agree closely, better than most in this batch. The seven time blocks on slide 3 match the wiki plan's suggested structure exactly (0-10, 10-25, 25-40, 40-55, 55-70, 70-82, 82-90), and each slide footer repeats its band. All six sources of uncertainty the plan asks for (sampling variability, measurement error, missing data, label noise, heterogeneity, model assumptions) appear on slides 8 to 17. The plan's 25-40 request to 'briefly compare uncertainty for a mean/proportion with uncertainty for a model performance metric' is slide 25. The 40-55 request to separate confidence from prediction intervals is slide 27. The 55-70 request for reliability diagrams, Brier score and log loss at an intuitive level is slides 37, 39 and 40. The plan's instruction to keep formulas minimal is respected: only three formulas appear in the whole deck (CI structure on slide 20, Brier on 39, log loss on 40), and no derivations. All five stated learning outcomes are delivered.", "Four disagreements, none serious. (1) The plan suggests 'a medical risk prediction model, a loan default model, or a.

Coverage
["Fills the 90 minutes, and the pacing is realistic rather than optimistic. The PDF is 55 pages carrying 51 numbered frames (slides 10, 22, 38 and 48 are duplicated as question and answer overlays). Net of five section dividers and three backup slides (49, 50, 51), that is about 43 content slides for 90 minutes, inside the consortium's 30-60 guideline and close to the one-slide-per-minute rule of thumb.", "Interactivity meets the requirement. Four clearly marked checkpoints (slide 5 open discussion, slides 10, 22 and 38 multiple choice with worked answer overlays) plus a four-part exit check on slide 48 with model answers. They are well spaced, roughly one every 15 minutes, and each sits at the point where the concept has just been introduced rather than being bolted on.", "All five.

Bottom line
We are happy to sign this off. The items above are worth doing before it is taught, but none of them needs to come back to us for another round.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026
