entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (signed off with minor fixes). Technically accurate, current, and unusually well structured for a 90-minute statistics lecture, with a fully verifiable bibliography and clearly labelled fictional case data; it needs per-slide source lines for the leakage and validation-hierarchy frameworks, four quiz slides that stop printing their own answers, one metric misfiled, and one human-facing subgroup example the lesson plan asks for  5 must-fix item(s); 20 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Technically accurate, current, and unusually well structured for a 90-minute statistics lecture, with a fully verifiable bibliography and clearly labelled fictional case data; it needs per-slide source lines for the leakage and validation-hierarchy frameworks, four quiz slides that stop printing their own answers, one metric misfiled, and one human-facing subgroup example the lesson plan asks for and the pump-only case cannot deliver.

What works

Every one of the ten bibliography entries on slide 50 checks out. I verified authors, year, venue, volume and pages for all ten. This is rare and it means a lecturer can hand the reference list to students without re-checking it.
Slides 5 and 44 both carry the label "fictional teaching-case results" directly on the figure. Invented numbers in a deck that ships under CC BY-NC-SA get screenshotted and quoted; labelling them on the artwork itself is the right call and most decks in this programme do not do it.
Slide 13 is the best slide in the deck. Splitting develop / select / evaluate into three statistical jobs, with the line "If a dataset changes the procedure, it is development information, even when we call it a test set", states in one sentence the thing practitioners get wrong most often.
Slide 32 teaches leakage through human decisions: the team looks at test errors, changes the model, re-reports the same test set, and "No rows moved". This route is the one that actually happens in industry and it is usually absent from statistics teaching, which stops at joining the wrong table.
Slide 26 gives an operational test rather than a definition: "could this exact information be obtained before the decision in real use?" Combined with the seven-point audit on slide 34, a student leaves with something they can run on a paper or a project, which is what the lesson plan asked for.
What to fix before this is taught

Established published frameworks are reproduced with no source note on the slide, and the canonical leakage reference is missing from the bibliography. (Slides 27, 31, 34 and 40; bibliography on slide 50)
The deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and gets copied onward, so an unattributed framework travels as if it were the author's. Slide 27's five leakage routes and slide 34's audit are a condensed relabelling of the published leakage taxonomies: Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich and Stitelman (2012), ACM TKDD 6(4) Article 15, which is the canonical formulation and is not in the bibliography at all, and Kapoor and Narayanan (2023), which is cited but only at the end and whose paper is built around an eight-type leakage.
Fix: Add a one-line source note in the footer of slides 27, 34, 40 and 42 naming the framework's authors. Add to the bibliography: Kaufman, S., Rosset, S., Perlich, C., & Stitelman, O. (2012), ACM TKDD 6(4), Art. 15; Justice, A. C., Covinsky, K. E., & Berlin, J. A. (1999), Ann Intern Med 130(6), 515-524; Reilly, B. M., & Evans, A. T. (2006), Ann Intern Med 144(3), 201-209;.
Four of the five interactive elements display their own answer on the page that asks the question. (Slides 5, 14, 23 and 33)
Slide 33 asks which parts of a pipeline invalidate the test performance and the "Message to keep" banner on that same page reads "All four leak information". Slide 23's question page carries "Here, grouping by pump prevents repeated-unit leakage; a temporal hold-out directly tests next-year use", which is answers B and C. Slide 14's question page carries "final evaluation must occur after the search stops", which points at C. Slide 5 is worse: the question and both columns of model answers sit on one page with no.
Fix: Suppress the "Message to keep" banner on the question page of each pair and show it only on the answer page, or replace it with a neutral prompt. Split slide 5 into a question overlay and an answer overlay to match the pattern already used on slides 14, 23, 33 and 49.
Brier score is listed as evidence for calibration only. (Slide 36, "Calibration" row of the metrics table)
The Brier score is a strictly proper scoring rule that decomposes into reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty (Murphy, 1973). Resolution is a discrimination-like component, so the Brier score is not calibration evidence: it can improve while calibration gets worse, and two models with identical Brier scores can have very different reliability. Teaching it as the calibration metric in a lecture whose learning outcome is to differentiate what each kind of validation evidence can and cannot prove undercuts the.
Fix: Keep calibration curve, slope and intercept in the Calibration row. Give the Brier score its own row, "overall probabilistic accuracy", with a one-line note that it decomposes into calibration and resolution components and therefore does not isolate either.
The lesson plan asks for subgroup performance across demographic groups and for patient-level splits; the pump-only running case delivers neither. (Slides 43, 44 and 45, against the wiki blocks 25-40 min and 68-80 min)
The wiki's 68-80 block says to show "how performance can differ across sites, devices, demographic groups, or time periods" and the 25-40 block lists "patient-level" splits. The deck covers sites, devices and time well, but the only subgroups that ever appear are "Older pump type" and "New pump type" on slide 44, and slide 43 says only "Decision-relevant strata". Slide 45 is a genuinely good slide about overinterpreting subgroup evidence, but with pump types as the running subgroup a student never meets the reason.
Fix: Add one slide, or a parallel right-hand column on slides 43-45, translating the same subgroup finding into one of the human-facing cases the lesson plan already names (a clinical risk model or a credit model): the same table, but with the strata being people and the consequence being a denied loan or a missed diagnosis. This closes the plan mismatch, the.
The n labels in the subgroup figure have no unit, and the deck's own rule three slides earlier says they must. (Slide 44 (n=1,800 / 620 / 410 / 270 / 95))
Slide 29 tells students "Report numbers of units, not only numbers of rows" and "A large row count does not imply a large independent sample". Slide 38 repeats it and slide 45 repeats it again. The figure on slide 44 then prints bare n values with no statement of whether they count pumps or pump-months. The running case is 1,000 pumps with monthly records over three years, so 1,800 is very unlikely to be pumps; if these are pump-months, the 95% intervals drawn on the chart are too narrow, which is precisely the.
Fix: Label the axis with the unit and both counts, for example "n = 300 pumps / 1,800 pump-months, 74 failures", and widen the intervals if they were computed on pump-months. Add the event count for each bar, since slide 45 requires it.
Also noted on the second pass

The whole H-128 file was in the review pack and answers both of the review's open questions. This is the biggest process miss and it is what makes must-fix 4 and the plan_vs_material hedge collapse. H-128 also supplies the best available evidence for must-fix 3, since its own summary table separates the Brier score from calibration slope and intercept and its bibliography already cites Murphy (1973). Read the.
Possible numerical inconsistency between slide 4 and slide 44, on the deck's headline figure, unflagged. Slide 4 states the running case as AUROC 0.91 random hold-out, 0.76 next year, 0.64 new site. Slide 44 replots the same three tests, plus two pump-type subgroups, on an axis whose printed tick range is 0.60 to 0.90. A point at 0.91 and its upper confidence arm cannot sit on that axis, and a Site D interval around.
Plan and material disagree on self-standing status, and nobody flagged it. The wiki says 'Self-standing: Yes' and 'Learning Events to be completed before: None.' The deck uses AUROC from slide 4 onward without ever defining it, uses calibration curve, slope and Brier score on slide 36 without definition, and slide 7 is an explicit build on H-128. Either the wiki should list H-128 as expected preparation, or the deck.
Slide 2's footer reads '0-5 min', which is not one of the seven blocks in the wiki schedule or in slide 3's own reproduction of that schedule. Trivial on its own, but the review praises the footers as a complete pacing system a substitute lecturer can run from, so the one footer that breaks the scheme should be named rather than left for the second author to find.
Smaller fixes

Slide 19, step 5, and slide 38, bullet 2: say explicitly that the fold-to-fold standard deviation underestimates the true error bar. Varoquaux (2018) is already in the bibliography and that is exactly its finding (roughly plus or minus 10% at n=100, with the standard error across folds strongly.
Slide 36, Decision value row: 'net benefit' is decision curve analysis, Vickers and Elkin (2006), Medical Decision Making 26(6), 565-574. Name it on the slide, since students who go looking for 'net benefit' without the term will not find the method.
Slide 47 is a validation reporting checklist and TRIPOD+AI is already in the bibliography but is never named on a slide. Naming it on 47 connects the lecture to the reporting standard practitioners are actually asked to produce against, at the cost of four words.
The PDF supplied for review contains no lecturer notes. The per-slide 'Message to keep' plus the time-block footer covers a lot of the gap, but the eight figure-only slides (11, 18, 21, 28, 37, 40, 44, 46) have no talk track at all, and those are the ones a substitute lecturer will stall on. If a.
No regulatory or standards hook anywhere in 90 minutes, which is a gap for a programme with a legal dimension. One slide would do it, and the deck has already taught the mechanism. Current position, verified this week: EU AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Art 15 requires declared accuracy.
Slide 22, left column: 'preprocessing is fitted within each split' is not a condition under which random splitting is reasonable, it is a requirement for every split design. It sits oddly in a list of three genuine conditions. Move it out, or restate it as a caveat under the table.
Cawley and Talbot's title on slide 50 is truncated: the full title is 'On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation'. Volume, year and pages (JMLR 11, 2079-2107, 2010) are correct.
Optional addition to the bibliography: Riley et al., BMJ 2024;384:e074821, part 3 of the same series, on calculating sample size for an external validation study. Parts 1 and 2 are already cited, and part 3 is precisely the 'the interval is too wide to decide' problem that slide 44 raises and does.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 20 items in total. The notable results:

Stone, M. (1974), JRSS B 36(2) - CONFIRMED, DOI 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1974.tb00994.x. Note on pages: Oxford Academic lists the article as 111-133; the 111-147 range used on slide 50 is the with-discussion range used by JSTOR and by most bibliographies. Both are in circulation and the deck's version is defensible, not an.
Varma, S. & Simon, R. (2006), 'Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection', BMC Bioinformatics 7, 91 - CONFIRMED, DOI 10.1186/1471-2105-7-91, PMID 16504092, published 23 Feb 2006, NCI Biometric Research Branch. Supports the claim on slide 14.
Cawley, G. C. & Talbot, N. L. C. (2010), JMLR 11, 2079-2107 - CONFIRMED via jmlr.org. Title on slide 50 is truncated by four words ('...in performance evaluation').
Roberts, D. R., et al. (2017), Ecography 40, 913-929 - CONFIRMED, DOI 10.1111/ecog.02881, issue 8, 14 authors. The paper's finding (ignoring structure in cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error; use block cross-validation) is what slides 21 and 22 teach.
Varoquaux, G. (2018), NeuroImage 180, 68-77 - CONFIRMED, DOI 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2017.06.061, PMID 28655633, arXiv 1706.07581. Its central finding, that the standard error across folds strongly underestimates the true error bar, is not surfaced anywhere on the slides; see smaller fixes.
Kapoor, S. & Narayanan, A. (2023), Patterns 4(9), 100804 - CONFIRMED, DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100804, PMID 37720327, published 4 Aug 2023. Confirmed that the paper's contribution is a taxonomy of eight types of leakage across 17 fields and 294 affected papers, which is why slide 27's route table needs an on-slide.
Plan against material
"They agree closely, more closely than most LEs in this batch. Slide 3's block table reproduces the wiki's seven time blocks exactly (0-10, 10-25, 25-40, 40-55, 55-68, 68-80, 80-90) and every bullet in the wiki's 'Suggested lesson structure' has a slide behind it. The wiki's five learning outcomes map cleanly onto slide 2, which adds 'grouped' to the list of validation designs and drops the word 'internal' from the restatement, though internal validation is properly covered on slide 40. The wiki's demand for 'a practical leakage-detection checklist' is met by slide 34, and 'a validation report structure: data split, leakage prevention, metrics with uncertainty, subgroup/external validation, robustness checks, and known limitations' is met point for point by slide 47. The wiki's closing takeaway, that validation is not a ceremonial test but the design logic that tells us whether a result deserves trust, is the message line on slide 49.\n\nTwo disagreements. First, the subgroup content: the wiki asks for performance differences across 'sites, devices, demographic groups, or time.

Coverage
"Yes, it fills 90 minutes, and if anything it is slightly over-full rather than thin. 54 pages for 90 minutes is about 1.7 minutes per page, inside the consortium's 30-60 slide guidance for a lecture LE. The five learning outcomes are all delivered: LO1 on slides 6 and 9, LO2 on slides 19-22 and 40-43, LO3 on slides 11-13 and 25-34, LO4 on slides 15 and 46, and LO5 on slides 39, 47, 48 and the exit check on 49.\n\nThe load is unevenly distributed across blocks and a lecturer will feel it. Counting from the time footers printed on each page: the 40-55 block carries 11 pages in 15 minutes, including a four-option discussion question and a seven-point audit slide, while the 68-80 block carries 5 pages in 12 minutes. The 25-40 block carries 10 pages in 15 minutes. The 80-90 block has 6 pages.

Bottom line
We are happy to sign this off. The items above are worth doing before it is taught, but none of them needs to come back to us for another round.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: H-130 Statistics in practice
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (signed off with minor fixes). Technically the most solid practical we have reviewed in this batch: I re-executed all 21 code cells on a much newer Python stack and every stored number, including every figure hard-coded inside the collapsed model answers, reproduced exactly, so the three fixes needed are additive and small (a licence and attribution cell, one missing per-site threshold cell, and a programme-level answer on whet 3 must-fix item(s); 8 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8545.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Technically the most solid practical we have reviewed in this batch: I re-executed all 21 code cells on a much newer Python stack and every stored number, including every figure hard-coded inside the collapsed model answers, reproduced exactly, so the three fixes needed are additive and small (a licence and attribution cell, one missing per-site threshold cell, and a programme-level answer on whether this file is H-130 or H-130 plus H-131).

What works

Reproducibility is verified, not asserted. I extracted all 21 code cells and ran them on Python 3.14 with numpy 2.5.3, pandas 3.0.5, scikit-learn 1.9.0 and matplotlib, well ahead of what the author would have used. Every stored output reproduced to the printed digit: prevalence 19.5% with bootstrap interval 16.6% to 22.2% (Cell 15), AUROC 0.781 with interval 0.741 to 0.819 (Cell 26), Brier 0.132 and mean predicted.
The synthetic data generator (Cell 6, make_pump_data) is engineered rather than decorative. Each planted complication produces one teaching point and each point lands hard: the post-outcome work order moves AUROC from 0.781 to 0.973 (Cell 23), the fully grown tree goes from development AUROC 1.000 and Brier 0.000 to test AUROC 0.578 (Cell 18), the South 2026 sensor drift of -0.75 mm/s produces a +15.0 point.
The Brier skill score treatment in Cell 40 is more careful than most published material. It names the reference forecast, gives the formula, then states that the reference 'is a mathematical yardstick rather than a deployable model, because it uses an observed failure rate that nobody knows in advance', and still warns that the normalisation does not remove case-mix differences. Both caveats are usually dropped. The.
Cell 24 is the best paragraph in the file. Asking whether a leaky model would become acceptable at AUROC 0.99 on a larger externally collected dataset, and answering that more data only estimates an infeasible procedure more precisely, is exactly the error practitioners make when a validation result looks too good. It is a better framing than the usual 'do not leak' instruction.
Bootstrap intervals are attached to decision-relevant quantities, not only to the headline metric. Cell 36 reports sensitivity, precision among inspected, inspection rate, and non-failing units inspected per 1,000, each with a 95% interval. Most teaching material stops at a confidence interval around AUROC and leaves the operational rates as point estimates.
What to fix before this is taught

The notebook file carries no author, no institution, no funding acknowledgement and no licence statement. (Cell 1 (title banner) and Cell 55 (references), that is, the top and bottom of the .ipynb)
The wiki page states that the materials are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. A .ipynb travels separately from its wiki page: students download it, open it in Colab, and forward it. In its current form a downstream copy carries nothing that identifies BME or Andras Gezsi, so the BY condition cannot survive redistribution, and PANORAIMA and the EU co-financing get no credit either. Every other deck in this programme should be held to the same rule.
Fix: Add a short markdown cell at the end (or a line in the Cell 1 banner) reading: author Andras Gezsi, BME; PANORAIMA learning event H-130; licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; plus the EU co-financing line used on the wiki. Roughly four lines of text.
The notebook banner and the filename claim two learning event codes, H_130 and H_131, while the wiki page under review is H-130 alone at 120 minutes, and the notebook's own timetable budgets exactly 120 minutes. (Cell 1 banner ('H_130-H_131 · Horizontal learning event · 120 minutes'), and the filename H130_H131_Statistics_in_Practice_final.ipynb)
The internal run-of-show in Cell 3 and Cell 54 fills 0 to 120 minutes with no spare capacity, so this file cannot also be the material for a second 120-minute learning event. Either H-131 has been left with no distinct material, or the banner is wrong. A lecturer rostered to teach H-131 who opens this file will find a session already fully budgeted for H-130, and will not know what is supposed to be different.
Fix: Programme level decision, not a content change. If H-130 and H-131 are a deliberate pair, say so on both wiki pages and split the notebook into the two blocks each one covers. If H-131 is a separate event, remove H_131 from the banner and the filename. If they were merged, close H-131 on the wiki. I cannot check the H-131 wiki page from here (the wiki is VPN gated), so the.
No cell computes threshold consequences per site, so the question Activity 5 actually asks cannot be answered from the notebook's own output, and the facilitator guide points learners at output that does not exist. (Cell 43 (site results) and Cell 47 (Activity 5); the dangling instruction is in Cell 54, 'Timing contingencies', early-finisher bullet)
The wiki plan's 82 to 98 minute block requires the lecturer to ask 'whether the same threshold would be acceptable for all subgroups', and Cell 47 asks 'Is the proposed 20% threshold ready for routine use at all three sites?'. Cell 43 gives only AUROC and mean predicted risk by site, so a student can infer that South is miscalibrated but cannot see what the 20% rule actually does site by site. Worse, Cell 54 tells early finishers to 'compare the bootstrap intervals and South-site confusion counts', and no cell.
Fix: Add one prepared code cell after Cell 43 that loops over sites and calls the existing metric_summary at THRESHOLD, printing sensitivity, precision, inspection rate and the four confusion counts per site. The helper already exists, so this is roughly eight lines and no new machinery. Then add the resulting numbers to the Activity 5 suggested interpretation in Cell 47.
Also noted on the second pass

Robustness check C is partly hollow and nobody says so. Cell 46's predict_with_south_correction does perturbed.loc[site == 'South', 'vibration_mm_s'] += correction. Vibration is NaN for 58 of the 318 South 2026 rows, and NaN plus 0.75 is still NaN, so 58 rows are silently left uncorrected and then filled by the pipeline's development-set median. The sensitivity analysis therefore covers 82% of the rows it claims to.
Missingness is planted, displayed, then abandoned. Cell 7 lists it as one of five deliberate complications, Cell 11 shows 18.2% at South 2026 against 1.9% to 4.8% everywhere else, and no activity, checkpoint or facilitator prompt ever returns to it. The wiki's 98 to 112 block names 'missing-data perturbation' as one of the suitable robustness checks. The review's coverage_note says outcome 4 gets three checks.
The must_fix 1 fix text tells the author to add 'the EU co-financing line used on the wiki'. That line currently reads 'The PANORAIMA programme was Co-Financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union Under Grant No ???.' on all 25 wiki pages I have here, including H-130. Instructing an author to copy a placeholder into a file built for redistribution is a bad instruction. Either give the grant.
The paired-code question is a pattern, not a one-off, and saying so makes the finding land better. H-132 in this same batch has the same author (BME, Andras Gezsi), a wiki page for H-132 alone at 120 minutes, and a material file named H_132-H_133_Typical_approach_to_AI_project.pptx. So H_130-H_131 and H_132-H_133 are the same convention. Raise it once as a programme-level naming question covering both, rather than.
Smaller fixes

Log loss is computed but never shown. metric_summary in Cell 6 returns 'log loss' (I get 0.4215 on the 2026 test) and no cell ever displays it. The wiki plan's 65 to 82 minute block says 'Compute or inspect Brier score/log loss'. Either add it to the print block in Cell 28 next to the Brier score,.
The AUROC statement in Cell 19 omits ties: AUROC is P(failing ranked higher) plus half P(tie). With continuous logistic scores the tie mass here is effectively zero, so Cell 20's printed '78.1% of the time' is fine as it stands. But this is a statistics practical, the same sentence is repeated in.
References (Cell 55) are all real and correctly cited, but the two papers closest to what this notebook actually teaches are missing. Add Van Calster, Nieboer, Vergouwe, De Cock, Pencina and Steyerberg (2016), 'A calibration hierarchy for risk models was defined: from utopia to empirical data',.
The population framing in Cell 4 wobbles. It states 'The intended deployment is all three sites in 2026', while Cell 18 uses 2026 as the temporal test set and Cell 51 question 3 talks about 'next-year deployment'. A careful student will ask how you deploy into a year whose outcomes you have already.
The five-element conclusion structure in Cell 48 (result, uncertainty, probability quality, validation and robustness, limitation and next step) is sound but unattributed. Since TRIPOD+AI is already in the reference list, a line saying the structure is adapted from its reporting principles would.
Subgroup analysis stops at site. The wiki's own teacher instructions list 'demographic subgroup' among the suitable grouping variables, and this is a human-centred AI programme. Two sentences in Cell 47 or the Cell 54 guide, noting that the identical machinery is how one evaluates person-level.
bootstrap_distribution in Cell 6 silently skips any AUROC resample containing a single outcome class, so n_boot is an upper bound rather than the count used. With 19.5% prevalence at n=800, and even for Central at 26 failures in 225 rows, the probability of this firing is effectively zero, so no.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 8 items in total. The notable results:

All six references in Cell 55 verified as real, correctly attributed and correctly cited. Efron, B. and Tibshirani, R.J. (1993), An Introduction to the Bootstrap, Chapman & Hall (Monographs on Statistics and Applied Probability), confirmed. Gneiting, T. and Raftery, A.E. (2007), 'Strictly proper scoring rules,.
Re-executed the material rather than reading it. I extracted all 21 code cells to a script and ran them under Python 3.14 with numpy 2.5.3, pandas 3.0.5, scikit-learn 1.9.0 and matplotlib, a stack considerably newer than the author's. Every stored output reproduced to the printed digit: 2026 prevalence 19.5% with.
Checked every number hard-coded inside the collapsed model answers, because those are where drift usually hides. Cell 38 claims 'roughly 213 of 1,000 units' flagged at the 20% threshold: I compute 21.25%, which is 212.5 per 1,000. Correct. Cell 38 claims the model 'catches only about half of future failures':.
Checked the statistical definitions independently rather than taking them on trust. The Brier skill score formula in Cell 40 matches the code in Cell 6, and the constant-reference Brier column in Cell 41 uses p(1-p), which is exactly the mean squared error of the sample-optimal constant forecast, so the two are.
Computed the evidence the notebook is missing, so the author can paste it in. At the 20% threshold, by site: Central n=225, sensitivity 53.8%, precision 37.8%, 164 inspected per 1,000, prevalence 11.6%; North n=257, sensitivity 47.2%, precision 28.8%, 230 per 1,000, prevalence 14.0%; South n=318, sensitivity 51.1%,.
Searched for uncredited reproduction of published material and found none. Every table and figure is computed from the notebook's own synthetic data. The reliability-band table, the misconceptions table and the run-of-show table in Cell 54 are original prose, not lifted from a published framework. The five-element.
Plan against material
"They agree on substance. All five wiki learning outcomes appear in Cell 3 in the same order and in compatible wording, and each is delivered by named cells. The prerequisite chain is honoured: Cell 1 explicitly continues the pump-failure case from H-128 and H-129, which are the two events the wiki lists as required before.\n\nFour differences, in order of how much they matter.\n\nFirst, the H-130 versus H-131 code question, covered in the must-fix list. This is the one the programme has to answer.\n\nSecond, the timetables differ by a few minutes per block. Wiki: 0-10, 10-25, 25-45, 45-65, 65-82, 82-98, 98-112, 112-120. Notebook (Cell 3 and Cell 54): 0-10, 10-22, 22-37, 37-58, 58-76, 76-92, 92-108, 108-120. The sequence and content match block for block, so this is bookkeeping rather than disagreement, and the notebook is the version to follow because it is what the lecturer actually runs. The wiki timetable should be updated to match so the two do not drift further apart.\n\nThird, the subgroup-threshold gap in the must-fix list. The wiki's 82-98 block asks whether the same.

Coverage
"The 120 minutes are real and honestly budgeted, and the risk is overrun rather than underrun. Section 3 alone (37 to 58 minutes, Cells 17 to 26) carries the temporal split, a constant baseline, two models, the ROC explainer, the leakage demonstration and an AUROC bootstrap in 21 minutes. That is tight. The author has anticipated it: Cell 54 gives contingencies for running 15 and 30 minutes behind, and the post-class review (Cell 51) and the random-partition extension (Cells 52 to 53) are both marked optional and excluded from the timetable, which is the correct way to build slack.\n\nOn outcomes, mapped to the wiki wording: outcome 1 (uncertainty summaries for a descriptive quantity and a performance metric) is delivered by Cell 15 for prevalence and Cell 26 for AUROC, with Cell 36.

Bottom line
We are happy to sign this off. The items above are worth doing before it is taught, but none of them needs to come back to us for another round.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: H-132 Typical approach to AI project
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (REVISION REQUESTED). The content is well written and the email-triage running case is carried through properly, but the deck credits the wrong author and the wrong EU funding programme, sets a 90 percent accuracy deploy gate on a problem it has just described as imbalanced, and contains none of the seven group activities the wiki lesson plan schedules, so it needs one revision pass before it is taught. 8 must-fix item(s); 11 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8547.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
The content is well written and the email-triage running case is carried through properly, but the deck credits the wrong author and the wrong EU funding programme, sets a 90 percent accuracy deploy gate on a problem it has just described as imbalanced, and contains none of the seven group activities the wiki lesson plan schedules, so it needs one revision pass before it is taught.

What works

The running case is well chosen and actually carried through. Slides 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 25 and 27 all stay on customer support email triage, and each stage's answer follows from the one before it. The wiki plan asks for exactly this and the author delivered it. Most decks we review abandon their example by the third section.
Slide 9 is the best slide in the deck. Putting three business-problem statements next to three AI-task statements is the right level of abstraction for the distinction between a real-world problem and an ML task, and the closing line ('an AI project starts by translating a real-world problem into a well-defined prediction or decision task') is the sentence students should leave with.
Human oversight is designed into the case rather than added as an ethics slide. Slide 6 frames the AI as supporting routing, slide 10 says the agent can accept or override, and slide 25 asks the four questions that matter in practice: where does the prediction appear, who sees it, what happens next, can the user override it. That is the programme's human-centred orientation done properly.
Slide 12 gets baselines right, including the question most courses skip: is AI worth the additional complexity at all. Pairing it with slide 30's 'would you approve the project' gives students a genuine go/no-go judgement to make rather than a definition to recall.
Slide 11's explicit out-of-scope column (generate responses, answer technical questions, multiple languages, full automation) is good practice and is rarely taught. Naming what the first version will not do is the single most useful scoping habit in industry.
What must be fixed before sign-off

The funding acknowledgement names the wrong EU programme. Slide 32 says the project is 'co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union under grant DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, grant agreement. (Slide 32 (Acknowledgements); wiki section 'Acknowledgements, thanks')
This deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and gets copied onward, and EU funding acknowledgements carry contractual wording obligations. Every downstream copy inherits the error. It is almost certainly a consortium template problem rather than this author's mistake, so it is worth raising above the LE as well as fixing here.
Fix: Replace with the Digital Europe Programme wording, for example: 'Co-funded by the European Union under the Digital Europe Programme, call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, grant agreement number 101189994.' Fill the grant number into the wiki Acknowledgements section at the same time, and ask the WP lead to check the master template, because other LE decks will carry the same.
The title slide credits a different author from the wiki. Slide 1 carries 'Laszlo Fetter' under the title. The wiki Management information block lists Author Person 1 as Andras Gezsi (BME), with Author Organisation 2 as. (Slide 1 vs wiki 'Management information')
Under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 the attribution line is the part reusers are required to reproduce. Two records disagreeing about who wrote the material makes correct downstream attribution impossible, and it also makes the wiki an unreliable index of who to contact about this LE. Both people are real BME staff, so this reads as a genuine record mismatch rather than a placeholder.
Fix: Decide who authored the material and make the two agree. If both contributed, name both on slide 1 and fill Author Person 2 on the wiki. Also fill the blank Author Person 2 field for TUD or remove Author Organisation 2 if TUD did not contribute.
Slide 23 sets 'Accuracy >= 90%' as the deployment criterion for a multiclass problem that slide 16 has just described as imbalanced ('Many Billing emails but few Sales emails', 'the model may become biased toward. (Slide 23 ('How Do We Know If the Model Is Good?'), read against slide 16 ('Is the Data Good Enough?'))
This is the one point in the deck where a student could take away a technically wrong rule and apply it at work. It also breaks the deck's internal logic: slide 23's own header says to use metrics that reflect the project's goals 'not just overall accuracy', and then the only concrete number given is overall accuracy. The wiki plan asks for one primary metric, one secondary metric, one robustness check and one go/no-go threshold, and a single accuracy figure covers none of that properly.
Fix: Replace the accuracy target with a per-class criterion, for example 'macro-averaged F1 above the baseline' as the primary metric with 'recall of at least X on every category including the rare ones' as the secondary, and keep 'higher than the baseline' as the gate. Bring precision, recall and F1 out of the notes and onto the slide with the confusion matrix idea, and add one.
The split design is taught loosely and contradicts the drift material later in the deck. Slide 22 is titled 'Training and Validation' but its body and notes describe only a training set and a test set, so validation and. (Slide 22 ('How Should We Test the Model?' / 'Training and Validation') vs slide 26 ('AI Projects Don't End at Deployment'))
At master level, train, validation and test are three distinct things with different jobs (fitting, model selection, unbiased estimate), and conflating the last two is how students learn to tune on the test set. The temporal point is not a refinement here, it is the correct method for this case, and the deck already contains the evidence for why.
Fix: Separate the three sets in one line on slide 22, and add a second line: for systems whose inputs change over time, split by date so the test period comes after the training period. That connects slide 22 to slide 26 and gives groups something concrete to write into canvas section 5 ('How will you split the data for training and testing?').
The wiki lesson plan schedules seven in-lecture group activities (at 10-25, 25-40, 40-58, 58-72, 72-88, 88-100 and 100-112 minutes) plus group presentations at 112-120. The deck contains none of them. There is no. (Deck as a whole vs wiki 'Instructions for teachers', 'Suggested lesson structure')
This is the difference between the LE the wiki describes (Interactive, 120 minutes, canvas built section by section in groups) and the LE the deck delivers (a lecture that hands out the finished answers, then asks groups to fill in a canvas whose answers are on the slides they just saw). Groups will copy rather than decide. It also breaks the consortium format rule of thumb that interactive sessions run 5 to 10 slides. A lecturer who was not involved in building this cannot recover the plan from the deck.
Fix: Two things. First, add seven short activity slides matching the plan's blocks, each stating the task, the time box and which canvas section it fills, so the timing lives in the deck and not only on the wiki. Second, give the groups a different case from the one the slides work through. Keep email triage as the worked example and hand groups one of the other cases the plan.
Two of the risks named in the wiki learning outcomes are absent from the material. Learning outcome 4 lists leakage explicitly, and the plan's 40-58 block asks whether labels 'encode bias or future information'. The. (Deck sections 'Planning the Data' (slides 14-17) and 'Deployment and Monitoring' (slides 24-27); wiki Learning Outcome 4)
These are the two failure modes that actually bite this exact use case, so leaving them out is a missed opportunity as well as an unmet outcome. Historical tickets carry fields written after routing (resolution team, closing notes, handling time), and training on those gives a model that scores well offline and fails live. The feedback loop is sharper still: once the AI recommends a category and the agent accepts it, the accepted recommendation becomes the next round of training labels, so the model trains on its.
Fix: Add one slide in the data section: which fields existed at prediction time and which were created afterwards, with two or three concrete examples from the ticket system. Add three lines to slide 26 on the feedback loop, including the practical mitigation of logging whether the agent accepted or overrode each recommendation and keeping a small stream of independently labelled.
The canvas is missing three elements the learning outcomes and the lesson plan require. Learning outcome 5 asks for a canvas 'including assumptions, milestones, validation plan, risks, and next-step decisions'. The. (Canvas docx sections 1 and 7; slide 27)
Outcome 5 is the only competence-level outcome in the LE, so the canvas is the assessed artefact. As it stands, students cannot demonstrate the outcome as written. Likelihood and impact are also what turn a risk list into a prioritised one, which is the professional skill here, and without decision gates the canvas has no place to record when the project would be stopped.
Fix: Add an assumptions box to canvas section 1 ('What are we assuming that, if false, would sink this project?') and a milestones line to section 2. Extend section 7 to risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner, decision gate, and change slide 27's table to the same six columns so the slide and the canvas match.
The deck carries no references at all. There is no source slide, no citation on any slide, and no reading list. The lifecycle it teaches (problem, data, model, evaluation, deployment, monitoring) is the standard process. (Whole deck, in particular slides 5, 19, 20 and the canvas docx title)
The consortium checklist asks explicitly whether claims and frameworks are sourced and traceable, and these decks are redistributed under CC BY-NC-SA, which makes provenance a licensing question and not only an academic one. There is also a content cost: at master level, students in a session called 'Typical approach to AI project' should leave knowing the names of the process models they will meet in a real team. I checked the deck for lifted tables and figures and found none, so this is missing attribution.
Fix: Add one references slide before the acknowledgements with, at minimum: CRISP-DM as the origin of the lifecycle; Studer et al., 'Towards CRISP-ML(Q)', Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction 3(2):392-413, 2021, DOI 10.3390/make3020020, for the quality-assured ML version; ISO/IEC 5338:2023 (AI system life cycle processes) as the standard a compliance-minded employer will name;.
Also noted on the second pass

Current practice in 2026, and this is the biggest gap for our role. The slide 19 notes teach the ladder manual process, then rule-based, then simple classifier, then advanced language model, with the LLM at the far end as the thing you graduate to. In practice today a zero-shot or few-shot LLM classifier is usually the first thing a team tries for four-way email routing, and it needs no labelled history at all. That.
The plan's 72-88 block names calibration and subgroup checks. Neither appears in the deck, and the word calibration appears nowhere in it. This matters concretely: slide 27's first mitigation is 'Human review of uncertain predictions', which only works if the model's confidence is calibrated. The review flags the missing confidence score as a smaller fix but never connects it to the plan's explicit calibration.
The plan's 100-112 block also names incident handling and version control. Slide 26 covers monitoring and retraining and neither of those. The review flags feedback loops from that block but not these two.
The CEF wording is a batch-wide template defect, and the review can prove it rather than guess. The identical sentence appears in 25 material files across this review batch and in every LE wiki page in it, all with the grant number left as '???'. Say so with that evidence and route it to the WP lead. As currently written the one_line says 'the deck credits the wrong author and the wrong EU funding programme', which.
Smaller fixes

Slide 6 says the company receives 'thousands of customer emails every day'; slide 8 says 'Hundreds of customer emails arrive every day'. Pick one. The number drives both the business case and whether there is enough training data, so students will notice.
Slide 14's third training example is '"Cancel my subscription." / Account Management', but Account Management is not one of the four categories defined on slides 10, 11 and 14 (Technical Support, Billing, Sales, General Inquiry). Either use one of the four or make the fifth category deliberate and.
Slide 27's first mitigation is 'Human review of uncertain predictions', but no slide explains how the system knows a prediction is uncertain. The whole human-in-the-loop design on slides 25 and 27 rests on a confidence score and a threshold that the deck never teaches. Add two lines in the.
Seven of the 33 slides (5, 7, 13, 18, 21, 24, 28) carry a title and a slide number and nothing else. That is acceptable for section dividers, but slide 19 is a content slide with only a heading and a one-line caption, and its substance (manual process, then rule-based system, then simple.
Slide 2 lists all 31 remaining slide titles on one page. Projected, this is unreadable. Cut it to the seven section names, or keep the full index as a handout page and hide it in the presentation.
Slides 8 and 15 use a low-9 quotation mark as the closing quote in the example emails ('...still can't access my account.,,' and '...charged twice for my subscription.,,'). It is a character-set slip and it shows on screen.
Slide 1 carries the date 07/28/2026 in US format. In a European consortium deck that is ambiguous, and a fixed date makes the deck look stale within a year. Use a version number or drop it.
Slide 17 handles privacy generically. One concrete anchor would help students see that these questions have answers: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) data minimisation for the 'does the model really need this information?' question, and a line noting that this use case is not an Annex III high-risk system.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 11 items in total. The notable results:

Andras Gezsi (wiki Author Person 1) is real and correctly placed: associate professor at BME, Department of Measurement and Information Systems / AI and Systems Engineering, staff page at mit.bme.hu/general/staff/gezsi, Google Scholar profile with ~1,100 citations, research in Bayesian networks and machine learning..
Laszlo Fetter (named on slide 1) is also real and also at BME: listed as teaching staff on the BME Artificial Intelligence course BMEVIMIAC16 (edu.vik.bme.hu) for 2025/26. So the title slide credits a genuine BME colleague, just not the person the wiki records as the author. This is a records mismatch, not a.
Grant agreement 101189994 is PANORAIMA. Confirmed on panoraima.eu ('Co-funded by EU Project 101189994') and via HaDEA's listing of AI projects it manages. Consortium of 16 partners coordinated by Stichting Hogeschool Utrecht. Verified.
Call topic DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU ('Specialised education programmes in key capacity areas') is a Digital Europe Programme topic on the EU Funding and Tenders portal, open 21 November 2023 to 21 March 2024, budget EUR 30 million, managed by HaDEA. It is NOT a Connecting Europe Facility call. Slide 32 and.
CRISP-ML(Q): Studer, Bui, Drescher, Hanuschkin, Winkler, Peters, Mueller-Birn, 'Towards CRISP-ML(Q): A Machine Learning Process Model with Quality Assurance Methodology', Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction, 2021, 3(2), 392-413, DOI 10.3390/make3020020, open access at MDPI, preprint arXiv:2003.05155. Year,.
ISO/IEC 5338:2023, 'Information technology - Artificial intelligence - AI system life cycle processes', first edition 2023, iso.org standard number 81118. Built on ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207 with AI-specific processes from ISO/IEC 22989 and 23053. Verified. Recommended as a citation, not present in the deck.
Plan against material
["They agree on the content sequence and disagree on the format, and where they disagree the wiki plan is right.", "", "Agreement. The deck's seven sections follow the wiki's block order exactly: problem formulation, scope and baseline, data and labels, modelling strategy, evaluation, implementation, deployment and monitoring, then a closing review. The plan asks for a single running case revisited from multiple angles and the deck does that. The plan says the output should be a project canvas rather than code, and the deck and the canvas docx both hold that line. The plan's central intuition ('a successful AI project is not mainly about choosing the most advanced model') is the deck's thesis, stated on slides 5, 12, 19, 20 and 31. The plan's critical-thinking questions (Is AI really needed? Would a simpler baseline solve it? What could go wrong after deployment? Who is responsible if it fails?) map onto slides 12, 27, 29 and 30 and onto the canvas.", "", "Disagreement 1, interactivity. This is the material one. The plan is a 120-minute interactive session with roughly 90 minutes of.

Coverage
["Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert. RealAI builds and operates production ML systems, including text classification and human-in-the-loop routing of the kind used as the running case here.", "", "Duration. It does not fill 120 minutes as delivered, and it is not short of material either. The problem is which 120 minutes. The 24 content slides carry about 2,700 words of speaker notes, which is roughly 25 minutes of narration and, with pauses and the slide 8 discussion, about 50 to 60 minutes of lecture. That is a good fit for the roughly 30 minutes of lecturing the plan allows plus overrun, but it leaves a lecturer who owns only this deck with 60 minutes and no instructions. The seven group activities that fill those 60 minutes exist only on the wiki. Add them to the deck with.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What must be fixed before sign-off' need addressing, after which we will re-review. Everything else here is offered as improvement, not as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.heading: Correction from RealAI: our duration comment, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 120 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 34 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.28. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: H-147 Time series forecasting for demand, cost and capacity
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (REVISION REQUESTED). A well-built, accurate introductory lecture that gets the practitioner's order of operations right (define the decision, then the model), but it ships with the wrong author on the title slide, no references anywhere, and the last two blocks of its own lesson plan (decision costs, stress testing, post-deployment monitoring) only half delivered; the fixes are short. 5 must-fix item(s); 12 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8548.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
A well-built, accurate introductory lecture that gets the practitioner's order of operations right (define the decision, then the model), but it ships with the wrong author on the title slide, no references anywhere, and the last two blocks of its own lesson plan (decision costs, stress testing, post-deployment monitoring) only half delivered; the fixes are short.

What works

Slide 9 ("Before You Build a Forecast") and slide 17 ("Defining a Forecast Problem") put target, horizon, update frequency and decision before any model choice, and slide 17 walks the hospital case through all four. That is the order practitioners actually work in and most introductory forecasting decks get it backwards. The note on slide 17 that "many forecasting failures originate from poorly defined objectives.
Slide 23 ("Why Do We Need a Baseline?") earns its place. The exam-score analogy (82% means nothing until you know the class average) makes the point in one beat, and the note that a complex model should only be adopted if it clearly beats the simple alternatives is the right professional standard, stated plainly.
Slide 22 is headed "One Reasonable Set of Choices", not "Correct Answers", and the note reinforces that analysts compare several approaches and pick on evidence. That hedging is honest and it matches how the work is done. Keep the wording exactly as it is.
The leakage treatment is correct and lands in two places, not one. Slide 26 gives the rule (train on the past, test on the future) and slide 18's notes add the trap that actually catches people: an external variable is only usable if it will be available at prediction time. Many decks state the first and omit the second.
Speaker notes are genuinely usable by a lecturer who did not write the deck. Every content slide has substantive notes, the two quiz slides carry explicit timing cues ("give them about a minute"), and slide 22's notes explain the reasoning behind each suggested answer rather than just asserting it. This clears the teachability bar comfortably.
What must be fixed before sign-off

The title slide credits "László Fetter". The wiki records the author as BME · András Gézsi. (Slide 1 (title slide); wiki Management information section)
These decks are distributed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and get copied onward with the title slide attached. The byline is the attribution. It has to name the person the consortium records as the author, and right now the deck and the wiki name two different people. I could not find a "László Fetter" at BME in any public source; András Gézsi is verifiable as an associate professor in BME's Department of Artificial Intelligence and Systems Engineering. Whoever is right, the two records must agree before this is published.
Fix: Correct the title slide byline to match the recorded author, or, if László Fetter genuinely contributed, add him as Author Person 2 on the wiki and credit both on slide 1. Do not leave the deck and the wiki disagreeing.
The deck contains no references, no further reading and no source notes on any slide. The wiki lists "None" for references for students, optional reading, and recommended reading for teachers. (Whole deck; wiki Expected preparation section)
The guidelines require that claims, frameworks and figures be sourced or traceable. Slide 12's four-way split of trend / seasonality / cycle / irregular event, including the distinguishing point that a cycle is "longer-term fluctuations without a fixed period", is the taxonomy from Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed., OTexts, 2021), section 2.3, which defines a cycle as occurring when the data exhibit rises and falls that are not of a fixed frequency, and seasonality as always.
Fix: Add one references slide before Acknowledgements and populate the wiki reading fields. The obvious anchor is Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (FPP3) because it is free online and CC-licensed, so there is no cost or licensing friction. Add a source note on slide 12 naming it. For slide 25, cite Hyndman & Koehler (2006), International Journal of Forecasting 22(4), 679-688,.
The deck has no treatment of what goes wrong. There is no slide on failure modes, limitations or the ways a forecast can do harm, and the asymmetric cost of under- versus over-forecasting is absent from every slide and. (Missing between slides 27 and 29; plan block 50-60 minutes; wiki Learning Outcome 5)
The lesson plan explicitly promises asymmetric consequences of under- versus over-forecasting in the 50-60 minute block, and Learning Outcome 5 requires students to evaluate a setup by considering decision costs. Neither is delivered. This matters most for the running example the deck chose: under-forecasting hospital bed demand and over-forecasting it are not symmetric errors, and the whole reason a manager wants a range rather than a point is that the two sides cost different amounts. Without it, slide 27's.
Fix: Add one slide after 27. Two items carry it. First, asymmetric cost: staffing one nurse short is not the mirror image of staffing one nurse spare, so pick the quantile that reflects the cost ratio rather than forecasting the mean. Second, and this is the point most likely to be new to students: the history you train on is often not the quantity you want. Hospital bed occupancy.
The 40-50 and 50-60 minute blocks of the lesson plan are only partly delivered. Rolling-origin evaluation and backtesting appear only in a speaker note, the stress-testing content is absent entirely, quantile forecasts. (Slides 26, 27 and 30 versus wiki Instructions for teachers, blocks 40-50 and 50-60)
The plan asks for chronological split, rolling-origin evaluation and backtesting (slide 26 has the chronological split on the slide and the other two buried in the last line of the notes, where a lecturer skimming presenter view will miss them); for MAPE or sMAPE (sMAPE never appears); for checks across different periods, unusual weeks, subgroups, high-demand periods and structural breaks (no slide covers any of this); for prediction intervals, quantile forecasts and scenarios (slide 27 has intervals and scenarios.
Fix: Promote rolling-origin from the notes to the body of slide 26, with the standard diagram of the origin sliding forward. Add a short slide covering behaviour on the hard segments (flu peaks, holiday weeks, the period after a structural break) and one line on monitoring and retraining after deployment, then add "monitor after deployment" as a fifth item on slide 30 so the.
The acknowledgements slide attributes the funding to the Connecting Europe Facility. The call topic it cites, DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, belongs to the Digital Europe Programme. (Slide 32 (Acknowledgements); also the wiki Acknowledgements section)
DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU is confirmed as a Digital Europe Programme call topic, opened 21 November 2023 and administered by HaDEA, not a CEF instrument. The slide names the correct topic code and grant number (101189994) but the wrong funding programme. This is public-facing boilerplate on a CC-licensed document, so the error propagates to every copy.
Fix: Not this author's text to fix. This is consortium boilerplate and almost certainly identical across every PANORAIMA deck, so route it to the programme office rather than to BME. The wiki version has a related problem: its Acknowledgements section still reads "under Grant № ???". Both should be corrected centrally in one pass.
Also noted on the second pass

Slide 12 conflates two different things in one box. "Irregular Event: Unexpected shock, outlier, or structural changes" merges a one-off outlier, which you generally want a model to ignore, with a structural break, after which the earlier history is actively misleading and the model has to be refit on the post-break period. Wiki Learning Outcome 3 lists them separately ("irregular shocks, noise, and structural.
Prerequisites and overlap with sibling Learning Events are not assessed anywhere in the review, and the reviewer checklist covers this. The wiki says "Learning Events to be completed before: None", yet slides 20 to 22 ask students to choose between gradient boosting, random forests, neural networks and ARIMA, and slide 25 assumes MAE and RMSE are already familiar. Nothing in the deck or the plan tells a lecturer.
The same author's H-128 and H-129, both in this review batch, already carry a large part of what the review asks H-147 to add. H-129 covers leakage in depth (future/target, repeated-unit, preprocessing and selection leakage, plus temporal validation) and H-128 covers prediction intervals, calibration and, at line 409 of its extraction, "Monitor inputs, outcomes, performance and calibration after deployment". So the.
Slide 3 also drops wiki Learning Outcome 1 (forecasting as predicting future values from temporally ordered observations), not only Learning Outcome 2. The review flags the missing forecasting-targets outcome and stops there. Two of the five wiki outcomes have no counterpart in the deck's stated objectives.
Smaller fixes

Section structure, slides 11 to 18. The divider on slide 11 announces "Time Series Fundamentals", slides 12 to 14 deliver it, then slides 15 to 18 (Different Decisions Require Different Forecasts, One Dataset Multiple Forecasting Tasks, Defining a Forecast Problem, What Influences a Forecast).
Slide 20 and slide 23: the words "naive" and "seasonal naive" never appear. Slide 23 describes exactly these (last observed value, seasonal repeat) without naming them. Every textbook and every library a student will touch next (statsmodels, sktime, darts) uses those two terms. Name them on slide.
Slide 20 omits the mechanism by which machine learning models actually forecast: you construct lag features, rolling statistics and calendar features and then run a normal regressor. The plan explicitly lists regression with lag/calendar/external features as a family. Without it, slides 21 and 22.
Autocorrelation is never named. The plan asks for it explicitly at 20-30 minutes (nearby time points are often more similar than distant ones). Slide 10's notes carry the intuition but not the word. Add the term on slide 10 or 12; it is the one piece of vocabulary students will need to read.
Slide 25: add sMAPE, which the plan asks for by name, and add MASE. MASE is worth the thirty seconds because it is defined as error relative to the naive baseline, so it ties slide 25 straight back to slide 23 and makes the baseline point operational rather than rhetorical. Also worth one line:.
Slide 26 body text reads confusingly in isolation: "Hospital Example Monday to Predict Tuesday. Thursday's admissions are NOT available yet." The notes make the logic clear but the slide text jumps from Tuesday to Thursday with no bridge. If the accompanying figure carries the bridge this is fine;.
Currency gap in the model taxonomy, slide 20. For a deck dated 2026 the split is statistical versus machine learning, with nothing on pretrained time series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai, TimeGPT) that forecast zero-shot with no fitting on the target series. These are now benchmarked.
Slides 20 and 25 assume continuous, well-populated series. Much real demand data is intermittent, with long runs of zeros, which breaks MAPE outright and defeats most of what is on slide 20. One line naming the problem and Croston's method (Croston, Operational Research Quarterly 23, 1972, 289-303).
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 12 items in total. The notable results:

Slide 12's trend / seasonality / cycle taxonomy against Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed., OTexts), section 2.3 at otexts.com/fpp3/tspatterns.html. Fetched and compared. The source defines trend as a long-term increase or decrease in the data, seasonality as always of a fixed and.
Hyndman & Koehler (2006), Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. Verified: International Journal of Forecasting 22(4), 679-688, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2006.03.001. Origin of MASE, and the reference I recommend adding to slide 25. Confirmed via Monash research portal, RePEc and ScienceDirect.
Tashman (2000), Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review. Verified: International Journal of Forecasting 16(4), 437-450. Correct reference for the rolling-origin evaluation I recommend promoting onto slide 26.
The M4 competition. Verified: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos (2020), IJF 36(1), 54-74, 100,000 series and 61 methods, with the finding that hybrid and combination approaches led and that computational cost rose sharply for the top methods. Relevant to slide 20's statistical-versus-ML framing.
The M5 competition. Verified: M5 Accuracy results published in IJF in January 2022, 42,840 Walmart series; the first M competition in which all top methods were pure machine learning and beat every statistical benchmark, with the leading method 22.4% more accurate than the best statistical benchmark (exponential.
The M5 Uncertainty competition. Verified: IJF 2022, nine quantiles (0.005 to 0.995) scored with weighted scaled pinball loss, with probabilistic accuracy degrading at more granular levels. Cited in support of adding quantile forecasts to slide 27, which the plan asks for and the deck omits.
Plan against material
They agree on the first three blocks and drift apart on the last two. Blocks 0-10 and 10-20 land cleanly: the plan asks for familiar operational examples, a definition of a time series, and the specification questions (target, time unit, horizon, update frequency, aggregation, intended use), and slides 6, 7, 9, 10, 15, 16 and 17 deliver all of it, with slide 17 doing the scoping walkthrough almost line for line. Block 20-30 lands except for one item: trend, seasonality, cycles, outliers and shocks are on slide 12, calendar effects arrive later on slide 18 in a different framing, and why shuffling breaks the problem is on slide 26, but autocorrelation, which the plan names explicitly, is never stated as a concept. Block 30-40 is partial: the plan lists seven model families (naive, seasonal naive, moving average, exponential smoothing, ARIMA-like, regression with lag/calendar/external features, ML) and slide 20 shows five, dropping the two naive baselines and the lag-feature regression family; the baseline material the plan insists on is present and good, but on slide 23 rather than.

Coverage
33 slides, of which 21 are content once you strip the title, index, objectives, agenda, six section dividers, acknowledgements and disclaimer. Format guidance asks for roughly one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture, so the raw count sits at the low end. In practice it will run closer to 50 minutes than 60: the speaker notes are dense, roughly two minutes of material per content slide if delivered properly, and the three activities (slides 13/14, 21/22, 31) will absorb three to four minutes each, giving about 42 minutes of exposition plus 10 of activity. A lecturer who moves briskly will finish early with nothing queued. That is convenient rather than a problem, because the material the plan promises and the deck omits is roughly the size of the gap: promoting.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What must be fixed before sign-off' need addressing, after which we will re-review. Everything else here is offered as improvement, not as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026
