entries.title: H-191 Operating AI in Production: Monitoring, SLAs, Retraining and Governance Gates
entries.author: HAW · Ahmad Khalidi
entries.review_note: H-191's plan covers the MLOps principles, components, stages and roles from one 2023 paper, but none of its outcomes or blocks deal with SLAs, drift, retraining or governance gates, although HC-195 (Ready for pilot) relies on H-191 for that depth. The outcomes can't be assessed, the instructions are one line per block, the legal side is missing, HC-205 is missing as a prerequisite and most wiki fields are blank.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): lesson plan in development, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review: we read the H-191 wiki page as pulled on 17 September 2026 (content from revision 5862 of 18 May 2026), the SharePoint lesson plan "H-191 Operating AI in Production Monitoring SLAs Retraining and Governance Gates.docx" (HAW Horizontal Lesson Plans, 28 April 2026) and the material folder 4.1 Horizontal/H-191, which is empty. Submitted as it stands this would be a major revision, because the plan teaches the MLOps overview of Kreuzberger et al. (2023) and has no outcome or teaching block for the SLAs, drift, retraining and governance gates in its title; before a formal review the outcomes and timed instructions need rebuilding, every PanoLessonPlan field needs filling, and the status needs to move to "Lesson plan: review".

What works

The source is a sound choice and the plan reports it accurately. Kreuzberger, Kühl and Hirschl (IEEE Access 11, 2023) is peer reviewed and openly readable, and the lists in your four outcomes match the paper: nine principles (P1-P9), nine components (C1-C9), four architecture stages (A-D) and seven roles (R1-R7). Citation and DOI are correct.
The paper already contains parts of the rebuild. The plan names the Model Registry (C6), the Monitoring Component (C9) and the Feedback loops principle (P9), and the paper covers champion/challenger testing (p. 31875) and three retraining triggers: a statistical threshold, new feature data, or a schedule (p. 31876). Build the monitoring, retraining and gate blocks from these.
Every block has a duration, the durations add up to the 60 minutes, and block 5 already tries to get students talking.
Must fix

The plan does not teach its title. SLAs, drift, retraining and governance gates have no learning outcome and no teaching block. (Title, Keywords, Learning Outcomes, Instructions for teachers)
The title, set when the page was created on 24 April 2026, is "Operating AI in Production: Monitoring, SLAs, Retraining and Governance Gates", and the keywords repeat it. The outcomes and instructions never use "SLA", "drift", "gate", "governance" or "retraining"; the closest they get is the principle name "Continuous ML training & evaluation". Monitoring is one of nine principles and one of nine components. The five blocks follow sections IV.A, IV.B, IV.C and V of Kreuzberger et al., and in the paper serving, monitoring, the feedback loop and drift-triggered retraining are steps 25 to 28 of stage D, about a page (pp. 31875-31876).
HC-195 Model Risk Management & The AI Life Cycle (HU, Ready for pilot) depends on this event. Its lesson plan docx lists H-191 as a strong prerequisite, its slide 26 lists it as a hard prerequisite, and the plan says: "MLOps, model drift, retraining pipelines are treated in greater depth in Operating AI in Production, keep the treatment here at the conceptual/governance level." A student who comes from H-191 as currently planned gets none of that depth.
The pipeline overview also repeats earlier events: HC-020 Designing a machine learning system, where you are second author, covers deployment and "concept drift, performance degradation, retraining, feedback loops, and human oversight" (minutes 40-60), and H-132 covers "performance drift, data drift, feedback loops, retraining, incident handling, version control" (minutes 100-112).
Fix: rebuild the outcomes and blocks around the title and keep Kreuzberger et al. as a short reference architecture at the start (about 5 minutes). A worked proposal is under Suggested outcomes and timing below. Retitling would leave HC-195 without the prerequisite it was built on, so we do not recommend it.
The learning outcomes cannot be assessed. (Learning Outcomes, all four)
They read "Students learn about the nine principles", "Students learn what technical components", "Students get a general understanding of how a MLOps end-to-end architecture can look like" and "Students understand the necessary roles". None says what a student can do at the end or at what level. Several sibling plans, for example HC-020 and H-132, give the verb and level: HC-020 has "Explain (knowledge, intermediate level) the main components of a learning system". As written the outcomes ask for recall of 29 named items (9 + 9 + 4 + 7), which is below master level. Most students in a Horizontal event will not build pipelines; they will sign off monitoring plans, agree SLAs and decide whether a retrained model goes live. Write the outcomes for those decisions.
Fix: 4 or 5 outcomes, each with an observable verb, the knowledge/skill/competence tag and level, and each mapped to a timed block. See the proposal below.
A different teacher could not run this session from the instructions. (Instructions for teachers)
Each block is one line starting "Introduction to" or "Introduce". There are no talking points, no example or case, no pointer to which figure or table of the paper to show, no questions to ask, no wrap-up and no buffer. 29 named items in the 55 minutes after the intro leaves under two minutes per item, too little time to explain any of them. HC-020 names the concepts for every block and ends with a takeaway; H-132 adds a running case and a group activity in each block.
Fix: for each block write the purpose, the concepts in teaching order, what the teacher shows, any student task with its timing and model answer, and the one sentence students should take away. Use one running case for the whole hour so monitoring, retraining and gates are applied to the same system.
Interactivity is one optional activity, and it does not ask students to judge anything. (Instructions, block 5: "This part can be used as a short interactive format, where the students reflect on in which role they see themselves in MLOps")
The programme's format checklist for lecture slides asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements, and the reviewer checklist asks whether the material builds professional judgement rather than only definitions. Here there is one element, marked optional, sharing its 10 minutes with teaching seven roles, and placing yourself in a role involves no judgement. The roles content also overlaps with H-194 Organizing for AI: Roles, RACI, and Board Oversight (planned, no author yet); we only flag that.
Fix: replace it with 2 or 3 short decision tasks, each with an answer note for the teacher. The proposal below has three.
The governance and legal side of the title is missing. (Title "Governance Gates"; Learning Outcomes; Instructions)
The programme guidelines ask materials to cover legal as well as scientific and technical dimensions. For high-risk systems the EU AI Act sets obligations that bear directly on monitoring, logging and changes to a deployed system:
Art. 12: high-risk systems must technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over their lifetime, including events relevant to post-market monitoring and to monitoring by deployers.
Art. 19(1) and Art. 26(6): providers and deployers keep those logs, to the extent the logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months, unless other Union or national law provides otherwise. Deployers of a provider-hosted model often do not hold the logs.
Art. 26(5): deployers monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use; where they have reason to consider the system presents a risk, they inform the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority and suspend use.
Art. 72, with Art. 17(1)(h): providers run a documented post-market monitoring system based on a post-market monitoring plan, which is part of the technical documentation and of the quality management system.
Art. 73: providers report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority, at the latest 15 days after becoming aware of them, with shorter limits for the most severe cases.
Art. 3(23) and Art. 43(4): a substantial modification (a change not foreseen in the initial conformity assessment that affects compliance or the intended purpose) needs a new conformity assessment. For systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market, changes pre-determined by the provider at the initial assessment and recorded in the technical documentation are not a substantial modification. A promotion gate should check whether a retrained model stays inside what was foreseen. Whether a scheduled offline retrain counts as "continuing to learn" is not settled, so present it as an open question.
Art. 15(4): high-risk systems that continue to learn must reduce the risk of biased outputs influencing future inputs (feedback loops).
Dates: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I products. Legal summaries report that it also changed Art. 72(3), so the post-market monitoring plan template now comes in Commission guidance rather than an implementing act; we have not read the amending provision. Check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex before putting any date or article wording on a slide.
Fix: one block of about 10 minutes on gates: what an automated promotion gate checks and logs, and which of the articles above apply when the system is high-risk. Leave what "high-risk" means and the legal detail to HC-205 EU AI Act Basics (its slides 17 and 18 already list Arts. 12, 26, 72 and 73) and HC-215 The Risk-Based Approach and Post-Market Monitoring, and organisational stage-gates to HC-195.
Most PanoLessonPlan fields are empty or thin. (see Wiki page completeness below)
Six fields are blank and two hold the same single citation. Some blanks are template defaults, but only you can fill them for this event.
Fix: fill every field as listed under Wiki page completeness, including a full step-by-step teacher script.
Should fix

The reading list is one paper whose evidence dates from 2021, and it does not cover the title. (References and background for students; Recommended for teachers, both identical)
Kreuzberger et al. rests on a review of 27 articles, a tool review and eight expert interviews held June to August 2021 (section III). It has nothing on service levels, governance gates, regulation or LLM-based systems, and the teacher entry adds nothing to the student entry.
Cite the IEEE Access version with page numbers. The free arXiv preprint (2205.02302) that teachers are likely to find first differs: it says "MLOps project initiation" instead of "product initiation" and has neither the concept drift sentence nor the champion/challenger passage discussed here.
Fix: see the reading lists under Wiki page completeness.
The paper's concept drift wording is loose, and its sensor example is a data quality failure. (Kreuzberger et al., section V, stage D, p. 31875)
The paper says concept drifts occur "when the input data changes over time e.g., when a sensor breaks". Gama et al. (ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), 2014) define concept drift as any change in the joint distribution p(X,y) and separate real concept drift, where p(y|X) changes, from virtual drift, where only p(X) changes. Much of current practice, and HC-195 slides 9 and 10, uses the narrower terms: data or covariate drift for a change in p(X), concept drift for a change in p(y|X) (Moreno-Torres et al., Pattern Recognition 45(1), 2012). A broken sensor is best taught as neither: it is a data quality failure that validation checks should catch before any drift statistic does. The three cases need different responses: a pipeline fix, an investigation (input drift may or may not hurt performance), new labels.
Fix: add a teacher note, teach the three cases separately with one example each, and use the same terms as HC-195 so students do not meet two vocabularies in consecutive events.
"Feedback loop" means two different things in the sources this event will use. (Learning Outcomes, principle "Feedback loops")
In Kreuzberger et al. (P9) a feedback loop is an engineering flow: monitoring results go back to experimentation, data engineering and the retraining scheduler. In AI Act Art. 15(4) it is a risk: biased outputs shaping future inputs, for example a fraud model whose flags decide which cases get investigated and so which labels exist at all.
Fix: name both meanings and use the second as the human-centred example in the retraining block.
Prerequisites and forward links need work. (Learning Events to be completed before; Instructions)
The field gives only the title "Introduction to Machine Learning: types and tasks". HC-019 does not teach evaluation metrics, and students cannot set a model-quality objective or a promotion threshold without them; H-122 Model Training, Evaluation and Generalization covers precision, recall and the confusion matrix (minutes 105-115). HC-020 covers the pipeline this lecture builds on. Nothing on the declared path teaches what "high-risk" means under the AI Act; HC-205 does, and HC-195 lists it as a prerequisite as well.
Fix: list HC-019, HC-020, H-122 and HC-205 by code. The wiki has no successor field, so name the follow-on events in the instructions: HC-195 (organisational stage-gates, model inventory, kill switch), HC-215 (post-market monitoring law), H-197 Incident Response and Supply Chain Integrity and H-227 Access Control, Logging, and Emergency Access. H-197 has no author yet, so point to it as a planned event.
Agree the split with the neighbouring authors. With Marieke Peeters (HU) on HC-195: its slide 21 already uses alert tiers with "Human review within defined SLA", slide 22 lists scheduled, performance-based and event-based retraining triggers, and plan section 4 covers the risks of retraining such as regression on subgroups. Decide which event defines SLAs, thresholds and triggers and which one applies them. With Edit Tomasovszky (BME) and Michael Gille (HAW) on HC-205 and HC-215, so the gates block points to their legal content instead of repeating it.
Current practice the title implies is not in the plan. (Whole plan)
For students: SLI, SLO and SLA as separate things (Google SRE book, ch. 4, which separates an SLA from an SLO by whether missing it has explicit consequences). In practice external SLAs usually cover availability and latency, while model quality is an internal SLO, because labels arrive late and the incoming data is outside the provider's control.
For students: label delay and proxy metrics; performance per subgroup; shadow deployment, canary, champion/challenger and rollback through the model registry.
For students: LLM-based systems in production. Most outputs have no ground-truth label, so evaluation sets and human review become the monitoring signal; model and prompt versions need pinning; hosted models change on the provider's schedule; cost per request becomes an objective. One element in the monitoring or release block is enough.
For the lecturer notes, not the student outcomes: error budgets (SRE book, ch. 3); drift statistics (PSI, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Jensen-Shannon or Wasserstein distance) and their false alarms; label-free performance estimation and why it fails under concept drift; training-serving skew; and, if you show MLflow, that its fixed Staging/Production stages were deprecated in version 2.9 in favour of aliases and tags, so older tutorials show a deprecated workflow.
Fix: choose what fits 60 minutes, but the SLO/SLA distinction, label delay and release strategies belong in any lecture with this title.
The human-centred angle is missing. (Whole plan)
Nothing in the plan covers the people affected when a model degrades for one group while the overall metric holds, or when a retrained model regresses on a subgroup that was fine before.
Fix: make per-subgroup monitoring, override and complaint rates from human reviewers, and a human sign-off step for high-risk promotions explicit parts of the monitoring and gate blocks.
The main source is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. (for the material stage)
Kreuzberger et al. carries a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence line on p. 31866. You can show its figures unmodified with attribution in non-commercial teaching material, but a redrawn or adapted Figure 4 is a derivative the licence does not permit, and the figure cannot be relabelled CC BY-NC-SA with the rest of the deck.
Fix: use Figure 4 unmodified with its own licence line on the slide, or draw your own simplified architecture that is not a copy of Figure 4 and cite the paper for the concepts.
Build the material to the format checklist from the start. (Lesson materials; SharePoint folder 4.1 Horizontal/H-191, empty)
Fix: RAISE-U template, PowerPoint with lecturer notes on every slide, the plan's block timings shown in the notes, a task sheet with model answers, a references slide, and the licence of each third-party figure on its slide.
Smaller things

Instructions, block 5: "nessecary" should be "necessary". The same typo is in the SharePoint docx.
Learning Outcomes: outcomes 2 and 3 are separated by a blank line, not "$". Use "$" between every outcome and check the rendered page shows each outcome as its own item.
Wiki page completeness

Self-standing (empty; also blank on other pages, so partly a template default): state "No" and give the prerequisite codes.
Learning Outcomes (not assessable): 4 or 5 outcomes with verb, knowledge/skill/competence tag and level, as proposed below.
Learning Events to be completed before (title only): HC-019, HC-020, H-122 and HC-205, by code.
Keywords (thin): fix the capitals in "model Monitoring" and add SLO, SLI, data drift, concept drift, model registry, champion/challenger, post-market monitoring, EU AI Act.
Obligatory for students (empty): about 45 minutes of reading. For example: Beyer, B., Jones, C., Petoff, J. and Murphy, N. R. (eds.), Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly, 2016, ch. 4 "Service Level Objectives" (free at sre.google), and Kreuzberger et al. (2023) sections IV.A and V. Blank Expected preparation is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally; please still fill it for this event.
Optional for students (empty): Huyen, C., Designing Machine Learning Systems, O'Reilly, 2022, ch. 8 "Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring" and ch. 9 "Continual Learning and Test in Production" (not open access, so say how students get it, for example through the library); Shankar, S., Garcia, R., Hellerstein, J. M. and Parameswaran, A. G., "Operationalizing Machine Learning: An Interview Study", arXiv:2209.09125, 2022.
References and background for students (one item): keep Kreuzberger et al. (IEEE Access version) and add Gama, J., Žliobaitė, I., Bifet, A., Pechenizkiy, M. and Bouchachia, A., "A survey on concept drift adaptation", ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), article 44, 2014, doi:10.1145/2523813; Breck, E., Cai, S., Nielsen, E., Salib, M. and Sculley, D., "The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction", IEEE Big Data 2017, pp. 1123-1132, doi:10.1109/BigData.2017.8258038.
Recommended for teachers (copy of the student entry): Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Arts. 3(23), 12, 15(4), 17(1)(h), 19, 26(5)-(6), 43(4), 72 and 73, from the consolidated text on EUR-Lex; SRE book ch. 3 and 4; Moreno-Torres, J. G., Raeder, T., Alaiz-Rodríguez, R., Chawla, N. V. and Herrera, F., "A unifying view on dataset shift in classification", Pattern Recognition 45(1), pp. 521-530, 2012, doi:10.1016/j.patcog.2011.06.019; the HC-195 lesson plan and deck and the HC-205 deck, to agree the split.
Acknowledgements (empty): the funding line the template adds credits the Connecting Europe Facility instead of the Digital Europe Programme and leaves the grant number as "???". That is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally, not your error. Add your own acknowledgements and the credit and licence for any Kreuzberger et al. figure you use.
Original contributions (empty): say which parts are adapted from Kreuzberger et al. or other sources and which are original.
Lesson materials (empty): list and link each SharePoint file once it exists, with any third-party licence noted per file. The stub in this section is a known template issue RealAI has raised centrally; the file list is still yours to fill.
Instructions for teachers (thin): a full timed script a teacher who did not write it can run, as set out under Must fix.
Author Organisation 2 and Author Person 2 (empty): assigning a second author is WP4's call, not yours, but nobody currently does the didactic and format check for H-191. Please ask WP4 to assign one before the plan moves to review.
Suggested outcomes and timing (adapt freely)

Outcome 1. Explain (knowledge, intermediate level) what changes when a model moves from experiment to production, using the MLOps components of Kreuzberger et al. (2023) as a reference architecture.
Outcome 2. Distinguish (cognitive skill, intermediate level) SLIs, SLOs and SLAs for an ML service, and write one service objective and one model-quality objective for a given case, including how delayed labels affect the second.
Outcome 3. Design (cognitive skill, intermediate level) a monitoring plan for a deployed model that states the signals watched (service health, data quality, input drift, performance once labels arrive, performance per subgroup), the alert threshold and who responds.
Outcome 4. Compare (cognitive skill, intermediate level) retraining triggers (scheduled, threshold-based, event-based) and release strategies (shadow, canary, champion/challenger, rollback through the model registry), and justify a choice for a given case.
Outcome 5. Evaluate (competence, intermediate level) whether a retrained model should replace the production model, stating what the promotion gate checks and logs and where EU AI Act rules for high-risk systems change that gate.
0-5 min. Opening case: a credit model whose service dashboards stay green while its decisions get worse after the applicant population shifts. Ask the room what would have told them, and when.
5-10 min (outcome 1). Reference architecture: Kreuzberger et al. Figure 4, unmodified with its licence line. Walk only the model registry, the metadata store, the monitoring component and the feedback loop. Link back to HC-020; roles in one sentence, pointing to H-194.
10-20 min (outcome 2). Service levels: SLI, SLO, SLA; service objectives (p95 latency, availability, error rate) against model-quality objectives measured once labels arrive. Task 1, pairs, 4 min: write one of each for the opening case. Answer note: a service objective such as "p95 latency under 300 ms over 30 days" can go into an SLA; a quality objective such as "recall on defaults of at least 0.80, measured each quarter on loans whose outcome is known" stays internal, because it lags by months and depends on data the provider does not control.
20-33 min (outcome 3). Monitoring and drift: data quality failure, data drift and concept drift with one example each; label delay; per-subgroup monitoring. Name the drift statistics and keep their details in the lecturer notes. Task 2, groups, 5 min: triage three alerts (a PSI jump on one input feature, a p95 latency SLO breach, a 3-point recall drop for one age band once labels arrive) and say who acts and what they check first. Answer note: the latency breach goes to on-call now; the subgroup recall drop carries the most harm and goes to the model owner, with rollback as an option; the PSI jump alone needs investigation before any action, because input drift does not always mean worse performance.
33-42 min (outcome 4). Retraining and release: the three trigger types (HC-195 slide 22 names them too, so keep this short), what the retraining pipeline runs, shadow, canary, champion/challenger, rollback. Risks: regression on subgroups, retraining on bad data, feedback loops in the Art. 15(4) sense.
42-52 min (outcome 5). Governance gates: automated checks before promotion (data validation, evaluation against the current champion on a fixed holdout and per subgroup, sign-off step for high-risk use), what is logged, and which AI Act articles apply. Task 3, pairs, 4 min: "The retrained challenger beats the champion overall but has 4 percentage points lower recall on one subgroup. Do you promote it, and what do you log?" Answer note: not automatically. The gate should block or escalate to a named owner, who checks whether the gap is outside the documented tolerance and whether the change stays within what was pre-determined; log both evaluations, the decision, who took it and why.
52-56 min. Debrief Task 3, recap, and point forward to HC-195, HC-215 and H-197.
56-60 min. Buffer and student questions.
If this does not fit in 60 minutes, move legal detail to HC-205 and HC-215 rather than rushing the operations blocks, or split the event in two.

Plan against SharePoint and material

Wiki against SharePoint docx: outcomes, instructions and literature are identical. The docx gives the prerequisite code (HC-019), the author email and "Type: Lecture"; the wiki adds job role and reviewer; the blank line between outcomes 2 and 3 is only on the wiki. entries.title: HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02
entries.author: HAW · Ahmad Khalidi
entries.review_note: HC-017 needs a major revision before formal review: its outcomes and 58-word teacher instructions can be neither assessed nor taught from, and its chain-of-thought block rests on a trust claim and an uncontrolled experiment that current evidence does not support.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): lesson plan in development, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We read the HC-017 wiki page as it stood on 17 September 2026 (revision 8474 of 4 September, which only added the reviewer; the content is from your edits of 18 May 2026) and the SharePoint lesson plan "HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02.docx" (28 April 2026); the HC-017 material folder is empty and this Talk page had no earlier comments. This is early feedback on a plan in development, not a formal review: on the current text the plan needs a major revision, and the Must fix items below should be done before the status moves to "Lesson plan: review".

When you asked us to review HC-016, you asked whether its design carries to HC-017, so our 11 September review on the HC-016 Talk page already covered the session shape, the outcome wording, the missing documentation and ethics clauses, the reasoning-model problem, the "it’s" typo and the funding line. Nothing on this page has changed since, which is fine: you said you are busy until the end of September. We repeat those points here so they sit on the right page, with two changes: the outcomes suggested below replace the two we gave on HC-016, and we no longer predict the thinking off/on result, because your pilot should settle it.

What works

Putting chain-of-thought straight after HC-016 works. HC-016 Introduction slides 13 and 14 already have students open a model's thinking trace, and slide 15 lists "LLMs can “think” before giving an answer" among its key takeaways. HC-017 can start from something students have seen instead of from a definition.
The time split suits a Practice event. 40 of the 60 minutes are student experiments, and each experiment block is followed by a discussion slot, which keeps HC-016's experiment-then-reflect pattern.
Block 4's idea, using an LLM to critique and rewrite a prompt, has a worked example in your own reading. The OpenAI cookbook notebook rewrites a summarisation prompt and scores the original and the rewritten prompt with a GPT-4o grader over 100 news articles. The 20-minute slot is long enough for two scored cycles once the block has inputs and criteria (see Must fix).
All three backgrStPrep links resolved on 17 September 2026 and are on topic.
Must fix

The learning outcomes describe what happens in the room and cannot be assessed. (learningOutcomes, both entries)
Entry 1: "The students experiment with chain-of-thought- and meta-prompting, so they learn how more structured and well-defined expectations of the LLM’s output can improve the LLM’s performance and improves it’s trustworthiness." Entry 2: "The students use intelligent ChatBots, like ChatGPT, Gemini, ... to refine the designed prompts. This way the students learn to design and refine their prompts in cycles with the help of LLMs." "Experiment with" and "use" name activities, and "so they learn" and "This way the students learn" cannot be marked. Neither entry has a level tag, while every outcome on HC-016 has one ("on a beginner level", "on an intermediate level"). Entry 1 also puts both techniques in one clause that fits neither: "more structured and well-defined expectations of the LLM’s output" describes output specification, which is HC-016's Output Indicator, while chain-of-thought asks the model for intermediate reasoning steps. Neither entry has the documentation or ethics clause that HC-016's outcomes carry.
Fix: one capability per outcome, verb plus object plus level, no trailing "so they learn". For example: (a) "The student applies chain-of-thought prompting to a fixed set of multi-step tasks, with the model's built-in thinking switched off and on, and records the effect on correctness and token use in the Prompt Log, on an intermediate level." (b) "The student uses an LLM to rewrite a prompt and compares the original and the rewritten prompt on the same inputs against stated criteria, on an intermediate level." (c) "The student checks whether an LLM-rewritten prompt still asks for what they intended, and explains why a visible reasoning chain is not a reliable account of how a model reached its answer, on a beginner level."
The plan tells the teacher to present chain-of-thought and meta-prompting as making the LLM more trustworthy. For chain-of-thought, research shows the reasoning text can misstate why the model answered; for meta-prompting, the plan gives no evidence. (learningOutcomes entry 1, "improves it’s trustworthiness"; instructions block 1, "how they can be used to increase the LLM’s performance and trustworthiness")
Turpin, Michael, Perez and Bowman (NeurIPS 2023) found that chain-of-thought explanations "can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction". When they reordered the options in few-shot examples so the right answer was always "(A)", models followed that pattern and their explanations did not mention it. Chen et al. (Anthropic, 2025) planted hints in prompts to reasoning models and found that the reasoning often mentioned the hint in fewer than 20% of the cases where the model used it. They still find reading the reasoning useful for noticing unwanted behaviour, but not sufficient to rule it out. None of the three readings supports a trust gain from meta-prompting. HC-016 Introduction slide 14 ("The thinking process reveals valuable information about the reasoning steps of the model") and the third takeaway on slide 15 ("There are instructions hidden in the thinking process of the model that lead the model to produce favourable results.") already make the same assumption, and HC-017 as written would repeat it.
Fix: take "trustworthiness" out of outcome 1 and block 1. Teach that a reasoning chain makes an answer easier to check, and that a fluent chain can come with a wrong answer or leave out what drove it. Add a short check inside the chain-of-thought block: on one task, students add a leading hint ("A professor says the answer is 12") and note whether the answer moves and whether the reasoning mentions the hint. Pilot this as well. Chen et al. measured large reasoning models, and a small local model may state the hint openly; if it does, write that into the teacher notes and show the Turpin et al. "(A)" example on a slide instead. Add both papers to recommTePrep. When you revise HC-016, qualify slides 14 and 15 the same way.
The chain-of-thought experiment names no model and no thinking setting, and every likely set-up already has a thinking mode, so results will differ across the room with nothing to explain them. (instructions block 2, "Students experiment with meta-prompts and chain-of-thoughts."; learningOutcomes entry 2, "intelligent ChatBots, like ChatGPT, Gemini, ...")
OpenAI's reasoning best practices say "Avoid chain-of-thought prompts" for its reasoning models, since they reason internally. Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (Wharton, June 2025) ran eight models on GPQA Diamond and found that asking for step-by-step reasoning gave non-reasoning models a small average gain with more variable answers, and gave reasoning models little gain for more tokens and time. Every likely set-up has a thinking setting. gemma-4-e4b from HC-016 has a thinking mode that Google's Gemma 4 documentation switches on with the <|think|> token in the system instruction. Since 14 September 2026 ChatGPT Plus and Pro no longer move from Instant to Thinking on their own, and other plans behave differently. The Gemini app has Fast, Thinking and Pro, with a Standard or Extended thinking level on Fast and Pro. Students on different set-ups will get different results and the 5-minute reflection will have no shared result to discuss. One run per condition at default temperature also cannot separate the prompt's effect from chance; your HC-016 worked log shows the remedy, with three runs at temperature 0 all returning 73.
This corrects our HC-016 review, which said gemma-4-e4b's thinking is on by default. Google's documentation describes it as something you switch on, and whether it is on in LM Studio depends on the build and the system prompt. Check it in the pilot.
Fix: run it on one model at temperature 0 as a 2 by 2: thinking off or on, plain prompt or "Let's think step by step". Use 4 to 6 short tasks with one checkable answer each, taken from work students will recognise, such as an invoice total with VAT and a discount or whether an applicant meets a three-rule policy. To fit 20 minutes, half the pairs run with thinking off and half with thinking on, each pair runs both prompt versions, and the room pools right-or-wrong counts and token counts on one shared sheet. Pilot and time the task set on the class model before building slides, and write your counts into the teacher notes; if a pair cannot finish in 15 minutes, cut tasks and keep the reflection slot. Do not assume the result for a small model: Wei et al. (2022) saw chain-of-thought gains only at about 100B parameters, with smaller models writing fluent but illogical chains, and current small models are trained differently. The reflection question then becomes a practice question: when is the gain worth the extra tokens and waiting time?
"Meta-prompting" is never defined, the two readings on it describe different techniques, and under the OpenAI definition block 4 teaches it a second time. (instructions blocks 1, 2 and 4; backgrStPrep links 1 and 3)
The OpenAI cookbook: "Meta-prompting is a technique where you use an LLM to generate or improve prompts." The DAIR.AI Prompt Engineering Guide page says meta prompting "focuses on the structural and syntactical aspects of tasks and problems rather than their specific content details", uses abstracted examples as templates, and says nothing about using an LLM to rewrite prompts. The paper it cites, Zhang, Yuan and Yao (arXiv:2311.11482), centres on task structure, although its Recursive Meta Prompting extension does have a model propose prompt edits. A third usage, Suzgun and Kalai (arXiv:2401.12954), has one model conduct expert instances of itself, which is close to HC-018's prompt chaining and agentic workflows block. Under OpenAI's definition, block 4 ("Students experiment refining their prompts using intelligent ChatBots.") is meta-prompting, so the session covers it in block 2 and again in block 4 under another name.
Fix: pick one definition and write it into the plan. We suggest OpenAI's, because it matches block 4 and your own cookbook reading. Then make block 2 chain-of-thought only and block 4 meta-prompting with an evaluation step. Mention the structure-template sense in one sentence or drop the DAIR.AI meta prompting reading. Leave the conductor pattern to HC-018 and say so in both plans.
Block 4 has no way to tell whether a rewritten prompt is better. (instructions block 4)
"(20 minutes) Students experiment refining their prompts using intelligent ChatBots." There is no starting prompt, no test inputs, no criteria and no stop condition. A chatbot's rewrite is usually longer and more formal, so students will judge it by how it looks. Your cookbook reading scores both versions on the same sample, and HC-016's worked Prompt Log holds the question fixed while one thing changes.
Fix: give students one prompt from work (for example, summarise a customer complaint for a case handler), 3 to 5 fixed inputs and a 3-item checklist. They score the original, ask the LLM to improve it, score the rewrite on the same inputs, and do one more cycle. Each cycle also logs one yes or no: does the rewrite still ask for what I meant? That is the human-centred question for this block: whose intent is in the final prompt, and would you notice if the chatbot changed it?
The teacher instructions are five one-line blocks. A teacher who did not write the plan cannot run the session from them. (instructions)
58 words for 60 minutes. HC-016's instructions run to 236 words, not counting links, and link every file. HC-017 names no task, model, prompt, file, discussion question or expected result, and both reflection blocks read "Students discuss and reflect on experiences made." Nothing says how the session ends: what students hand in or keep, and how a teacher can see whether the outcomes were met.
Fix: for each block give the minute range, what the teacher shows and on which slide, what students do with which input, what they log, two or three discussion questions with the answers to expect, and a fallback if the tool fails. Close with what students hand in, for example the HC-017 Prompt Log, and whether it is collected. Example for the first reflection: "(30-35 min) Two or three pairs read out their pooled counts. Ask: where did 'Let's think step by step' change the answer, and where did it only make it longer? Did the reasoning mention the planted hint when the answer moved? Would you pay the extra tokens for this gain in a production system? Expected, from the pilot: [your numbers]." Keep the 10-minute introduction to the definitions, the thinking switch and the task briefing, and leave the faithfulness discussion to this reflection slot, where students have their own hint result.
The plan is written as one 60-minute session that depends on HC-016, but the page does not say so. (instructions; self-standing; obligStPrep; expectedLEs)
The blocks add up to 10 + 20 + 5 + 20 + 5 with no homework and no setup time, while HC-016 runs over two sittings with student work in between. The experiments need the model students installed in HC-016, yet self-standing and obligStPrep are empty and expectedLEs names the preceding event without its code. On the HC-016 Talk page we asked you to decide between single-session and flipped for HC-017 and HC-018.
Fix: confirm the shape and state it in the first line of the instructions. If it stays single-session, set self-standing to "No", obligStPrep to the text under Wiki page completeness, and expectedLEs to "HC-016 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 01".
Seven PanoLessonPlan fields are empty, and on the rendered page the empty preparation fields tell students "None." (self-standing, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx, origContrib, lessonMaterials)
An empty preparation field is displayed as "None.", which is why HC-016's page, with the same empty obligStPrep, reads "Obligatory for students: None." For HC-017 that tells students they need nothing before a class that runs on a model installed in the previous event.
Fix: fill each field as listed under Wiki page completeness. lessonMaterials can wait until the material exists; the others can be filled now.
Should fix

The plan sends students to consumer chatbots with no guidance on accounts or data. (learningOutcomes entry 2; obligStPrep empty)
On consumer ChatGPT plans, conversations are used for model training by default unless "Improve the model for everyone" is switched off (OpenAI Help Center); ChatGPT Edu, Business and Enterprise do not train on inputs by default. Students will paste prompts that may contain their own or other people's text. A consumer chatbot also shows no token counts and has no temperature control, so outcome (a) and the 2 by 2 only run as planned on the local model.
Fix: default both blocks to the local model students installed in HC-016. If your pilot shows it is too weak as a prompt rewriter, name an institution-licensed chatbot for block 4 only and say which Prompt Log columns stay blank there. Add a teacher note: no personal data or third-party text in prompts, and if consumer accounts are used, show students the training setting first.
The readings are secondary web pages with unclear labels and no primary sources. (backgrStPrep)
"Prompt-Engineering on Chain-of-Thoughts" and "Prompt Engineering on Meta-Prompting" are pages of the DAIR.AI Prompt Engineering Guide, and the labels do not say so. The chain-of-thought page cites only 2022 work (Wei et al., Kojima et al., Auto-CoT) and says nothing about reasoning models or faithfulness. At master level students should be able to reach the papers the claims rest on.
Fix: relabel the links and add the two primary papers, as listed under Wiki page completeness.
HC-017 needs its own version of the Prompt Log, with an answer key. (no material yet; HC-016's Prompt Log.xlsx has the columns Task, Instruction, Context, Input Data, Output Indicator, LLM Thoughts, LLM Response, Comments)
None of those columns records the technique, the thinking setting, the temperature, whether the answer was right, or who changed the prompt. Without them the 2 by 2 and the refinement cycles cannot be read back in the reflection slots. HC-016 shipped a worked example log next to the blank template, and HC-017 needs the same.
Fix: for block 2 add Technique, Thinking (on/off), Temperature, Correct (against the answer key) and Tokens; for block 4 add Prompt version, Changed by (student or LLM) and Still my intent (yes/no). Ship the task set with its answer key and a worked example log.
Chain-of-thought is already taught in HC-164 and HC-166, and three SU prompt engineering events may overlap once they have content. (HC-164 Intro to agentic AI.pdf page 15; HC-166 Intro to agentic AI.pdf pages 15, 22 and 45; Horizontal master list)
HC-164 page 15: "Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) dramatically improves performance on complex multi-step reasoning, enabling agents to decompose complex goals." HC-166 lists chain-of-thought as a reasoning mechanism (page 15) and a planning strategy (pages 22 and 45). Both are SU events by Ioannis Patias and are "Ready for pilot". HC-164 makes the unqualified performance claim this review questions for HC-017, so the two events could teach students opposite things. H-096 "Creating Effective Prompts", H-098a/b "Quality, Reasoning, and Contextual Understanding" and H-102a/b "Advanced Prompt Engineering Systems and Applications" are on the list with no status, no named authors and empty material folders, so we could not compare them.
Fix: add one sentence to the HC-017 instructions on how it relates to HC-164 and HC-166 (HC-017 tests the technique hands-on; HC-164 presents it as an agent planning method), and tell Ioannis Patias what HC-017 will say about faithfulness. We flag the SU events for the programme-level distinctiveness check.
The SharePoint docx and the wiki have drifted. (HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02.docx against the wiki page)
The docx (28 April) lists "HC-016 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 01" as preceding LE and names only you as author. The wiki (edited 13 to 18 May) drops the HC-016 code from expectedLEs and lists Stefano Marrone (UNINA) as second author, added on 13 May. The three literature links point to the same URLs in both, and the outcomes and instructions are word for word the same.
Fix: treat the wiki as the master. When you rewrite the plan, update the docx or mark it superseded, so two versions of HC-017 are not in circulation.
The second author has not commented yet. (Talk page)
Stefano Marrone (UNINA) is second author. The guidelines give the second author the didactic check and the format scan, which is where timing and teachability gaps like the ones above should be caught.
Fix: ask Stefano to read the rewritten plan before the status moves to "Lesson plan: review".
Smaller things

Language in learningOutcomes and instructions: "can improve the LLM’s performance and improves it’s trustworthiness" should read "can improve ... and improve its"; "chain-of-thought- and meta-prompting" should be "chain-of-thought and meta-prompting"; "chain-of-thoughts" in instructions blocks 1 and 2 and in the second reading label should be "chain-of-thought"; "intelligent ChatBots, like ChatGPT, Gemini, ..." should be "LLM chatbots such as ChatGPT or Gemini"; "reflect on experiences made" should be "reflect on their results".
The title "Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02" does not say what the event covers. A subtitle such as "Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02: Chain-of-Thought and Meta-Prompting" keeps the series numbering and makes the event findable among 144 Horizontal events.
The OpenAI cookbook notebook improves the prompt with o1-preview, which OpenAI removed from the API on 28 July 2025. Add a note next to the link that students running it need to swap in a current reasoning model.
Known template issues RealAI has raised centrally: the acknowledgement credits the Connecting Europe Facility with "Grant № ???" where PANORAIMA is Digital Europe grant 101189994, empty preparation fields display as "None.", and the Lesson materials section names no files on the pages we checked. The funding line needs nothing from you. The preparation fields, ackThx and lessonMaterials are still yours to fill.
Wiki page completeness

learningOutcomes: too thin. Two activity statements with no level. Replace with three outcomes along the lines of (a) to (c) under Must fix.
instructions: too thin. 58 words for 60 minutes. Give minute ranges, the slide or file per block, the task and its inputs, what to log, discussion questions with expected answers, a fallback if the tool fails, and what students hand in.
keywords: too thin. Two terms. Use "chain-of-thought prompting", "reasoning models", "chain-of-thought faithfulness", "meta-prompting", "prompt evaluation", with one spelling of chain-of-thought across the page.
expectedLEs: filled, no code. Use "HC-016 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 01", as your docx already does.
self-standing: empty. "No", if HC-017 stays a single session that relies on HC-016's model setup and Prompt Log.
obligStPrep: empty, displays "None.". For example: "Completion of HC-016. LM Studio with the HC-016 model installed and tested before class. Bring your HC-016 Prompt Log." If a chatbot is used instead, name it and the account needed.
optionStPrep: empty, displays "None.". For example Wei et al. (2022), sections 1 to 3, and the OpenAI meta-prompting notebook.
backgrStPrep: filled. Relabel the DAIR.AI links as "DAIR.AI Prompt Engineering Guide: Chain-of-Thought Prompting" and "DAIR.AI Prompt Engineering Guide: Meta Prompting" (or drop the second, per the definition point). Add Wei, J. et al. (2022), "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models", NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2201.11903, and Kojima, T. et al. (2022), "Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners", NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2205.11916.
recommTePrep: empty, displays "None.". OpenAI, "Reasoning best practices" (developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices); Meincke, L., Mollick, E., Mollick, L. and Shapiro, D. (2025), "Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting", arXiv:2506.07142; Turpin, M., Michael, J., Perez, E. and Bowman, S. R. (2023), "Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting", NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.04388; Chen, Y. et al. (2025), "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think", arXiv:2505.05410. Add practical notes: run and time the task set and the hint check on the class model at temperature 0 and record the results, and check how thinking is switched on and off in the LM Studio build students have.
ackThx: empty. Name anyone who contributed to or piloted the session, or write "None".
origContrib: empty. Say whether the tasks, examples or prompts are adapted from existing sources and cite them, or state that they are original. This field is empty on all 34 RealAI Horizontal pages we hold, so it is a programme-wide gap, and it still needs filling here.
lessonMaterials: empty. Once the material exists, list every file: slides, task set with answer key, HC-017 Prompt Log template and worked example log.
mandatory, further, revStatus, surfLink and surfMaterials are empty on all 34 RealAI Horizontal pages we hold. We are not asking authors to fill them unless WP4 assigns them to authors.
Once the Must fix items are done, move the status to "Lesson plan: review" and we will do the formal review.

entries.title: HC-018 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 03
entries.author: HAW · Ahmad Khalidi
entries.review_note: HC-018 is a four-block outline: the timings add up to 60 min, but there are no tasks, no tool, no assessable outcomes and no prep fields, and the prerequisite title is wrong; system prompts repeat HC-016, and block 4 overlaps HC-164/HC-166 (checked against their material).

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): lesson plan in development, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We read wiki revision 8472 of HC-018 (4 September 2026, our reviewer assignment; the last content edit is revision 5866 by Ahmad Khalidi, 18 May 2026), the SharePoint lesson plan "HC-018 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 03.docx" (28 April 2026) and the HC-018 material folder, which is empty. The status is "Lesson plan: development", so this is early feedback, not a formal review: the plan needs major work, and the Must fix items below should be done and the status moved to "Lesson plan: review" before we do the formal plan review.

Several points about HC-018 were already in our HC-016 review of 11 September: the prerequisite title, the blank self-standing field, outcomes without level tags, the missing documentation and ethics clauses, the empty student preparation, and the flipped or single-session decision. The page has not changed since, so they are repeated here on HC-018's own page. Where our suggestions differ from that review, we say so.

Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert (LLM applications and agentic systems).

What works

The four timed blocks add up to the declared 60 minutes, and 40 of them are planned as student work or debrief, which is the intended shape for a Practice event. The blocks still need content, see Must fix. (Instructions for teachers: 10 + 30 + 10 + 10)
Putting prompt chaining before agentic workflows is a sensible order. (learningOutcomes; instructions blocks 1 and 4) Anthropic's engineering guide "Building effective agents" (19 December 2024) lists prompt chaining as its first workflow pattern: a sequence of LLM calls where each processes the previous output, with optional programmatic checks ("gates") on intermediate steps.
Both readings are live, and the generated knowledge page links to the original paper, so a student can follow it back to the source. (backgrStPrep)
The wiki and the SharePoint docx agree on duration, type, keywords, outcomes, the four timed blocks and the two readings, so there is no drift between the two copies yet. (HC-018 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 03.docx, 28 April 2026, against the wiki fields)
Must fix

Most of the lesson plan is still empty or one line. (self-standing, obligStPrep, optionStPrep, recommTePrep, ackThx, origContrib and lessonMaterials are blank; learningOutcomes, keywords, backgrStPrep and instructions are one or two lines each)
That is normal for a page in development, but a teacher who did not write the plan cannot run HC-018 from the page as it stands. Blank Expected preparation fields render as "None." (a known template behaviour, see Smaller things), which tells teachers and students that nothing is needed, while this session needs at least a working chat model with a system prompt field and a way to log runs.
Fix: fill every field listed under Wiki page completeness below before moving the status to "Lesson plan: review". For lessonMaterials, name the planned files now and add the SharePoint links once the files exist; the links are a condition for "Learning materials: review".
The outcomes describe an activity, not a capability a teacher can assess, and block 4 is covered only by a trailing clause. (learningOutcomes: "The student experiments with advanced prompting strategies, like system prompts, prompt chaining, and knowledge prompting." and "This way the student learns to use advanced prompting techniques, which introduces the student to more complex agentic workflows.")
"Experiments with" names what happens in the room. "This way the student learns" and "introduces the student to" cannot be assessed. There is no level tag, while HC-016 tags each of its five outcomes ("on a beginner level", "on an intermediate level"). No outcome covers documenting the runs or the human side of these techniques.
Fix: one outcome per capability, verb plus object plus level, no trailing clause. These build on the examples in our HC-016 review; the system prompt outcome moves from beginner to intermediate because it now includes testing against conflicting messages:
The student writes a system prompt that sets scope, answer format and a refusal rule for a reusable chat, and tests it against user messages that conflict with it, on an intermediate level.
The student decomposes a task into a chain of three prompts, checks each intermediate output before passing it on, records every step in the Prompt Log, and identifies which step caused an error in the final answer, on an intermediate level.
The student compares answers built on model-generated facts with answers built on a supplied source, checks the generated facts against that source, and explains when generated facts are not safe to rely on, on a beginner level.
The student describes how a tool-based agentic workflow orchestrates a chain like the one above, distinguishes it from an agent that chooses its own steps and tools, and says where a human check belongs, on a beginner level.
The 30-minute task block has no tasks. (Instructions for teachers, block 2: "(30 minutes) Students work individually or in groups on tasks regarding the advanced prompting strategies.")
This is 30 of the 60 minutes. The plan does not name the tool, the input, the split across three techniques, the grouping, what students record or what a good result looks like. LM Studio and the Prompt Log are not mentioned, so a teacher cannot tell whether HC-016's setup is assumed. HC-016 shipped task slides, a Prompt Log and a worked example log; HC-018's plan needs that level of detail before material is built.
Fix: write each task into the instructions with its time, exact input and expected output, and name the tool. A version to trial on the HC-016 setup (the times are our estimates; measure them, see Should fix):
(8 min) System prompt. Students write a system prompt for a reusable chat, for example a study helper for this course, that sets scope, answer format and one refusal rule. They test it with three prepared user messages: one in scope, one out of scope, one that tells the model to ignore its instructions. They log which rules held.
(12 min) Prompt chaining. Every student gets the same one-page text. Step 1 extracts quotes relevant to a fixed question. Step 2 answers using only those quotes. Step 3 checks the answer against the quotes and lists any claim without support. Students then change one quote in the step 1 output by hand and rerun steps 2 and 3, to see whether the check catches it. Use a text you wrote yourselves or one whose licence allows reuse in CC BY-NC-SA material, and record it in origContrib.
(10 min) Generated facts against a source. Three prepared questions that you have checked the classroom model sometimes gets wrong. Students answer each after "first generate relevant facts, then answer", then again with a short supplied source paragraph instead, and mark each generated fact as supported by the source or not. Put a fact key with sources in the teacher notes, otherwise the marking cannot be checked in 10 minutes.
Add a worked Prompt Log for these tasks, as you did for HC-016, with a column for thinking on or off per run. If a teacher uses a hosted chatbot instead of LM Studio, say where the system prompt goes (for example a custom GPT, a Gemini Gem or a Claude Project), check whether that feature needs a paid account, and tell students to put no personal or confidential data into prompts on a hosted service.
Generated knowledge prompting is planned without its main limitation, and block 4 does not separate it from retrieval. (learningOutcomes and instructions block 1: "knowledge prompting"; backgrStPrep: "Prompt-Engineering on Generated Knowledge Prompting"; instructions block 4: "prompt strategies, like prompt chaining or knowledge prompting, are tool based and orchestrated")
The linked page describes generated knowledge prompting from Liu et al., ACL 2022: the model writes background facts, then answers with them. Generated facts can be wrong. In the paper's human evaluation (section 4.4) of up to 50 GPT-3 knowledge statements per dataset on NumerSense and QASC, sampled because they changed T5-11b's answer, 83% were factually correct and 13% were harmful, meaning they argued against the correct answer or for a wrong one; of the harmful statements that misled the model, 86% were not factual. That is a small selected sample, not a general error rate, but the risk is real. The published method also picks among 20 statements per question by answer score, which a chat window does not show; the promptingguide page says it simplified this and does not discuss wrong facts.
Block 4 is broadly right that agentic workflows are tool based, but it does not say what changes: there the model usually does not write its own facts, a retrieval or search tool fetches them from a source someone can check. Anthropic's guide describes the basic building block as "an LLM enhanced with augmentations such as retrieval, tools, and memory".
On the HC-016 model there is a further problem, the one our HC-016 review raised for chain-of-thought in HC-017: with thinking on, gemma-4-e4b already writes its own reasoning before it answers, so a with-and-without comparison measures little. Google's Gemma 4 model card says thinking is switched on by a token at the start of the system prompt, and there are open LM Studio reports that thinking cannot be switched off on Gemma 4 builds (lmstudio-bug-tracker issues #1805, #2046 and #2274).
Fix: call it "generated knowledge prompting" throughout and cite Liu et al. 2022. Teach the risk with the generated facts task above. Run that task with thinking off, record the setting for every run, and test the toggle on the classroom build before class. In block 4, add one sentence contrasting generated facts with retrieval.
The plan has no human-centred content yet, and the debrief has no questions. (learningOutcomes; keywords; instructions block 3: "Students discuss results and reflect on experiences made.")
In a chain, a wrong step 1 output is passed to later steps unless someone checks it, and a document fed into a chain can carry instructions the chain then follows. Anthropic's guide names "the potential for compounding errors" as a cost of agents and recommends "extensive testing in sandboxed environments". HC-016 closes its Context, Output Indicator and Temperature experiments with a question on ethical values, appropriateness or bias (IPE_1_Assignments.pptx slides 13, 16 and 22). HC-018 has no equivalent question, and nothing asks students to make and justify a decision a practitioner would face.
Fix: write the debrief questions into block 3, each with the answer you expect. For example: Which step in your chain produced the error, and could you tell from the final answer alone? Did your step 3 check catch the changed quote? Which generated facts were wrong, and would a user have noticed? Your manager wants this chain to summarise customer complaints for a weekly report: would you let it run without a human check, and if not, where does the check go and who does it? In the block text, link forward to HC-168 Limitations and Risks of Agentic AI (Part 1) (PDF page 17 on compounding inaccuracies, page 40 on human-in-the-loop against human-on-the-loop), HC-170 (Part 2) (page 9 on direct and indirect prompt injection and tool-use hijacking) and HC-034 Agentic bias (slide 14 on the accountability gap in multi-step agentic workflows). Add H-049 Prompt injection and Jailbreaking Attacks once it has an author and material; today it has neither.
One of the three "advanced" techniques is already taught and debriefed in HC-016, and the plan does not say what HC-018 adds to HC-016 or HC-017. (learningOutcomes and instructions block 1: "advanced prompting strategies, like system prompts"; against HC-016 IPE_1_Assignments.pptx slides 17 and 18, IPE_1_Discussions.pptx slide 6, and the HC-016 wiki block at 15-20 min on the System Prompt reflection)
HC-016 Assignments slide 18 already has students create a chat called System Prompt and move context and output indicator into the system prompt field, because "Often we don't want to repeat context and output indicators for every prompt"; Discussions slide 6 asks for the pros and cons. The keyword "custom chats" could mean that same reusable chat or something beyond it, and the plan does not say which. The step from HC-017 is not stated either: generated knowledge prompting, like HC-017's chain-of-thought, has the model write intermediate text before it answers. HC-017 also moves students to hosted chatbots ("The students use intelligent ChatBots, like ChatGPT, Gemini") while HC-016 runs on LM Studio, so the tool for HC-018 is open.
Fix: add a sentence to block 1 stating what is new against HC-016 and HC-017. Our suggestion: testing a system prompt against conflicting user messages, chaining with checks between steps, and generated facts checked against a supplied source. Name the tool the series uses from HC-018 on.
The prerequisite has HC-017's code but HC-018's own title, and self-standing is blank. (expectedLEs: "HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 03"; self-standing: empty. The same wrong title is in the SharePoint docx under "Preceding LEs".)
HC-017's title is "Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02". HC-017 is itself a lesson plan in development with an empty SharePoint folder, and its chain-of-thought block still has the thinking-mode issue from our HC-016 review, so HC-018's place in the series depends on decisions not yet taken.
Fix: "HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02" in the wiki and the docx. Set self-standing to "No", since HC-018 builds on HC-016 and HC-017.
Should fix

The timing is tight for three techniques on a local model. (Instructions for teachers, blocks 1 and 2)
Ten minutes to introduce three techniques is about three minutes each. The screenshot on HC-016 IPE_1_Introduction.pptx slide 12 shows one short gemma-4-e4b reply with thinking on: 463 tokens at 16.30 tok/sec after "Thought for 20.42 seconds", so roughly 28 seconds. The chain task needs five generations (three steps, then steps 2 and 3 again), each on a longer input. HC-018 has no homework, so everything has to fit in class, and the flipped or single-session question from our HC-016 review is still open.
Fix: time one full run of each task on a typical student laptop and write the measured time into the plan. If it does not fit, run the chain with thinking off and say so, or turn the generated facts task into a teacher demo. Add a fallback: the teacher runs the chain on the projector and students do the checks. Decide flipped or single-session for the series and write the answer on this page.
Block 4 is 10 minutes of new lecture after the debrief, and it overlaps HC-164 and HC-166. (Instructions block 4: "(10 minutes) Introduction to agentic workflows, where prompt strategies, like prompt chaining or knowledge prompting, are tool based and orchestrated.")
We read the HC-164 and HC-166 PDFs on SharePoint (Introduction to Agentic AI, Parts 1 and 2, Ready for pilot). Neither teaches system prompts or prompt chaining, so blocks 1 to 3 are distinct. Block 4 overlaps HC-164 PDF page 16 "Example: LLM Workflow Agent" (plans tasks, calls APIs/tools, evaluates outcomes) and HC-166 pages 29 (retrieval errors), 44 (vector databases) and 58 (a multi-step workflow scenario with tool calls). H-096 Creating Effective Prompts and H-102a/b Advanced Prompt Engineering Systems and Applications overlap by title only; all three have no status and empty SharePoint folders. Ten minutes at the end cannot introduce agentic workflows, and block 4 links forward to nothing.
Fix: turn block 4 into a short demo of what students just did by hand, and place it before the debrief so the questions can cover it. The teacher runs the same three-step chain from a script against LM Studio's local server (OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint, which also takes tool calls), with the step 3 check written as code, then shows the difference between that fixed workflow and an agent using Anthropic's definitions: workflows are "orchestrated through predefined code paths", agents "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage". LM Studio's docs warn that smaller models "may output improperly formatted tool calls", so test the demo and keep a recorded run as fallback; if it uses MCP servers, use only trusted ones. Put the forward link to HC-164 in the block 4 text, since the template has no successor field (a gap RealAI has raised centrally), and agree the boundary with the HC-164 authors, Ioannis Patias and András Gézsi. András is already your co-author on HC-020 and HC-023.
Smaller things

"reflect on experiences made" (instructions block 3, and HC-017 blocks 3 and 5): "reflect on what they observed" is clearer.
The title "Introduction to Prompt Engineering 03" does not tell a catalogue reader what the event covers, and the plan calls the content "advanced". If titles are not fixed by the WP lead, consider "Prompt Engineering 03: System Prompts, Prompt Chaining and Generated Knowledge".
The docx names only Ahmad Khalidi as author; the wiki adds Stefano Marrone (UNINA), since 13 May. Keep the wiki as the master copy and update the docx or mark it superseded. There is no second-author comment yet, and the guidelines give the second author the didactic check, so ask Stefano for it before the status moves.
Template issues: the page renders "Co-Financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union Under Grant № ???", "None." under all four Expected preparation fields when they are blank, and a Lesson materials section that names no file. These are known template issues RealAI has raised centrally, not your fault. Please still fill your own ackThx, the four preparation fields and lessonMaterials.
Wiki page completeness

self-standing: empty. Set to "No".
learningOutcomes: too thin (two sentences, no level tags, not assessable, block 4 only in a trailing clause). Replace with the four outcomes above or your own in the same form.
expectedLEs: wrong title. Change to "HC-017 Introduction to Prompt Engineering 02".
keywords: too thin (two terms, neither used in the outcomes or instructions). Replace with: system prompt, prompt chaining, generated knowledge prompting, agentic workflow, tool use, human oversight.
obligStPrep: empty, renders as "None.". If HC-018 runs on the HC-016 setup, students need LM Studio and gemma-4-e4b installed and tested before class (the model download alone is 5.90 GB, per our HC-016 review), a laptop meeting the minimum memory and free disk you state, and their HC-016 Prompt Log. Say so.
optionStPrep: empty. For example the Wu, Terry and Cai 2022 paper (introduction and user study) or the Anthropic guide.
backgrStPrep: too thin. Both pages are fine as a first read, but the chaining page says chaining makes each stage easier to debug without giving a method for checking intermediate output, and the knowledge page does not mention wrong facts. Keep them and add a primary source per technique:
Liu, J., Liu, A., Lu, X., Welleck, S., West, P., Le Bras, R., Choi, Y. and Hajishirzi, H. (2022). Generated Knowledge Prompting for Commonsense Reasoning. Proceedings of ACL 2022 (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 3154-3169. https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.225/
Wu, T., Terry, M. and Cai, C. J. (2022). AI Chains: Transparent and Controllable Human-AI Interaction by Chaining Large Language Model Prompts. CHI 2022. https://doi.org/10.1145/3491102.3517582. In a 20-person user study, chaining improved output quality, transparency, controllability and sense of collaboration, and participants debugged chains by testing single steps.
Anthropic (2024). Building effective agents. 19 December 2024. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
recommTePrep: empty. Liu et al. 2022 section 4.4; the Anthropic guide; the LM Studio docs on tool use and MCP; Schulhoff, S. et al., The Prompt Report: A Systematic Survey of Prompt Engineering Techniques, arXiv:2406.06608, for one shared vocabulary across HC-016 to HC-018; and one timed run of every task on the classroom model with the thinking setting noted.
ackThx: empty. Add your own thanks (for example anyone who tested the tasks) or a deliberate "None"; the funding line is the template issue above.
origContrib: empty. Name any external text or material you reuse, such as the input text for the chaining task and its licence, otherwise write "None".
lessonMaterials: empty. Name the planned files now: slides, task sheet, chaining input text, question set with source paragraphs and fact key, HC-018 Prompt Log, worked example log, block 4 demo script. Add the SharePoint link for each once it exists.
instructions: too thin. Rewrite minute by minute, as HC-016 does: for each block what the teacher does, which file or slide, the exact task text, what students record, the debrief questions with expected answers, the forward links, and the fallback if the local model is too slow.
When you pick HC-018 up again, the outcomes and the task block are the two to write first, since the rest of the plan follows from them.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST

The supervised half has good worked examples (llamas, Titanic, housing, the slide 21 messy-data exercise). But four of Béla's seven 27 July points (4 to 7) are still in the 20 Aug deck, point 2 is open and points 1 and 3 are only partly covered. The ML taxonomy contradicts itself (slides 12/23/30/36). long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 17 September 2026, 13:40 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed the HC-019 wiki page as pulled on 17 September 2026 (revision 8471; last content edits by Sietske on 8 July and Béla on 27 July) and the one SharePoint file, HC-019 Introduction Machine Learning Types and Tasks.pptx (39 slides, 12 with speaker notes, saved 20 August 2026); there is no lesson-plan document, so the wiki is the only plan. Verdict: major revision, with the seven items under Must fix as the conditions for sign-off.

Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert, machine learning in industry practice.

What works
