Must fix

The deck gives three incompatible pictures of how machine learning divides up, and its own reinforcement learning example fits none of them. (Slides 12, 23, 30 and 36; Béla's points 4 and 5)
Slides 12 and 23 split machine learning into supervised and unsupervised only. Slide 30 hangs "Reinforcement learning" off to the side of "Machine Learning types" and draws "Possible implementation strategy: Deep learning" under classification, regression, clustering and dimensionality reduction only. Slide 36 then lists three peers: "Supervised learning needs labeled data, unsupervised learning takes unlabeled data, reinforcement learning creates own data". The video on slide 37 is Haarnoja et al., "Learning to Walk via Deep Reinforcement Learning" (RSS 2019), which is deep reinforcement learning, and slide 30 has no place for it. Slides 11 and 34 also list "next words/tokens" as a task; that is self-supervised learning, which no slide names. The Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system (C(2025) 5053 final, 29 July 2025) give supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning as examples of machine learning approaches (paragraph 32), treat self-supervised learning as a subcategory of unsupervised learning with next-token language models as an example (paragraph 36), and describe deep learning as layered neural network architectures for representation learning (paragraph 38), not as a branch of one approach.
Fix: Draw one diagram and reuse it on slides 12, 23 and 30, adding to it rather than redrawing it: three peers (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), self-supervised named under unsupervised, and deep learning as a band running under all three. Rewrite the slide 36 bullet to match. Béla is second author here and first author of HC-021 and HC-022, so please agree the diagram between you so the introductions match. RealAI has raised the programme-wide version centrally, because HC-148, HC-154 and HC-158 draw it differently again. -- ST: adjusted the diagram according to the suggestions made here.
Learning outcome 1 (differences and relationships between AI, machine learning and deep learning) rests on three dictionary definitions, and deep learning is summed up as "resembling human learning". (Slides 8, 9, 31 and 36; Béla's point 6)
Slides 8, 9 and 31 quote Oxford Learner's Dictionaries (we checked, the quotes are accurate). Slide 31 defines deep learning through "computers designed to work in a similar way to the human brain", and slide 36 turns that into "Deep learning is a form of machine learning resembling human learning", close to the dictionary's own example sentence, "Deep learning imitates the way in which humans acquire knowledge". A learner's dictionary explains everyday English; it is not a technical source for a master's course. Neural networks were loosely inspired by neurons, but fitting millions of weights by gradient descent does not resemble how people learn, and a graduate who tells a client it does will overstate what the model understands. The definition also fails Béla's test, and the network on slide 31 (input layer, three hidden layers, output layer) is exactly the 5-layer MLP he asks about. For the relationships half of the outcome, slide 36 only asserts "Machine learning is a subarea of artificial intelligence": no slide shows how the three nest, no slide gives an example of AI that is not machine learning, and no activity tests the outcome.
Fix: Replace the slide 31 definition with a structural one: machine learning with neural networks of many layers, each layer learning a more abstract representation of the data, so features are learned rather than hand-built. Cite LeCun, Bengio and Hinton, "Deep learning", Nature 521, 436-444 (2015), or paragraph 38 of the Commission guidelines. Say on the slide that "deep" has no agreed layer count; that is the answer to Béla's question. Rewrite the slide 36 bullet as "Deep learning uses many-layered neural networks and is used in supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning." Add a nested picture of AI, machine learning and deep learning with one example at each level, including a rule-based system as AI without machine learning (paragraph 39 of the guidelines calls these logic- and knowledge-based approaches), and add one question on it to the slide 34 exercise. Add a source for the slide 31 network figure. -- ST: I have struggled with this, because the learners are really new to machine learning. They don't know yet what a neural network is, so the definition proposed here may confuse too much. I have tried to settle for a good compromise, also mentioning that the image is not a deep learning network, but a deep learning network does look like a complex version of the image.
Slide 10 carries a page of a copyrighted novel that the CC BY-NC-SA licence on slide 39 cannot cover, and slide 28 and most images carry no credit. (Slides 10 and 28, and most image slides)
Licence problem. Slide 10 shows the opening page of chapter 1 of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (J.K. Rowling, Bloomsbury) as the example of text data, with no credit. Slide 39 releases "All materials" under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and that cannot include a page of the novel.
Credit problem. Slide 28's eight lines are the step headings and stopping criteria of Pulkit Sharma's Analytics Vidhya article "K-Means Clustering Algorithm" (https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2019/08/comprehensive-guide-k-means-clustering/, last updated 3 December 2025, footer "All rights reserved") nearly word for word and in the same order, with articles and a few words dropped: "Recompute the centroids of newly formed clusters" becomes "Recompute centroids of newly formed clusters", "Maximum number of iterations is reached" becomes "Max number of iterations reached". The rest of the article is not reproduced and the k-means procedure itself is standard; what is missing is the credit. The animated GIF on the same slide has no visible credit; its alt text points to Ruslan Brilenkov, "Understanding K-Means Clustering: Hands-on Visual Approach" (Artificial Intelligence in Plain English, Medium).
No source or licence is given for the alpaca photo (slides 4 and 6), the llama and alpaca photos (slide 5), the car table, cat photos and inbox screenshot (slide 10), the house photos (slides 16 and 17), the Albert Heijn logo and app screens, the Netflix screenshot and the two scatter plots (slide 25), the iris photos and scatter plot (slide 26), the network diagram (slide 31) and the robot photo (slide 32, which looks like a frame from the slide 37 video). Slide 27 credits ISLR, but that figure still needs the publisher's permission or a note that it is excluded from the CC licence.
Fix: Replace the slide 10 book page with public-domain text (a Project Gutenberg page) or a paragraph you wrote. [ST: replaced the book page with a screen shot from the English wikipedia page on Harry Potter, including a reference]. Rewrite slide 28 in your own words from a textbook and cite it: ISLR, which you already use on slide 27, gives k-means as Algorithm 10.1 in the first edition (chapter 12 in the 2021 second edition). Since HC-021 slides 19 to 29 teach k-means step by step, you can also cut slide 28 to one sentence and name HC-021 in the lesson plan. Credit the GIF to Brilenkov, or replace it if its terms do not allow reuse. [ST: removed slide 28, because it is indeed covered in HC-021.] Add a source line to every image you keep, check the reuse terms for the ISLR figure, and replace anything you cannot license. [ST: changed the image on slide 27 to a created version based on the HC-021 slides. For the llama, alpaca, cats and house photos: would it be allowed to include stock-photos that Microsoft Office offers within Powerpoint? And how to credit those? Because I can find quite some alpaca (no llamas though), houses and cats in there.]. The blanket licence sentence on the wiki pages is a template matter RealAI has raised centrally, and the slide 39 disclaimer is the same template wording; the per-image credits are yours.
The lesson plan schedules dimensionality reduction, deep and reinforcement learning tasks, and domain use cases that the deck does not contain. (Wiki Instructions for teachers against slides 24 to 34)
The wiki says "25 - 40 minutes: unsupervised learning examples: clustering, dimensionality reduction". Slides 24 to 28 are all clustering; dimensionality reduction appears only as a box on slides 12, 23 and 30 and as "Reducing complexity" in the slide 11 list. "40 - 50 minutes: deep learning and reinforcement learning tasks": slides 31 and 32 define both and show no task. "50 - 60 minutes: use cases from various domains and wrap up": slide 34 repeats the slide 11 list and there are no use cases. The learning outcomes never mention reinforcement learning, although slides 29 to 32 and slide 36 teach it.
Fix: Dimensionality reduction is an unsupervised task (paragraph 35 of the Commission guidelines), so keep it as a box in the one diagram, but do not promise a block you have no slides for. Either add one example slide on the iris data you already show, projecting the four measurements onto two principal components (on the UCI file the first component carries about 92% of the variance on raw measurements and about 73% after standardising; setosa separates, versicolor and virginica overlap), or rewrite the 25-40 minute line to name clustering only and point to HC-021, whose plan gives dimensionality reduction 30-40 minutes. [ST: good observation. I opted for the latter option, I think the lecture as it is shows enough new examples to students.] For the 40-50 minute block, show one deep learning task (an image or text example) and one reinforcement learning task (the slide 37 walking robot, with its reward stated). For the last block, add three or four short cases from sectors your students will work in (health, public services, finance, manufacturing), each naming the task, the data, whether labels exist, the learning type and who is affected when the output is wrong. Add reinforcement learning to learning outcome 2. [ST: added reinforcement learning to learning outcome 2 both on the wiki page and in the slides].
Learning outcome 4 is practised once, with no answer key and with task names that do not match the taxonomy, and the deep learning and reinforcement learning section has no speaker notes. (Slides 11 and 34; slides 4 to 6 and 21; notes on slides 27 to 32, 36 and 37)
The slide 34 note reads "Have students discuss these tasks, and/or the ones written on the whiteboard. Which of the machine learning types seems appropriate for which task?" and stops. Several items have no single answer from what the deck teaches. "next words/tokens" is self-supervised, which the deck never names. Anomaly detection is supervised when you have labelled fraud cases and unsupervised when you do not. Ranking and recommendation are usually trained on user behaviour as supervised or collaborative-filtering problems, yet slide 25 has shown recommendation as clustering. The list also uses different names from the diagram: "Prediction: values" and "Reducing complexity" on slides 11 and 34 against "Regression" and "Dimensionality reduction" on slides 12, 23 and 30, while slides 15 and 19 label both the classification and the regression rows "predict". Students have to map one vocabulary onto the other without being told how. Slides 4 to 6 never state which animal is shown, and slide 21 gives no answers. Only 12 of 39 slides have notes with text: slides 27, 28, 30, 36 and 37 have note pages holding only the slide number, and slides 29, 31 and 32 have no note page, so the section where Béla found four technical problems has no teaching guidance.
Fix: Use one set of task names on slides 11 and 34 and in the diagram. Write an answer key into the slide 34 note, one line per task, with the rule students apply: are labels available, and is the output a category, a number, a grouping or an action. Put the answer to slides 4 to 6 in the slide 6 note. For slide 21: the first target is feature1 squared; the second is feature1 plus feature2, with the "a", the blank and the final 10 as the planted defects. Give every content slide a note a different lecturer could teach from.
The deck has no content on who is affected when a prediction is wrong. (Whole deck; Titanic slides 14 and 15)
The reviewer guidelines ask for risks, trade-offs and ethical issues and for professional judgement, and the programme is built on a human-centred orientation. No slide or note in HC-019 asks who a model's output affects. Slides 14 and 15 already have the data for it: in the Kaggle training file 74% of women and 19% of men survived, and 63% of first-class against 24% of third-class passengers, so sex and class are among the strongest predictors a model will pick up.
Fix: Add one slide after slide 15 asking what happens if you train the same way on historical hiring or lending data: whose past decisions the labels record, and who carries the cost of a wrong prediction. It takes about three minutes. Ask the same question in each use case for the last block.
Most of the wiki page is empty, and Instructions for teachers is five timing lines. (PanoLessonPlan fields; field by field under Wiki page completeness below)
Ten fields you can fill now are blank, keywords has five terms, and Instructions for teachers gives five timing lines for 60 minutes with no slide numbers, no activity instructions and no expected answers. A lecturer at another institution cannot run HC-019 from this page.
Fix: Fill every field as listed under Wiki page completeness.
Should fix

Slide 25 presents two recommender systems as the example of clustering. (Slide 25 and its note)
Netflix's own account of its recommender (Gomez-Uribe and Hunt, ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems 6(4), 2015, section 2.9) says it combines supervised classification and regression, unsupervised methods including clustering, and matrix factorization. For the Albert Heijn Bonus Box, AH says offers are personalised from purchase history; we found no public account of the method, so the note's "suggests products that users with similar behavior regarding to groceries are buying" says more than anyone outside AH can check.
Fix: Use a case that is clustering, such as segmenting customers for a campaign or grouping incoming support tickets, or keep Netflix and say clustering is one ingredient among several. The same paper describes a feedback loop in which titles get watched because they were recommended; one line on that adds a point about the people on the receiving end.
Slide 26 shows species labels on a clustering slide, and its note describes a target "at the dataset level". (Slide 26 and its note)
The scatter plot is coloured "Class 0, Class 1, Class 2", which are the true species. The note says "there is no target on the individual iris level, but there is a target at the dataset level we are using to train". Clustering has no target at any level, and this sentence confuses the supervised and unsupervised distinction that learning outcome 2 tests. The note also says we can "even distinguish three groups". k-means with k = 3 on all four measurements puts all 50 setosa together, but 14 virginica fall in the versicolor cluster and 2 versicolor in the virginica cluster: 134 of 150 flowers, about 89% agreement with species.
Fix: Show the plot uncoloured, then the k-means result, then the species colouring, so students see that clusters and classes are not the same thing. Delete the "dataset level" sentence.
Béla's points 2 and 3: data size, test data and how a model is checked. (Slides 5, 14, 15, 18, 19 and 26)
The slide 9 note stresses "huge amounts of DATA", but no slide or note gives a dataset size: the Titanic training file has 891 passengers, iris 150 flowers, King County 21,613 sales. How much is enough depends on the task: 150 rows is plenty for k-means on four measurements, four photos is nowhere near enough to learn to tell images apart. On slide 15 the five "predict" passengers (IDs 596 to 600) come from Kaggle's training file, so their outcomes are known (0, 1, 0, 0, 1). The only word on checking a model is the slide 15 note, "evaluate how often it is correct". 342 of 891 passengers survived, so predicting "did not survive" for everyone is already right 62% of the time, and nothing is said about checking a regression or a clustering. RealAI has raised centrally that none of the machine learning introductions in the Horizontal track teaches evaluation. On slide 19 the "train" rows are the first five rows of the file (October 2014 to February 2015) and the "predict" rows the last five (May 2014 to February 2015), so some rows to predict are older than the rows trained on.
Fix: Put the dataset sizes in the notes of slides 5, 14, 18 and 26. On slide 15, hide the outcomes, let the room predict, reveal and count, then give the 62% baseline in one sentence. Add one line on how a regression is checked (the average size of the error on sales the model has not seen) and one on why a clustering has no correct answer to check against. On slide 19, add a note that a price model used on future sales should be tested on later sales than it was trained on, and leave the detail to HC-020, whose plan covers splitting and leakage at 20-30 minutes. Once the WP4 lead confirms where evaluation is taught, name that event in the plan.
Slide 32 on reinforcement learning (Béla's point 7). (Slide 32)
Keep "Learn by trial-and-error" and "Feedback is a scalar reward". "Data generated by agent itself" matches paragraph 37 of the Commission guidelines ("learn from data collected from their own experience"), but Béla is right that it is not always true: offline reinforcement learning trains on logged data. The missing idea is the one Béla names: the consequences of an action, including the reward, can play out many steps later, so the learner does not get feedback at every step.
Fix: Add that bullet, correct "awards" to "rewards", cite Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd edition, MIT Press, 2018 (Béla quoted a 2014-15 draft), and add a note on the slide 37 video saying what the robot is rewarded for.
Overlap and sequence with other learning events are not stated on this page. (Wiki page; slide 3)
HC-019 has sort number 50, ahead of HC-020 (60), HC-021 (70) and HC-022 (80). HC-021 teaches k-means step by step (slides 19 to 29) and HC-022 teaches classification against regression. HC-158 carries slide 9's machine learning definition word for word, a close variant of slide 11's task list and the slide 34 discussion question; RealAI raised this centrally, and the file dates do not show which came first. In the other direction, H-191 (Operating AI in Production) already lists "Introduction to Machine Learning: types and tasks" as its prerequisite, the only forward link to HC-019 among the 34 Horizontal plans we review. Slide 8 defines AI only as systems that "copy intelligent human behaviour". (Slide 8)
Article 3(1) of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) defines an AI system by what it does: it infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions. It says nothing about human behaviour and covers most of the slide 11 tasks. Not all of them: the Commission guidelines (paragraphs 49 to 51) place simple baseline predictors, such as always predicting the historical average, outside the definition, and the "did not survive" Titanic baseline above is one.
Fix: Put the Article 3(1) definition next to the dictionary one and ask the room which one a compliance officer would use, and whether the Titanic baseline counts as an AI system.
Nothing on large pretrained models, which is where most students will meet machine learning at work. (Slides 11, 30, 31 and 34)
The only trace is "next words/tokens" on slides 11 and 34. The language and image models in use today are pretrained on unlabelled data (self-supervised) and then adapted with labelled examples and human feedback. References are two blog posts and a video link. (Slide 37)

Fix: Add ISLR 2nd edition (James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, 2021, free PDF at statlearning.com), Sutton and Barto 2018 (free online) and the Commission guidelines above. Give the video its title and authors (Haarnoja et al., RSS 2019). Replace the Akkio guide with a non-commercial source.

Hi Sietske and Béla, thank you for the v2 deck and your reply of 13 October. We re-read both against our review of 17 September and our Action summary of 14 October; those entries stay above as the record. RealAI keeps the longer, more instructional review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard.

Verdict: major revision still stands, but the deck is much closer.

Closed since our review:
* Taxonomy wording is the same on slides 12, 23 and 29 (we have not re-read the drawn figures); deep learning is defined structurally on slide 30 and nested on slide 37.
* Slide 10 cites a source, the k-means slide and GIF are gone, the slide 27 figure is your own drawing, and the slide 6, 21 and 35 notes now give answers.

Still open: the "who is affected" slide (nothing yet on harm, fairness or who bears the cost); image sources on slides 4 to 6, 10 and the house photos from slide 16; dataset sizes and how predictions are checked; the slide 25 recommender example; and the wiki page (Self-standing, Expected preparation, Learning Events before, Lesson materials link, and Acknowledgements still "Grant № ???").

A short follow-up is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off. When the open items are done, tell us on this Discussion page and email the review inbox so we can re-review.

entries.review_note: Lesson plan reviewed 17 Sep 2026 13:41 CEST, posted Talk rev 8612. Status at review: 'Lesson plan: review'. REVISION REQUESTED (major). The stage sequence and the problem formulation block are sound. But another teacher could not run the plan from the wiki, outcomes 3 to 5 have no activity behind them, evaluation is named four times and taught nowhere, and all four Expected preparation fields are empty. long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan, 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST
long_form.text:
We reviewed the HC-020 lesson plan on the wiki as of András Gézsi's revision of 30 June 2026 ("Ready for LP review", pulled 17 September 2026; the 4 September edit only assigned reviewers) and BME_lessonplan_H020.docx in SharePoint, last modified 14 April 2026. Verdict: major revision, mainly because another teacher could not run the plan from the wiki text, and model evaluation is named four times but never taught.

The HC-020 material folder is empty and the Talk page did not exist, so this covers the plan only. Reviewer expertise: subject-matter expert (industry AI practice).

What works

The event sits in the right place. HC-021, HC-022 and HC-023 all declare HC-020 as their prerequisite, and a system view before model families is the order a practitioner would choose. The stages in Instructions for teachers (problem formulation, data pipeline, model development, deployment, monitoring) match how production teams split the work and how the standard references do, for example Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems (O'Reilly, 2022), and ISO/IEC 23053:2022.
The 10-20 block asks the questions a practitioner starts with: "what is the prediction target, what is the unit of prediction, what inputs are available, and what success means", followed by "different formulations of the same real-world problem may lead to very different systems". Unit of prediction matters in practice: a model that scores each hospital visit is a different system from one that scores each patient, even on the same records. Keep this block and build on it.
The failure modes named are ones that break deployed systems: leakage (outcome 4 and the 20-30 block), "batch vs real-time inference" and "the difference between offline evaluation and real-world use" (40-50), and "feedback loops, and human oversight" (50-60). Sculley et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (NeurIPS 28, 2015, pp. 2503-2511), list hidden feedback loops among the main ML-specific risks.
The docx carries two good design decisions: one running example revisited at every stage with six fixed questions (from "what is the task?" to "how do we know when it stops working well?"), and "The lecture should remain model-agnostic." Both belong on the wiki (see Must fix).
Every outcome carries verb, category and level, and the verbs go from Explain to Evaluate in a sensible order.
Must fix

Another teacher could not run the plan from the wiki, and the better guidance is only in the docx. (Instructions for teachers, whole field; BME_lessonplan_H020.docx, the paragraphs before the "When? / What?" table)
The wiki says "Present a simple real-world example" and never names one. Each block is a list of topics to "Introduce", "Explain", "Define", "Discuss" or "Summarize", with no example, no question with an expected answer and no student task. The docx says "Use one (or more) running example(s) throughout the lecture, such as: spam detection, medical risk prediction, recommendation, or image classification", lists six questions to revisit at every stage, and says supervised and unsupervised content "belongs mainly to H021 and H022". None of that is on the wiki, which is the version the programme publishes.
Fix: Pick one running example and write it into the wiki. We suggest medical risk prediction from your own list: it is a binary task, which the evaluation part needs, and the published cases under Should fix fit it. For each block write a few sentences another teacher can follow: the point, the example applied to it, the question to ask and the expected answer. The H-132 wiki plan, which lists you as first author, already works this way (one running case and a group activity per block), so use it as the model. Move the docx framing paragraph and its six questions onto the wiki, then keep the docx in sync or mark it superseded.
Outcomes 3, 4 and 5 have no activity behind them, and the plan has one student prompt. (Learning Outcomes 3 "Differentiate (cognitive skill, intermediate level)", 4 "Analyze (cognitive skill, intermediate level)" and 5 "Evaluate (competence, intermediate level) whether a proposed learning pipeline is coherent and suitable for a given application scenario"; Instructions for teachers, all six blocks)
The only student prompt is in 0-10, "ask what steps are needed before and after training", and no expected answer is given. Outcome 5 needs an exercise where students judge a pipeline. There is none, so a teacher has no way to check it. The reviewer checklist asks where students can "make, justify or evaluate decisions", and the format scan for lecture slides asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements. Schedule them in the plan now so the deck can carry them.
Fix: Add three interactive elements, each with an answer key in the teacher instructions. (1) The opening question, with the list of steps you expect. (2) A 3 minute spot-the-leak check in the data block: four one-line scenarios, for example a scaler fitted on the full dataset before splitting, the same patient in training and test data, a random split on time-stamped records, and a feature recorded only after the outcome. (3) A 12 minute pipeline critique: a one-page proposed pipeline for the running example with four or five planted flaws (a leak, a metric that ignores the costly error, batch scoring where the decision needs real time, no monitoring plan, no way for a clinician to override). Pairs find and justify the flaws and the teacher debriefs from the key. Outcomes 4 and 5 are assessed there. To make room, merge deployment and monitoring. One timing that adds up, including the additions under Should fix: 0-8 running example, opening question and, if you keep open entry, a 2 minute recap of features, label and target; 8-17 problem formulation with the Obermeyer case; 17-26 data pipeline with the leak check; 26-35 model development (2 minutes, including pretrained and bought models) and evaluation (7 minutes); 35-45 deployment and monitoring with one deployment case; 45-57 pipeline critique and debrief; 57-60 wrap-up naming HC-021, HC-022 and HC-023.
Evaluation is named in four places and taught in none. (Learning Outcomes, outcome 1: "model development, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring"; 10-20 block: "what success means"; 30-40 block: "training, and evaluation"; 40-50 block: "the difference between offline evaluation and real-world use")
No block says what is measured, what it is compared with, or which kind of error matters more. Outcome 5 asks students to judge whether a pipeline is "suitable for a given application scenario", which needs some way to say what good enough looks like. In our cross-series pass of 9 to 13 September we found that no PANORAIMA-authored file in the 25 Horizontal events of that pass defines a confusion matrix, and that the four machine learning introductions contain no precision, recall or F1. We asked WP4 whether an evaluation event exists elsewhere, naming HC-020 and H-014 as candidates. HC-020 does not cover it. Two events outside that pass do: the H-108 deck ("Fundamentals of machine learning.pdf", page 25, numbered slide 26) defines the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and F1, and the H-122 plan schedules them at 105-115 minutes. Both sit at sort numbers 620 and 690, after HC-020 (60) and after HC-021, HC-022 and HC-023 (70 to 90). HC-023's notes on slide 16 (Information Extraction) ask "what could go wrong if this is 95% accurate?" and use it to introduce the idea that accuracy figures hide where the errors fall. HC-020 is the earlier event where that idea can first be set up.
Fix: Give evaluation about 7 minutes in the model block, at system level and on the running example. Turn the success criterion from 10-20 into something measurable. Name the two error types in words (a patient flagged who did not need it, a patient missed who did) and say who carries each. Show that one accuracy figure hides both and can hide a subgroup where the model does much worse. Contrast the offline metric with the outcome the hospital actually cares about. Leave the formulas to H-108 and H-122 and the full evaluation plan, with baselines and go/no-go thresholds, to H-132, and name those events in the plan. Use the same terms as H-108 slide 26. The ordering, with metric definitions arriving after the events that use them, is a programme-level question that we will put to WP4.
All four Expected preparation fields are empty and Keywords has one entry. (obligStPrep, optionStPrep, backgrStPrep, recommTePrep; keywords "ML pipelines and architectures")
An empty preparation field renders as "None." on the public page. For a lecture that asks students to judge a pipeline, that tells students there is nothing to read and teachers there is nothing to prepare. A single broad keyword also makes the event hard to tell apart from HC-195, H-132 and H-191, which cover related ground.
Fix: Fill all four preparation fields and add specific keywords. Also fill ackThx, origContrib and further where they apply, and lessonMaterials once material exists. Suggested content is in the Wiki page completeness block below. Blank Expected preparation is a series-wide pattern RealAI has raised centrally (see Smaller things), but only you can fill these fields for HC-020.
Should fix

HC-020 overlaps with six other events, and the plan names none of them. (Learning Outcomes 1 and 4; 20-30, 30-40 and 50-60 blocks; final takeaway)
HC-195, Model Risk Management & The AI Life Cycle (HU, 60 minute lecture, Ready for pilot), is the closest. Its slide 7 says "coherence across the pipeline matters as much as performance at any single step", and HC-020's final takeaway is "designing a good learning system requires coherence across all stages, not only a good model". HC-195 slides 8 and 9 also cover proxy target errors, "Data leakage: future information inadvertently included in training features", feedback loops, and data and concept drift, and slide 17 is a decommissioning gate.
H-132, Typical approach to AI project, which also lists you as first author, has as outcome 1 "Explain the typical lifecycle of an AI project from problem formulation through data collection, modelling, evaluation, implementation, deployment, and monitoring", which is close to HC-020's outcome 1. Its slide 20 says "A trained model is only one component of a deployed AI system", the same point as HC-020's 30-40 bullet "the model is one component inside the larger system".
H-191, Operating AI in Production (Ahmad Khalidi, your Author Person 2; Lesson plan: development), lists "Continuous monitoring and Feedback loops" in its outcomes and "Model Drift$retraining pipelines" in its keywords. That is the content of HC-020's 50-60 block: "concept drift, performance degradation, retraining, feedback loops". H-191 declares HC-019, not HC-020, as its prerequisite.
H-108 outcome 2 lists "the main stages of a machine learning workflow: data collection, data preparation, model training, evaluation, and inference", and H-122 schedules "data splitting, training set, validation set, test set, hyperparameter tuning, data leakage" at 35-60 minutes. HC-022 teaches the validation and test sets in its 20-30 block and on slides 26 and 27.
Fix: Write the division into the plan and name these events where HC-020 points to them. One workable split: HC-020 gives the design view and names the failure modes at introductory level; HC-195 takes risk governance and stage gates; H-132 applies the lifecycle as a project canvas; H-191 covers running models in production; H-108 and H-122 teach splitting and metrics in depth; HC-022 covers generalisation and overfitting. Agree the split with the authors of HC-195 and H-191. Distinctiveness is decided at programme level, so treat this as input to that check.
The prerequisite decision is not stated, and the forward links name no events. (Management information, "Learning Events to be completed before", which renders "None."; Administrative information, "Self-standing: Yes"; 30-40 block: "Briefly connect to later LEs on supervised and unsupervised learning")
"None." matches the docx, so open entry looks deliberate. The plan still uses supervised-learning vocabulary without introducing it: the 0-10 prompt asks what happens "before and after training", and the 20-30 block uses labeling and train/validation/test sets. HC-019, Introduction to Machine Learning: types and tasks (sort number 50, directly before HC-020), teaches supervised and unsupervised learning, classification and regression, and a train and test split in its slide 15 notes, but no validation set. The forward pointer in 30-40 names no code, while the docx names H021 and H022, and HC-023 also declares HC-020.
Fix: Choose one route and write it down. Either keep open entry and add the 2 minute recap of features, label and target to the first block, or add HC-019 to Learning Events to be completed before and set Self-standing to match; we raised the same clash between Self-standing and the prerequisite field on HC-021. Name HC-021, HC-022 and HC-023 by code in the 30-40 and 50-60 blocks.
The data block lists preprocessing before splitting and does not say what must be fitted on training data only. (20-30 block: "data collection, preprocessing, labeling, splitting into train/validation/test sets, and the importance of preventing leakage")
Anything estimated from the data (imputation values, scaling parameters, feature selection, target encoding) that is fitted before the split carries test information into training. Kapoor and Narayanan, "Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science", Patterns 4(9), 100804 (2023), call this leakage type L1.2, "Pre-processing on training and test set". Their survey found leakage affecting 294 papers across 17 fields. Leakage is in outcome 4, and a teacher reading the list in order could teach the steps the wrong way round.
Fix: Say which steps can run before the split (deduplication, format fixes) and which must be fitted on training data only. Name the other leaks students will meet: the same person on both sides of the split, random splits on time-ordered data, and features not available at prediction time. These also give you the spot-the-leak scenarios. Kapoor and Narayanan's taxonomy table is a good teacher reference.
The shift and drift terms are non-standard and split across two blocks. (Learning Outcomes, outcome 4: "train–test mismatch, deployment mismatch"; 40-50 block: "distribution shift and mismatched assumptions"; 50-60 block: "concept drift, performance degradation")
"Train–test mismatch", "deployment mismatch" and "mismatched assumptions" are not terms a student can look up. The standard vocabulary is dataset shift: covariate shift (the inputs change), prior probability or label shift (the class balance changes) and concept shift or drift (the relationship between inputs and outcome changes). See Moreno-Torres et al., "A unifying view on dataset shift in classification", Pattern Recognition 45(1):521-530 (2012). Practitioners also say training-serving skew. Google's Rules of Machine Learning, in the introduction to its Training-Serving Skew section, gives three causes: a discrepancy between how data is handled in the training and serving pipelines, a change in the data between training and serving, and a feedback loop between the model and the algorithm. Rule #37 then measures skew as the gap between training and holdout data, between holdout and next-day data, and between next-day and live data. The monitoring block also lists what goes wrong but not what to watch, and true labels can arrive late: a 30-day readmission label exists only 30 days after discharge.
Fix: Use the standard terms in outcome 4 and in the instructions, and teach shift once, in the merged deployment and monitoring block. Say what can be monitored before labels arrive (input and prediction distributions, data quality checks, alert rates) and what can be checked once they arrive (performance on the delayed labels). Point to HC-195 and H-191 for alert thresholds, owners and retraining.
The formulation questions do not ask who is affected by a wrong prediction. (10-20 block; Learning Outcomes, outcome 2: "intended use context"; 50-60 block: "human oversight")
People affected by the system appear only as "human oversight" in the last block, while the guidelines ask that students understand "how AI in this context impacts people, by design". The standard case fits the plan's own sentence about different formulations. Obermeyer et al., "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations", Science 366(6464):447-453 (2019): a widely used US care-management algorithm predicted healthcare cost as a stand-in for health need. Less is spent on Black patients with the same level of need, so Black patients at a given risk score were considerably sicker than White patients. The authors estimated that correcting it would raise the share of Black patients flagged for extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%. The cause was the choice of cost as the label.
Fix: Use this case in the formulation block with a 2 minute question: what would you predict instead of cost, and what would that label take to collect? Add two formulation questions: who carries a false positive and who carries a false negative, and how can someone contest the output. Point to HC-029 and HC-030 for bias and fairness definitions.
The deployment block names the gap between offline and real-world performance but gives the teacher no case to show it. (40-50 block: "integration into workflow, and the difference between offline evaluation and real-world use")
Two verified cases each take a few minutes. Wong et al., "External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients", JAMA Internal Medicine 181(8):1065-1070 (2021): the developer had reported AUC 0.76 to 0.83; at Michigan Medicine it was 0.63, it alerted on 18% of hospitalisations and it missed 67% of patients with sepsis. Beede et al., "A Human-Centered Evaluation of a Deep Learning System Deployed in Clinics for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy", CHI 2020: in 11 clinics in Thailand about 21% of images were rejected as ungradable, and the paper links this to conditions in the clinics such as lighting, which disrupted the screening workflow. Wong shows a vendor model used widely without local validation. Beede shows an accurate model that did not fit the clinic workflow.
Fix: Add both as teacher references and put one on a slide in the deployment block. Both fit the hospital running example.
The plan does not say what changes when the model is pretrained or bought. (30-40 block: "representation, model choice, training, and evaluation"; docx: "The lecture should remain model-agnostic")
Keeping the lecture model-agnostic is fine. In 2026, though, many teams do not train a model at all: they call a general-purpose model through an API, fine-tune an open-weight model, or buy a vendor product like the sepsis model above. A student who hears "representation, model choice, training" will not know which parts of the pipeline still apply. All of them do, and the design work moves toward problem formulation, local evaluation data and monitoring.
Fix: Add two sentences with one example to the model block, and point to HC-023 and H-014 for language models.
The plan has no legal content, although three of its stages map onto AI Act articles that other events teach. (20-30 and 50-60 blocks; Expected preparation)
For high-risk systems, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Article 10 requires training, validation and testing data sets to be relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose. Article 14(4)(b) requires the system to be provided so that the people assigned to oversight are enabled to remain aware of automation bias. Article 72 requires providers to run post-market monitoring that actively and systematically collects and analyses performance data over the system's lifetime. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026, moved the application dates to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for AI in Annex I products. A hospital risk model that qualifies as a medical device falls under the later date. HC-205's deck already refers to Articles 10, 14 and 72, HC-043 covers Article 14 and automation bias, and HC-215, The Risk-Based Approach and Post-Market Monitoring, is in development.
Fix: Add a dated teacher note that maps the three stages to these articles, gives both dates, and points students to HC-205, HC-043 and HC-215. No extra class time is needed. If the dated AI Act reference block RealAI has asked WP4 to commission is issued, use its wording.
Five outcomes for a 60 minute lecture, and outcome 3 restates outcome 1. (Learning Outcomes 1 and 3)
Outcome 3, "Differentiate ... between model-level thinking and system-level thinking in machine learning applications", is the framing of outcome 1 and of the final takeaway, and no block asks students to differentiate anything.
Fix: Merge outcome 3 into outcome 1 or 5. That leaves four outcomes, each with an activity behind it once the exercises above are in.
No didactic review from the second author is recorded. (Management information, Author Person 2: Ahmad Khalidi (HAW); Talk page)
The Talk page did not exist before this review, and Ahmad Khalidi's only page edit was on 18 May 2026, before the plan text was written. The guidelines make the second-author review one of the two parts of the review process, and it carries the distinctiveness and connections checks.
Fix: Record the second-author review on this Talk page, including the split between HC-020 and H-191.
Smaller things

Title and credits differ between the two versions. Wiki: "Designing a machine learning system". Docx: "Designing a Learning System: From Problem Formulation to Deployment", with Co-author "?" and Reviewer "?". The docx subtitle also stops at deployment while the plan runs to monitoring. Align the docx with the wiki or mark it superseded.
Outcomes 1 and 2 and the 0-10 and 50-60 blocks say "learning system", outcome 5 says "learning pipeline", and the title (LEvTitle) says "machine learning system". Use one term throughout.
The keyword "ML pipelines and architectures" promises architectures, and the plan is deliberately model-agnostic. If the term comes from a fixed programme list, keep it and add the specific keywords next to it.
The 0-10 block defines the pipeline as running "from problem formulation to maintained use". ISO/IEC 22989:2022 includes retirement as a life cycle stage. Add one line to the monitoring block on when to switch a model off or replace it, and point to HC-195's decommissioning gate (slide 17).
When the deck is built: speaker notes on every slide, as in the HC-023 and H-132 decks; the 2 to 4 interactive elements marked on the slides; a references slide; a source line for each borrowed figure or case; and every file named, with its licence, in Lesson materials.
Known template issues RealAI has raised centrally, not the author's fault: Acknowledgements credits the Connecting Europe Facility with "Grant № ???" (PANORAIMA is Digital Europe, grant 101189994), Expected preparation reads "None." on almost every page, and Lesson materials names no file. Please still fill your own fields for HC-020.
Wiki page completeness

learningOutcomes: five outcomes with verb, category and level. Merge outcome 3, use standard shift terms in outcome 4, and make sure each remaining outcome has an activity (see Must fix).
expectedLEs: empty, renders "None.". Keep it only if open entry is the stated choice; otherwise add HC-019 (see Should fix).
keywords: one entry. Suggested: problem formulation$prediction target$unit of prediction$data pipeline$data leakage$training, validation and test sets$model evaluation$false positives and false negatives$batch and real-time inference$training-serving skew$dataset shift$concept drift$model monitoring$feedback loops$human oversight
obligStPrep: empty. For example Sculley et al. (2015), Figure 1 and the section on feedback loops. The paper has no maths but uses engineering vocabulary, so for a job role of "any" give students two or three questions to read it with. If nothing is required, write why.
optionStPrep: empty. For example Huyen (2022), chapters 1 and 2; Paleyes, Urma and Lawrence, "Challenges in Deploying Machine Learning: A Survey of Case Studies", ACM Computing Surveys 55(6), article 114 (2022).
backgrStPrep: empty. For example Kapoor and Narayanan (2023); Obermeyer et al. (2019); Google, Rules of Machine Learning.
recommTePrep: empty. For example Huyen (2022), chapter 6 on model development and offline evaluation and chapter 8 on distribution shifts and monitoring; Moreno-Torres et al. (2012); Wong et al. (2021); Beede et al. (2020); ISO/IEC 22989:2022 and ISO/IEC 23053:2022 for vocabulary; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Articles 10, 14 and 72 with the Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 dates; and the H-108, H-122, H-132 and H-191 plans and the HC-195 deck, so the teacher knows what is covered elsewhere.
ackThx: empty. Add anyone or any source you want credited. The template sentence around it is the central issue noted above.
lessonMaterials: empty. When material exists, list every file by name, with a licence line for any third-party content.
instructions: present, but a timed topic list. Needs the running example, what the teacher says, questions with expected answers, and the exercises (see Must fix).
origContrib and further: empty. Note any figure or case you adapt, for example a redrawn Sculley et al. Figure 1.
mandatory: empty here and on all 34 Horizontal plans RealAI reviews, so we read it as a programme field.
self-standing ("Yes"), jobrole ("any") and status ("Lesson plan: review") are set and valid. Self-standing has to match the prerequisite decision.
Send us the revised plan before the slides are built and we will look at it.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 17 September 2026, 13:41 CEST

entries.title: HC-021 Introduction to Unsupervised Machine Learning
entries.author: BME · Béla Pataki
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (REVISION REQUESTED). The clustering half of this deck is genuinely good teaching, but the deck delivers only one of the four unsupervised task types the lesson plan and learning outcomes promise, runs roughly 15 minutes short of its 60 minute slot, and carries five statements (slides 8, 18, 42, 43) that need correcting before it is taught. 5 must-fix item(s); 10 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8549.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
The clustering half of this deck is genuinely good teaching, but the deck delivers only one of the four unsupervised task types the lesson plan and learning outcomes promise, runs roughly 15 minutes short of its 60 minute slot, and carries five statements (slides 8, 18, 42, 43) that need correcting before it is taught.

What works

Slides 19 to 29, the k-means walkthrough, are the best thing in the deck. Building one run step by step over a single scatter, with the cluster boundaries redrawn each time the centres move, shows students why the reassignment step exists instead of just stating it. Slide 26 is the reason it works: it holds the intermediate state where points are still assigned to a centre that is no longer the closest one. Most.
Slides 9 to 12 are a well-ordered piece of teaching. The deck asks what similar means, answers "depends on the problem" three separate times for colour, text and the cap, and only then produces the weighted distance formula on slide 12. Intuition first, formula second, and it puts the deck's most important message (clustering output is a consequence of analyst choices) in the first fifteen minutes rather than in the.
Three interactive slides (13, 38, 39), each with a worked answer in the speaker notes. This clears the guidelines' 2 to 4 requirement with margin. Slides 38 and 39 are the strongest pair: asking whether k-means at k=5 and single-linkage at a given threshold will agree, then asking what would have to change to make them agree, forces students to reason about the two algorithms' assumptions rather than recall their.
Slide 18's health example, where every parameter sits inside its normal range but the combination is abnormal, is a concrete and practice-accurate illustration of why multivariate anomaly detection is not the same as per-feature thresholding. That distinction is one practitioners actually get wrong, and one sentence on a slide handles it.
Slide 42 is honest about the technical limitations and is close to complete on that side: dependence on the features chosen, dependence on initial conditions with k-means starting centres named explicitly, different algorithms giving different answers, no ground truth for evaluation. Nothing on that list is padding.
What must be fixed before sign-off

Three of the four unsupervised task types named in the learning outcomes are never taught. Dimensionality reduction gets one clause on slide 17 and one bullet each on slides 18 and 40. Representation learning gets the. (Whole deck; the gap is clearest between slide 18 and slide 40. Against wiki 'Instructions for teachers' blocks 10-20, 30-40 and 40-50 minutes.)
Learning outcome 2 asks students to differentiate between clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection and representation learning, and outcome 3 asks them to describe how unsupervised methods organize, compress or summarize data. A student cannot differentiate between four things after being shown one. The plan also assigns a full 10 minute block to dimensionality reduction and another to anomaly detection plus representation learning, and there are no slides for either. The plan's 10-20 minute block,.
Fix: Add a task-type overview slide after slide 8 that names the four types and what each one is for, matching the plan's 10-20 minute block. Then add roughly 8 to 10 slides: two or three on dimensionality reduction (compression and visualisation as distinct goals, PCA as the linear workhorse, t-SNE or UMAP as the exploration tool with a warning that distances between clusters in a.
Slide 8's first example is the beer-and-diapers story, presented as fact, attributed to the early days of webshops, and labelled as clustering. All three are wrong. The anecdote traces to a 1992 NCR/Teradata study of. (Slide 8, titled 'Examples of Unsupervised Clustering'. All four bullets.)
This is the first content example students meet and it sets their mental model of what clustering is. Three of the four examples are not clustering, so the slide teaches the wrong boundary for the technique. The beer-and-diapers claim is also unsourced and unverifiable as stated, and the deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so the error gets copied onward with the consortium's name on it. The gendered gloss ('one for their wives, the other for themselves') is an unsourced stereotype sitting in the opening example of.
Fix: Retitle the slide 'Examples of unsupervised learning' and label each bullet with its actual task type, which also does useful work for learning outcome 2. Either drop the beer-and-diapers story or keep it and say plainly that it is data mining folklore whose famous version did not happen, cite Agrawal, Imielinski and Swami, SIGMOD 1993, for association rule mining, and drop.
Slide 42 says 'Biased grouping prohibited by the AI Act, e.g. grouping on skin colour, or sexual orientation, etc.' The AI Act does not contain a general prohibition on biased grouping. Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation. (Slide 42, second bullet.)
This is the only legal claim in the deck, on a programme whose slides are expected to cover the legal dimension, and it is both overbroad and pointed at the wrong example. A student who takes this away will believe the AI Act polices clustering generally, and will not know which instrument actually applies to the case in front of them. No article is cited, so a lecturer cannot check it and a student cannot follow it up.
Fix: Split the bullet in two. First: biometric categorisation to infer sensitive characteristics is prohibited under Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, in force since 2 February 2025, and note the labelling and filtering exception. Second, and more useful for this deck: the practice risk in clustering is proxy discrimination, where a model that never sees a protected.
Slide 18 says Semmelweis discovered that puerperal fever was rare among street births compared with clinic births, that this showed him two important groups, and that 'he didn't know the exact cause'. The last part is. (Slide 18, first bullet block.)
The analogy the slide wants (grouping reveals structure without explaining it) is a good one, but it is built on a version of the history that is inaccurate on both the comparison and the outcome. BME is in Budapest and Semmelweis is the example students in the room are most likely to already know, so getting it loose is conspicuous. It also weakens the point: Semmelweis is a better example of what happens after clustering, when someone forms and tests a causal hypothesis about why the groups differ.
Fix: Rewrite as two sentences. The mortality gap between the doctors' clinic and the midwives' clinic was the observed structure, and the structure alone did not say why. Semmelweis then formed a hypothesis about material carried from the autopsy room and tested it with chlorinated lime handwashing, cutting mortality from about 98 to about 13 per 1,000. That is the honest version.
The closing summary reads as boilerplate carried over from a supervised learning deck and was not adapted. It lists 'Imbalanced data set' and 'Noise in the examples (input or output noise)' as problems. There is no. (Slide 43, both halves.)
This is the last slide students see and the one they copy into their notes, and it contradicts the definition the deck gave on slide 6. The lesson plan's 50-60 minute block ends on 'unsupervised learning is about discovering potentially useful structure, not recovering a single ground truth answer'. That sentence appears nowhere on the slides. Slide 42 gets close with 'we don't have ground truth' but the deck then closes on the wrong note.
Fix: Rewrite slide 43 against slide 6. Drop 'output noise' and either drop 'imbalanced data set' or restate it as what it means here, which is that k-means splits large clusters and merges small ones when cluster sizes are very unequal. Replace 'Different AI models could (and should) be used' with the concrete version: run more than one algorithm and more than one parameter.
Also noted on the second pass

Slide 31 states something the deck's own algorithm then contradicts, and this is a harder technical error than the Semmelweis point the review led with. Slide 31: 'Define distance limit. Two elements could only be in the same cluster if their distance is less than the limit.' Slides 32 to 36 then merge the two closest elements or clusters whenever that pair is within the limit, which is single linkage. Under that.
The deck does not credit its second author. Slide 1 says only 'Béla Pataki, BME'. The wiki lists Author Organisation 2 UNINA and Author Person 2 Stefano Marrone. Neither name appears anywhere in the 45 slides. This is a plan and material disagreement with teeth, because the deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and downstream users attribute from the title slide. Either add the second author to slide 1 or, if Marrone did.
Slide 7 is where the scope problem starts and the review never names it. 'Basic Goal of Unsupervised Learning: We look for groups where there is a high degree of similarity... Clustering.' The deck defines the goal of unsupervised learning as clustering, and slide 8 follows with the title 'Examples of Unsupervised Clustering'. must_fix 1 points at the gap between slides 18 and 40 but gives the author no single slide.
The wiki contradicts itself in a way the review did not catch. Administrative information says 'Self-standing: Yes' while Management information lists 'Learning Events to be completed before: HC-020_Designing_a_machine_learning_system'. The review flagged the separate contradiction between that prerequisite and the four 'None.' entries under Expected preparation, but not this one. Both need resolving in the same.
Smaller fixes

Slide 2 says students will 'Understand' the core idea. The wiki says 'Explain (knowledge, intermediate level)'. Align the slide to the wiki, and note that 'understand' is not a verb you can assess.
Slides 14 to 17 carry the same speaker note pasted four times, with 'grpoups' misspelled on slides 14 and 15 and corrected on 16 and 17. The note also describes two clusters and some outliers, which is not yet true on slide 14, where the figure only sets up the five-person table. Give each build.
Slides 19 to 37 have no speaker notes at all. That is 19 build slides carrying short captions and a lot of visual state. This is precisely where a lecturer who did not write the deck needs a script: what the animation is showing, what to say while it moves, what students usually ask. One note per.
Feature scaling is never mentioned. Slides 19 to 30 use body mass against height as the running example, which is the textbook case where unscaled Euclidean distance is driven by whichever variable has the larger numeric spread. The deck handles this implicitly through the weighted distance on.
Slide 17's colour axis is ordered White, Blue, Red, Yellow, Green, Black. That ordering is arbitrary, so any horizontal distance a student reads off the figure is an artefact of a choice the author made. Slide 17 then draws a real conclusion from that figure, that height can be dropped from the.
Name the algorithms. Slide 3 and slides 30 to 37 say 'bottom-up'; the standard names are agglomerative hierarchical clustering and, for the specific merge rule used on slide 34, single linkage. Students who go looking for 'bottom-up clustering' will not find the library function. Worth adding that.
Slide 20 says the starting centres are chosen randomly and slide 42 flags dependence on them, which is good. Add one sentence naming k-means++ and multiple restarts. It matters practically: scikit-learn's current default is init='k-means++' with n_init='auto', which resolves to a single run, so the.
Nothing in the deck says how to choose k or the distance limit. Slide 41 says it is promising when you already know how many clusters to expect, which in practice you usually do not. Add the standard options (elbow, silhouette, gap statistic) or at least the honest version, that you run several.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 10 items in total. The notable results:

Beer and diapers (slide 8). Traced to a 1992 NCR/Teradata study for American Stores' Osco Drug by Thomas Blischok and Karen Heath over about 1.2 million market baskets from roughly 25 stores; a beer and diapers co-occurrence in the 5-7pm window was observed. The famous follow-on, that Osco moved the products together.
Unabomber (slide 8). Verified and essentially correct as stated. Ted Kaczynski, American domestic terrorist. The manifesto was published in the Washington Post in September 1995 specifically in the hope that someone would recognise the writing style; his brother David Kaczynski recognised phrases including.
Semmelweis (slide 18). Verified against the James Lind Library's account. First clinic (medical students) mortality 98.4 per 1,000 births 1840-1846 against second clinic (midwives) 36.2 per 1,000. Handwashing in chloride of lime introduced May 1847 following Kolletschka's death; first clinic mortality 12.7 per 1,000.
EU AI Act, biased grouping (slide 42). Checked against Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and against Commission implementation guidance coverage. The prohibition is on AI systems that categorise natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union.
AI Act timing. Confirmed that Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, deferring the Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 and the Annex I embedded-systems date to 2 August 2028, and that the Article 5.
Funding details (slide 44 and wiki). Grant agreement number 101189994 verified as PANORAIMA, running January 2025 to January 2029, under call topic DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU. One error, and it is programme-level boilerplate rather than this author's: both slide 44 and the wiki acknowledgement say the project.
Plan against material
"They agree on the first third and diverge sharply after that.\n\nWhere they agree. The plan's 0-10 minute block (intuitive examples, define unlabeled data, contrast with supervised) maps cleanly onto slides 4 to 8. The 20-30 block (clustering as grouping similar examples, similarity and distance, results depend on representation and assumptions) maps onto slides 9 to 18 and is arguably the best-executed part of the deck. The plan's requirement that students see representation dependence is met three times over on slides 10, 11 and 17.\n\nWhere they diverge. The plan's 10-20 minute block introduces the four task types and explains what each tries to achieve. No slide does this; slide 3 lists them in the agenda and the deck moves on. The 30-40 block is dimensionality reduction with simple motivating examples; the deck has no dimensionality reduction slides, only feature selection framed as omitting an unhelpful axis (slide 17) and a bullet on slide 40. The 40-50 block is anomaly detection and representation learning; the deck covers anomalies incidentally as clustering residue and.

Coverage
"As written this deck does not fill 60 minutes, and it does not deliver learning outcomes 2 and 3.\n\nOn timing. Forty-five slides sits inside the guidelines' 30 to 60 range, but the raw count is misleading here. Slides 19 to 29 are eleven build steps of a single k-means run, and slides 30 to 37 are eight build steps of a single hierarchical run. Those 19 slides are two worked examples, not 19 minutes of content; a lecturer will get through them in 12 to 15 minutes. Slides 14 to 17 are another four-step build of one figure. Counting build sequences as the single slides they are, the deck has roughly 25 distinct pieces of content. My estimate is 40 to 45 minutes as written, including the three interactive slides at three to four minutes each. The 15 minute shortfall lines up almost exactly.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What must be fixed before sign-off' need addressing, after which we will re-review. Everything else here is offered as improvement, not as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

Thanks, Terry. 
That’s really useful. I’ll go through it and make changes where necessary.
Béla
