entries.title: HC-022 Introduction to Supervised Machine Learning
entries.author: BME · Béla Pataki
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (REVISION REQUESTED). The content is accurate and unusually well designed for an intro lecture, but the teacher guide points at the wrong slide numbers, the wiki timeline runs in a different order from the deck, and the best exercise in the deck (slide 20) has no answer key, so a lecturer other than the author cannot teach this as delivered. 7 must-fix item(s); 11 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8550.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
The content is accurate and unusually well designed for an intro lecture, but the teacher guide points at the wrong slide numbers, the wiki timeline runs in a different order from the deck, and the best exercise in the deck (slide 20) has no answer key, so a lecturer other than the author cannot teach this as delivered.

What works

Slides 17 to 19 show an actual decision tree training step: an incorrect case arrives (C195, kidney problem), a new test is added, the tree grows, and the slide names the two things a training step decides (which parameter to test, and what limit to use). Most introductory decks show a finished tree and call that training. This is the best content in the deck and it is worth protecting in any revision.
Slide 20 is well constructed. In the nine row table, Country is the only feature that separates the labels perfectly (all Greece rows +, all Czechia and Hungary rows -), while interest rate ranges overlap between Greece and Czechia and neither Management changes nor Stock buybacks separates anything. A student can read the table in thirty seconds and reach the conclusion themselves. This is shortcut learning taught.
Slide 27 teaches a real practitioner failure mode that intro courses almost never cover: training, validation and test sets drawn from different subpopulations (cities, towns, villages) give a performance number that means nothing. Naming this at intro level is good judgement.
Slide 22 does the class imbalance point with explicit arithmetic (6/100 = 0.06) rather than hand-waving. Students see why a low average error can be worthless.
Slide 9 puts interpretability and human-AI interaction early, before any technical content, and frames it around what a person can and cannot reconstruct about a trained model. That placement suits a human-centred programme and it is a deliberate choice, not filler.
What must be fixed before sign-off

The ForTeachers PDF suggests breaks after slide 10 ("Tell your opinion #1") and slide 17 ("Tell your opinion #2"). The two "Tell your opinion!" slides are actually 13 and 20. (HC-022_ForTeachers_IntroductionToSupervisedLearinng.pdf, break suggestions and the ambiguity note)
The numbers are off by exactly three, which is consistent with the PDF being written before slides 1 to 3 (title, learning outcomes, session overview) were added to the front. A lecturer following the PDF pauses on slide 10 (the classification definition) and slide 17 (the first decision tree slide) instead of on the two discussion slides. Worse, the PDF's answer note about the classification versus regression ambiguity would be applied to slide 10, which contains nothing ambiguous. The one piece of guidance a.
Fix: Change 10 to 13 and 17 to 20 in the PDF. Add the slide titles as well as the numbers so the guide survives the next edit to the deck.
The wiki "Instructions for teachers" runs the session in a different order from the deck. The wiki puts training, validation, testing and generalization in the 20 to 30 minute block and the challenges (overfitting,. (Wiki, Instructions for teachers, the 20-30 and 40-50 blocks)
A lecturer who was not involved in writing this cannot follow the wiki timings against this deck. The deck's order is the better one, because overfitting on slides 23 to 25 motivates the validation split on slide 26 rather than arriving after it. Slide 9 is one of the stronger parts of the deck and it is invisible in the plan, so a lecturer working from the wiki may skip it.
Fix: Rewrite the wiki blocks to match the deck, not the other way round. A workable version: 0-10 slides 4 to 8; 10-15 slide 9 (human-AI interaction); 15-25 slides 10 to 13 including discussion 1; 25-30 slide 14; 30-40 slides 15 to 20 including discussion 2; 40-50 slides 21 to 25; 50-60 slides 26 to 28. Put slide number ranges in the wiki blocks so the mapping is checkable.
Slide 20 (the stock price table) has no model answer anywhere. The ForTeachers PDF covers only the first discussion. (Slide 20, and the ForTeachers PDF which stops after discussion 1)
This is the most valuable exercise in the deck and the answer is not obvious under time pressure. The intended point is that Country is the only feature that separates the labels cleanly, so the model learns "Greece means up" and nothing about finance. A lecturer who did not build the table will either miss that or, worse, let students land on interest rates, which do not separate the classes (Greece 1.5 to 2.2 overlaps Czechia 1.45 to 2.3). Without an answer key the exercise gets cut, and then the session runs.
Fix: Add a note to the ForTeachers PDF: the model learns Country as the sole predictor; no other single feature splits the nine rows; this is a proxy or shortcut feature with no causal link to the target; ask students what happens when a Greek company with a bad quarter arrives. One extra sentence connecting this to proxy features in credit and hiring decisions would earn the.
Slide 4 opens the lecture with the chess example: the child moves, the supervisor says "good move" or "bad move", the slide adds "You don't tell him why!", and after thousands of games the child plays well. That is. (Slide 4)
Sutton and Barto draw the supervised versus reinforcement line at exactly this point. Evaluative feedback tells the learner how good the action taken was without indicating the best action; instructive feedback gives the correct output for the input. Slide 4 describes evaluative feedback on a chosen action, and chess is their standard illustration of it. This is the first thing students see in the lecture, and any student who later meets reinforcement learning hits a direct contradiction. Slide 5 (the journalist).
Fix: Either reframe slide 4 as "given this position and this move, predict good or bad", which makes it supervised, or keep the example and add one line saying that learning to play from good and bad feedback alone is reinforcement learning, and that the supervised version is predicting the label for a position and move you are handed. One sentence is enough. Add a matching line to.
Slide 2 states learning outcome 4 as "data quality, label quality, and overfitting". The wiki learning outcome reads "data quality, label quality, feature representation, and overfitting". Feature representation has. (Slide 2, bullet 4, against the wiki Management information learning outcomes)
The wiki is the record the programme is assessed against, so the two must agree. The concept is present by example (slide 19 chooses which parameter to test, slide 21 learns flowers instead of the dog, slide 20 learns Country instead of finance) but it is never named, so students cannot connect the three examples to a single idea they will meet again.
Fix: Cheapest fix: put "feature representation" back into slide 2, and add one line on slide 21 naming what the three examples have in common (the model learns whatever feature separates the training data, not the feature you meant it to use). If the author would rather not cover it, amend the wiki outcome instead, but do not leave the two disagreeing.
Slide 2's final bullet, "Why is it important to understand basics of supervised learning, when you use AI tools", is listed under "Students will be able to" but no slide answers it. Slide 9 and the last bullet of slide. (Slide 2, final bullet; nothing in slides 4 to 28 delivers it)
This is a horizontal lecture with job role "any", so a good share of students will meet supervised learning only as users of AI tools rather than as builders. The deck promises them the answer and does not give it. There is also a currency gap behind the promise. The workflow taught here (collect labelled examples, train from scratch, stop on the validation curve) is the picture a practitioner would have recognised ten years ago. In 2026 most people meet supervised learning as fine-tuning or adapting an existing.
Fix: Add one closing slide before the summary answering the slide 2 promise directly. Three points would do it: the labelled examples someone collected still determine what the tool can and cannot do; the training, validation and test split is why a vendor's accuracy number may not hold on your data; and the interpretability problem from slide 9 is why you cannot ask the tool why.
Two problems in the back matter. First, slide 30 states that "All materials are made available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0" with no carve-out, while the deck contains third party photographs. Only slides 11 and 14 carry a. (Slides 29 and 30, plus the uncredited images on slides 12, 15, 16 and 21)
A CC licence only covers the rights the licensor actually holds. Creative Commons is explicit that third party content cannot be swept in, and its own guidance recommends the wording "Except where otherwise noted, this work is available under [licence]" with the excluded elements marked. The Unsplash License permits the use but does not let a third party relicense the photo under ShareAlike. These decks are meant to be copied onward, so a blanket claim that is not true of every element is a real problem for.
Fix: Change slide 30's opening line to "Except where otherwise noted, all materials are made available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0", and add a source line to every photograph and figure that does not have one (slides 12, 15, 16, 21). Then check whether the images on slides 15, 16 and 21 are the author's own or third party, since the licence position differs. On the funder wording: this.
Also noted on the second pass

The deck has no speaker notes on any slide. Zero. This is the single strongest piece of evidence for the review's own headline claim and it is not in the review. The consortium format scan requires that lecture slides 'contain lecturer notes that make the slides usable for a lecturer who was not involved in developing the material'. HC-021, by the same author in the same batch, does have notes, including a full.
Slide 3, the deck's own session overview, contradicts the deck's delivery order. It lists 'Generalization: Training, Validation, Testing' fifth, before 'Training steps using different models' and 'Basic Problems', but the deck delivers generalization last on slides 26-27. It also omits both discussion slides. This is a plan-material mismatch entirely inside the deck, and it is the piece of evidence that decides.
No source is given anywhere for the two clinical decision thresholds the deck presents as fact: systolic BP > 140 mmHg on slides 17 and 18, and protein in urine > 150 mg on slide 19. The reviewer verified both thresholds themselves and then did not ask the author to cite either. Under our own standing rule, a threshold presented on a slide that ships under CC BY-NC-SA and gets copied onward needs a source line. The.
Related practice-lens gap on the same slides: slides 17 to 19 present a triage decision tree that outputs 'Heart problem', 'Broken arm', 'Kidney problem' and 'Diarrhea' from two or three parameters, with no line saying it is illustrative and not a clinical algorithm. In a human-centred programme, with a CC-licensed deck built by a computer-aided-diagnosis researcher, one sentence of caveat is cheap and its absence.
Smaller fixes

Slide 16: the title is truncated to "Basic Workflow of Supervised". Missing "Learning". This is on screen for students.
Slide 20: the header says "predict stock prices" but the labels are + and -, which makes it a binary classification. Slide 11 gave stock price prediction as its example of regression. Students meet the contradiction seven slides after being taught the distinction. Reword slide 20 to "predict.
Slide 19: "Protein in urine > 150 mg" needs a time basis. Write "> 150 mg/24 h". The number itself is right.
Slide 25 appears in the extracted text as a duplicate of slide 24 with the "Noisy border" label removed. Confirm it carries a different figure. If it does not, delete it.
Slide 2 uses "Understand" for outcomes 1 and 3 where the wiki uses "Explain" and "Describe". The wiki verbs are the assessable ones. Match the slide to the wiki.
Slide 2's final bullet is a sentence fragment sitting under "Students will be able to" and has no question mark. Reformat it as a question or move it out of the outcomes list.
Slide 26 presents the validation set only as a stopping criterion. In practice it is used mostly for model and hyperparameter selection, and "when to stop" is not the main use for several of the model families on slides 15 to 19. One sentence would widen it correctly.
Cross-validation is never named. With small datasets, which is the situation the deck describes on slide 21, a single fixed three-way split is not what practitioners do. One line on slide 26 is enough at this level.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 11 items in total. The notable results:

Grant 101189994 and call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU (slide 29): the grant number and call ID are correct, project duration January 2025 to January 2029. But the call sits under the Digital Europe Programme, not the Connecting Europe Facility as slide 29 and the wiki both state. Confirmed against the EU Funding.
Supervised versus reinforcement learning framing of the chess example (slide 4): checked against Sutton and Barto's evaluative versus instructive feedback distinction. Evaluative feedback tells the learner how good the action taken was without indicating the best action; instructive feedback gives the correct action.
Systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg as a decision threshold (slides 17 and 18): current. The 2024 ESC guideline keeps hypertension at office BP at or above 140/90 mmHg, and added a new "elevated BP" band of 120-139/70-89 mmHg below it. The slide's threshold is not outdated.
Protein in urine above 150 mg (slide 19): the value is correct. Normal urinary protein excretion is below 150 mg per 24 hours and proteinuria is defined above that. The slide omits the time basis; see smaller fixes.
"Dutch Spaniel" (slide 21): I checked this expecting an error and did not find one. Dutch Spaniel and Dutch Decoy Spaniel are both recognised alternative names for the Kooikerhondje (Nederlandse Kooikerhondje). No change needed. Puli is correctly a Hungarian breed.
"Photo by Gabor Koszegi on Unsplash" (slides 11 and 14): the photographer exists on Unsplash (@gabor_koszegi, landscape photographer, around 250 photos). The credit is real and correctly formed. Attribution is not required by the Unsplash License but the author gave it anyway, which is good practice.
Plan against material
["They agree on scope and outcomes and disagree on order and on one outcome element.", "Agreement: the wiki lists five learning outcomes and slide 2 carries all five in the same sequence. Every topic the wiki names is present in the deck, with two exceptions noted below. Duration, type, track and job role match. The deck correctly contains no cross-references to other learning events, which is what the guidelines ask for (references to other LEs belong in the lesson plan, not the slides), and the HC-020 prerequisite is recorded in the wiki where it should be.", "Disagreement 1, order. The wiki's six ten-minute blocks put training, validation, testing and generalization at 20 to 30 minutes and the challenges at 40 to 50. The deck runs workflow (slide 14), model families (15 to 20), problems (21 to 25), then validation and test (26 to 27). The deck is right and the wiki should be changed. Putting overfitting before the validation split is the better sequence because it gives students a reason to care about the split.", "Disagreement 2, an unscheduled segment. Slide 9, Effect on.

Coverage
The deck is 30 slides, of which 25 are content (slides 4 to 28) once the title, outcomes, overview, acknowledgement and disclaimer slides are removed. That is below the guidelines' rule of thumb of 30 to 60 slides for a lecture-based learning event, and the effective count is lower still because slides 15 and 16 are one build, 17 to 19 are one build, and 23 to 25 are another. That leaves roughly 20 distinct content beats. Timing verdict: it fills 60 minutes only if both discussion slides are run properly at five minutes or more each. Straight lecture delivery of slides 4 to 28 comes in nearer 45 minutes. The risk is concrete rather than theoretical, because the second discussion (slide 20) has no answer key, so a lecturer who did not write it is likely to cut it short, and then the.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What must be fixed before sign-off' need addressing, after which we will re-review. Everything else here is offered as improvement, not as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

Thanks, Terry. That’s really useful. I’ll go through it and make changes where necessary. Béla

action_summary.text:
Béla and Stefano, this is the short, actionable version of our review of 9 September 2026; the full text stays above as the record. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: Major revision. The content is accurate, but a lecturer who did not write it cannot teach it as delivered.

Please do next:
# Correct the ForTeachers PDF break suggestions from slides 10 and 17 to slides 13 and 20, with slide titles.
# Add a model answer for slide 20 to the ForTeachers PDF: Country is the only feature that separates the labels.
# Rewrite the wiki "Instructions for teachers" blocks in deck order, with slide ranges, including slide 9.
# Reframe slide 4 (chess) as predicting a label for a given position and move, or state that it is reinforcement learning.
# Match slide 2 outcome 4 to the wiki ("feature representation"), and add a closing slide answering the final bullet of slide 2.
# Change slide 30 to "Except where otherwise noted", and add source lines to the images on slides 12, 15, 16 and 21.
# Add speaker notes to every slide, and change "Connecting Europe Facility" to "Digital Europe Programme" on slide 29.

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):
* Expected preparation: all four fields say "None".
* Lesson materials: add links to the deck and the ForTeachers PDF.
* Acknowledgements: replace "Grant № ???" with 101189994, and change the programme to Digital Europe Programme.

A short summary is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off.

When the items are done, tell us on this Discussion page and email the review inbox, so we can re-review.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 14 October 2026, 20:54 CEST

entries.title: HC-023 Introduction to Natural Language Processing
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (signed off with minor fixes). A genuinely good 60-minute breadth lecture on NLP that matches its lesson plan block for block and is teachable by someone who did not write it; three one-line corrections are needed first, the most important being an author credit that disagrees with the wiki and an EU funding instrument that is named wrongly on the acknowledgement slide. 3 must-fix item(s); 11 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8546.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
A genuinely good 60-minute breadth lecture on NLP that matches its lesson plan block for block and is teachable by someone who did not write it; three one-line corrections are needed first, the most important being an author credit that disagrees with the wiki and an EU funding instrument that is named wrongly on the acknowledgement slide.

What works

Slide 30, "Neural =/= LLM", is the best slide in the deck and the most useful one for professional practice. It separates neural NLP from LLMs using two concrete counterexamples, embedding models (including cross-modal ones such as CLIP) and single-task focused classifiers. Conflating the two is the misconception that produces bad build decisions and inflated inference bills in real projects. I do not often see it.
Slide 29, "Old school, still cool", is the corrective a mixed audience needs. A regular expression for phone numbers and Naive Bayes for spam are the right two examples. The speaker note question, "your project has 200 labelled examples and a lawyer who must explain every decision, what do you build?", is a real procurement conversation compressed into one sentence.
Slide 33, "When is NLP the right tool?", is where learning outcome 5 actually gets rehearsed rather than asserted. Three suitability questions plus three standing risks (bias, privacy, human in the loop), and the speaker note works a patient-message triage case through all three questions rather than reading bullets. The note also tells the lecturer this slide must not be dropped for time and names a task slide to.
The speaker notes are the strongest part of the material. Each agenda slide states which block it opens and what the block must achieve. Slide 12's note names Translation and Dialogue Systems as the two slides to compress when running behind. Slide 24's note tells the lecturer explicitly not to go into word2vec or transformer mechanics. A lecturer who was not involved in developing this deck can pick it up and teach.
Slide 28's note flags its own simplification: the pros and cons columns are approximations, and some statistical methods need no labels at all (n-gram language models are given as the example). That is accurate and intellectually honest, and it is rare in an intro deck.
What to fix before this is taught

The title slide credits Matyas Antal and Andras Gezsi. The wiki Management information section lists Author Person 1 as Andras Gezsi (BME) and Author Person 2 as Ahmad Khalidi (HAW). Matyas Antal does not appear on the. (Slide 1 (title page), against wiki section "Management information")
These decks ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and get copied onward. Attribution is a licence term, not a formality. One of the two records is wrong and neither the lecturer nor a downstream reuser can tell which. It also makes the second-author didactic review trail unclear, since the wiki names Ahmad Khalidi in that slot.
Fix: Decide who the co-author is and make slide 1 and the wiki Management information section say the same names and organisations. If both people contributed, list both in both places.
The acknowledgement text states the project is "co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union" while naming call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU and grant agreement 101189994. Those two. (Slide 37 (Acknowledgements), and wiki section "Acknowledgements, thanks")
This is a public deliverable of an EU-funded project, redistributed under an open licence. Naming the wrong funding instrument in a mandatory acknowledgement is a reporting and compliance problem, not a typo, and it propagates to every copy. The wiki placeholder "???" is separately visible to anyone reading the lesson plan.
Fix: Change "Connecting Europe Facility" to "Digital Europe Programme" in the acknowledgement paragraph, and fill the grant number into the wiki (101189994). This is consortium boilerplate rather than the author's own wording, so raise it with the coordinator so the corrected text is applied across all Learning Events rather than only this one. Do not let this item alone hold up.
Slide 31 states as a flat bullet that LLMs "Understand meaning, context and real-world knowledge". Slide 32 then lists "Still not perfect understanding of context" and "Hallucinations" as dangers. The deck asserts and. (Slide 31 ("The era of LLMs"), bullet 2)
"LLMs understand meaning and real-world knowledge" is the precise misconception a responsible AI programme exists to correct, and it is the claim that leads practitioners to deploy a model into a decision where a confident fabrication does damage. Stated without qualification on a slide that students photograph, it outweighs the correction on the next slide. It also sits badly with slide 19's note, which tells the lecturer that LLMs answer even when the answer is not in the source.
Fix: Reword to something the deck can defend, for example "Encode a great deal of context and world knowledge from training data, without any guarantee of correctness". One line, no restructuring. Keep bullets 1 and 3 as they are.
Also noted on the second pass

Block 6 has no agenda slide and no agenda entry, and it is the block carrying learning outcome 5. The agenda list on slides 4, 8, 12, 21 and 27 has five bullets ending at "How approaches evolved". Nothing on it covers slides 31 to 35 (LLMs, dangers, when NLP is the right tool, discussion, takeaways). Slide 2's note tells the lecturer to say the recurring agenda means "people always know where they are", which stops.
Slide 19 body text is ungrammatical on a projected, student-facing bullet: "Like summarization, requires both to understanding and generation". Should read "requires both understanding and generation". The review quotes slide 19's speaker note in two separate places and still missed the error on the slide itself. Worth catching, because the second author's format scan may not reach content-level wording.
Wiki Administrative information records "Self-standing: Yes" while Management information lists two Learning Events to be completed before (HC-020, HC-022), and slide 1's note repeats both as prerequisites. One of those two wiki fields is wrong. This belongs alongside the review's existing plan-versus-material items 2 and 4, since it is the same section of the wiki and the same author fixes it in one pass.
Slide 3 objective 5 truncates the wiki outcome. Slide reads "Evaluate whether a real-world language problem is suitable for NLP"; wiki outcome 5 reads "...and what kinds of limitations or risks may arise". The dropped half is precisely the half slide 33 delivers, and slide 33's own note quotes the outcome in full. The review flagged objective 3's verb and stopped there. Same one-line fix, same slide.
Smaller fixes

Slide footer numbering is out by three against the deck's own index. Slides 1, 11, 26 and 33 have no footer number (they use the two-column layout, which appears to lack the placeholder), so the printed numbers drift: slide 12 shows 11, slide 27 shows 25, slide 34 shows 31, and the final slide.
Slide 2: the index entries read "37 Acknowledgements (mandatory)" and "38 Disclaimer (mandatory)". "(mandatory)" is an internal production label and it is on a student-facing slide. Delete both parentheticals.
Retrieval-augmented generation is never named. Slide 19's note says finding the right source is hard, and slide 30's note says embedding models are used in search and retrieval everywhere. Those two sentences describe RAG without giving it its name, and RAG is how most organisations actually deploy.
No regulatory anchor anywhere in the deck. Nothing stated is out of date, because no regulation is cited, but for a human-centred AI programme this is a gap the reviewer role should flag. Two cheap additions, both current as of today: on slide 20 (Dialogue Systems), note that in the EU a system.
Slide 3, objective 3: change "Understand" to "Describe" to match the wiki outcome. "Understand" is not an assessable verb.
Slide 36, Eisenstein entry: add the year and note the format. It is Jacob Eisenstein, Introduction to Natural Language Processing, MIT Press, 2019 (ISBN 9780262042840). It sits between three free resources without any signal that it is a paid book, which will frustrate students. A pre-publication.
Slide 30 names CLIP with no source. On an intro slide a model name does not need an academic citation, but since the deck is redistributed, add it to slide 36: Radford et al., "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision", ICML 2021 (PMLR v139), arXiv:2103.00020.
Slide 29's note says Naive Bayes "still filters spam at enormous scale". Defensible as a teaching statement, and Bayesian filters are still standard components in open-source mail stacks, but the largest mail providers moved to neural ensembles years ago. Soften to "is still deployed as a cheap.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 11 items in total. The notable results:

Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft, web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/. Fetched, HTTP 200. Still a draft; the current release on the page is dated 19 August 2026. Chapter 1 is "Introduction" and chapter 2 is "Words and Tokens". Slide 36's pointer to chapters 1 to 2 as the match for.
Eisenstein, Introduction to Natural Language Processing. Verified: Jacob Eisenstein, MIT Press, 2019, ISBN 9780262042840, Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series. Author and publisher on slide 36 are correct. Year and ISBN are absent from the slide.
Hugging Face LLM Course, huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter1/1. Fetched, HTTP 200, page live. Hugging Face's own text says the course originally focused on NLP and has evolved to emphasise LLMs. Slide 36's phrasing "successor to their NLP course" is a fair description of that, so no correction needed.
spaCy displaCy entity demo, demos.explosion.ai/displacy-ent. HTTP 200, page live, and it is the named entity visualiser the slide describes. No deprecation or redirect notice found. Safe to keep recommending.
CLIP (slide 30). Verified as Radford et al., "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision", ICML 2021, PMLR volume 139, arXiv:2103.00020. It is correctly used on the slide as an example of a model spanning image and text. No citation is given anywhere in the deck.
PANORAIMA funding. Verified that grant agreement 101189994 is a Digital Europe Programme project under call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU (DIGITAL-SKILLS-5), managed by HaDEA, running 01/01/2025 to 31/01/2029, coordinated by Stichting Hogeschool Utrecht, 16 partners. The DIGITAL- call prefix is Digital Europe.
Plan against material
"They agree on substance, and the agreement is unusually tight. The plan's six ten-minute blocks map onto the deck one for one, and the deck marks each transition with a repeated agenda slide plus a speaker note naming the block and its time window. 0 to 10 (intro, definition, why language is hard as a data type) is slides 5 to 7. 10 to 20 (ambiguity, synonymy, polysemy, compositionality, context, variability) is slides 9 to 11, and slide 10 uses exactly the plan's vocabulary. 20 to 30 (the seven task families) is slides 13 to 20, all seven present and in the plan's order. 30 to 40 (tokens, features, bag of words, embeddings, representation determines what can be learned) is slides 22 to 26, including the plan's emphasis point as its own slide (25). 40 to 50 (rule-based, statistical, neural, what each contributes and where each is limited) is slides 28 to 30. 50 to 60 (LLMs placed in context without depth, summary, closing takeaway) is slides 31 to 35, and slide 35's note even reuses the plan's closing formulation about making language computable without throwing away the.

Coverage
"Yes on both counts, with one timing risk worth naming.\n\nLength. 38 slides for 60 minutes, inside the 30 to 60 guideline. Of those, nine carry no teaching load (title, index, five agenda slides, acknowledgements, disclaimer) and take about three minutes between them. Four interactive elements consume 12 to 13 minutes by the notes' own budgets (2 + 3 + 3 + 4 to 5). That leaves roughly 44 minutes for 25 substantive slides, about 1.7 minutes each. Comfortable, not padded.\n\nOutcomes. All five are delivered and four of them are rehearsed rather than only stated. Outcome 1 lands on slide 6. Outcome 2 gets seven slides and is tested implicitly on slide 34's note, which asks each contributor to name the task family their example belongs to. Outcome 3 gets slides 9 to 11 and is tested at slide.

Bottom line
We are happy to sign this off. The items above are worth doing before it is taught, but none of them needs to come back to us for another round.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: HC-040 Explainability, Right to Explanation, XAI
entries.author: BME · András Gézsi
entries.review_note: Material reviewed 9 Sep 2026 (REVISION REQUESTED). Pedagogically strong deck built around one well-chosen running example, but it names SHAP, LIME and counterfactuals with zero citations and discusses the "right to explanation" without naming a single law, which for a Learning Event with "Right to Explanation" in its title has to be fixed before it is taught. 6 must-fix item(s); 14 citations/statistics/frameworks verified against source. Posted to Talk page rev 8551.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Learning material, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Pedagogically strong deck built around one well-chosen running example, but it names SHAP, LIME and counterfactuals with zero citations and discusses the "right to explanation" without naming a single law, which for a Learning Event with "Right to Explanation" in its title has to be fixed before it is taught.

What works

The single running example is the best thing here. One university admissions model is introduced on slide 6 and then carried through slides 7, 19, 20, 23, 28, 32 and 33 without ever being dropped for a new domain. Most XAI decks change example every third slide. This one lets students see the same decision from four stakeholder viewpoints, which is exactly what the LE's fifth learning outcome asks for.
Slide 19's caption is the single most valuable line in the deck: feature importance measures influence, "not whether that influence is fair, causal, or appropriate". The speaker note reinforces it. Practitioners get this wrong constantly, including in production model documentation, and it is rarely stated this plainly in an introductory lecture.
Slide 24's four limitations (approximate, misleading, unstable, not a guarantee) are accurate and match the actual methods literature on post-hoc explanation instability. The deck does not oversell XAI, which is the failure mode of most teaching material on this topic.
Slide 29 correctly debunks the popular belief that there is a blanket right to a full explanation of every AI decision, and correctly separates being informed, requesting human review, and contesting. The substance is right. Only the sourcing is missing.
Slide 16 makes the point that publishing source code is not explainability. That is a real and common professional confusion, especially in procurement and open-source policy discussions, and it is well framed.
What must be fixed before sign-off

The deck contains no citations at all. Across all 37 slides and all speaker notes there is not one author name, year, DOI, URL, or reference slide. SHAP (slide 20), LIME (slides 21 and 22) and counterfactual. (Slides 20, 21, 22, 23, 35; no References slide exists (see the slide index on slide 2))
These decks ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and are redistributed by RAISE-U. Teaching a named published method with no source is an attribution failure, and it also leaves the material impossible to update, because a future maintainer cannot tell which version of a method or which claim came from where. Every other reviewable element in the deck is traceable except the science.
Fix: Add a References slide before slide 36 and cite the primary sources on the slides that use them. Verified: Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S.-I. (2017). A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions. NeurIPS 30. Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S., & Guestrin, C. (2016). "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier. KDD '16, doi:10.1145/2939672.2939778..
The four-family taxonomy of explanation methods introduced on slide 18 (feature importance, counterfactual, similar-case, rule-based) is the same four-way split as the local explanation types in Leijnen et al. (2025),. (Slide 18 and its speaker notes; wiki lesson plan, Expected preparation section)
The wiki already tells students where this taxonomy comes from and the slides do not, so the deck is the weaker artefact of the two. On a CC BY-NC-SA deck that gets copied onward, reproducing a published taxonomy without naming it is the kind of finding we block on. If the author arrived at the same four families independently, that is fine, but the source should still be pointed at because the recommended reading is already in the plan.
Fix: Add a source line on slide 18: "Explanation types after Leijnen, S., Maathuis, H., van Montfort, K., van Otterloo, S., Sent, D., Stalenhoef, M., van Turnhout, K., & Zwaal, R. (2025). Guideline for user interface design of explainable AI. HU University of Applied Sciences Utrecht." I confirmed the publication, the year and the full author list on the HU site.
Slide 29, the slide that carries the LE's own title topic, names no legal instrument. It says rights "may" exist and that "legal requirements differ across jurisdictions", and stops there. GDPR, AI Act, Article 22 and. (Slide 29, "The Right to Explanation", and its speaker notes)
An LE called "Explainability, Right to Explanation, XAI" taught in the EU in 2026 cannot leave the legal basis unnamed. As written, a lecturer who was not the author has nothing to answer a student who asks "which right, under what law, from when?" The bullets are correct but unfalsifiable and unmaintainable. This is also the block the lesson plan allocates ten full minutes to (30-40 minutes).
Fix: Name the instruments on the slide. Verified as of this review: GDPR Art 22 (automated individual decision-making) with Art 15(1)(h) meaningful information about the logic involved; the academic dispute over whether the GDPR contains a right to explanation (Wachter, Mittelstadt & Floridi, International Data Privacy Law 7(2), 2017, 76-99, arguing it does not; Selbst & Powles,.
The running example is a university admissions system, which is a listed high-risk use case under AI Act Annex III point 3(a), "AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural. (Slides 6, 26 and 29)
This is the strongest professional-practice point available in the deck and it is sitting unused. The author picked, presumably by accident, the one example that is expressly named in Annex III, and it is the example that makes AI Act Art 86 directly applicable rather than hypothetical. As it stands, students learn that explainability need is a matter of judgement about consequences, when for this exact system it is a matter of legal classification.
Fix: On slide 6 add one line: this system falls under Annex III(3)(a) of the AI Act, so it is high-risk. On slide 26 add the regulatory basis alongside the intuition, and note the corollary that spam filtering and movie recommendation are not Annex III. On slide 29 close the loop: an applicant rejected by this system has an Art 86 right against the deployer. Note the timing when.
The deck does not follow the timing in the lesson plan for the second half. The plan gives 30-40 minutes to the ethical and legal dimension and 40-50 minutes to the user dimension. The deck has slides 28 and 29 for the. (Wiki "Instructions for teachers", 30-40 and 40-50 blocks, against slides 28, 29 and 30)
A lecturer who was not involved in developing this material and who follows the wiki timing will run out of material around minute 35 and then have one slide to fill ten minutes on the user dimension. The first half maps cleanly onto the plan, so the mismatch will not be obvious until the lecturer is already in the room.
Fix: Either build out the two thin blocks (the legal content in the item above is most of what the 30-40 block needs, and the 40-50 block needs the expert-level versus user-level explanation mismatch that the plan asks for and that the recommended Leijnen et al. guideline supplies), or revise the wiki timing to match what the deck actually delivers and say where the extra minutes.
The title slide credits László Fetter. The wiki lists Author Person 1 as András Gézsi (BME) and Author Person 2 as Sieuwert van Otterloo (HU). László Fetter appears nowhere on the wiki. (Slide 1, against the wiki Management information section)
The deck is published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so the byline is the attribution of record. Right now the wiki and the artefact name different people. László Fetter is a real BME AI instructor, so this looks like an unrecorded contributor rather than an error in substance, but it still has to be reconciled.
Fix: Decide who the authors are and make slide 1 and the wiki Management information agree. If Fetter authored the slides for Gézsi, list both.
Also noted on the second pass

Slide 3's Learning Objectives do not match the wiki's five registered learning outcomes. Slide 3 lists "Describe common explainability methods (SHAP, LIME, counterfactuals)", which is not a registered outcome, and drops wiki outcome 3 (differentiate technical, ethical and user-facing dimensions including traceability, transparency, justice, acceptance, understanding) entirely. This is the same class of.
Slides 30 and 33 contradict slide 24, and this is the professional-practice finding RealAI should be adding. Slide 30 gives the decision-maker the question "Can I rely on this prediction?" and answers it with "Confidence and supporting evidence". Slide 33 then answers it with SHAP. SHAP attributes a prediction, it says nothing about whether that prediction is reliable, and slide 24 has already warned that.
The Art 22 "solely automated" point is buried in claims_checked and never becomes an actionable finding. Slide 6's note frames the AI as "intended to support admissions officers rather than replace them completely", and slide 28 offers "request a human review if necessary". The deck never says that a human who rubber-stamps does not take a decision out of Art 22, which is exactly what C-634/21 complicates. The.
The plan's 20-30 block asks for "faithful vs approximate explanations" and the deck never uses the word faithful. Slide 24 covers "Approximate" but the contrast the plan names is absent. This is the same finding as the local-versus-global one they did make, and it comes from the same sentence of the lesson plan.
Smaller fixes

Slide 2, the slide index, does not match the actual slide titles. The index lists "Interpretable vs. Black-box Models", "Explaining Black-box Models", "Transparency, Explainability & Traceability", "Is Transparency Enough?", "Overview of Explainability Methods" and "LIME in Practice", but the.
Slides 21 and 22 have the same title and byte-identical body text, including the same emoji flow diagram text. The speaker note on 22 refers to axes, data points and a decision boundary, so the two slides evidently carry different figures. Retitle 22 to "LIME in Practice" as the index already calls.
Slide 20, SHAP row for School type reads "◀── 0.02": a left-pointing (negative) bar with a positive number. Write it as -0.02, or flip the arrow. A student reading the numbers off the slide will get the sign wrong.
Slide 36 names the wrong EU funding programme. PANORAIMA, grant agreement 101189994 under call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, is funded by the Digital Europe Programme, not the Connecting Europe Facility. The grant number and call ID on the slide are correct. This is consortium boilerplate.
The lesson plan asks for "local vs global explanations" in the 20-30 minute block. The deck teaches the distinction (slide 19 is global, slides 20-23 are local) but never names it on a slide. Add the two words to slide 19 or 18; students need the vocabulary to read any XAI documentation.
The learning outcomes and keywords list "justice" as one of the ethical dimensions, and the teacher instructions ask the lecturer to cover "procedural fairness". Neither term appears on any slide. Slide 28 covers fairness as bias detection only, which is a different idea. Either add procedural.
Slides 11 and 12 state the accuracy-versus-interpretability trade-off as settled fact ("modern AI often sacrifices interpretability in exchange for predictive performance"). For structured tabular data of exactly the kind in the admissions example, that claim is contested: Rudin, C. (2019), Stop.
Slides 13 and 14 have titles and speaker notes but no body text, so they are image-only. Add a one-line caption to each so the deck still works as a student handout or when printed.
What we verified
We checked the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material against their sources, 14 items in total. The notable results:

SHAP primary source: confirmed. Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S.-I. (2017), A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, Curran Associates. NeurIPS 2017 oral. Not cited anywhere in the deck.
LIME primary source: confirmed. Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S., & Guestrin, C. (2016), "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier, Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD, doi:10.1145/2939672.2939778. Not cited anywhere in the deck.
Counterfactual explanations primary source: confirmed. Wachter, S., Mittelstadt, B., & Russell (2018), Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box: Automated Decisions and the GDPR, Harvard Journal of Law & Technology 31(2), 841-887 (arXiv:1711.00399, SSRN 3063289). Slide 23's framing, smallest change.
Right-to-explanation dispute: both sides confirmed. Wachter, Mittelstadt & Floridi (2017), Why a right to explanation of automated decision-making does not exist in the GDPR, International Data Privacy Law 7(2), 76-99; and Selbst & Powles (2017), Meaningful information and the right to explanation, IDPL 7(4), 233-242..
AI Act Article 86: confirmed. Right to explanation of individual decision-making, applies to affected persons subject to a deployer's decision based on an Annex III high-risk system (excluding Annex III point 2), where the decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly and adversely affects health, safety.
AI Act Annex III point 3(a): confirmed, quoted from the consolidated text: "AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels". The deck's running example is squarely inside this. Never mentioned in the deck.
Plan against material
["They agree on structure and on the first two time blocks, and disagree on three things.","Agreement: the plan's 0-10 block (black-box problem, concrete scenario, ask why people demand explanations, scope the lecture as technical/ethical/user-centred) maps exactly onto slides 5-8 and 10. The 10-20 block (define and distinguish black box, interpretability, explainability, transparency, traceability, and show that explainability is not revealing the code) maps exactly onto slides 11-16, including the \"revealing the code is not enough\" point which slide 16 delivers precisely as instructed. The 20-30 block is delivered by slides 17-24, with LIME and SHAP kept conceptual as the plan requires, and the limits list on slide 24 matching the plan's four named limits almost word for word. The 50-60 block maps onto slides 31-35, and the plan's final takeaway (\"explainability can support trustworthy AI, but it is not a complete substitute for validity, fairness, or accountability\") is delivered verbatim in spirit on slide 35.","Disagreement 1, timing. The plan gives ten minutes to the.

Coverage
["Length is adequate but not generous. 37 slides, of which 6 are section dividers with no body text (5, 9, 17, 25, 27, 31) and 6 are front and back matter (1, 2, 3, 4, 36, 37), leaving about 25 teaching slides. That is at the thin end of the consortium's one-slide-per-minute rule of thumb, but the speaker notes are dense and there are five points where the lecturer is told to collect answers from the room (slides 5, 7, 26, 32, 34), so with real discussion this runs 45 to 55 minutes. The gap is not spread evenly: the first 30 minutes are well stocked and the 30-50 minute stretch has three slides for twenty minutes of plan.","Interactivity meets the format requirement. Slide 7 (would this rejection message satisfy you?), slide 32 (four stakeholders, students propose methods before the.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What must be fixed before sign-off' need addressing, after which we will re-review. Everything else here is offered as improvement, not as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: HC-148 Definitions of AI
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: Well-structured and genuinely broad introduction to AI definitions, but the EU AI Act slide quotes the withdrawn 2021 draft definition under a regulation number that belongs to a different EU act entirely, and the deck credits none of its sources, so it cannot be taught or redistributed as it stands.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

Well-structured and genuinely broad introduction to AI definitions, but the EU AI Act slide quotes the withdrawn 2021 draft definition under a regulation number that belongs to a different EU act entirely, and the deck credits none of its sources, so it cannot be taught or redistributed as it stands.

What already works

Three legal definitions from three jurisdictions (EU, OECD, US) in one 120-minute intro lecture is more than most definitional decks attempt, and 15 U.S. Code 9401 is rarely taught in European material. The OECD slide is quoted correctly word for word, including the closing sentence on autonomy and adaptiveness, and both dates on it (adopted 22 May 2019, revised 3 May 2024) are right. The US.
The four discussion questions (Introduction, Metaphysics of AI, Epistemology of AI, Summary and conclusions) meet the consortium's 2 to 4 interactive elements and are placed sensibly: one to open, two in the middle where attention drops, one to close. The metaphysics question about whether AI systems are just code and hardware or something more works for a mixed-background room because answering.
The 'distributed agency' bullet on the Metaphysics of AI slide is the best content in the deck. Saying that agency is a relational property of the network of people, software and environment, and that no single component bears full responsibility unless the network was designed to concentrate it, maps directly onto the accountability arguments students will meet in real AI Act compliance work..
The 'Ethical and social implications of AI' slide carries the right six items (alignment, bias and fairness, autonomous weapons, job displacement, privacy and surveillance, transparency and explainability) and putting them inside the definitions lecture rather than deferring them to a separate ethics LE fits the programme's human-centred framing.
What we would change

The quoted EU AI Act definition is the withdrawn April 2021 Commission proposal text, not the adopted law, and the Annex I techniques list on the following slide was deleted from the final Act. (Slide 'Legal definitions of AI', first EU slide and the following slide beginning 'Annex I lists the following techniques and approaches')
Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted reads: 'a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments'. The 'software that is developed with one or more of the.
Suggested fix: Replace the quoted text with the adopted Article 3(1) wording. Keep the 2021 proposal text only if it is explicitly labelled as the withdrawn proposal, which actually makes a good teaching point about why the EU moved from a technique list to a functional definition. Delete or relabel the Annex I slide. Add a pointer to the Commission's.
The EU AI Act is cited as 'Regulation (EU) 2024/1798'. That number belongs to a completely different instrument. (Slide 'Legal definitions of AI', first EU slide, first line)
The AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Decision (EU) 2024/1798 concerns financial contributions to the European Development Fund. A student who follows the citation to EUR-Lex lands on a budget instrument. These decks ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and get copied onward, so a wrong regulation number propagates.
Suggested fix: Change to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and add the OJ reference so it is traceable.
The scientific-definitions section reproduces Russell and Norvig's framework, and the weak/strong AI section uses Searle's terms, with no attribution anywhere in the deck. There is no references slide. (Slides 'Scientific definitions of AI', 'Acting humanly: The Turing test', 'Rationality', 'Foundations of AI', and 'Weak vs. strong AI')
The two-by-two of think/act crossed with humanly/rationally, the two-dimensions framing beneath it, the expected-utility account of rationality, and the seven contributing disciplines listed in the order Philosophy, Mathematics, Psychology, Economics, Linguistics, Neuroscience, Control theory are Chapter 1 of Russell and Norvig, 'Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach' (Figure 1.1 and Section 1.2). 'Strong AI' and 'weak AI' are Searle's terms from 'Minds, Brains, and.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide and put a source line on each of these slides. Russell and Norvig (4th ed., 2021) for the four approaches and the foundations list, Searle (1980) for strong/weak AI, Turing (1950) is already named on its slide and only needs the full reference (Mind, LIX(236), 433-460). Add Russell and Norvig Chapter 1 to.
No coverage of general-purpose AI models. A 2026 lecture that gives three statutory definitions of 'AI system' does not give the statutory definition of a general-purpose AI model. (Whole legal section, and slide 'Main AI-related areas' where 'generative AI' appears only as one item in a list)
Article 3(63) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 defines a general-purpose AI model, and the provider obligations in Articles 53 and 55 have applied since 2 August 2025. This is the definition that most students will actually have to apply at work, and it is the one the field has been arguing about since 2023. Its absence is also why the Hamburg reviewers wrote that the deck 'has the feel of something written 5 years ago'. Separately, the stated learning outcome promises a.
Suggested fix: One slide is enough for the definitional gap: quote Article 3(63), note that a GPAI model sits inside a system and that the AI Act regulates the two differently, and say the obligations are already in force. For the technological dimension, one further slide on what an AI system needs to be built and run would close the outcome.
The wrap-up slide has no body text. 'Summary and conclusions' contains only the discussion question 'What is and what is not AI?' (Slide 'Summary and conclusions')
The lesson plan gives this block 10 minutes and ties it to the outcome that students understand what is and is not AI. A lecturer who did not write the deck reaches this slide with nothing on screen and nothing in presenter view, because the file is a PDF with no notes. The same problem affects 'Basic AI concepts' and 'Main AI-related areas', which are bare term lists carrying 30 minutes of plan time between them with no explanatory text.
Suggested fix: Add three or four closing statements to the summary slide: what the three legal definitions have in common, where they differ, and one or two borderline cases (a chess engine, a route planner, a spreadsheet with a regression in it) so the closing question has something to bite on. The second author's suggested examples on the Talk page.
Also noticed

The plan's time budget does not match the deck's content mass, and the review praises the alignment instead of flagging it. This is the biggest miss and it is squarely in scope, since the guidelines say the mapping between lecturer instructions and learning materials must be checkable. Legal definitions gets 10 minutes for four slides of quoted statute (EU definition, the.
The '(???)' on the 'Weak vs. strong AI' slide (deck line 120, '(???) has self-awareness and consciousness') is a leftover authorial uncertainty marker that projects to students. The review reads it charitably as a deliberate hedge. By our own standard on placeholders reaching the lecturer, it belongs on the defect list alongside the wiki's 'Grant № ???'. Ask for it to be.
The AIMA problem is a licensing question, not only an attribution one, and the proposed fix does not solve it. Slide titles 'Acting humanly: The Turing test', 'Rationality' and 'Foundations of AI', the two-dimensions framing, and the discipline sub-topic phrasing ('mind as a physical system, foundations of learning, language and rationality'; '(un)decidability,.
Smaller points

Slide 'Weak vs. strong AI': 'cannot generalize knowledge from one domain to another' is stated absolutely. Frontier models in 2026 transfer across domains to a degree that makes this hard to defend in a room, and a student will say so. Rephrase as a matter of degree rather than.
Same slide: Searle's 'strong AI' is a claim about mind and understanding, while AGI is a claim about breadth of capability. The deck merges them, then hedges with '(???) has self-awareness and consciousness', which suggests the author already sees the tension. Split the two.
Same slide: 'the type of AI that exists today' should be argued rather than asserted in 2026. One sentence saying why is enough.
Slide 'Artificial intelligence and computer science' defines AI as tasks that 'normally require human intelligence'. That is the definition the field now warns about, because tasks stop counting as AI once they work. Given the lecture closes on 'what is and what is not AI', one.
Slide 'Epistemology of AI' names word2vec and BERT as the embedding examples. Those are 2013 and 2018. Add one current representative so the slide does not date the whole deck.
Slide 'Metaphysics of AI': 'dual ontology' and 'distributed agency' are a specific philosophical position, not consensus. Distributed responsibility across human and artificial agents is associated with Floridi in particular. Name whose framework this is, or mark it as one.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 12 items. The notable results:

EU AI Act number. The deck cites 'Regulation (EU) 2024/1798'. Checked EUR-Lex: the AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; 2024/1798 is a Decision on European Development Fund financial contributions. The deck's number is wrong.
EU AI Act Article 3(1) text. Checked against the adopted regulation and the artificialintelligenceact.eu Article 3 text. The adopted definition is the machine-based-system / varying-levels-of-autonomy / infers-from-input wording. The deck's quoted text ('software developed with one or more of the.
EU AI Act Annex I. Confirmed that Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is the list of Union harmonisation legislation (Sections A and B), not the ML / logic-based / statistical techniques list the deck reproduces. That techniques list existed only in the 2021 proposal.
Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system. Confirmed as C(2025) 924 final, published 6 February 2025, non-binding, breaking Article 3(1) into seven elements. Not cited in the deck; recommended as the fix reference.
OECD definition and dates. Confirmed the Recommendation was adopted 22 May 2019 and revised 3 May 2024, and that the revised definition reads exactly as the deck quotes it, including the closing sentence on levels of autonomy and adaptiveness. Deck is correct.
Plan against material
"They agree on structure. The deck follows the plan's eight blocks in the plan's order, and the plan's sub-bullets for the philosophy block (what is intelligence, can machines think, ethical implications, metaphysics, epistemology) and for the main-areas block (core, applied, supporting, interdisciplinary, emerging) map one to one onto slides. The named legal sources in the plan (EU AI Act, OECD Principles, 15 U.S. Code 9401) are all present. Four disagreements. First, the wiki Acknowledgements still reads 'Grant No. ???' while the deck carries 101189994; the deck is right and the wiki should be updated. Second, the plan promises a 10-minute wrap-up delivering 'what is and what is not AI', and the deck's summary slide carries only the question, so the plan is right and the material is short. Third, the wiki lists 'None' for all four Expected preparation fields including references for.

Coverage
"Against the consortium rule of thumb of roughly one slide per teaching minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture LE, 27 slides (the second author's count) does not fill 120 minutes on paper. The real picture is more mixed. Two slides, 'Basic AI concepts' and 'Main AI-related areas', carry 30 minutes of plan time between them and are bare term lists, so about a quarter of the session is lecturer talk with nothing on screen and no notes to guide it. That is under-supported rather than under-length. entries.title: HC-150 Introduction to Knowledge Modeling and Reasoning (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: HC-150 teaches the right material in the right order and maps cleanly onto its lesson plan, but large parts of it are taken from Brachman and Levesque's textbook slides and from Kejriwal's knowledge graph work with no attribution anywhere in the deck, which has to be fixed before a CC BY-NC-SA deck goes out.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

HC-150 teaches the right material in the right order and maps cleanly onto its lesson plan, but large parts of it are taken from Brachman and Levesque's textbook slides and from Kejriwal's knowledge graph work with no attribution anywhere in the deck, which has to be fixed before a CC BY-NC-SA deck goes out.

What already works

Content selection is right for the programme. Teaching frames and production rule systems in 2026 is unfashionable, and correct. A student who later meets a rules engine in an insurer's underwriting stack, or a clinical terminology in a hospital data model, needs exactly slides 15 to 20. The formalism list on slide 6 is the right set and is not padded.
The plan-to-slide mapping is clean and in order. All seven blocks in Instructions for teachers land on contiguous slides in sequence: 20 min key concepts on slides 2 to 7, 10 min knowledge-based systems on 8 to 9, 25 min logic and FOL on 10 to 14, 15 min production rules on 15 to 17, 15 min object-oriented on 18 to 20, 25 min ontologies and knowledge graphs on 21 to 27, 10 min wrap-up on 28. That.
Slides 13 and 14 are the only two worked examples in the deck and they are the right two: a propositional refutation showing the empty clause, and an FOL resolution with the unifier labelled on each step. They are pitched correctly and a student can follow them. The problem with those slides is where they came from, not what they teach.
Slide 12 states the explicit versus implicit knowledge distinction crisply (KB, and the set of everything the KB entails). That is the single most useful idea in the deck for someone who will later be asked why a knowledge base 'already knows' something nobody typed into it.
What we would change

Substantial verbatim reproduction of Hector Levesque's public slide set for Brachman and Levesque, Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (Morgan Kaufmann, 2004), with no attribution anywhere in the deck. (Slides 4, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20)
I downloaded Levesque's public slides (cs.toronto.edu/~hector/PublicKRSlides.pdf, 288 pages, each page footed '(c) Brachman & Levesque 2005', slide 2 states 'from the book of the same name by Ronald J. Brachman and Hector J. Levesque, Morgan Kaufmann Publishers, San Francisco, CA, 2004') and diffed it against HC-150. Slide 16 is word for word: 'Basic operation: cycle of / 1. recognize / find conflict set: rules whose conditions are satisfied by the current WM / 2. resolve /.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide naming Brachman, R. J. and Levesque, H. J., Knowledge Representation and Reasoning, Morgan Kaufmann, 2004, and put a short source line on each slide that draws on it. For slides 13 and 14, either redraw the two derivations as native PowerPoint figures with a 'after Brachman and Levesque (2004)' credit, or obtain.
Slide 25's knowledge graph figure and the definitions on slides 23 and 24 come from Mayank Kejriwal's work and are uncredited. (Slides 23, 24, 25)
The graph on slide 25 (Fido is-a Dog, Fido stole bone_1, bone_1 located-in yard_1, yard_1 belongs-to Mary, Mary is-a Person, with filled ovals for the ontology concepts) is Kejriwal's standard worked example from Domain-Specific Knowledge Graph Construction (Springer, 2019), chapter 1, reused in Kejriwal, Knoblock and Szekely, Knowledge Graphs: Fundamentals, Techniques, and Applications (MIT Press, 2021). I verified the triple set against published descriptions of that.
Suggested fix: Credit the figure on slide 25 and cite whichever Kejriwal source the definitions on slides 23 and 24 were taken from. Add both to the references slide.
The two ontology definitions are given as if they were common property. Neither names an author. (Slides 21 and 22)
The 4-tuple O = <C, R, I, A> on slide 21 is the Karlsruhe formulation, from Stumme, Ehrig, Handschuh, Hotho, Maedche and colleagues, 'The Karlsruhe View on Ontologies', University of Karlsruhe AIFB technical report, 2003, and carried into Ehrig and Sure, 'Ontology Mapping: An Integrated Approach', ESWS 2004. Slide 22's paragraph on conceptualization tracks Gruber (1993, 'A translation approach to portable ontology specifications', and 1995, 'Toward principles for the design.
Suggested fix: Name Gruber on slide 22 with a year, and give slide 21's 4-tuple its Karlsruhe source. Two lines of text.
Slide 8 attributes the Knowledge Representation Hypothesis to 'Brian Smith' with no date and no source. (Slide 8)
The quotation itself is accurate; I checked it word for word against two independent sources. The attribution is not. The author is Brian Cantwell Smith, and the hypothesis comes from his 1982 MIT doctoral thesis Reflection and Semantics in a Procedural Language (MIT-LCS-TR-272), most often cited through the 1985 reprint in Brachman and Levesque (eds.), Readings in Knowledge Representation. 'Brian Smith' with no year is not findable by a student, and it is also the exact.
Suggested fix: Change to 'Brian Cantwell Smith (1982)' and add the full reference to the references slide.
Frames are taught across three slides with no mention of Marvin Minsky. (Slides 18, 19, 20)
Frames are Minsky's, from 'A Framework for Representing Knowledge' (1975), in Winston (ed.), The Psychology of Computer Vision, McGraw-Hill, originally MIT AI Memo 306, 1974. The Levesque slide that HC-150's slide 18 was copied from carries the line 'basic idea originally proposed by Marvin Minsky'. HC-150 kept the definition and dropped that line. So this is an attribution that was present in the source and got removed, which is worse than an omission.
Suggested fix: Put Minsky (1975) back on slide 18 and add him to the references.
The funding statement names the wrong EU programme. (Slide 29 (Acknowledgements), and the wiki Acknowledgements section)
The slide says the project 'is co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union under grant DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, grant agreement number 101189994'. DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU is a Digital Europe Programme call, not a Connecting Europe Facility call. I confirmed grant agreement 101189994 and the DIGITAL-SKILLS-5 call against the EU Funding and Tenders portal topic page and against partner project pages, which describe PANORAIMA as a.
Suggested fix: Escalate to the coordinator and correct the boilerplate across all decks to name the Digital Europe Programme. Fill in the grant number on the wiki Acknowledgements section.
The 10-minute wrap-up promised by the lesson plan has no content behind it. (Slide 28, against Instructions for teachers, final bullet)
Instructions for teachers allocate 10 minutes to 'analysis of the modeling capabilities of the considered formalisms for knowledge representation and reasoning'. Slide 28 restates that sentence as a heading and then asks a discussion question. There is no comparison. A lecturer who did not write this deck has ten minutes to fill and nothing to fill it with, and this is also the one slide where the reviewer checklist's professional judgement requirement would naturally be.
Suggested fix: Add one comparison table across the five formalisms taught (FOL, production rules, frames, ontologies, knowledge graphs) with columns for expressiveness, decidability and reasoning cost, typical tooling, what it is good at, and what it costs to maintain. Then the discussion question on slide 28 has something to work against.
Learning Outcome 2 is not delivered by the material. (Slide 9, against wiki Learning Outcomes, second bullet)
The outcome is that students 'can distinguish the main types of knowledge-based AI systems and know their basic characteristics'. Slide 9 offers a two-way split, symbolic versus connectionist, and gives no characteristics of either beyond whether they accept the Knowledge Representation Hypothesis. Expert systems, case-based reasoning and hybrid or neuro-symbolic systems do not appear anywhere in the deck. The plan is right about what students should be able to do; the.
Suggested fix: Expand slide 9 into two slides: one on the types of knowledge-based system with a line each on what characterises them, and one motivating slide on expert systems (MYCIN and XCON historically, and a current example such as a rules engine in underwriting or a clinical decision support system) so students see what the rest of the lecture.
Also noticed

Slide 12, the metavariable is broken. The slide reads "KB |= a: a is a further consequence of what is believed" and "implicit knowledge: { a | KB |= a }". In the source (Levesque p32) that symbol is alpha. Somewhere between the source and PowerPoint it became a plain Latin "a". A student reading slide 12 cannot tell whether "a" is a constant of the language or a metavariable.
Slide 11 says "Well-constructed formulas (wffs)". The standard term is well-formed formulas, which is what the abbreviation stands for. HC-152, by the same author, in the same mini-journey, says "well-formed formulas (WFFs)" and later "Well-Formed Formulas". Two names for the same object across Part 1 and Part 2, and only the Part 2 name matches the abbreviation both parts use.
Slide 4 changes Brachman and Levesque's "some putative agent" to "some intelligent agent". "Putative" is doing work in the original: the agent is only supposed to hold beliefs, which is the point the intentional stance and the Knowledge Representation Hypothesis on slide 8 both rest on. Swapping in "intelligent" removes that and makes slide 4 sit awkwardly against slide 8..
Smaller points

Slide 6 lists neural networks as a knowledge representation formalism. Slide 9 defines connectionist systems as being 'based on non-acceptance of the Knowledge Representation Hypothesis' and gives neural networks as the example. Students will ask which it is. One sentence.
Slide 27 typo: 'Dynamic kowledge updates'. Missing n.
Slide 27 lists seven benefits of knowledge graphs with no mechanism and no example behind any of them. As written it is a claims list a student cannot evaluate. This is also the obvious slide for retrieval over a knowledge graph to ground an LLM, which is the reason most.
Slide 26 asserts that knowledge graphs and ontologies play a central role in modern search engines, and that search engines combine machine learning models with them, with no source and no example beyond the Google Knowledge Graph name-check on slide 24. Either cite it or cut it.
Slide 23 defines a knowledge graph only as a set of triples. Labelled property graphs are the other half of the field in practice and now have an ISO standard: GQL, ISO/IEC 39075:2024, published April 2024, the first new ISO database query language standard since SQL. One.
No standards are named in Part 1 at all: no RDF, RDFS, SPARQL or SHACL. OWL does arrive properly in HC-152, along with Protege and HermiT/Pellet/FaCT++, so this is only partly a gap. But the knowledge graph half of HC-150 (slides 21 to 27, the largest single time block at 25.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 14 items. The notable results:

Knowledge Representation Hypothesis quotation on slide 8: verified word for word, including 'a)' and 'b)' clause structure, against two independent sources. Correct as quoted. Attribution is wrong: it is Brian Cantwell Smith, 1982 MIT thesis Reflection and Semantics in a Procedural Language.
Source of slides 4, 10, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20: confirmed by downloading Hector Levesque's public slide set at cs.toronto.edu/~hector/PublicKRSlides.pdf, converting it to text and diffing. 288 pages, 'from the book of the same name by Ronald J. Brachman and Hector J. Levesque, Morgan.
Slides 13 and 14 as images: confirmed with pdfimages that both slides carry embedded bitmaps, and rendered them. Slide 13 is Levesque's slide 54 (the [FirstGrade] to [Girl] refutation, 'Derivation has 9 clauses, 4 new'); slide 14 is Levesque's slide 59 (GradStudent(sue) to HardWorker(sue), 'Label.
Slide 25 knowledge graph figure: verified that the triple set (Fido is-a Dog, Fido stole bone_1, bone_1 is-a Bone, bone_1 located-in yard_1, yard_1 is-a Yard, yard_1 belongs-to Mary, Mary is-a Person) is Mayank Kejriwal's published example, from Domain-Specific Knowledge Graph Construction.
Slides 23 and 24 knowledge graph definitions: could NOT verify the exact source. The abstract-definition and functional-definition phrasing, and the 'if the KG was constructed correctly (with 100% accuracy) over a trustworthy data source' clause, read as taken from a specific text and the.
Plan against material
"They agree on structure and disagree on two substantive points.\n\nStructure agrees, and unusually well. All seven blocks in Instructions for teachers map onto contiguous slides in the stated order: key concepts (20 min) to slides 2 to 7; knowledge-based systems and the Knowledge Representation Hypothesis (10 min) to slides 8 to 9; formal logic and FOL (25 min) to slides 10 to 14; production rule systems (15 min) to slides 15 to 17; object-oriented representation (15 min) to slides 18 to 20; ontologies and knowledge graphs (25 min) to slides 21 to 27; wrap-up (10 min) to slide 28. Nothing in the deck is unaccounted for and nothing in the plan is missing a home. Traceability from lecturer instructions to slides is checkable, which is what the guidelines ask for.\n\nFirst disagreement: the plan's final 10-minute block promises a comparative analysis of the formalisms. Slide 28 restates.

Coverage
"The material does not comfortably fill 120 minutes, and it delivers two of the three learning outcomes.\n\nOn duration: 27 content slides for 120 minutes sits below the format scan's 30 to 60 range for a lecture-based Learning Event. More telling than the count is where the thin slides are. The FOL block (slides 11 and 12) is a list of topic headings, and slide 11 has none of the alphabet, terms or well-formed formula definitions the plan allots 25 minutes to. The production rules block (slides 15 to 17) is denser but has no worked trace of a single recognize-resolve-act cycle, so it would run eight to ten minutes rather than 15. Same for frames on slides 18 to 20, which give the syntax.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

follow_up.text:
Hi Maria and András, thank you for the revision-1 deck of 11 October. We re-read it against our early feedback of 9 September and our Action summary of 14 October; those entries stay above as the record. RealAI keeps the longer, more instructional review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard.

Status: the wiki says "Ready for pilot", but RealAI has not signed this off and 5 of our 8 main points are still open. Please set the status back to "Learning materials: review" until they are done, so the programme does not treat it as pilot-ready.

Closed since our feedback: "Well-formed formulas" on slide 11, the "knowledge" typo on slide 27, and the neural-network contradiction between slides 6 and 9 (removed, see below).

Partly done: the Resources slide 29 lists three references; slides 13 and 14 say "illustration copied from [2]"; the Kejriwal figure on slide 25 is credited; "Brian Smith, 1982" is on slide 8.

Still open, in this order:
# The funding line on slide 30 and the wiki still names the Connecting Europe Facility; PANORAIMA is a Digital Europe Programme grant.
# Learning outcome 2 (types of knowledge-based systems) has no content: slide 9 now only defines the term.
# Source lines for the word-for-word slides 5, 10, 12 and 15 to 20, and citations on slides 23 and 24.
# Gruber and the Karlsruhe definition on slides 21 and 22; Minsky (1975) for the frames on slides 18 to 20.

New: "illustration copied from [2]" means Levesque's slides, marked (c) Brachman and Levesque 2005, are pasted in; they cannot sit under CC BY-NC-SA, so redraw them or get permission. Reference [1] gives the publisher as Elsevier; it is Morgan Kaufmann.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 15 October 2026, 15:24 CEST
