entries.title: HC-152 Introduction to Knowledge Modeling and Reasoning (Part 2)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: The lecture half is sound and written by a genuine subject expert, but the 60-minute Protege half is delegated wholesale to two third-party PDFs with no scoped exercise, and four technical statements plus the whole OWL version story need correcting before anyone teaches this.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

The lecture half is sound and written by a genuine subject expert, but the 60-minute Protege half is delegated wholesale to two third-party PDFs with no scoped exercise, and four technical statements plus the whole OWL version story need correcting before anyone teaches this.

What already works

Author expertise is real and checkable. Maria Nisheva-Pavlova is Professor at the Faculty of Mathematics and Informatics, Sofia University, with knowledge-based systems and semantic technologies among her listed research areas. This is her subject and it shows in the FOL treatment.
The FOL syntax slides ("Expressing knowledge using the language of FOL" through the terms and free/bound slide) are correct, complete and in the right order: constants, variables, predicates with arity, functions, connectives, quantifiers, recursive definition of WFFs, recursive definition of terms, free vs bound. The worked free/bound example is correct, with x bound and y free. Nothing in this.
The entailment definition on "Satisfaction and entailment" is stated correctly and formally, and the TBox/ABox split on the "Description logics" slide is the standard one. A student who takes away only those two items has taken away something right.
The informal framing of resolution on "The Resolution rule of infrence" (assume the opposite, look for a contradiction) is pitched well for a 30-minute block. Resolution is refutation-based and leading with that intuition beats opening with clause form.
What we would change

The entire 60-minute hands-on block is one slide that says "Follow a Protege OWL tutorial (e.g. [1] or [2])". There is no scoped exercise, no expected output, no timing, no version pinning, no install instructions, no. (Slide "Working example: Creating and reasoning on an OWL ontology using Protege")
Reference [1] is a 90-page guide and reference [2] is a 50-slide lecture deck. Neither is a 60-minute exercise. A lecturer who did not write this LE cannot run the second hour, and half the class time is unspecified. This is the single biggest reason the LE cannot be signed off today.
Suggested fix: Pick one tutorial and name the exact sections. DeBellis sections 4.1 to 4.13 is about the right 60-minute scope (build the class hierarchy, add object properties, add existential restrictions, run HermiT, see the classification, find the inconsistent class). Papacchini's videogame ontology is the alternative and has the advantage of a.
OWL is described as having three sublanguages, OWL Lite, OWL DL and OWL Full. That is OWL 1 (2004). OWL 2 is never mentioned anywhere in the deck. (Slide "The Web Ontology Language")
The current standard is OWL 2, a W3C Recommendation whose Second Edition is dated 11 December 2012. It defines OWL 2 DL and OWL 2 Full plus three profiles, OWL 2 EL, OWL 2 QL and OWL 2 RL. OWL Lite is an OWL 1 species and is not part of OWL 2. Protege 5.6, which students are told to install, is an OWL 2 editor, and the tutorial they are told to follow uses OWL 2 features: Papacchini's syntax table lists ObjectMinCardinality / ObjectMaxCardinality with a class filler, which.
Suggested fix: Rewrite the slide around OWL 2: cite the W3C OWL 2 Overview (Second Edition, 11 December 2012), state that OWL 2 DL and OWL 2 Full are the two species, and introduce EL, QL and RL as profiles chosen for reasoning cost, with one line each on what they buy (EL: polynomial classification, used by SNOMED CT; QL: query answering over.
"Realization: finding a model that satisfies a set of axioms" is not what realization means in description logics. (Slide "Description logics", in the list of main reasoning tasks (fourth bullet, after subsumption, instance checking and consistency checking))
Realization is an ABox task: given an individual, compute the most specific concepts of which it is an instance, that is, its direct types under the subsumption ordering. What the slide describes (finding a satisfying model) is consistency checking, which is already the bullet directly above it. So the slide gives two different names to the same task and leaves the actual fourth task untaught. This matters because realization is exactly what students will watch the reasoner.
Suggested fix: Replace with: "Realization: for a given individual, computing the most specific concepts it belongs to (its direct types)." Attribute the task list to Baader et al., The Description Logic Handbook, which is where this four-task framing comes from and which is currently uncited.
"An interpretation assigns a truth value (true or false) to each atomic statement in the language." That is the semantics of propositional logic, not first-order logic, and it contradicts the slide immediately before it. (Slide "Satisfaction and entailment", second sentence)
The preceding "Semantics (meaning)" slide correctly says a FOL interpretation gives a domain of discourse and maps constants to objects, predicates to sets of tuples and functions to functions. Truth values of atoms then follow from that plus a variable assignment. Two consecutive slides now define "interpretation" two incompatible ways, in the block that carries the learning outcome about entailment relations. A student reading the handout cannot tell which one is right.
Suggested fix: Cut the sentence and instead write: "An interpretation together with an assignment to the free variables determines a truth value for every formula. A set of formulas is satisfied by an interpretation if all of them are true under it; such an interpretation is called a model of the set." That also fixes the loose "interpretation (or.
"FOL is undecidable (which means that no algorithm can determine, in finite time, whether a given FOL formula is valid ... or satisfiable)". The gloss in the brackets is wrong for validity. (Slide "Description logics", the paragraph contrasting FOL with DLs)
Validity in FOL is undecidable but semi-decidable: the set of valid first-order sentences is recursively enumerable, so a complete proof procedure does terminate in finite time on every valid formula. It is only invalid formulas on which it may run forever. As written, the slide implies automated theorem provers cannot work at all, which is odd two slides after teaching resolution, and it is resolution's refutation-completeness that gives you the semi-decision procedure..
Suggested fix: Say: "Validity in FOL is undecidable but semi-decidable. A complete proof procedure such as resolution will always terminate on a valid formula, but may run forever on an invalid one. DLs are designed as fragments where both validity and satisfiability are decidable, so a reasoner always terminates." That also connects the resolution.
"OWL DL is supported by a wide range of reasoners (e.g., HermiT, Pellet, FaCT++)". Two of the three named will not be in the tool students install. (Slide "The Web Ontology Language" / OWL DL constructors, final bullet)
Protege 5.6 ships HermiT and ELK. FaCT++ has had no release since 2016 and its 1.6.5 plugin is reported broken on Protege 5.6.5 (open issue on the protegeproject repo). The Pellet plugin has a complicated availability history after the project moved hosts; students will not find it in the default install either. So the deck names a 2010-era line-up, omits the reasoner that is actually bundled, and sets students hunting for plugins during a 60-minute lab.
Suggested fix: Change to: "Protege 5.6 ships with HermiT (general OWL 2 DL) and ELK (fast, restricted to OWL 2 EL). Openllet and Konclude are the maintained alternatives; Konclude currently has the best benchmark performance on large ontologies. FaCT++ is unmaintained and does not run on current Protege." Add a lecturer note saying to use HermiT for.
The open world assumption and the absence of a unique name assumption are never mentioned anywhere in the deck. (Missing across the "Description logics" and "The Web Ontology Language" slides; surfaces in the lab)
This is the single thing that most confuses newcomers to OWL, and both tutorials the LE points at deal with it explicitly (DeBellis section 4.13 "Automated Classification and Open World Reasoning" and 11.1 "OWA and Monotonic Reasoning"). Students who have just been taught closed-world habits will build a class, run HermiT, and not understand why the individual they expected to be classified was not, or why two differently named individuals are not assumed distinct. Sending.
Suggested fix: Add one slide before the working example: OWL reasoning is open world (what is not stated is unknown, not false) and has no unique name assumption (two names may denote the same individual unless you assert owl:differentFrom). Give the one-line consequence for the lab: a reasoner will not infer that a pizza has only the toppings you.
The DeBellis guide is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0. It is shipped inside a learning event whose wiki page states "The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0." (Wiki section "Lesson materials" vs the file HC-152_Protege tutorial 1.pdf, section 1.1 Licensing)
The two licences are incompatible in that direction. ShareAlike means adaptations of BY-SA material may only be released under BY-SA 4.0 or a later BY-SA version; you cannot add a NonCommercial restriction to it. Blanket-labelling the LE package CC BY-NC-SA misstates the licence of one of the three files. These decks are copied onward under an open licence, so a wrong licence label propagates. The Papacchini deck carries no licence statement at all, so its redistribution.
Suggested fix: Do not redistribute either PDF inside the LE package. Link to them instead (DeBellis at https://www.michaeldebellis.com/post/new-protege-pizza-tutorial, Papacchini at the Liverpool URL already cited), and note on the Lesson materials wiki section that the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 statement covers the PANORAIMA-authored presentation only. If the.
The wiki lesson plan says Expected preparation is "None" on all four fields, but the material requires students to have installed Protege (a Java desktop application) before the session and to have working FOL. (Wiki section "Expected preparation" vs slide "Working example")
"Select and, if necessary, install the appropriate version of Protege ontology editor" as an in-class activity will eat 10 to 20 minutes of the 60-minute lab on a mixed room of Windows and Mac laptops, with the usual JVM and Gatekeeper problems. The wiki also lists "References and background for students: None" while the deck hands students two references and instructs them to work through one.
Suggested fix: On the wiki, set Obligatory for students to: install Protege 5.6.x from https://protege.stanford.edu/ before the session and confirm it opens. Set References and background to the two references already on the deck's References slide. Add a note that the lab assumes HC-150 (or whichever LE is Part 1) has been completed.
Also noticed

The funding acknowledgement names the wrong EU programme, on the deck and on the wiki. Deck Acknowledgements slide: "co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union under grant DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU". I fetched the EC funding portal topic record for that identifier: it sits under frameworkProgramme "DIGITAL", "Digital Europe Programme.
Substantial FOL duplication between HC-150 (Part 1) and HC-152 (Part 2), which the guidelines explicitly ask the reviewer to flag under Distinctiveness of the Learning Event. HC-150's lesson plan allots 25 minutes to "Knowledge modeling and reasoning using the language of first-order logic", and its slides cover Syntax of FOL (alphabet, terms, wffs, quantifiers), Semantics of.
The review's smaller_fix on resolution needing clausal form and Skolemisation is only half right, because of the above. HC-150 already names "clausal representation of the KB" in its Reasoning in FOL block. So the correct ask for HC-152 is a cross-reference back to HC-150 plus one line naming Skolemisation and unification, not fresh standalone content. As drafted, the author.
Smaller points

Slide "The Resolution rule of infrence": the title is misspelled (infrence). Also the slide ends with the word "Example:" and no extractable text after it. If the example is a bitmap, it will not be readable in handouts or by a screen reader and a lecturer cannot rebuild the.
Slide "The Resolution rule of infrence": resolution over FOL needs conversion to clausal form (prenex form, Skolemisation) and unification. Neither is named. One line saying so would stop students concluding that resolution applies directly to arbitrary formulas.
Slide "Introduction": "Temporal logics: extend FOL with temporal operators" and "Modal logics: extend FOL with modal operators" are loose. LTL, CTL and the standard modal systems are propositional. Say "extend propositional or first-order logic".
Slide "Introduction": the FOL example is "For all x, if x is a bird, then x can fly", which is the textbook counterexample used to motivate non-monotonic reasoning. Using it uncommented immediately before teaching monotonic entailment is a missed opportunity at best. Either.
References slide, reference [1]: the ResearchGate link returns 403 to a plain request and increasingly needs an account. Cite the author's own page, https://www.michaeldebellis.com/post/new-protege-pizza-tutorial, which is open, carries the supporting ontology files, and is.
Inside the Papacchini deck (HC-152_Protege tutorial 2.pdf), the link given twice as the "Official Tutorial", http://mowl-power.cs.man.ac.uk/protegeowltutorial/resources/ProtegeOWLTutorialP4_v1_3.pdf, is dead: it times out. If that deck ships with the LE, the dead link needs a.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 12 items. The notable results:

Protege current version: confirmed live and maintained at https://protege.stanford.edu/ (200 OK). Release history shows the 5.6 series through 5.6.9, released March 2026. The DeBellis guide targets 5.5 and the Papacchini deck targets 5.1, so both tutorials are behind the tool students will install,.
OWL version claim: checked the W3C OWL 2 Overview (Second Edition), dated 11 December 2012. It defines OWL 2 DL and OWL 2 Full plus the EL, QL and RL profiles. OWL Lite is an OWL 1 (2004) species and does not appear as a category in OWL 2. The deck's "three sublanguages: OWL Lite, OWL DL, OWL Full".
Realization: checked against the description logic literature (Baader and Nutt, Basic Description Logics, in The Description Logic Handbook). Realization is the ABox task of computing the most specific concepts an individual belongs to, related to the most specific concepts that are minimal under.
FOL undecidability: confirmed Church (1936) and Turing (1936) settled the Entscheidungsproblem negatively, and confirmed that the set of valid first-order sentences is computably enumerable, so derivability is semi-decidable. The deck's gloss that no algorithm can determine validity in finite time.
Reasoner currency: FaCT++ has had no release since 2016, and there is an open protegeproject issue reporting that the FaCT++ 1.6.5 plugin does not work with Protege 5.6.5 on Windows 11. The Pellet plugin's availability was disrupted by the project's move to GitHub; Openllet is the maintained fork.
Plan against material
Aligned on the first hour, not on the second. The plan's 10-minute introduction, 30-minute FOL block (satisfaction, entailment, resolution, description logics) and 20-minute OWL block all map onto identifiable slides in the right order, and the deck's headings echo the plan's bullets almost word for word. That part is checkable and it checks out. The last plan bullet does not hold: it promises "Introduction to the Protege ontology editor. Creating a learning ontology using Protege. Checking the consistency and classification of the ontology - 60 min", and the material contains no introduction to the Protege editor at all. There is one slide telling students to install it and follow somebody else's tutorial. On this point the plan is right and the material is missing; the material should be brought up to the plan, not the plan trimmed to the material. Two smaller contradictions: the wiki.

Coverage
The lecture 60 minutes is plausibly filled but only because the slides are dense. I count roughly 20 content slides plus title, references, acknowledgement and disclaimer, against the guidelines' rule of thumb of about one slide per minute. Several slides here carry a full screen of prose (the syntax slides, the DL slide), so 20 slides genuinely can run 50 to 60 minutes when spoken. It will feel like a wall of text; that is the second author's call, not mine, but it is worth saying that nothing on these slides is a figure, table or diagram. The lab 60 minutes cannot be judged to fill anything, because nothing is specified: an unbounded pointer at a 90-page guide is not a 60-minute exercise..

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

action_summary.text:
Maria and András, this is the short version of our 9 September 2026 feedback; the full text stays above. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: major revision. The lecture half is sound, but "Ready for pilot" is premature without a formal review.

Since our review:
* Partly done: slide 13 now cites [1], but shows no readable example; slide 11 still says "infrence".
* Still open: slides 10, 15, 16, 18, 19 and 20, the tutorial PDFs and licence statement are unchanged.

Please do next:
# Replace slide 20 with one scoped 60-minute Protégé 5.6 exercise: exact tutorial sections, timing and expected output.
# Rewrite slide 18 around OWL 2 (DL, Full, profiles EL, QL, RL); drop OWL Lite.
# Delete the slide 10 sentence on atomic truth values; correct slide 15 (validity is semi-decidable) and slide 16 (realization means most specific concepts).
# Replace Pellet and FaCT++ on slide 19 with ELK; add a slide before slide 20 on open world and no unique name assumption.
# Remove both tutorial PDFs, link to them instead, and limit the CC BY-NC-SA statement (slide 23, wiki) to your own deck.
# Correct the funding programme on slide 22; fix "infrence" and the example on slides 11 and 13; name clausal form and Skolemisation.
# Work through the smaller points in our 9 September text.

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off): Expected preparation (all "None"), Lesson materials (add links), Acknowledgements ("Grant № ???") and Instructions for teachers (add lab guidance) need completing.

When these are done, tell us on the Discussion page and email the review inbox for re-review.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 14 October 2026, 20:54 CEST

The revised deck differs from the old one only by a "(WFFs)" label, a new reference [1] (Brachman and Levesque slides) cited on the resolution "Example [1]" slide, and the tutorial references renumbered to [2] and [3]; no wiki fields and no slide content we raised were changed.
reread.headline: Almost nothing in HC-152 is closed: the author renumbered the references and cited a source for the resolution example, moved the status to Ready for pilot, and left all 9 must-fix items (Protege lab, OWL 2, realization, interpretation, FOL decidability, reasoners, open world, licence, preparation field) as they were.

points.point: The 60-minute Protege block is one slide pointing to two third-party PDFs, with no scoped exercise, sections, timing, version or install steps.
points.evidence: Slide 20 still reads 'Follow a Protégé OWL tutorial (e.g. [2] or [3]) to create a learning ontology... Check the consistency and classify the ontology.' Only the reference numbers changed. No section ranges, no expected output, no timing. Wiki 'Instructions for teachers' still just says '60 min'.

points.point: OWL described as OWL Lite/DL/Full (OWL 1); OWL 2 and its profiles never mentioned.
points.evidence: Slide 18 still says 'one of the three sublanguages of OWL (the others being OWL Lite and OWL Full)'. A search of the revised pptx and pdf text finds no 'OWL 2', EL, QL or RL.

points.point: 'Realization' defined wrongly as finding a model; Description Logic Handbook not cited.
points.evidence: Slide 16 still reads 'Realization: finding a model that satisfies a set of axioms'. No Baader citation was added to the references.

points.point: Slide 'Satisfaction and entailment' gives the propositional definition of interpretation, contradicting the semantics slide.
points.evidence: Slide 10 still says 'An interpretation assigns a truth value (true or false) to each atomic statement in the language.' Unchanged.

points.point: FOL validity wrongly described as not decidable in finite time; it is semi-decidable.
points.evidence: Slide 15 still says 'no algorithm can determine, in finite time, whether a given FOL formula is valid... or satisfiable'. No mention of semi-decidability.

points.point: Reasoner list (HermiT, Pellet, FaCT++) does not match what Protege 5.6 ships (HermiT, ELK).
points.evidence: Slide 19 still reads '(e.g., HermiT, Pellet, FaCT++)'. ELK is not mentioned and there is no lecturer note to use HermiT.

points.point: Open world assumption and no unique name assumption not covered anywhere before the lab.
points.evidence: No new slide was added; the deck is still 23 slides and a text search for 'open world' or 'unique name' finds nothing.

points.point: DeBellis guide (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Papacchini deck (no licence) shipped inside an LE labelled CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
points.evidence: Both HC-152_Protege tutorial PDFs are still in the HC-152 folder (unchanged since 20 Jul). Wiki 'Lesson materials' still says 'The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.' with no carve-out. Slide 23 disclaimer still says 'All materials'.

points.point: Wiki 'Expected preparation' says None everywhere although students must install Protege and need Part 1.
points.evidence: Current wiki text: Obligatory for students: None. Optional: None. References and background for students: None. Recommended for teachers: None. 'Learning Events to be completed before: HC-148, HC-150' is present but is the same as before and does not cover the Protege install.

points.point: Funding acknowledgement names the wrong EU programme (CEF instead of Digital Europe), on the deck and the wiki.
points.evidence: Slide 22 still says 'Connecting Europe Facility... DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU'. Wiki still says 'Co-Financed by the Connecting Europe Facility... Under Grant № ???.' Both unchanged.

points.point: FOL syntax/semantics largely duplicates HC-150 (Part 1); distinctiveness not addressed.
points.evidence: Slides 4 to 10 (syntax, WFFs, terms, semantics) are unchanged and there is no cross-reference to HC-150 anywhere in the deck.

entries.title: HC-154 Introduction to Generative AI (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: HC-154 has the right structure and a sound outline, but it carries no citations at all, three technical statements are wrong, diffusion models are absent from a 2026 generative AI introduction, and the 40-minute transformer block has no diagram and no formula, so it cannot deliver the two transformer learning outcomes as it stands.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

HC-154 has the right structure and a sound outline, but it carries no citations at all, three technical statements are wrong, diffusion models are absent from a 2026 generative AI introduction, and the 40-minute transformer block has no diagram and no formula, so it cannot deliver the two transformer learning outcomes as it stands.

What already works

The deck follows the lesson plan's five sections in the exact order given in the wiki, with a section divider for each. A lecturer who reads the plan can find their place in the deck immediately. That mapping is often broken in these materials and here it holds.
Slide 10 is a good interactive prompt. Asking what signs suggest a text, image or video was AI-generated needs no setup, works with any cohort, and sits at the right point, after the ethics slide and before the technical sections. It is the one place in the deck where students have to form a judgement rather than receive a definition.
Slide 25 pairs autoregressive models with the correct example per modality: PixelCNN for images, WaveNet for audio, GPT for text. I checked all three against the original papers and the mapping is right. It also names the real limitation, that sequential generation is slow, rather than skipping it.
Slides 14 and 15 stage the GAN training loop correctly and in the right order: generator maps noise to pseudo-data, discriminator sees both real and generated inputs, feedback adjusts both, and the two loss functions are described separately with what each measures. This is the clearest technical passage in the deck.
What we would change

The deck contains no citations anywhere and has no references slide. (Whole deck; most visible on slides 12, 19, 25, 27, 31, 32 and 38)
Every named model and mechanism is presented with no source. GANs, VAEs, the transformer, GPT, BERT, PixelCNN, WaveNet and StyleGAN are all named and none is attributed to anyone. The materials ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and are meant to be copied onward, so uncredited technical content becomes an attribution problem for every downstream user, not just for this deck. Master's students also need to see that this field has a primary literature they can go and read, and at.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide before the acknowledgements and put a short inline citation on each slide that names a model. Verified minimum set: Goodfellow, Pouget-Abadie, Mirza, Xu, Warde-Farley, Ozair, Courville and Bengio, Generative Adversarial Nets, NeurIPS 2014, arXiv 1406.2661; Kingma and Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, arXiv.
Slides 16 and 22 carry a figure and nothing else. No title, no caption, no source line. (Slides 16 and 22)
The PDF text layer for both slides contains only the page number, so both are images with no accompanying text at all. From their position, slide 16 follows the GAN loss functions and slide 22 follows the autoencoder loss, so they are presumably a GAN schematic and an autoencoder schematic. I cannot tell from the text extraction where either came from, which is exactly the problem. Under CC BY-NC-SA a reused third-party figure needs its own credit and a licence compatible.
Suggested fix: Give both slides a title, a one-line caption saying what the figure shows, and a source line. If either figure came from a paper, textbook, blog or another slide deck, name it and confirm the licence allows redistribution under CC BY-NC-SA. If the author drew them, state that so downstream users know they are safe to reuse.
The transformer and attention section does not contain enough substance to deliver learning outcomes 3 and 4. (Slides 27 to 30)
Slide 27 is titled 'Building blocks of the transformer architecture' and then lists two building blocks: input embeddings and self-attention. Multi-head attention, the query, key and value construction, scaled dot-product attention, the feed-forward sublayers, residual connections with layer normalisation, and the encoder versus decoder stacks are all missing. There is no architecture diagram anywhere in the deck and no formula. Slides 28 to 30 describe self-attention in.
Suggested fix: Add an architecture diagram showing the encoder and decoder stacks; a slide on Q, K and V with the scaled dot-product attention expression softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V; a slide on multi-head attention explaining why several heads are used; and a short worked example showing attention weights over one sentence so students see what the.
Diffusion models are not mentioned once, and the deck presents GANs as the leading route to image generation. (Section 2 overall, slides 11 to 25; specifically slides 17 and 18)
The deck is dated August 2026. Slide 17 tells students that image generation is 'perhaps the most popular application of GANs', that GANs produce images 'often indistinguishable from real photos', and attributes deepfakes and super-resolution to GANs. In current practice, image, video and audio generation is dominated by diffusion and flow-matching models, usually operating inside a VAE latent space, with GANs retained for narrower jobs such as upscaling and style transfer..
Suggested fix: Add diffusion as a fourth family in section 2: forward noising and the learned reverse process, why training is more stable than adversarial training, latent diffusion for compute cost, and the sampling-speed trade-off against GANs. Cite Ho, Jain and Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, arXiv 2006.11239, NeurIPS 2020, and.
Slide 32 says BERT 'uses a completely new kind of architecture known as the bidirectional transformer'. (Slide 32)
BERT is not a new architecture. Devlin et al. describe it as a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder based on the original implementation in Vaswani et al. 2017. It is a stack of standard transformer encoder layers. What was new was the pretraining objective, masked language modelling, which allows each position to attend to both left and right context. Calling the architecture new hides the distinction students actually need, which is that GPT is decoder-only with.
Suggested fix: Rewrite to: BERT is an encoder-only stack of standard transformer encoder layers, and bidirectionality comes from the masked language modelling objective rather than from a new architecture. Then add one slide putting GPT and BERT side by side, decoder-only and causal versus encoder-only and bidirectional, with the citation for each.
Slide 6 lists 'Mostly semi-supervised learning' as a major characteristic of generative AI. (Slide 6)
Semi-supervised learning means training on a small labelled set together with a large unlabelled set. That is not how any of the models in this deck are trained. GANs and VAEs are unsupervised, and GPT and BERT pretraining is self-supervised, where the training signal is derived from the data itself. The GPT-1 paper did use the word semi-supervised for unsupervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, so the wording has a defensible origin, but stated flatly as.
Suggested fix: Replace with 'mostly self-supervised or unsupervised training' and add one line explaining that the training signal comes from the data itself, for example predicting the next token or reconstructing a masked one. This also sets up the GPT and BERT objectives on slides 31 and 32.
Slide 13 says 'The discriminator is a variant of the critic.' (Slide 13)
This reverses the relationship. The discriminator is the original component in Goodfellow et al. 2014 and outputs a probability that its input is real. The critic came later, introduced in Wasserstein GAN by Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou in 2017, which drops the classification framing and scores samples so that the difference in expected scores approximates a Wasserstein distance. As written, a student will assume the critic is the standard component and the discriminator a.
Suggested fix: State that the discriminator is a binary classifier producing the probability that the input is real. If the critic is mentioned at all, present it as the WGAN variant with a citation to Arjovsky et al. 2017. Remove the pronoun.
The VAE section never explains what makes a VAE variational, and slide 19 misstates what the decoder does. (Slides 19 to 24, especially 19 and 21)
Slide 19 says the decoder is 'for reconstructing data samples in the latent space'. The decoder maps from the latent space back to data space; it does not reconstruct in the latent space. Slide 19 also promises a loss function that balances reconstruction quality against 'regularity of the latent space', and then slide 21 gives only the plain autoencoder MSE loss and never says what the regularity term is. Across slides 19 to 24 the KL divergence, the prior over latents, the.
Suggested fix: Correct the decoder line on slide 19. Add one slide showing the two-term objective, reconstruction plus KL to the prior, and one slide on the reparameterisation trick and why gradients cannot pass through a raw sampling step. Cite Kingma and Welling 2013 on both.
Neither slide 5 nor slide 8 does what its title promises, so the first learning outcome rests on application lists. (Slides 5 and 8)
Slide 5 is titled 'What is generative AI?' and answers with four 'primary elements' that are all uses: content generation, data augmentation, creativity, personalisation. Slide 8 is titled 'Place of generative AI in the AI ecosystem' and lists text generation, image and video synthesis, music and drug discovery, which are applications again, not a place in any ecosystem. Generative AI is never contrasted with discriminative modelling, never located relative to machine.
Suggested fix: Put an actual definition on slide 5: a model that learns a distribution over data and samples new data from it, p(x) or p(x | condition), as against a discriminative model that learns p(y | x). Turn slide 8 into a containment diagram from AI through machine learning and deep learning to generative models and foundation models, and mark.
The deck will not fill 120 minutes, and the time inside section 2 is distributed against the plan's own priorities. (Whole deck against the plan's 120 minutes; the 45-minute section 2 in particular)
44 slides, of which about 34 carry content and two of those are wordless figures. The consortium rule of thumb is roughly one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture Learning Event, so this deck sits at the bottom of that range for a session at the top of the duration range. Delivered as written I would expect 60 to 75 minutes. Inside the 45-minute overview block, GANs get seven slides, VAEs six and autoregressive models exactly one, slide 25, with four bullets..
Suggested fix: Expand autoregressive models to three or four slides covering the sequential factorisation of the joint distribution, teacher forcing, and why sampling is slow. Add the transformer material described above. Add two more interactive elements, for example a quick poll after section 2 asking which family a named product uses, and a paired.
The ethics slide and the AI-detection discussion question do not mention the EU transparency rule that now governs exactly this. (Slides 9 and 10)
Slide 9 raises deepfakes and misinformation. Slide 10 asks students what signs suggest that content was AI-generated. Article 50 of the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, has applied since 2 August 2026 and requires providers of generative systems to mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable and detectable format, and requires deployers to disclose deepfakes. I checked whether the recent deferral touched this: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 pushed the.
Suggested fix: Add two or three lines to slide 9 naming Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and its marking and disclosure duties, and reframe slide 10 to ask both what technical signs a student can spot and what the provider was legally required to embed. Do not describe this as the 'limited risk' tier; that phrase is not statutory language in the.
Slide 43 names the wrong EU funding programme. (Slide 43, and the Acknowledgements section of the HC-154 wiki page)
The slide says the project is co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility. PANORAIMA is funded under the Digital Europe Programme. The call topic printed on the same slide, DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, is a Digital Europe Programme topic, and grant agreement 101189994 is a Digital Europe Programme grant. The Connecting Europe Facility is a separate instrument. This sits on the acknowledgements slide of a deck licensed for redistribution, so the misstatement travels.
Suggested fix: Change the slide to the Digital Europe Programme wording and copy the correct grant details onto the wiki, replacing the '???'. This boilerplate is almost certainly identical across every deck in the programme, so raise it with whoever owns the RAISE-U template rather than correcting HC-154 in isolation.
Also noticed

Part 2 is HC-156, it is in the same review batch, and it has no diffusion content either. HC-156's plan gives 35 minutes to 'generative AI for image and video synthesis' and its slide 22 teaches that 'Deepfakes primarily rely on GANs'. The currency gap is a mini-journey defect, not an HC-154 defect, and should be raised with the author across both LEs at once.
The AI Act is missing from HC-156, where the plan actually puts it. HC-156's 20-minute 'Ethics and bias' block includes 'regulation and legal impact of generative AI', and its regulation slide names GDPR and never names Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 or Article 50. That is the stronger version of must-fix 11 and it was not made.
BERT is taught as a generative model. Slide 31's section heading is 'Generative pretrained models: GPT, BERT'. BERT is encoder-only, trained by masked language modelling, and does not learn and sample p(x) the way the rest of the deck defines generative modelling. This compounds the slide 32 architecture error and it is the conceptual half of that error, which the review.
Smaller points

Slide 27: 'Transformers are inherently order-unaware and don't understand any linearity between the provided sequence.' Linearity is the wrong word. Say the architecture has no built-in notion of token order, which is why positional encodings are added. One extra sentence on.
Slide 31: GPT described as a 'one-way transformer model'. Use decoder-only with causal (masked) self-attention. One-way is not standard terminology and students will not find it in the literature.
Slide 32: next sentence prediction is presented as simply how BERT is trained. Add a line noting that RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) found dropping NSP improved results and that later encoder models generally omit it, so students do not carry a superseded picture forward.
Slide 38: 'applying noise to audio, e.g., translations, rotations, scaling, flipping.' Translations, rotations, scaling and flipping are image transforms, not audio noise. The sentence has two examples fused into one. Split it: geometric transforms for images, noise injection,.
Slide 40: 'oscillations or collapse.' Name mode collapse explicitly, since it is the failure students will actually hear about, and add posterior collapse for VAEs alongside it. The section covers optimisation of generative models and these are the two failure modes specific to.
Slide 24: 'VAEs possess a better ability at robust detection of the anomalies as they measure the underlying uncertainty in the data.' This is contested in the anomaly-detection literature and is stated here as settled. Either cite a source or soften to say VAEs give a.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 16 items. The notable results:

Goodfellow et al., Generative Adversarial Nets, NeurIPS 2014, arXiv 1406.2661. Verified. Full author list: Ian Goodfellow, Jean Pouget-Abadie, Mehdi Mirza, Bing Xu, David Warde-Farley, Sherjil Ozair, Aaron Courville, Yoshua Bengio. Not cited anywhere in the deck.
Kingma and Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, arXiv 1312.6114, submitted 20 December 2013. Verified. This is the source of the VAE and of the reparameterisation trick that the deck's VAE section omits. Not cited.
Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017, arXiv 1706.03762. Verified, eight authors. The transformer content on slides 27 to 30 traces to this paper and does not cite it.
Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova, BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding, arXiv 1810.04805, submitted October 2018, published NAACL 2019. Verified via the arXiv listing. Also verified the substantive point: BERT's architecture is described in the literature.
WGAN critic versus GAN discriminator. Verified. The critic was introduced in Wasserstein GAN (Arjovsky, Chintala, Bottou, 2017) as a replacement for the discriminator, scoring samples so the difference in expected values approximates the Wasserstein distance under Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality..
Plan against material
"They agree on structure and disagree on content in four places.\n\nAgreement: the deck's five sections match the plan's five bullets in the same order, and the 'challenges and limitations' sub-bullet the plan places under transformers does appear there, on slides 34 and 35. The learning objectives on slide 2 restate the wiki's five learning outcomes almost word for word. That alignment is real and worth crediting.\n\nDisagreements, and which side is right:\n\n1. The plan is right, the material is wrong. The plan gives 15 minutes to 'what is generative AI, place of generative AI in the AI ecosystem' and the keyword list opens with 'definition of generative AI'. Slides 5 and 8 supply application lists instead, and no definition appears anywhere in the deck. Fix the slides, not the plan.\n\n2. The plan is right, the material under-delivers. The plan allocates 40 minutes to transformers.

Coverage
"The material does not fill 120 minutes and it delivers three of the five learning outcomes.\n\nVolume: 44 slides, of which one is the title, one the objectives, one the agenda, five are section dividers and two are the acknowledgements and disclaimer. That leaves about 34 content slides, two of which (16 and 22) are figures with no text. Most of the remaining slides carry three or four bullets. Against the consortium's one-slide-per-minute guide, this is a 60 to 75 minute lecture in a 120 minute slot. The gap is concentrated in section 3, where 40 minutes of plan time meets four content slides.\n\nOutcomes, one by one. Outcome 1, understand the essence of generative AI: not met, because.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.heading: Correction from RealAI: our duration comment, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 120 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 44 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.37. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

# Expand slides 27 to 30 with an encoder-decoder diagram, Q, K, V with the scaled dot-product formula, multi-head attention and a worked example.
# Add diffusion as a fourth family in section 2, the VAE KL term and reparameterisation on slides 19 to 24, and rebalance slide 17.
# Add a references slide and inline citations on slides naming models, and give slides 16 and 22 a title, caption and source line.

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):

entries.title: HC-156 Introduction to Generative AI (Part 2)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: Clear structure and an unusually honest limitations section, but the legal slide omits the EU AI Act entirely, image, video and music generation is taught as GANs and VAEs with no mention of diffusion, and not one statistic in the deck is sourced, so we cannot close this today.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

Clear structure and an unusually honest limitations section, but the legal slide omits the EU AI Act entirely, image, video and music generation is taught as GANs and VAEs with no mention of diffusion, and not one statistic in the deck is sourced, so we cannot close this today.

What already works

Slide 12 gives the cleanest explanation in the deck. The contrast between extractive summarization (concatenating the most relevant parts) and abstractive summarization (condensing into coherent new text) is correct, compact and pitched right for a mixed-background master's audience.
Slides 9 and 10 describe the pretraining and fine-tuning pipeline accurately without hand-waving. The framing of pretraining as next-word prediction that yields grammar plus factual knowledge as a side effect is the right level of detail for an introduction.
Slides 43 and 44 are the best part of the deck. Most introductory generative AI material stops at capabilities. This one names accuracy, reasoning, bias, privacy and IP exposure with hosted models, and emotional limits, and it does so without softening. The instinct is right even where the numbers need repair.
Slide 45 pairs agentic AI with causal AI and explains causal AI as the reasoning layer that decides which actions are worth taking and grounds agents against false signals. That is a sharper framing than the usual 'agents are coming' slide and it gives a lecturer something real to talk about.
What we would change

The 'Current regulatory landscape' slide does not mention the EU AI Act. (Slide 38 (and slide 39, 'Future trends'))
Learning outcome 4 is that students are aware of the legal issues of using generative AI tools. The slide covers GDPR and 'organizations exploring content authentication' and stops there. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is the governing instrument for exactly this deck's subject matter, and its Article 50 transparency obligations became applicable on 2 August 2026, the month this deck is dated. Article 50 covers chatbot disclosure, deepfake labelling and machine-readable marking.
Suggested fix: Rewrite slide 38 around three anchors: GDPR for personal data, the AI Act Article 50 transparency duties for synthetic content and chatbots, and AI Act Articles 53 and 55 for general-purpose model providers. Give students the dates, because they are the part that keeps moving: Article 50 applicable 2 August 2026, with systems already on.
Image, video and music generation are taught as GAN- and VAE-based. Diffusion is not mentioned once in 48 slides. (Slides 22, 23, 24, 25 (and slide 26, molecular generation))
Slide 22 states deepfakes 'primarily rely on GANs'. Diffusion models overtook GANs for image and video synthesis around 2022 and now lead on essentially every quality benchmark; GANs survive mainly for face synthesis and as finishing stages in face-swap pipelines. Current music tools are transformer and diffusion based, not GAN and VAE based. Students taught this deck will describe the previous generation of the technology in a job interview. This is the single biggest.
Suggested fix: Add one slide on diffusion (forward noising, learned denoising, latent diffusion for efficiency) before the GAN slide, then position GANs and VAEs as the earlier generation that is still used in specific places. Keep VAEs where they belong, in the latent-space discussion. Say plainly which approach dominates today for each modality:.
Two unrelated studies, three years apart, are merged into one undated sentence about hallucination rates. (Slide 43, first bullet)
The slide says 'By August, 2026, the rate of hallucinations remains between 3% and 27% in corporate deployments, with errors reaching up to 45% on factual tasks.' The 3 to 27 percent range is Vectara's Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model leaderboard as reported in November 2023, where OpenAI models sat near 3 percent and Google's PaLM chat at 27 percent. It measured grounded summarization on a benchmark, not corporate deployments, and Vectara retired that dataset in.
Suggested fix: Split into two sourced bullets. Cite Vectara HHEM by name with the year and say it measures grounded summarization on a benchmark, and note the leaderboard moved to a harder dataset in November 2025 so old numbers are not comparable. Cite the EBU/BBC study by name and date and state accurately what it measured: 45 percent of news answers.
BERT is described as a generative model used for machine translation. (Slide 13, 'Transformer-based translation')
BERT is an encoder-only masked language model. It produces contextual embeddings for classification, extraction and question answering. It is not a generative model and it is not a translation model. The slide sits under a bullet claiming generative models translate 'by taking advantage of the same principles used in text generation', so the one named example contradicts the point it is meant to illustrate. Students carry named examples forward.
Suggested fix: Replace BERT with encoder-decoder or decoder-only transformers. Cite Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017), whose original result was machine translation, and give a current example such as an open translation model or a general-purpose LLM. If BERT is worth keeping at all, keep it in a one-line contrast: encoder-only models.
'Deepfakes are the most significant application of generative AI.' (Slide 21, first bullet)
It is not true, and it contradicts the deck's own slides 5 and 6, which name healthcare, finance, creative media and education as the key applications. It also narrows the lesson plan's bullet 'generative AI for image and video synthesis' down to deepfakes alone. Text-to-image and text-to-video systems, which are the tools students in the room actually use, do not appear anywhere in 48 slides. Opening the visual-generation section on a misuse case sets the wrong frame for.
Suggested fix: Open the section with text-to-image and text-to-video generation as the mainstream application, then treat deepfakes as the misuse case that follows from the same technology. That also gives the ethics section on slide 36 something to point back to, and it restores the coverage the lesson plan asked for.
The deck tells students the copyright status of AI-generated art is 'not very widely discussed within legal frameworks'. (Slide 37, 'Ownership and copyright')
This is the opposite of the position in 2026, and it undercuts learning outcome 4. The US Copyright Office published its Part 2 report on copyrightability in January 2025. The DC Circuit affirmed the human authorship requirement in Thaler v. Perlmutter in March 2025, and the Supreme Court declined review. The England and Wales High Court gave judgment in Getty Images v Stability AI in November 2025, finding for Getty on trade marks while dismissing the secondary copyright.
Suggested fix: Replace the sentence with the actual state of play: human authorship is required for registration in the US, the training-data question is being litigated on both sides of the Atlantic with mixed outcomes, and EU providers carry a copyright policy obligation under the AI Act. Name two or three cases with dates so the slide can be updated.
There is not a single citation anywhere in the deck, and the wiki lists no references either. (Whole deck; acutely slides 41, 42, 43, 44. Wiki section 'Expected preparation')
48 slides, no reference slide, no source line under any statistic, and the wiki's 'References and background for students' says None. Every number on slides 41 to 43 is unattributed, and two of them we could not trace to any source at all. These slides ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so they get copied onward with the figures intact and no way for a downstream lecturer or student to check where any of it came from. This is the clearest failure against the consortium's.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide before the acknowledgements, and put a short source line in the footer of every slide carrying a statistic. Populate the wiki's 'References and background for students' with three or four readings, and 'Recommended for teachers' with the sources behind the wrap-up figures.
Two headline statistics in the wrap-up could not be traced to any source, and one of them is low. (Slide 41 ('30% of cases in customer service ... 50% by 2027') and slide 42 ('4 out of 5 university students now use generative AI tools'))
We searched for both. The customer service pairing does not match any published Gartner forecast we could find; the nearest published figures have different numbers and different scope (40 percent of customer service issues resolved by unofficial third-party generative AI tools by 2027, from December 2024; agentic AI autonomously resolving 80 percent of common issues by 2029). The student figure is understated: HEPI's Student Generative AI Survey 2026 reports 95 percent of.
Suggested fix: Either source both figures properly or replace them. For the student figure the HEPI 2026 survey is the obvious substitute and it makes the point more forcefully. For customer service, cite whichever Gartner press release the number came from and quote its actual scope and horizon, or drop the forward projection and keep only what can be.
Also noticed

Slide 41's science bullet is unchecked. 'AI is leading to breakthroughs in drug discovery, protein folding, energy production, and astronomy' (lines 495 to 497). Protein folding is the AlphaFold line, which is structure prediction rather than generative modelling in the sense this deck teaches, and the deck cannot explain the part that is generative because it never mentions.
The deck names no tool a student could open. Grep for named systems returns only GPT, BERT, Google Translate, Google Assistant and Siri. There is no ChatGPT, no current assistant, no image, video or music tool anywhere in 48 slides, and the two assistants named on slide 16 are the pre-LLM generation. For a practice-oriented review this is a direct hit on 'credible.
Retrieval and grounding are absent from the whole deck. Grep returns no hit for retrieval augmentation, grounding for accuracy, or context window. The only 'grounding' is on slide 45 about agents. The deck spends slide 43 on hallucination as a persistent limitation and never names the mitigation every practitioner reaches for first. A student leaves thinking hallucination is.
Smaller points

Slide 18 is titled 'Bias and ethical issues' but the body is entirely about coherence breaking down over long conversations. The title is wrong and the real bias material is on slide 34. Rename it to something like 'Coherence and consistency'.
Slide 17 presents chatbots for mental health support and companionship as a popular success with no caution, and slide 44 then says AI cannot replace the human approach in mental health support. The deck contradicts itself 27 slides apart. Slide 17 also misses 2025 to 2026.
Slide 15 describes 'Architecture of conversational agents' as intent classification followed by response generation. That is the pre-LLM Dialogflow and Rasa pipeline. Label it as the classic architecture and contrast it with how LLM assistants actually work, or students will.
Slides 9 and 10 give the pipeline as pretraining, fine-tuning, generation. Alignment (instruction tuning and RLHF or preference optimisation) is missing, and it is the step that turns a next-word predictor into a usable assistant. One bullet fixes it.
Slide 38 says organizations are 'exploring standards on content authentication'. They have shipped one. Name C2PA and Content Credentials: specification v2.4 (April 2026), fast-tracked as ISO/DIS 22144, with JPEG Trust adopted as ISO/IEC 21617-1:2025. 'Exploring' understates the.
Slides 30 to 32 present generative AI for personalized treatment planning as current practice ('increasingly used today'). No mention of clinical validation, EU MDR or IVDR, FDA clearance, or the fact that no generative model is approved as a medical device for treatment.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 12 items. The notable results:

'BERT and other generative models have been used for machine translation' (slide 13). Checked and found wrong. BERT is an encoder-only masked language model producing contextual embeddings; encoder-only models suit classification, NER and question answering, not generation tasks such as machine.
'Hallucinations remain between 3% and 27%' presented as an August 2026 figure (slide 43). Traced to Vectara's Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model leaderboard as reported in November 2023: OpenAI models near 3 percent, Google PaLM chat at 27 percent, measured on grounded summarization, not on.
'Errors reaching up to 45% on factual tasks' (slide 43). Traced to the EBU and BBC study 'News Integrity in AI Assistants', October 2025: 3,000 responses, 14 languages, 45 percent contained at least one significant issue, 81 percent had some problem, 31 percent had significant sourcing problems,.
'30% of customer service cases already resolved by AI, expected to reach 50% by 2027' (slide 41). Could not verify. No published Gartner forecast matching these numbers and this scope was found. The nearest published figures are different: 40 percent of customer service issues fully resolved by.
'4 out of 5 university students now use generative AI tools' (slide 42). Could not match to a current source, and it is low. HEPI's Student Generative AI Survey 2026 reports 95 percent of students using generative AI in at least one way and 94 percent using it for assessed work; the 2025 edition.
Plan against material
"They agree on structure and disagree on emphasis in two places.\n\nAgreement: the deck's five sections map one-to-one onto the five bullets in the wiki's 'Instructions for teachers', in the same order, and every sub-bullet in the plan has at least one slide behind it. Text generation with GPT models, summarization and translation, conversational agents, image and video, music and audio, healthcare, bias handling, deepfake and AI-art ethics, regulation, and a wrap-up on status and limitations are all present. The four learning outcomes on the wiki are reproduced verbatim on slide 2. That is better alignment than we usually see.\n\nFirst disagreement: the plan says 'generative AI for image and video synthesis'. The deck (slides 21 to 23) covers only deepfakes, face swapping and voice synthesis. Text-to-image and text-to-video generation are absent from all 48 slides. The plan is right.

Coverage
"Length is inside the format rule of thumb, density is not. 48 slides of which about 38 carry content, against a 30 to 60 guideline, looks fine on paper. But the slides are short prose bullets: no figures, no diagrams, no worked example, no data, no screenshots, no demo. Delivered straight this deck runs 55 to 70 minutes, not 120. The 45-minute NLP block sits on 11 sparse slides (9 to 19), which is four minutes per slide of bullet text. To fill the session the lecturer has to supply examples, a live tool demonstration and extra discussion, and none of that is written down in the deck or the wiki.\n\nInteractivity is one discussion question, on slide 46, at the very end. The format checklist.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026
