entries.title: HC-158 The AI Landscape and Limitations of AI (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: Strong classical-AI content with an unusually good treatment of each subfield's limitations, but it reproduces Russell and Norvig's agent taxonomy and learning-agent figure without attribution, carries no sources at all, and its section order and time budget do not match the lesson plan, so a lecturer cannot run it to the plan as it stands.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

Strong classical-AI content with an unusually good treatment of each subfield's limitations, but it reproduces Russell and Norvig's agent taxonomy and learning-agent figure without attribution, carries no sources at all, and its section order and time budget do not match the lesson plan, so a lecturer cannot run it to the plan as it stands.

What already works

The closing 'biggest challenges' line on each of the four blocks in 'Overview of the main subfields of classical AI' is the best design decision in the deck. Limitations sit next to the technique that has them rather than being parked in an ethics section at the end, and the ones named are the right ones: state space explosion and heuristic design for search, knowledge acquisition and commonsense.
The classical AI coverage is genuinely uncommon and worth protecting. Semantic networks, frames with slots and procedures for inference control, abductive reasoning, hierarchical and probabilistic planning, all on the 'Basic AI concepts' slides. A 2026 intake that has only met chatbots will not pick this up anywhere else, and it is what makes HC-158 distinct from HC-019, HC-021 and HC-022. It.
The 'Learning process' slide is correct and correctly ordered: forward propagation, loss function, backpropagation, optimization. Mean squared error is paired to regression and cross-entropy to classification. Intro decks routinely muddle the loss/task pairing and this one does not.
The 'Reasoning' block gets deduction, induction and abduction right, including the directions (general to specific, specific to general) and abduction as forming plausible hypotheses rather than as a third flavour of deduction.
What we would change

Russell and Norvig material is reproduced without attribution. The 'Agents' slide in the Basic AI concepts section lists agent architectures as 'simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents,. (Slides 'Agents' (Basic AI concepts section) and 'Learning agent architecture' (Basic concepts of machine learning section). The PDF text export carries no page numbers, so slides are named by title throughout.)
These decks ship under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and get copied onward. Attribution is a licence condition for the downstream user and an academic-integrity condition here. Reproducing a named author's published taxonomy and figure with no credit is the finding we block on.
Suggested fix: Add a caption on the figure slide naming its source, and a source line on the 'Agents' slide: Russell, S. and Norvig, P., Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 2. If the figure is redrawn rather than copied, say 'after Russell and Norvig'. If it came from somewhere else, name that instead; either way the slide needs a.
The 'Overview of the main subfields of classical AI' section does not deliver the subfields the plan lists. The plan names six (machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, speech recognition,. (Slide 'Overview of the main subfields of classical AI'; compare Instructions for teachers, third bullet block.)
Learning outcome 2 is 'Students know the key subfields of AI'. A student leaves this session having never heard speech recognition named, and having seen computer vision only as a list of four task names. A lecturer preparing from the plan will also arrive expecting slides that do not exist.
Suggested fix: Either add speech recognition and computer vision as full blocks in the same format as the other four (definition, then biggest challenges), or amend the plan to the four subfields the deck actually teaches and add search to the list. The deck's format is good, so extending it is the cheaper route.
Section order and time allocation do not match the plan. The plan runs intro plus basic AI concepts (20 min), main types (15), subfields (55), ML (45), DL (30), wrap up (15). The deck runs nature of AI, main types,. (Whole deck order; Instructions for teachers, all bullet blocks. Specifically slides 'Basic AI concepts' through 'Bias in AI systems' versus slide 'Overview of the main subfields of classical AI'.)
This is the teachability failure. A lecturer who was not involved in writing the material cannot run this deck against the timing in the plan. They will be at the 55-minute block with one slide and then hit ten unbudgeted slides.
Suggested fix: Rewrite the Instructions for teachers to the deck's actual order and give each section the minutes its slides need, or move the 'Basic AI concepts' slides back to the front as the 20-minute review the plan describes. Decide where ethics and bias belongs: HC-161 has a 30-minute 'core principles of responsible AI' block, so it may be.
The deck contains no references or source list of any kind, and the three figures on the supervised ML slide are uncaptioned. 'Sample data:', 'Sample result:' and 'Sample regression data:' are label text with images. (Slide 'Supervised ML - main types of methods'; and the deck as a whole, which has no references slide before Acknowledgements.)
The reviewer checklist covers traceability, and the same gap was already raised on the sibling LE HC-148 by the Hamburg reviewers ('What are the sources of the materials used for the facts in the teaching materials'). Under CC BY-NC-SA the downstream adapter has to be able to trace figures. Uncaptioned sample data is also unteachable: a lecturer teaching this cold cannot say what the columns are.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide before Acknowledgements. Caption each figure with what the dataset is and where it came from. If the decision tree sample is the classic weather / play-tennis dataset, name it and its source.
The wrap-up has no content. The plan allocates 15 minutes to 'Wrap up: modern trends in AI development'. The deck's wrap-up is a single discussion question, 'What are the classical and modern AI areas and concepts?',. (Slide 'Wrap up'; Instructions for teachers, final bullet.)
Fifteen minutes of a 180-minute session has no material. The question also asks students about 'modern AI areas' that the deck never covered, so it cannot be answered from the session. HC-161 owns current research and applications, so the content does not need to be large, but this block cannot be empty.
Suggested fix: Add two or three slides closing the classical-to-modern arc and naming what Part 2 picks up. The obvious content is the transformer architecture and foundation models, which is also the one thing missing from 'Types of neural networks'. Keep it to a bridge so it does not duplicate HC-161.
Reinforcement learning is missing from the classification of ML types. The slide 'Basic classification of ML methods' lists only supervised and unsupervised learning. RL gets its own slide two slides later, but a. (Slide with 'Definition of machine learning' and 'Basic classification of ML methods', in the Basic concepts of machine learning section.)
Learning outcome 4 is 'Students distinguish the main types of machine learning' and the plan spells it out as 'supervised vs. unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning'. The slide that carries the taxonomy contradicts both the plan and the deck's own earlier slide.
Suggested fix: Add reinforcement learning to the classification slide as the third type, with a forward pointer to the RL slide. Add self-supervised learning as a one-line mention while you are there; it is named in HC-161's plan and it is how everything students meet in Part 2 is actually trained.
The overview of supervised methods omits ensemble methods entirely. The slide lists decision trees, naive Bayes, support vector machines, linear regression and logistic regression. No random forests, no gradient. (Slide 'Supervised ML - main types of methods'; Instructions for teachers, 'overview of the main types of methods for supervised ML'.)
This is the practice-relevance point. Gradient-boosted trees are the default first choice for tabular problems in industry, and random forests are the standard baseline. A student who leaves an overview of supervised methods without having heard of either will be surprised on their first project. Single decision trees, presented alone, also invite the wrong conclusion about how trees are used in practice.
Suggested fix: Add one line for ensembles on the same slide: random forest and gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) as the methods most used on tabular data, built from the decision trees already on the slide. This is a two-bullet addition, not a new section.
The funding acknowledgement names the wrong EU programme. It reads 'co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union under grant DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU'. DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU. (Slide 'Acknowledgements'. The same text appears on HC-148 and in the wiki 'Acknowledgements, thanks' section, so this is consortium boilerplate rather than this author's wording.)
The sentence names a call topic from one instrument and attributes the funding to a different instrument. It is on every deck, it goes out under CC BY-NC-SA, and it is the kind of thing a funder notices.
Suggested fix: Correct to the Digital Europe Programme, or to whichever instrument the grant agreement actually names. This should go to the coordinator to fix once across all decks and the wiki template, not to Maria Nisheva alone.
Broken text on a student-facing slide: 'learning new knowledge (e.g., learning decision trees, learning or learning Bayesian networks)'. The words 'learning or learning' are a duplication and the bullet does not parse. (Slide 'Common ML tasks', first bullet.)
It is on the slide students read, immediately above the discussion question that asks them to work with this list.
Suggested fix: Correct to 'learning decision trees, learning Bayesian networks'.
Also noticed

Ten slides carry no text at all: 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 31, 35, 38, 41 and 49. That is a fifth of the deck. Some are certainly figures, which makes must_fix 4 far larger than stated: every figure in this deck is uncaptioned and unsourced, not just the three on slides 32 to 34 and the one on 27. Slides 14 and 15 are two consecutive textless slides closing the subfields section, and.
The deck credits only one author. Slide 1 reads 'Made by: Maria Nisheva (SU)'. The wiki names Author Person 2 as Ahmad Khalidi (HAW). That is a wiki and material disagreement, and an attribution gap on a deliverable that ships under CC BY-NC-SA and gets copied onward. The review's whole first must_fix is about attribution and it did not catch the missing author on the title.
Lecturer notes are a listed format requirement, not a nice-to-have. The guidelines' lecture-slides checklist says the slides should 'contain lecturer notes that make the slides usable for a lecturer who was not involved in developing the material'. The review put the PDF-versus-PPTX point in smaller_fixes. With ten textless slides that a lecturer cannot reconstruct without the.
Smaller points

Slide 'Main types of AI systems': the closing summary paragraph talks only about weak and strong AI and never mentions superintelligence, which the slide introduced three lines above. Carry it into the summary or drop it from the slide.
Same slide: the superintelligence wording tracks Nick Bostrom's definition. Cite Bostrom (Superintelligence, 2014) or rephrase in the author's own words.
Slide 'Overview of the main subfields of classical AI': 'It is the historically first subfield of AI' is stated flatly about search. Newell, Shaw and Simon's Logic Theorist supports it, but McCulloch and Pitts (1943) and the perceptron (1957) complicate it. Hedge it or source it.
Slide 'Supervised ML - main types of methods': logistic regression is listed among the methods and the slide then shows regression sample data. Students consistently take it for a regression method. One line saying it is a classification method despite the name would prevent.
Slide 'Unsupervised ML - clustering methods' is two words. The deck's own 'Machine learning' slide in the Basic AI concepts section says unsupervised learning covers clustering, dimensionality reduction and association rule mining. Add PCA and one embedding method (UMAP or.
Discussion question after 'Common ML tasks' is well placed but needs a model answer for the lecturer. Anomaly detection is done both supervised and unsupervised, and object detection is supervised but sits in a list that mixes task types with application types. Without an answer.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 10 items. The notable results:

DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU: verified as a Digital Europe Programme call topic ('Specialised education programmes in key capacity areas', open 21 Nov 2023 to 21 Mar 2024, EUR 30m budget, 26 proposals received), via the European Digital Skills and Jobs Platform and the EC Funding and Tenders.
Grant agreement 101189994: could not verify independently. cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101189994 returns 404, which is consistent with a Digital Europe Programme grant (DIGITAL projects are administered by HaDEA and generally are not published on CORDIS) rather than evidence the number is wrong..
Russell and Norvig agent taxonomy: verified against an AIMA Chapter 2 lecture handout (University of Pittsburgh CS2710, Litman). The five-way taxonomy simple reflex / model-based reflex / goal-based / utility-based / learning agents is Russell and Norvig's, and the general learning agent.
Machine learning definition ('A type of artificial intelligence in which computers use huge amounts of data to learn how to do tasks rather than being programmed to do them'): source not verified. dictionary.cambridge.org returned HTTP 403 and this session's web search budget was already exhausted.
Superintelligence definition: not verified externally, for the same budget reason. From knowledge, the deck's phrasing ('surpasses human intelligence in all aspects, including creativity, problem solving, and social skills') tracks Nick Bostrom's definition closely, which reads 'scientific.
Plan against material
They disagree in four places, and where they disagree the plan is closer to right on content while the deck is closer to right on structure. 1. Subfields. The plan lists six subfields for the 55-minute block: machine learning, NLP, computer vision, speech recognition, planning and scheduling, KRR. The deck covers search, planning, KRR and NLP. Search is a good addition and belongs in the plan. Speech recognition is absent from the entire deck and computer vision is demoted to a bullet list elsewhere; those two need to be added to the deck rather than dropped from the plan, because learning outcome 2 depends on them. 2. Order and timing. The plan opens with 'nature of AI and the basic AI concepts' as one 20-minute block. The deck splits these: nature of AI opens the session, but the ten-slide 'Basic AI concepts' section sits after the subfields block. The deck's order is defensible, the.

Coverage
Outcomes. Outcome 1 (main types of AI systems) is delivered, and the deck adds superintelligence beyond the plan's two types. Outcome 3 (basic concepts and tasks of ML) is delivered at definition level. Outcome 5 (basic concepts of deep learning) is delivered well and covers everything the plan lists, including forward propagation, backpropagation, CNNs, RNNs and autoencoders. Outcome 2 (key subfields) is only partly delivered: speech recognition is absent and computer vision is a bullet list. Outcome 4 (distinguish the main types of ML) is undercut by the classification slide, which gives two types where the plan and the outcome need three. 180 minutes. The deck is roughly 35 to 40 slides.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

action_summary.text:
Hello Maria and Ahmad, this is the short, actionable version of our early feedback of 9 September 2026; the full text above stays as the record. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: Early feedback only, not yet a formal review. The classical-AI content and per-technique limitations are strong.

Please do next:
# Credit Russell and Norvig (AIMA, Chapter 2) on the 'Agents' slide and the 'Learning agent architecture' figure, or write "after Russell and Norvig".
# Add speech recognition and computer vision as full blocks in the subfields overview, or reduce the plan to the four subfields taught.
# Rewrite Instructions for teachers to the deck's real order, with minutes for every section, including 'Basic AI concepts'.
# Add a references slide before Acknowledgements and caption every figure, starting with the three images on 'Supervised ML - main types of methods'.
# Replace the single-question 'Wrap up' with two or three slides bridging to transformers, foundation models and Part 2.
# Add reinforcement learning to 'Basic classification of ML methods', and random forest and gradient boosting to the supervised methods slide.
# Fix "learning or learning" on 'Common ML tasks', and add Ahmad Khalidi to the title slide.

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):
* Expected preparation: all four fields read "None".
* Lesson materials: only the text "HC-158", no working link.
* Acknowledgements: grant number reads "???"; we will raise the funding wording with the coordinator.

A short summary is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off.

When the items are done, tell us on this Discussion page, email the review inbox, and move the status to review.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

HC-161 has a good backbone, especially the responsible AI principles and the eight-instrument regulatory survey, but the EU AI Act penalty figure is the never-enacted 2021 proposal number, the OECD principle list drops Accountability, Canada's AIDA is presented as live legislation when it died in January 2025, and the Causal AI comparison is a near-verbatim uncredited lift from a vendor blog, so it cannot be taught or redistributed under CC BY-NC-SA as it stands.

What already works

The nine responsible AI principles slides are the best part of the deck. Each principle gets an operational sentence rather than a slogan: fairness names the protected characteristics to test against (race, gender, age, disability), privacy names data minimisation, consent and anonymisation, reliability names fallback mechanisms, human-centricity says humans must be able to review and correct.
The regulatory section goes well beyond what the plan asked for. The plan lists three instruments; the deck covers eight (EU AI Act, OECD, NIST AI RMF, Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, UNESCO, Canada AIDA, China algorithmic recommendation provisions, Singapore Model Framework). Every one uses the same four fields (Status, Approach, Key Provisions, Enforcement). That parallel structure is.
The Quantum AI slide headed 'Current status and challenges' is honest and accurate: early research stage, noisy hardware, limited qubit counts, and most real work today running as hybrid quantum-classical with classical machines handling data processing and model control. That last point in particular is what practitioners see. It is the slide that partly rescues the quantum section.
The three introduction sub-slides frame the topic the way it is actually discussed in industry rather than in a textbook: trust as an adoption barrier with stakeholders refusing black-box recommendations, augmentation with humans retaining the final say in high-stakes decisions, and regulation as something to anticipate rather than react to. Good practice framing for a mixed job-role audience.
What we would change

The EU AI Act penalty figure is wrong. The slide states fines 'up to EUR 30 million or 6% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher'. (Regulatory frameworks section, slide 'European Union - EU AI Act', Enforcement bullet (the PDF text extraction carries no slide numbers; this is the first slide after the 'Existing regulatory frameworks for AI' divider))
EUR 30 million / 6% is the figure from the April 2021 Commission proposal (COM(2021) 206 final, Art 71(3)). It was never enacted. I checked Article 99 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 directly: the tiers are EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for Article 5 prohibited practices, EUR 15 000 000 or 3% for most other operator and notified body obligations, and EUR 7 500 000 or 1% for supplying incorrect or misleading information. A single flat number also hides.
Suggested fix: Replace the single Enforcement line with the three statutory tiers and cite Art 99 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Add the SME rule (for SMEs and start-ups the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount applies, not the higher), because it changes the answer for most companies students will work at.
The OECD list of five values-based principles is incomplete and uses superseded wording. The slide gives 'inclusive growth; sustainable development; human-centered values; transparency and explainability; robustness,. (Regulatory frameworks section, slide 'OECD Principles on AI', Key Provisions bullet)
I verified the OECD principle set. Principle 1.1 is one principle, 'inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being', not two; splitting it lets the count still read as five while Accountability (principle 1.5) is silently dropped. Accountability is not a footnote here, it is the principle that carries traceability and risk management after the May 2024 revision moved those provisions into it from robustness. The slide also uses the 2019 wording of principle 1.2;.
Suggested fix: List all five as: (1.1) inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; (1.2) respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; (1.3) transparency and explainability; (1.4) robustness, security and safety; (1.5) accountability. Change the Status line to 'Adopted May 2019, revised.
Canada's AIDA is presented as live legislation with a current enforcement regime. (Regulatory frameworks section, slide 'Canada - Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA)')
AIDA was Part 3 of Bill C-27. Parliament was prorogued on 6 January 2025 and Bill C-27 died on the Order Paper. I verified this: the privacy half returned in a later bill, AIDA has no successor, and Canada has no federal AI statute. The slide's Status ('introduced in June 2022'), its present-tense Key Provisions ('Prohibits certain harmful uses of AI, requires risk mitigation measures, mandates transparency and record-keeping') and its Enforcement line ('Potential fines up.
Suggested fix: Either drop the slide or rewrite it as a lapsed-bill case study: what AIDA proposed, why it drew criticism, that it died at prorogation in January 2025 with no replacement introduced, and that Canada currently regulates AI through existing privacy, consumer protection and human rights law. The case study version is arguably more valuable.
The Causal AI comparison is reproduced near-verbatim from a vendor blog post without attribution. (Current fields of AI research section, slide 'Causal AI', the five 'Key differences from traditional (correlation-based) AI' bullets (Basis of Analysis, Explainability, Bias and Reliability, Adaptability, Decision Making))
I found the source. LeewayHertz's article 'Causal AI: Use Cases, Need, Benefits, Challenges and Strategies' (leewayhertz.com/causal-ai/) carries a comparison table with the same five row labels in the same order and near-identical wording. Its Bias and Reliability row reads 'Less prone to bias as it relies on actual and comprehensive data for analyses' and its Adaptability row reads 'Highly adaptable; can uncover new issues and adapt to changing environments'; the slide.
Suggested fix: Either cite LeewayHertz explicitly on the slide, or replace the table with a version built from a citable academic source (Pearl's ladder of causation, or Scholkopf et al. 'Toward Causal Representation Learning', Proc. IEEE 2021) and rewrite the wording. The second option is better for a master-level deck because it also fixes the.
The claim 'Causal AI is less prone to bias as it relies on actual and comprehensive data for analyses' is wrong as stated. (Current fields of AI research section, slide 'Causal AI', Bias and Reliability bullet)
Causal methods address one specific bias, confounding, and only under assumptions that cannot be tested from the data: no unmeasured confounding, positivity, and a correctly specified causal graph. They do nothing about measurement bias, selection bias or unrepresentative sampling, and a wrong graph makes the estimate worse than a plain predictive model while looking more authoritative. Saying causal AI is safer because it uses 'actual and comprehensive data' inverts the.
Suggested fix: Rewrite the row to state the real trade-off: causal methods can remove confounding bias, but only if the causal structure is correct and all confounders are measured, and they are not a general defence against biased or unrepresentative data. Drop or cite the outperformance claim.
The EU AI Act slide has no application timeline and no mention of general-purpose AI obligations, and it presents 'limited risk' and 'minimal/no risk' as if they were statutory categories. (Regulatory frameworks section, slide 'European Union - EU AI Act', Status and Approach bullets)
'Entered into force on 1 August 2024' is correct but it is the least useful date, because almost nothing applied then. The dates that matter are 2 February 2025 for the Article 5 prohibitions, 2 August 2025 for GPAI provider obligations and governance, 2 August 2026 for general application, and, since Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 entered into force on 27 July 2026, 2 December 2027 for Annex III high-risk systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I embedded systems. The deck is dated.
Suggested fix: Add a timeline strip with the four application dates including the December 2027 and August 2028 deferrals, add a GPAI line, and label the four-box diagram as a common simplification while naming the actual articles underneath it. This is the single most important learning outcome in the wiki plan ('first of all with the EU AI Act') and.
The Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights is presented as current US federal policy with no indication that the surrounding policy framework was revoked in January 2025. (Regulatory frameworks section, slide 'United States - Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights')
The facts on the slide are right for October 2022: OSTP, five principles, non-binding. But it sits in a section titled 'Existing regulatory frameworks' with no date context, and the US federal posture changed in January 2025 when the prior AI executive order was revoked and federal AI policy was redirected. The Blueprint still exists as a published OSTP document but it no longer describes the direction of US federal policy. Presented flat alongside the EU AI Act, it will.
Suggested fix: Keep the slide but add a currency line: the Blueprint remains a published OSTP document from October 2022 and is widely cited, but the federal AI policy framework around it was revoked in January 2025, and US AI governance now runs largely through sectoral regulators, procurement requirements and state law (Colorado SB 24-205, the.
The deck does not carry 180 minutes of teaching material. Two of the six planned blocks have almost no content behind them. (Slide 'Modern applications of AI systems' (one slide for the 40-minute block) and slide 'Summary' plus the discussion question slide (two slides for the 20-minute block))
The wiki plan allocates 40 minutes to modern applications across eight domains. The deck gives all eight domains as a single bulleted list with no case, no example system, no failure mode and no numbers. A lecturer cannot get 40 minutes out of that without inventing the content themselves, which defeats the teachability requirement. The plan then allocates 20 minutes to 'analysis of possible scenarios for the development of AI'. The deck has a 'Summary' slide that appears in.
Suggested fix: Expand 'Modern applications' to at least one slide per domain group, each with a named real system, what it does, and one documented limitation or failure. That also lets the deck finally deliver the 'Limitations of AI' half of its own title. For the summary, give students two or three named scenarios to react to (for example continued.
The wiki lesson plan and the deck disagree on the regulatory section, and the deck carries no references anywhere. (Wiki 'Instructions for teachers', bullet 'Existing regulatory frameworks for AI - 40 min'; wiki 'Expected preparation'; and the whole deck)
The plan lists three instruments: EU AI Act, OECD Principles on AI, US Executive Order 13859. The deck covers eight and does not mention EO 13859 at all. The deck's choice is the better one, since EO 13859 is a 2019 policy directive with little current operational relevance, but a lecturer working from the wiki will look for an EO 13859 slide and not find it, and the 40-minute allocation is now spread across eight instruments rather than three. Separately, the deck contains.
Suggested fix: Update the wiki teacher instructions to list the eight instruments actually covered, drop EO 13859 or justify keeping it, and re-split the 40 minutes. Add a references slide to the deck with the primary sources (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 on EUR-Lex, the OECD Recommendation OECD/LEGAL/0449, NIST AI 100-1, the.
Also noticed

The deck does not credit the second author. Wiki lines 54-60 name Author Organisation 2 as HAW and Author Person 2 as Ahmad Khalidi. The deck title slide (lines 8-9) says only 'Made by: Maria Nisheva (SU)'. This is a wiki/material disagreement of exactly the kind the review is meant to catch, and it is an attribution defect in a deck that ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and is.
The section title 'Existing regulatory frameworks for AI' (deck line 231) is wrong for six of its eight entries. Only the EU AI Act and the China provisions are binding law. OECD, NIST AI RMF, the Blueprint, UNESCO and Singapore are all non-binding guidance, and AIDA is a dead bill. The per-slide Enforcement field carries the distinction, and the review rightly praises that,.
The quantum parallelism misconception appears twice, not once. The review flags only the bullet at deck lines 133-135. The same error is in the definitional paragraph at lines 119-125: qubits 'allowing quantum computers to process vast amounts of data in parallel'. That sentence is the one students will copy into their notes, so fixing only the bullet leaves the misconception.
Smaller points

Typo on the sustainability principle slide: 'Developing and using AI systems as an environmental footprint' should be 'has an environmental footprint'. Also, the principle is named 'Environmental and economic sustainability' but the body text only covers environmental. Add a.
China slide stops at the March 2022 algorithmic recommendation provisions. China's AI regime has moved on considerably since: the Deep Synthesis Provisions (in force January 2023), the Interim Measures for Generative AI Services (August 2023) and the labelling measures for.
Singapore slide covers the 2019 Model AI Governance Framework and its 2020 second edition. Add the Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI (May 2024), which is the version practitioners actually reference now.
NIST slide correctly gives AI RMF 1.0, January 2023, and the Govern / Map / Measure / Manage functions. Add the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024), which is the companion most organisations are working from.
The Gartner Hype Cycle slide uses the 2025 edition. By the time this is first taught the 2026 edition will be current. If the licensing issue is resolved and the figure stays, plan to swap it each year, and note the swap in the lecturer instructions so it does not silently go.
The introduction slide on regulation refers to 'frameworks from the EU, OECD, UN, and other bodies'. The deck covers UNESCO, which is a UN agency but is not 'the UN'. Either name UNESCO or add the UN General Assembly resolution of March 2024 so the reference has something behind.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 14 items. The notable results:

EU AI Act penalties. Fetched artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/ and confirmed the three statutory tiers of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art 99: EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art 5 prohibited practices), EUR 15 000 000 or 3% (most other operator and notified body.
EU AI Act entry into force. Deck says 1 August 2024. CORRECT, but it is the least informative date, since the obligations phase in separately.
EU AI Act deferral. Confirmed by search that Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI) was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, deferring Annex III standalone high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 and Annex I.
EU AI Act risk terminology. 'Limited risk' and 'minimal risk' are not terms used in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; the Act structures obligations by Art 5 prohibitions, Art 6 and Annexes I/III high-risk classification, Art 50 transparency duties and the Chapter V GPAI regime. Deck presents the four-box.
OECD AI Principles. Verified by search. Adopted May 2019, revised May 2024. The five principles are: inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness,.
Plan against material
"They agree on three of six blocks and diverge on three.\n\nAgree. The 'Current fields of AI research' block maps almost exactly: machine learning with its five sub-topics, NLP with six, computer vision with three, robotics with two, then causal AI and quantum AI each getting their own treatment, in the plan's order. The 'Core principles of responsible AI' block maps one to one, all nine principles, same order, same names. The 'Modern applications' block lists the same eight domains with the same sub-items, though see the coverage note on depth.\n\nDisagree, and the plan is wrong. The regulatory block. The plan says EU AI Act, OECD Principles on AI, US Executive Order 13859. The deck covers EU AI Act, OECD, NIST AI RMF, Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, UNESCO, Canada AIDA, China, Singapore, and never mentions EO 13859. The deck is right to drop EO 13859 and right to broaden the.

Coverage
"No, the material does not fill 180 minutes, and it delivers three of the four learning outcomes only partly.\n\nOn duration. Counting from the text extraction, the deck is roughly 30 slides including the title, one section divider, the acknowledgements and the licence, so about 26 content slides for a three-hour lecture. The consortium rule of thumb is about one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture-based event. The gap is not evenly spread: the responsible AI principles block (30 minutes planned) has five well-filled slides and is close to right, and the regulatory block (40 minutes planned) has eight slides and is close to right. The shortfall is concentrated in two places..

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 180 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 34 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.19. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: HC-172 Introduction to Data Analysis and Study Design (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: HC-172 follows its lesson plan block for block and most of the statistics is correct, but two arithmetic errors are printed on screen, two concepts are given the wrong name, three figures appear to be lifted from a textbook and one from a watermarked website, and the deck carries no references at all, so it cannot go out under CC BY-NC-SA as it stands.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

HC-172 follows its lesson plan block for block and most of the statistics is correct, but two arithmetic errors are printed on screen, two concepts are given the wrong name, three figures appear to be lifted from a textbook and one from a watermarked website, and the deck carries no references at all, so it cannot go out under CC BY-NC-SA as it stands.

What already works

The deck maps one to one onto the lesson plan. Slides 4 to 6 are the introduction, 7 to 15 the terms, 16 to 27 the key steps, 28 to 32 the classes, 33 to 44 descriptive statistics, 45 to 49 the wrap up, in the same order and with the same names as the six timed blocks in the plan. A lecturer can hold the plan next to the deck and always know where they are. That is not true of every deck in this.
Slides 34 to 37 are the strongest part of the material. They do not just list mean, median and mode, they argue why the median is preferred when extreme values are present, give the median position formula correctly for odd and even n, and bring in the trimmed mean, which most introductory decks skip. Slide 37 handles multimodal data and the no-mode case correctly.
The p-value definition on slide 15 is the correct one, 'the probability of observing a result as extreme or more extreme than the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true'. That is a sentence most introductory material gets wrong.
Slide 27's conceptual question about middle names in employee records is well chosen. It is a real data problem, it has no single right answer, and asking for two solutions forces a decision instead of recall. It is the only exercise in the deck, but it is a good one.
What we would change

The worked example prints Median(D) = (5.5+6.5) = 6. (Slide 39)
(5.5+6.5) is 12. The division by 2 is missing, so the equality shown on screen is false. This is the only worked calculation of central tendency in the whole deck, and it is the line students will copy into their notes. The answer 6 is right; the formula is not.
Suggested fix: Change to Median(D) = (5.5+6.5)/2 = 6. Mean 5.6 and Mode 8 on the same slide both check out.
The transformation shown is -17, 25, 39, 128, -39 mapping to 0.17, 0.25, 0.39, 1.28, -0.39. The first value loses its minus sign. (Slide 22, Data Transformation panel)
Every other value is divided by 100 and keeps its sign, including -39 to -0.39. So -17 has to map to -0.17. A scaling example that silently flips a sign teaches the opposite of what the slide intends, and any student who checks it will stop trusting the rest of the arithmetic.
Suggested fix: Change 0.17 to -0.17.
The Data Integration, Data Cleaning, Data Transformation and Data Reduction panels carry no source line. They match the four panels of the 'forms of data preprocessing' figure in Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining:. (Slides 19, 21 and 22)
The deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and is meant to be copied and adapted onward. PANORAIMA cannot relicense a Morgan Kaufmann figure under CC BY-NC-SA. Reproducing a published figure with no credit is the finding we treat as blocking in this project. I verified the book, edition, publisher and that chapter 3 is Data Preprocessing from the authors' own book site, but I could not run an image-level match in this session, so the author should confirm the origin rather than.
Suggested fix: Confirm where the panels came from. If it is that book, either redraw them from scratch and credit the source of the idea, or put a full figure citation on each slide and check that the reuse is permitted under the deck's licence. If they came from somewhere else, name that source.
The histogram of student weights carries a visible pmvidya.com watermark in its bottom right corner. The line chart beside it has no source, no axis labels and no scale. (Slide 12, left-hand histogram)
pmvidya.com is a live third-party site whose footer asserts copyright as (c) 2026 PM Vidya. The image is used with no credit and no evident permission in a deck distributed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The watermark is legible on screen, so students can see whose image it is.
Suggested fix: Replace both images with charts the author generates. That also fixes the readability, since the borrowed histogram's axis labels are too small to read at projection size.
Two statistics, neither citable. 'Gartner (2025) predicts that 60% of AI projects will be abandoned if not supported by AI-ready data' names a firm but no report or release. 'Over 90% of AI failures come from poor data. (Slide 5)
A bare month and year is not a citation. I could not find any source for the 90% figure. The Gartner statement as I know it is bounded by a horizon ('through 2026') that the slide drops, and that horizon changes what the number claims. These are the only two numbers in the deck and they are the first thing students see.
Suggested fix: Add the Gartner release title and date and restore the time horizon. Source the 90% figure properly or cut it. If it comes from a vendor blog rather than research, say so on the slide so students learn to make that distinction.
The 1.5 x IQR outlier fence is introduced as 'the empirical rule'. (Slide 42)
The empirical rule is the 68-95-99.7 rule for the normal distribution. It is a different rule and it depends on a distributional assumption the IQR fence exists to avoid. The 1.5 x IQR fence is Tukey's, from the box plot work he introduced in 1970 and published in Exploratory Data Analysis in 1977. Students who carry the wrong name forward will be marked wrong in the next statistics course, and slide 43 already uses box plots without connecting them to this rule.
Suggested fix: Call it Tukey's fence or the 1.5 x IQR rule and credit Tukey. The bolded sentence itself is stated correctly; only the name needs replacing. Slide 42 also has no title, unlike every other content slide.
'Sometimes this type of analytics, when done hands-on with a small dataset, is also known as causal analysis, since it involves at least one cause (usually more than one) and one effect.' (Slide 30)
Drilling into data by hand is not causal analysis. A causal claim needs a design that rules out confounding, either randomisation or an identification strategy on observational data. Dataset size has nothing to do with it. This is exactly the reasoning error that produces bad decisions in practice. It also contradicts HC-174, which teaches observational versus experimental studies and bias control as the way to get at causes.
Suggested fix: Cut the sentence. Replace it with one line saying diagnostic analytics generates hypotheses about causes, and that establishing a cause requires the study designs covered in HC-174.
'Validation: Analysts ensure the data used for AI is representative and unbiased, preventing poor model performance.' (Slide 46)
No analyst can ensure data is unbiased. Representativeness is only defined relative to a stated target population, and bias can be measured against chosen groups and documented, not eliminated by inspection. Stated this way, students leave thinking data bias is a checkbox that someone upstream ticks. For a human-centred AI programme that is the wrong message, and it sits in the closing section that ties this event to the rest of the curriculum.
Suggested fix: Rewrite as: analysts assess how representative the data is for a stated target population, measure and document known biases, and record what remains unknown. One sentence pointing at the programme's fairness content would close the loop.
51 slides with no references slide anywhere, and the only file delivered is Presentation HC-172.pdf, which contains no lecturer notes. (Whole deck, and the SharePoint folder WP4/Learning_Materials/4.1 Horizontal/HC-172)
The reviewer checklist asks that claims, frameworks and figures be traceable and that the material be teachable by a lecturer who was not involved in writing it. With no source list a second lecturer cannot check a single claim on slides 5, 10, 12, 19, 21, 22, 29 to 32 or 42. With no notes they cannot see what the author intended for a 45-minute block that contains 10 content slides. A PDF also cannot be adapted, which is precisely what the CC BY-NC-SA licence on slide 51.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide. Deliver the source PowerPoint alongside the PDF, with notes on at least the section dividers and on slides 22, 27, 36 and 42. Every SU deck in this batch from HC-148 to HC-186 is PDF only, so the packaging half of this is worth settling once at partner level rather than deck by deck.
Also noticed

Slide 6 has no title and no page number. It is the only slide in the deck missing its footer number - I checked all 51 - and it reads as a dangling continuation of slide 5's bullet list. The review flags slide 42 for having no title but not slide 6, which is the worse of the two because the lecturer loses their place indicator as well.
Slide 43 contradicts slide 42. It says box plots 'display the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and identify outliers'. Once outliers are plotted separately the whiskers stop at the most extreme non-outlier, not at the minimum and maximum. The deck teaches the 1.5 x IQR fence on the preceding slide and then defines the box plot as if the fence did not.
Slide 44's unreadability can be stated as a fact rather than an impression: pdfimages shows the embedded bitmap is 432 x 240 pixels, placed across roughly half the width of a 960 x 540 pt slide, so it renders at well under half the density it needs. Worth putting in the finding, because it removes the argument.
Smaller points

Slide 34: 'inflation frates' should read 'inflation rates'.
Slide 42 has no title, unlike every other content slide, and it carries one bullet that would sit naturally at the foot of slide 41.
Slide 40 defines variance as 'the average of the squared differences from the mean' and never separates the population divisor n from the sample divisor n-1. The first time a student computes this they hit Excel's VAR.P against VAR.S, or numpy's default ddof=0 against pandas'.
Slide 36: saying the median is the trimmed mean with p = 100% is a limiting statement, not a computation you can perform. Write 'in the limit' so students do not try it.
Slide 22: the Data Reduction panel shrinks both attributes (200 to 120) and rows (200 to 150), while slide 20 defines data reduction only as reducing dimensionality. Either change the figure or add numerosity reduction to the slide 20 text.
Slide 24 lists accuracy, precision, recall, F1, RMSE and R-squared but never says the evaluation happens on data the model has not seen. Add that phrase. It is the single most common mistake made by people who learn data analysis before they learn machine learning, and this deck.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 11 items. The notable results:

Stevens' levels of measurement (slide 10). Verified: the nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio taxonomy is S. S. Stevens, 'On the Theory of Scales of Measurement', Science 103(2684), 677-680, 7 June 1946. The slide's four definitions and examples are correct. The source is not named on the slide, which.
1.5 x IQR fence (slide 42). Verified: the box plot and its 1.5 x IQR fences are Tukey's, introduced 1970 and published in Exploratory Data Analysis, 1977. Also verified that the 'empirical rule' is the separate 68-95-99.7 rule for the normal distribution. The slide's name for the rule is wrong; the.
Han, Kamber and Pei (slides 19, 21, 22). Verified from the authors' own book site (hanj.cs.illinois.edu/bk3): Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, 3rd edition, Morgan Kaufmann, July 2011, ISBN 978-0123814791, chapter 3 is 'Data Preprocessing'. The four panels on slides 19, 21 and 22 match that.
pmvidya.com (slide 12). Verified: it is a live third-party educational site whose footer asserts copyright as '(c) 2026 PM Vidya'. Its watermark is visible on the histogram used on slide 12.
Gartner 60% claim (slide 5). Not verified in this session. Gartner's newsroom returns HTTP 403 to fetches and the web search budget was exhausted, so I could not retrieve the release. My recollection of the February 2025 Gartner statement is that it reads 'through 2026, organizations will abandon.
Plan against material
Structurally they agree, and closely. The plan's six timed blocks appear in the deck in the same order under the same headings: 0 to 10 introduction (slides 4 to 6), 10 to 30 main tasks and terms (7 to 15), 30 to 75 key steps (16 to 27), 75 to 90 main classes (28 to 32), 90 to 110 descriptive statistics (33 to 44), 110 to 120 wrap up (45 to 49). All seven sub-steps listed under "key steps" and all four classes and all three descriptive statistics categories appear as named slides. That mapping is checkable and it holds. Four things do not agree, and in each case the deck is closer to right than the wiki. Authorship. The lesson plan file on SharePoint (Lesson Plan HC-172.docx) names the authors as "Maria Nisheva, Kalinka Kaloyanova". The wiki names Maria Nisheva (SU) as Author 1 and Béla Pataki (BME) as Author 2. The title slide credits only "Maria Nisheva (SU)". Kalinka Kaloyanova is.

Coverage
The learning outcomes are mostly delivered, but the 120 minutes are not filled by what is on the slides. Outcomes 1, 3 and 4 (main terms, main classes, categories of descriptive statistics) are covered directly and adequately by slides 7 to 15, 28 to 32 and 33 to 44. Outcome 2, "understand the key steps in data analysis", is delivered at the level of naming the seven steps. Slides 17 to 26 list what happens at each step. Nothing asks a student to make a decision at any step, to choose between two options, or to say what goes wrong if a step is skipped. That is the gap between knowing the steps and understanding them. On timing: 51 slides, 46 of them content, for 120 minutes, which is about.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

Please do next:

entries.title: HC-174 Introduction to Data Analysis and Study Design (Part 2)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: A well organised and factually accurate lecture on classical study design, but the section titled "Definition of study design" never defines one, the deck carries no references at all, and nothing in it connects study design to AI or ML practice, which is what a PANORAIMA horizontal lecture should be doing.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

A well organised and factually accurate lecture on classical study design, but the section titled "Definition of study design" never defines one, the deck carries no references at all, and nothing in it connects study design to AI or ML practice, which is what a PANORAIMA horizontal lecture should be doing.

What already works

Slides 11 to 16 are the best part of the deck. The ten questions a study plan must answer are complete and correctly ordered, and each one gets both a 'what to do' line and a 'why it matters' line rather than a bare checklist. A student could work from this page set directly.
Every design definition is correct. Cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, ecological (slides 21 to 22), RCT, quasi-experimental and crossover (slides 24 to 25) are all described accurately, and each gets a concrete worked example rather than an abstract statement. The examples are well chosen and memorable.
Slide 21 says plainly that a cross-sectional study cannot determine causality. That is the single most common student error in this topic and it is good that it is stated up front rather than buried.
The deck maps section for section onto the lesson plan. The five agenda items on slide 3 are the five bullets in the Instructions for teachers, in the same order, with section dividers at slides 4, 10, 19, 27 and 31. A lecturer who did not write this can find their place. That is better alignment than we usually see.
What we would change

The section called "Definition of study design" contains no definition of study design. (Slides 10 to 18)
Learning outcome 1 is "Students understand what a study design is". Slide 10 announces the section, slide 11 jumps straight to "Main research questions a study plan should answer", and the words "study design" are never defined anywhere in the 35 slides. The deck also slides between "study design", "study plan" and "detailed study plan" (slides 11, 17, 18) as if they were the same object. In practice they are not: the design is the logical structure that determines what.
Suggested fix: Add one slide immediately after slide 10 that defines study design, and one line distinguishing design from plan or protocol. Something like: the study design is the arrangement of who is observed or assigned, to what, when, and against what comparison, which fixes the range of conclusions the data can support; the study plan or protocol.
Nothing in the deck connects study design to AI or machine learning work. (Whole deck; most visibly slides 20 to 25 and 28 to 30)
This is a horizontal learning event in an AI programme, job role "Any", and it sits in a data analysis mini-journey. Every example is clinical or social epidemiology: smoking and lung function, heart disease diets, diabetes over 20 years, national sugar consumption, blood pressure medication, two schools, pain medication. AI appears once, on slide 6, as a passing mention that ML "demands new skills and raises ethical considerations", and is then dropped. A student on the.
Suggested fix: Do not rewrite the deck. Add two slides and re-point some examples. First, a slide mapping the taxonomy on slides 20 to 25 onto AI evaluation: retrospective model evaluation on historical data is a cohort or case-control design and inherits their weaknesses; a silent or shadow deployment is a prospective observational study; an A/B test.
Phenomenology and ethnography are used in the wrap up but were never taught. (Slide 33, against section 3 on slides 19 to 25)
Section 3 presents the taxonomy of study designs as observational and experimental only. Slide 33 then tells students that phenomenology is the right approach for understanding patients' experiences of chronic pain and ethnography for studying emergency room teamwork. Neither word appears earlier in the deck. The wrap up therefore asks students to recognise a whole family of designs, the qualitative ones, that the lecture did not cover, and it also implies the earlier.
Suggested fix: Either add a third design family in section 3 (a single slide on qualitative designs naming phenomenology, ethnography, grounded theory and case study, plus one line on mixed methods, with a sentence on when each answers a question the quantitative designs cannot), or cut the two qualitative use cases from slide 33 and replace them with.
The deck contains no references, source notes or further reading. Not one, in 35 slides. (Whole deck; the gap sits between slide 33 and the Acknowledgements on slide 34. Also wiki, Expected preparation, where all four fields say "None.")
The design taxonomy on slides 20 to 25 and the key factors list on slides 28 to 30 are the standard teaching content of clinical epidemiology and research methods textbooks, and slide 33 imports two named qualitative research traditions. The quoted-sounding definition on slide 12 ("A hypothesis is a tentative explanation for an observation, phenomenon, or scientific problem that can be tested by further investigation") reads like a lifted definition. None of it is.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide before slide 34 and populate the wiki's "References and background for students" and "Recommended for teachers" fields. Three or four entries is enough: a standard research design text for slides 20 to 25, a source for the qualitative traditions on slide 33 (Creswell's work on qualitative approaches is the usual.
The 40 minute "Key factors" block is backed by three bullet slides. (Slides 28 to 30, against the fourth bullet of Instructions for teachers)
Ten factors are listed across three slides with one sentence each, and the plan allocates 40 minutes to them, a third of the session. That is roughly 13 minutes per slide of one-line definitions with no exercise, no worked example and no decision for students to make. In practice the lecturer will either run 25 minutes short or improvise, and neither is acceptable in material meant to be taught by someone who did not write it. This is also where our reviewer checklist bites.
Suggested fix: Break the 40 minutes into taught content plus at least one applied element. Two suggestions that would work: a worked sample size and power calculation on slide 29, done live with real numbers, and a short exercise where students are given a scenario with a fixed budget and are asked which of feasibility, sample size and external.
The lesson plan timing sums to 130 minutes for a 120 minute event, and the plan has no slot for the deck's one activity. (Wiki, Instructions for teachers (15 + 30 + 30 + 40 + 15), against slide 26)
The second author already flagged the arithmetic on the Talk page and is correct. The problem is slightly worse than stated: slide 26 is an interactive session with no time allocated to it anywhere in the plan, so the real overrun is more than the 10 minutes the second author counted. The plan is also silent on breaks, which the second author correctly raised for a 120 minute lecture.
Suggested fix: Rebuild the plan to 120 minutes including the activity and at least one break. A workable split: introduction 10, definition and study plan 25, types of study designs 30, break 10, activity on slide 26 with feedback 15, key factors 30, wrap up 10. Whatever the final numbers, put slide 26 in the plan with an explicit duration, mark the.
The Acknowledgements slide names the wrong EU funding instrument. (Slide 34, and the wiki Acknowledgements section)
Slide 34 states the project is "co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility of the European Union under grant DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, grant agreement number 101189994". DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU is a Digital Europe Programme call topic, not a Connecting Europe Facility one. I confirmed on the HaDEA call page for "Specialised Education Programmes in Key Capacity Areas", which states the funding programme as Digital Europe Programme (2021/2027). CEF and.
Suggested fix: This is consortium template text and not the author's error, so it should be corrected centrally and then pushed to every deck rather than fixed on HC-174 alone. Correct wording: co-funded by the European Union under the Digital Europe Programme, call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU, grant agreement number 101189994. Please have the.
Also noticed

The deck has twelve research questions on slides 11 to 16 and the plan's second bullet lists ten. "Where will the study take place?" (slide 13) and "When will the study occur?" (slide 14) are taught but are not in the lesson plan. This is a genuine plan and material disagreement, the deck is right, and the plan should be updated. The review missed it because it miscounted.
HC-172 does not define study design either. Grepping the Part 1 deck, the word "design" appears exactly once, in the title on the cover slide. So the mini-journey as a whole never defines its central term. Add this to must_fix 1. It closes off the obvious author reply, which is that the definition lives in Part 1.
Slide 1 credits only "Made by: Maria Nisheva (SU)". The wiki Management information names Author Organisation 2 BME and Author Person 2 Bela Pataki. The deck's authorship line and the wiki disagree. Given that we are raising attribution as a blocking issue elsewhere in this review, missing an attribution mismatch on the cover slide is awkward.
Smaller points

Slide 24 calls the RCT 'the gold standard for evaluating interventions' without qualification. That framing is dated as a standalone claim. Add one line that randomisation is often impossible or unethical, and that the current methodological answer is to emulate a target trial.
Slide 22 introduces the ecological study without naming the ecological fallacy. The fallacy is the main reason the design is taught. Add one sentence: a correlation observed at population level does not license an inference about individuals.
Slide 21 gives case-control studies without naming their two characteristic weaknesses, control selection and recall bias. Slide 29 names bias types generically but never attaches one to a design. Connect them.
Slide 29 covers sample size in one sentence with no mention of how power is actually calculated or what inputs it needs (effect size, variance, alpha, power). In a 40 minute block this should be a worked example.
Slides 28 to 30 have no mention of pre-registration, protocol registration or analysis plan lock-in, which is where the analysis plan bullet on slide 30 leads in practice. One sentence and a pointer to a registry would cover it.
Slide 30's ethics bullet stops at informed consent, confidentiality and minimising harm. For a European AI programme, add GDPR and the research provisions that govern secondary use of data, since that is the constraint students will actually meet.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 11 items. The notable results:

Grant agreement 101189994 belongs to PANORAIMA. Confirmed via the project site https://panoraima.eu/ which states 'Co-funded by EU Project 101189994'. CORDIS (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101189994) returned 404 and the Funding and Tenders Portal record did not render, so I could not read.
Call topic DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05-SPECIALEDU is funded by the Digital Europe Programme, not the Connecting Europe Facility. Confirmed on the HaDEA call page for Specialised Education Programmes in Key Capacity Areas.
Prerequisite HC-172. Verified against the WP4 wiki master dump: HC-172 is 'Introduction to Data Analysis and Study Design (Part 1)', 120 minutes, Lecture, author SU / Maria Nisheva, second author BME / Béla Pataki, status 'Learning materials: development'. The wiki's prerequisite for HC-174 is.
CONSORT 2025 exists and supersedes CONSORT 2010. Confirmed via EQUATOR (https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/consort/): Hopewell S, Chan AW, Collins GS and colleagues, published simultaneously in 2025 in BMJ 388:e081123, JAMA 333:1998-2005, Lancet, Nature Medicine 31:1776-1783 and.
TRIPOD+AI. Confirmed via PubMed: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, Riley RD, Beam AL, Van Calster B and colleagues, 'TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods', BMJ 2024, doi 10.1136/bmj-2023-078378, published 16.
Plan against material
["Broadly yes on structure, no on two points of substance and one of timing.", "Agreement: the five agenda items on slide 3 are the five bullets of the Instructions for teachers, in the same order, with matching section dividers at slides 4, 10, 19, 27 and 31. The ten research questions listed in the plan's second bullet appear on slides 11 to 16 in the same order and with the same wording. The two design families in the third bullet are slides 20 to 25. All ten items in the fourth bullet appear on slides 28 to 30 in the same order. The fifth bullet, wrap up and common use cases, is slides 32 to 33. The learning outcomes on slide 2 match the wiki's Learning Outcomes field word for word. The prerequisite HC-172 is correct, verified against the wiki master list as Part 1 by the same author.", "Disagreement 1, and the plan is right: the plan's second bullet is headed 'Definition of study.

Coverage
["No on volume, partially on outcomes.", "Volume: 35 slides, of which slide 1 is the title, 3 the agenda, 4, 10, 19, 27 and 31 are section dividers, and 34 and 35 are Acknowledgements and Disclaimer. That leaves 26 content slides for 120 minutes, roughly 4.6 minutes each. The consortium rule of thumb is about one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture based event, so this deck is well under. The shortfall is not evenly spread: the introduction (slides 5 to 9, five slides for 15 minutes) is close to right, while the key factors section (slides 28 to 30, three slides for 40 minutes) cannot fill its block. Section 3 on the design types (slides 20 to 25, six slides for 30 minutes).

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.heading: Correction from RealAI: our duration comment, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 120 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 35 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.29. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026
