entries.title: HC-176 Introduction to Data Types and Data Formats (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Kalinka Kaloyanova
entries.review_note: Reviewed 12 Sep 2026, posted Talk rev 8583. Status was 'Lesson plan: review', so the plan comments are the formal review and the material comments were given as early feedback. REVISION REQUESTED. The NOIR section of HC-176 is built on a sound spine and gets the hard interval-versus-ratio distinction right, but two of its four scale slides state the wrong rule, the operations table is an uncredited reproduction of Tan, Steinbach and Kumar, and roughly 70 of the planned 120 minutes have no slides at all, so it cannot be taught as it stands. 11 must-fix item(s); 12 definitions and citations verified against source.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan and material, 12 September 2026
long_form.text:
A note on sequencing before the review itself. This learning event is marked "Lesson plan: review" on the wiki, so strictly it is the plan that has been submitted to us and not the material. We reviewed the material anyway, because it is already in SharePoint and two of the points below are things a student would be taught incorrectly if nobody said so. Treat the plan comments as the formal review and the material comments as early feedback you can take or leave.

The NOIR section of HC-176 is built on a sound spine and gets the hard interval-versus-ratio distinction right, but two of its four scale slides state the wrong rule, the operations table is an uncredited reproduction of Tan, Steinbach and Kumar, and roughly 70 of the planned 120 minutes have no slides at all, so it cannot be taught as it stands.

What works

Slide 9 (VARIABLE TYPES) is the best slide in the deck. It puts the categorical/numeric axis, the discrete/continuous axis and the four NOIR scales on one page, each with a one-line rule and a concrete example. That is the right structure for this topic and it is compact enough to actually teach from.
The interval/ratio temperature pair is handled correctly, which is not common. Slide 9 uses 5, 10 and 15 degrees Celsius to show that intervals compare but ratios do not; slide 13 uses Kelvin as the ratio example. Many published decks get this exact pair wrong. Keep both.
Slide 4 (DATA AND DATA SETS) separates Type (what values are allowed and what operations are permitted) from Format (how the value is stored, transmitted or encoded). That is a clean and useful distinction and it is the correct frame for a lecture with this title.
Slide 15 (CROSS-CHECK) has the right idea. Putting the programming type and the measurement level side by side for the same six columns is exactly the bridge students need between the first half and the second half of the lecture. The signup_date row, string converted to datetime and classified as interval, is a well-chosen example.
Slide 16 (Interactive session) is well designed for the point it makes. Student No, Mobile No. and Email Id all look numeric or structured but are nominal, and that is the single most common classification mistake students make with real tables.
What needs fixing

About 70 of the planned 120 minutes have no slides. Composite data types, image/audio/video data, the wrap-up and common use cases, and data formats themselves are all absent. (Whole deck (18 slides, of which 13 are substantive). Measured against the wiki 'Instructions for teachers' timing line.)
The teacher instructions allocate 40 minutes to 'Primitive data types, examples & Composite data types, examples', 20 minutes to 'image, audio, video data' and 10 minutes to 'wrap up, common use cases'. Slide 5 covers five primitives in one table and nothing else. There is no slide on arrays, lists, tuples, dictionaries, structs, records or objects. There is no slide on image, audio or video data. There is no wrap-up slide and no use cases. The deck is also titled 'Data Types and Data Formats' but formats are defined once on slide 4 and never returned.
Fix: Either add the missing sections, or split HC-176 so the wiki timing line describes only what Part 1 actually contains and the remainder moves to the Part 2 lesson plan. If splitting, the wiki must say so and name the Part 2 code. Note also that the consortium rule of thumb is roughly one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture Learning Event; 13 substantive slides for 120 minutes is.
The ordinal scale is defined with the nominal definition. The slide says ordinal variables have 'no logical order'. (Slide 12 (ORDINAL SCALE), opening definition)
Order is the defining property of an ordinal variable. The sentence is a copy of the opening line of slide 10 (NOMINAL SCALE) and it contradicts the rest of its own slide, which gives T-shirt sizes {S, M, L, XL, XXL} as the example and then says relational operators, median and ranking are permitted. It also contradicts slide 9, which defines the ordinal scale correctly as 'values that can be ordered but without quantification of differences'. Students reading the definition sentence will write the wrong answer in the slide 16 exercise.
Fix: Replace with: 'Variables that take a value among a set of mutually exclusive codes that have a meaningful order, but where the distance between consecutive values is not defined or not equal.' Then the T-shirt example and the operations bullets follow correctly.
The nominal slide forbids the one comparison that nominal data does support. It lists the not-equal operator among the operations that are 'not permitted'. (Slide 10 (NOMINAL SCALE), Operations bullet: 'Arithmetic (+,-,* and /) and logical operations (<,>,≠, etc.) are not permitted.')
Distinctness, meaning equals and not-equals, is precisely the property that defines the nominal level. You can and constantly do ask whether two blood groups differ. The deck contradicts itself two slides later: slide 14 lists 'Distinctiveness: = and ≠' as property 1, which applies to categorical data. As written the slide tells students they cannot test two nominal values for inequality, which would rule out grouping, filtering and contingency tables.
Fix: Change to: 'Equality and inequality (= and ≠) are the only comparisons defined. Ordering (<, >), arithmetic (+, -, *, /) and any statistic that assumes order or distance are not meaningful.' Also correct the wording: <, > and ≠ are relational or comparison operators, not logical operators.
The four-property operations table is reproduced from Tan, Steinbach and Kumar without credit, and the reproduction drops the part that carries the meaning. (Slide 14 (OPERATIONS ON DATA))
I downloaded the authors' own Chapter 2 lecture notes for 'Introduction to Data Mining' by Tan, Steinbach and Kumar and extracted the text. They define exactly these four properties in this order with these symbols: 'Distinctness: = ≠ / Order: < > / Addition: + - / Multiplication: * /', then map them 'Nominal attribute: distinctness. Ordinal attribute: distinctness & order. Interval attribute: distinctness, order & addition. Ratio attribute: all 4 properties.' Slide 14 is that table with the same four rows, the same order and the same operator symbols,.
Fix: Restore the four-column mapping to nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio, and add the source line: Tan, P.-N., Steinbach, M. and Kumar, V., 'Introduction to Data Mining', Chapter 2. Cite the edition you used. Keep the two-level Categorical/Numerical bracket only as a secondary annotation if it helps, not as the mapping.
The worked cross-check table mixes NOIR levels with a word that is not a NOIR level, and mislabels two columns. (Slide 15 (CROSS-CHECK), rows 'age' and 'income')
The column heading is 'Data Science Type' and four of the six rows use NOIR terms (nominal, interval, nominal, ordinal). The age and income rows say 'numerical'. Both are ratio: age and income have a true zero and ratios of them are meaningful. This is the worked example immediately before the slide 16 exercise that asks students to give the NOIR category for eight attributes, including Scholarship amount, which is the same kind of quantity as income. Students will copy 'numerical' and be marked wrong.
Fix: Change age and income to 'ratio'. Keep signup_date as interval and satisfaction as ordinal, both are correct. If you want to keep the coarse categorical/numerical grouping visible, add it as a separate column rather than mixing the two vocabularies in one.
The NOIR typology is presented across three slides with no source. Stevens is never named. (Slides 3 (DATA), 8 (NOIR CLASIFICATION) and 9 (VARIABLE TYPES))
Slide 3 says 'a good understanding of data scales (also called scales of measurement) is important' and slide 8 says 'the mostly recommended scales of measurement'. Recommended by whom, and mostly by what measure, is not said. This is a named published framework: S. S. Stevens, 'On the Theory of Scales of Measurement', Science 103(2684): 677-680, 7 June 1946, DOI 10.1126/science.103.2684.677. I resolved the DOI and it is live. Under CC BY-NC-SA the framework must carry its attribution. The claim on slide 8 that 'the NOIR scale is the fundamental.
Fix: Add the Stevens 1946 citation to slide 8 and add a references slide at the end. At master level it is worth one further sentence noting that the typology has been challenged, particularly for the nominal and ordinal levels; the standard reference article names Duncan (1986) and Luce (1997) as critics, and I would check those two directly before printing them. Saying the framework is contested is.
The opening quotation is misattributed to W. Edwards Deming. (Slide 3 (DATA): '“In God we trust. All others must bring data”, W. Edwards Deming')
I checked the Wikiquote entry for Deming. The line is filed under Misattributed, not under Sourced. It appears without attribution to anyone in Mary Walton's 'The Deming Management Method' (1986, p. 96), and the earliest attestation recorded there is 1978. No occurrence in Deming's own writing has been traced. This matters more here than it normally would: the lecture is about data provenance and evidence, and it opens with a quotation whose provenance does not hold up. A student who checks it, which is a reasonable thing to ask of a master's student,.
Fix: Either remove it, or keep it and label it honestly: 'Widely attributed to W. Edwards Deming; no source in his writings has been traced.' The second option is better, because the attribution failure is itself the teaching point on this slide.
Gender is taught as the canonical symmetric binary variable with exactly two mutually exclusive values. (Slide 11 (BINARY SCALE): 'If two choices of a binary variable have equal importance, then it is called symmetric binary variable - Gender {male, female}')
As a statement about how the field is recorded in current practice this is wrong, not merely dated. Statistical agencies and mainstream data standards now separate sex recorded at birth from gender identity and provide more than two response categories plus explicit non-response handling. Anyone who has worked with real HR, health or survey data has met three-plus-category gender fields. Teaching {male, female} as a closed mutually exclusive binary in a human-centred AI programme sends students into practice with a schema that will fail on their first.
Fix: Replace the symmetric example with something genuinely symmetric and uncontested, for example a coin toss {heads, tails} or handedness {left, right}. Replace the asymmetric example with a medical test result {positive, negative}, and add one line on the consequence: for asymmetric binaries the co-absence of the trait is not informative, so Jaccard rather than simple matching. If you want to keep.
Interval is the only one of the four NOIR scales with no slide of its own. (Between slides 12 (ORDINAL SCALE) and 13 (RATIO SCALE))
Nominal, binary, ordinal and ratio each get a full slide with a definition, examples and permitted operations. Interval gets one bullet on slide 9. Slide 13 then opens with 'Ratio data - Interval data with a clear definition of zero' and says 'all arithmetic operations on interval data are applicable to ratio data', which is a forward reference to a slide that does not exist. Interval is also the level students find hardest, and the one where the practical mistakes happen: dates, Celsius, standardised test scores, Likert composites.
Fix: Add an INTERVAL SCALE slide in the same layout as the other three, before the ratio slide. Definition, examples (calendar dates, temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit), operations (addition and subtraction meaningful, multiplication and division not, mean and standard deviation valid, no meaningful ratio), and one sentence on the missing true zero. The signup_date row on slide 15 then has.
The wiki teacher instructions and the slide deck describe different sessions. (Wiki 'Instructions for teachers' against the full deck)
Four of the five blocks in the timing line do not match. Block 2 promises composite data types with examples and the deck has none. Block 4, image, audio and video data for 20 minutes, has no slides. Block 5, wrap up and common use cases for 10 minutes, has no slides. Block 3 is the only one that is well covered. The mapping between lecturer instructions and the actual materials is one of the things the consortium checklist asks the reviewer to confirm is checkable, and here it is not. The deck is right about what exists; the wiki is describing content.
Fix: Rewrite the timing line to match what Part 1 actually contains, and move the rest to the Part 2 lesson plan. Also fill in the wiki Acknowledgements, which still reads 'Under Grant № ???' while the deck carries the full grant agreement number, and complete the Keywords field, which stops at 'definition of data type, common data types,' and omits NOIR, scales of measurement, and quantitative and.
The credit on the material does not match the credit on the wiki. (Slide 1 title slide ('Made by: K. Kaloyanova') against the wiki Management information block)
The wiki records Author Organisation 1 SU / Author Person 1 Kalinka Kaloyanova and Author Organisation 2 BME / Author Person 2 András Gézsi. The deck credits only K. Kaloyanova. Under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 downstream users copy the credit line off the material, not off the wiki, so whichever is right, the two must agree before this is published.
Fix: Either add the second author to the title slide, or correct the wiki if BME did not contribute to Part 1. Confirm with both authors rather than picking one.
Also noted on the second pass

Slide 7 conflates two different meanings of 'qualitative' and the deck never reconciles them. Slide 7 defines qualitative data as 'non-numerical data that generally describe subjective attributes or characteristics' analysed by 'thematic analysis or content analysis', with examples 'descriptions, observations, interviews, and open-ended survey responses' (material lines 108-114). That is.
Slide 9 defines discrete as 'natural numbers' and continuous as 'real numbers' (material lines 138-139). Discrete means a finite or countably infinite value set. Tan et al.'s own slide, which the deck is otherwise tracking, says 'Has only a finite or countably infinite set of values'. Under the deck's definition a temperature change of minus 3, a signed count, or a zero count is not discrete. One.
Slide 13's two operations bullets contradict each other on the slide, not just by implication. 'All arithmetic operations on interval data are applicable to ratio data' followed immediately by 'In addition, multiplication & division are allowed' (material lines 220-224). If all arithmetic already carried over there is nothing left to add. This is the same interval/ratio boundary the reviewer.
Slide 12 lists 'count, min, max' as 'Calculations based on order are permitted' (material lines 205-207). Count is not order-based. It is available at the nominal level, which the deck itself implies on slide 10 by allowing mode. Min and max are fine.
Smaller fixes

Slide 2 heading reads 'DATA AND INFROMATION'. Typo, and it is the second slide the room sees.
Slide 8 heading reads 'NOIR CLASIFICATION'. Should be CLASSIFICATION.
Slide 10, blood group is given as {A, B, AB, 0} with a numeral zero. The modern standard is the letter O, from Landsteiner's 'ohne'; the numeral 0 was the older German convention of Hirszfeld and von Dungern. In a lecture about exact value encodings this distinction is worth getting right, and it.
Slide 11 says 'Different binary variables may have unequal importance'. The point is that the two values within one variable can have unequal importance, not that variables differ from each other. Reword.
Slide 10 calls <, > and the not-equal sign 'logical operations'. They are relational or comparison operators. Logical operators are AND, OR, NOT.
Slide 15 maps income to float. Say explicitly that money should be stored as fixed-point or decimal, not binary floating point. Students who take the table at face value will build the rounding bug themselves.
There is no references slide anywhere in the deck. Add one. At minimum it needs Stevens 1946 and Tan, Steinbach and Kumar; the Deming line and the symmetric/asymmetric binary distinction also need homes.
The symmetric against asymmetric binary distinction on slide 11 is standard textbook material and is usually credited to Han, Kamber and Pei, 'Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques'. I was not able to confirm the exact section in this session, so please verify the edition and section before citing.
What we verified
We checked the citations, definitions and named frameworks against their sources, 12 items. The notable results:

Stevens 1946: VERIFIED. Resolved DOI 10.1126/science.103.2684.677, which redirects live to science.org. Full citation confirmed against the standard reference article: Stevens, S. S., 'On the Theory of Scales of Measurement', Science, 103(2684): 677-680, 7 June 1946. This is the source of the.
Deming quotation, slide 3: VERIFIED AS MISATTRIBUTED. Checked the Wikiquote entry for W. Edwards Deming. 'In God we trust. All others must bring data' is listed under Misattributed, not Sourced. It appears with no attribution to Deming or anyone else in Mary Walton, 'The Deming Management Method' (1986), p. 96, and.
Tan, Steinbach and Kumar operations table, slide 14: VERIFIED AS UNCREDITED REPRODUCTION. Downloaded the authors' own Chapter 2 lecture notes for 'Introduction to Data Mining' from the University of Minnesota faculty page and extracted the text. The deck's four properties, their order and their operator symbols match.
Interval against ratio temperature examples, slides 9 and 13: VERIFIED CORRECT. Confirmed that Celsius is an interval scale (20 degrees C is not twice as hot as 10 degrees C, ratios are not meaningful) and Kelvin is a ratio scale. The deck gets both right, which is worth saying because this pair is commonly reversed.
Stevens typology is contested: VERIFIED THAT CRITICISM EXISTS. The standard reference article on levels of measurement states the typology 'is still being challenged by other theoreticians, particularly in the cases of the nominal and ordinal types' and names Duncan (1986) and Luce (1997). I did NOT open those two.
ABO blood group notation, slide 10: VERIFIED. The modern standard is the letter O, which Landsteiner chose from the German 'ohne'. The numeral 0 came from Hirszfeld and von Dungern and is the older convention. The deck's {A, B, AB, 0} uses the numeral.
Plan against material
They do not agree, and the wiki is the side that is wrong. The wiki timing line commits to five blocks totalling 120 minutes. Only block 1 (introducing data types, 10 min) and block 3 (data types in data science, NOIR, operations and examples, 40 min) exist in the deck. Block 2 promises composite data types with examples and there is no composite types slide anywhere. Block 4 promises 20 minutes on image, audio and video data and there is nothing. Block 5 promises a wrap-up and common use cases and there is neither. The deck is the honest artefact here; it is labelled 'Part 1' and delivers a coherent Part 1 on primitives and measurement scales. The lesson plan was written for the full topic and never trimmed. Two further wiki-side defects: the Acknowledgements section still carries the placeholder 'Under Grant No ???' while the deck carries the full grant agreement number, and the Keywords field is truncated mid-list at 'common data types,' with no NOIR or scales-of-measurement terms even though those are half the lecture. The wiki also says 'Learning Events to be completed before:.

Coverage
No on both counts. On duration: 18 slides, of which one is a title, one a section divider and two are back matter, leaves 13 substantive slides for 120 minutes. The consortium rule of thumb is roughly one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture Learning Event. Even generously, with the single exercise on slide 16 stretched to 15 minutes and heavy discussion on slides 9 to 14, this is a 50 to 60 minute session. Around 70 minutes has no material behind it. There is also only one interactive element where the checklist asks for two to four, and no answer key for it, which matters because several of the STUDENT attributes are genuinely arguable. I reviewed a PDF export, so I cannot see speaker notes; the source PowerPoint should be checked against the requirement that a lecturer.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What needs fixing' should be addressed, and we will re-review on whatever version you submit once the status moves to learning materials. Everything else here is offered as improvement rather than as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 12 September 2026

entries.review_note: Reviewed 12 Sep 2026, posted Talk rev 8584. Status was 'Lesson plan: review', so the plan comments are the formal review and the material comments were given as early feedback. REVISION REQUESTED. Sound structure and a genuinely good structured-versus-unstructured exercise, but the deck reproduces OpenStax and textbook material without slide-level attribution, gives one piece of wrong data-cleaning advice, misses the formats an AI graduate actually meets (Parquet, JSONL, Arrow), and cannot deliver its third learning outcome because there is no exercise anywhere. 8 must-fix item(s); 11 definitions and citations verified against source.

long_form.heading: Review (RealAI): Lesson plan and material, 12 September 2026
long_form.text:
A note on sequencing before the review itself. This learning event is marked "Lesson plan: review" on the wiki, so strictly it is the plan that has been submitted to us and not the material. We reviewed the material anyway, because it is already in SharePoint and two of the points below are things a student would be taught incorrectly if nobody said so. Treat the plan comments as the formal review and the material comments as early feedback you can take or leave.

Sound structure and a genuinely good structured-versus-unstructured exercise, but the deck reproduces OpenStax and textbook material without slide-level attribution, gives one piece of wrong data-cleaning advice, misses the formats an AI graduate actually meets (Parquet, JSONL, Arrow), and cannot deliver its third learning outcome because there is no exercise anywhere.

What works

The structured/unstructured exercise on slides 11 to 16 is the best thing in the deck. Three cases, each on a question slide followed by an answer slide, and the third case shows that whether data is structured is a property of how it has been processed rather than of the subject matter. That is a real concept, taught by making students commit to an answer first.
The five blocks on slides 3 to 37 follow the lesson plan's timing outline in order, with section divider slides at 19 and 29. A lecturer who was not involved in writing this can find their place against the wiki instructions without guessing.
The CSV/JSON/XML comparison table on slide 28 is pitched right. Pros, cons and typical use in three rows gives students something to reason with when they meet a format choice, which is what learning outcome 2 asks for.
Both books on the Resources slide (38) are real and appropriate for the level. I checked them. Ault, Liao and Musolino, Principles of Data Science, 2025, exists and is a serious introductory text; Chirag Shah, A Hands-On Introduction to Data Science, Cambridge University Press, 2020, exists and is widely used.
The RAISE-U template, the acknowledgement slide and the CC BY-NC-SA licence slide are present and correctly worded, apart from the funder name discussed below.
What needs fixing

Substantial content is reproduced from OpenStax, Principles of Data Science (2025), section 1.3, with no source line on any of the slides that use it, and the Resources entry names the wrong publisher. (Slides 3, 7, 8, 11-16 and 28; Resources slide 38)
I fetched OpenStax section 1.3 and compared it against the deck. The dataset definition on slide 3 ("a collection of observations or data entities organized for analysis and interpretation"), the unstructured-data definition on slide 8, the jacket dataset and its three attributes on slides 11 and 12, the search-keyword example and its free-form-text wording on slides 13 and 14, the processed-keyword case on slides 15 and 16, and the pros/cons/typical-use table on slide 28 all track the OpenStax text closely. Reuse is legitimate because OpenStax.
Fix: Add a source line to each of the slides listed, in the same style already used on slides 4, 6 and 9. Correct the Resources entry to: Ault, S.V., Nam Liao, S., Musolino, L., Principles of Data Science, OpenStax, Rice University, 2025, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, openstax.org. Add the licence statement and a note that the material has been adapted.
The preprocessing block uses distinctive worked examples with no citation, and they are not from OpenStax. (Slides 31 to 35)
I checked OpenStax section 2.4 and it contains none of these examples: no wine consumption or deaths, no exam scores in the 70 to 90 range, no 7.9000000095, no tomatoes and garlic recipe. The missing-data list on slide 33 (ignore the record, global constant, imputation, inference using a Bayesian formula or a decision tree, attribute-based derivation) is the classical Han, Kamber and Pei list, and the recipe wrangling example and the noisy-data examples read as reproduced from a textbook rather than written fresh. The only other resource listed is Shah,.
Fix: The author should say where slides 31 to 35 came from and add per-slide source lines. If the text is taken from Shah, either reduce it to short quoted extracts with a page-level citation or rewrite it in the author's own words. If the missing-data list comes from Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, cite it and add it to Resources.
Two in-slide sources are cited by title only, with no author, year or publisher, and neither appears on the Resources slide. (Slides 4, 6 and 9; Resources slide 38)
Slide 4 says only Source: "It's All Analytics". I checked: that is Scott Burk and Gary Miner, It's All Analytics!, Productivity Press, 2020, and there are three volumes in the series, so the title alone does not identify which book the table came from. Slides 6 and 9 say only Source: "Fundamentals of Data Science: Theory and Practice". I checked: that is Jugal K. Kalita, Dhruba K. Bhattacharyya and Swarup Roy, Academic Press / Elsevier, 2022. A reader of the redistributed deck cannot find either source from what is on the slide, and the format/analytics.
Fix: Give full citations on the slides (author, title, publisher, year, and page or table number for the slide 4 table) and add both books to the Resources slide.
The deck tells students to convert impossible negative values to their positive counterparts. (Slide 34, SMOOTING NOISY DATA, the "Correcting Faulty Entries via Logic" bullet)
Flipping the sign of a negative wine consumption or death count assumes the cause was a sign error. It could equally be a units error, a sentinel value such as -1 or -999 used to encode missing, a delta rather than a level, or a column shifted during import. Taking the absolute value silently manufactures a plausible-looking number and destroys the evidence that the record was broken. Students will copy this into practice, where it is exactly the class of edit that survives review because the output looks clean.
Fix: Rewrite the bullet: impossible values should be flagged and investigated, and set to missing if the cause cannot be established, with the correction recorded. Add one line that sentinel codes such as -1 and -999 are a common cause and must be checked against the data dictionary before any repair.
Learning outcome 3, "Students can apply basic data preprocessing techniques", is not delivered by this material. (Wiki Management information (Learning Outcomes) against slides 29 to 35)
Slides 29 to 35 describe preprocessing. Nothing anywhere asks a student to do it. There is no dataset, no notebook, no tool, no exercise, and the wiki lists no tutorial and no obligatory preparation. "Apply" cannot be assessed from a lecture that only names techniques. This is also the block where the timing is weakest: six content slides for the 30 minutes the plan allocates.
Fix: Either add a 15 to 20 minute hands-on block to the preprocessing section using a small dirty CSV (missing values, a duplicate row, an inconsistent name field, one impossible negative), or reword the outcome to "explain and select appropriate basic data preprocessing techniques" and align the wiki. The exercise is the better fix because it also fills the timing gap.
Two slides are duplicated verbatim. (Slides 10 and 18 (MULTIMODAL DATA); slides 40 and 41 (Disclaimer))
Slide 10 and slide 18 carry identical text. Slide 40 and slide 41 carry the identical licence text in two layouts. A lecturer in presenter view hits the same slide twice and has to improvise. The multimodal duplication also splits the topic across the exercise: multimodal data appears at slide 10, the exercise runs 11 to 16, then multimodality returns at 17 and 18. The lesson plan groups multimodal with structured and unstructured data in one 30 minute block, so the plan is right and the deck ordering is wrong.
Fix: Delete slide 10 and keep the multimodal pair at 17 and 18 as a single sequence after the exercise. Delete one of the two disclaimer slides.
The 10 minute wrap-up is one slide carrying no text. (Slides 36 and 37)
Slide 36 is a Wrap UP divider. Slide 37 has the title "Structured vs Unstructured Data" and no body text in the export, and it covers only one of the session's four topics. Nothing summarises data formats, nothing summarises preprocessing, and nothing points to the next learning event. The plan allocates 10 minutes to this.
Fix: If slide 37 is a figure, add a caption and a source line. Then add a real wrap-up: the format choice heuristic from slide 28 restated as a decision, three takeaways from the preprocessing block, and one line on where this leads next in the mini-journey.
The format coverage stops at CSV, JSON, XML and consumer binary formats, which is not what an AI graduate meets in practice. (Slides 20, 21, 27 and 28)
Slide 20 presents CSV, JSON and XML as "the most often used formats" and slide 27 lists JPEG, MP3, MP4, PDF and DOCX. For a data formats lecture in an AI master's programme in 2026 this leaves out everything students will meet on their first day of work: Parquet and ORC for columnar analytical storage, Avro and Arrow for serialisation and in-memory interchange, and JSONL / NDJSON, which is the working format for LLM training, evaluation and batch inference data. The row-oriented versus columnar distinction is the single idea that explains why a CSV that.
Fix: Add one slide after 27: row-oriented (CSV, JSONL) versus columnar (Parquet, ORC), what columnar buys you (compression, column pruning, predicate pushdown, typed schema), and one line on Arrow as the in-memory standard. Add JSONL to slide 21's table with "one JSON object per line, streaming and ML training data" as its use case. This is roughly two slides and it also helps the thin timing.
Also noted on the second pass

Slide 3 states the same definition twice, word for word. 'Format - the structure or encoding used to store, transmit, or represent data' appears near the top, and 'A data format is the structure or encoding used to store, transmit, or represent data' appears again lower on the same slide. The review caught the identical stutter on slide 30 but not this one, and it is the first content slide the.
Slide 3 is a verbatim repeat of HC-176 slide 4. The Part 1 deck in the same folder carries the same 'Type - a category that specifies what kind of value something can hold', the same Format sentence, and the same 'Data sets: a collection of observations or data entities organized for analysis and interpretation'. Two consequences the review missed. First, HC-178 learning outcome 1 ('explain data.
Slide 23 tells students that 'MS Excel and Google Sheets can be used to open CSV files in a more intuitive way as a table' with no warning attached. Opening a CSV in Excel is the single most common way a student silently corrupts a dataset: locale decimal and thousands separators, automatic date coercion of anything shaped like a date, leading zeros stripped from identifiers and postcodes, and.
Slide 25 says XML is 'a default mechanism for sharing data between different information systems'. That is out of date for 2026 and it contradicts slide 20 in the same block, which says JSON is 'most suitable for exchanging data between a user and a server'. A student reading both slides cannot tell which is the default. Worth one line.
Smaller fixes

Slide 30: the first sentence repeats itself ("An important stage in any data science task is data preprocessing is data preprocessing"), and the third bullet says preprocessing "involves obtaining irrelevant or duplicate data". It should say removing. As written it tells students to go and collect.
Typos: slide 34 heading reads SMOOTING, should be SMOOTHING. Slide 33 opens "There are case when". Slide 5 has "Local fIles" with a stray capital I. Wiki keyword list has "multimidality".
Slide 34: the 7.9000000095 example is labelled an equipment or entry error. That is floating point representation, not noise in the measurement. Either relabel it or use a real sensor-drift example, otherwise students will go looking for the wrong cause.
Slide 34: "a score of 12 would be considered an outlier and should likely be removed or investigated". Put investigated first and drop "removed". A genuinely low exam score is data, not noise, and removing it is how selection bias gets in.
Slide 33: add the MCAR / MAR / MNAR distinction and one line on consequences, namely that dropping records is only safe under MCAR, that mean imputation shrinks variance and weakens correlations, and that imputation must be fitted after the train/test split or it leaks. OpenStax section 2.4 already.
Slide 20: "XML is most suitable for complex datasets because of its hierarchical structure" while JSON gets only the client-server line. Students will leave thinking JSON is flat. It nests just as well. The real differences worth teaching are schema validation (XSD), namespaces, attributes versus.
Slide 24: a JSON document does not have to begin and end with curly braces. Under RFC 8259 a top-level array or scalar is valid, and top-level arrays are extremely common in API responses. Students who write a parser on this slide will break on the first array.
Slides 22 and 28: CSV cons say only "difficult to parse if there are special characters". Name the actual failure modes, since they are what students will hit: delimiter and quoting rules (RFC 4180), embedded newlines, and character encoding mismatches. Encoding is the most common single cause of.
What we verified
We checked the citations, definitions and named frameworks against their sources, 11 items. The notable results:

WebSearch was unavailable for this review (session budget exhausted at 200 calls), so all verification below was done by direct fetches. Two claims I could not verify are marked as such rather than asserted.
VERIFIED: Resources item 1. Fetched openstax.org/books/principles-data-science/pages/preface. Principles of Data Science, senior contributing authors Dr. Shaun V. Ault, Dr. Soohyun Nam Liao, Larry Musolino, published by OpenStax, 24 January 2025, licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The author names and the year on slide 38 are.
VERIFIED: Resources item 2. Open Library confirms Chirag Shah, Hands-On Introduction to Data Science, first published 2020. Cambridge University Press is correct. Note that Shah published separate Python and R editions in 2025, so the author may want to cite the current edition.
VERIFIED: source cited on slide 4. "It's All Analytics" is Scott Burk and Gary Miner, It's All Analytics!, Productivity Press (Taylor & Francis), 2020, confirmed via Open Library. The series has three volumes (Part II 2021 with David Sweenor, Part III 2023), so the bare title on the slide does not identify which one.
VERIFIED: source cited on slides 6 and 9. "Fundamentals of Data Science: Theory and Practice" is Jugal K. Kalita, Dhruba K. Bhattacharyya and Swarup Roy, Academic Press / Elsevier, 2022, confirmed via Open Library. Real book, correctly summarised on the slides, but cited by title only.
VERIFIED by comparison: OpenStax Principles of Data Science section 1.3 "Data and Datasets" is the source of the deck's dataset definition (slide 3), the unstructured data definition (slide 8), the jacket dataset exercise and its three attributes (slides 11 and 12), the search-keyword exercise including the free-form.
Plan against material
"They agree on shape and disagree on delivery.\n\nAgreement: the deck follows the wiki's teacher instructions block for block and in order. Data and datasets on slides 3 to 6, structured and unstructured plus multimodal on 7 to 18, dataset formats on 19 to 28, preprocessing on 29 to 35, wrap up on 36 and 37. Anyone teaching from the wiki instructions can follow the deck.\n\nDisagreements, and which side is right:\n\n1. Learning outcome 3 (\"apply basic data preprocessing techniques\"). The plan is right to want it; the material does not deliver it. There is no exercise, dataset or tool. Either the material gains an exercise or the outcome is reworded. See must-fix 5.\n\n2. Multimodal data placement. The plan groups multimodal with structured and unstructured in one 30 minute block. The deck splits it across the exercise (slide 10, then 17 and 18) and duplicates a slide doing so. The plan is right.\n\n3. Wrap up. The plan allocates 10 minutes. The material has one divider and one textless slide. The plan is right; the material is short.\n\n4. Authorship. The wiki lists Author.

Coverage
"It does not comfortably fill 120 minutes, and it delivers two of the three outcomes.\n\nLength: 41 slides, of which 37 are teaching slides and four are back matter (Resources, Acknowledgements, and two duplicate Disclaimers). The consortium rule of thumb is roughly one slide per minute and 30 to 60 slides for a lecture-based learning event. At 37 teaching slides for 120 minutes the lecturer has about 3.2 minutes per slide, and most of these slides carry four or five bullets. The preprocessing block is the worst case: six content slides (30 to 35) for the 30 minutes the plan allocates, with no exercise. The opening block is the second worst: four slides (3 to 6) for 20 minutes.\n\nInteractivity: the guidelines ask for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements. There is exactly one,.

Bottom line
We are not signing this off yet. The items under 'What needs fixing' should be addressed, and we will re-review on whatever version you submit once the status moves to learning materials. Everything else here is offered as improvement rather than as a condition.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 12 September 2026

entries.title: HC-180 Data Exploration and Preparation (Part 1)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: Sound, well-organised coverage of data quality and preprocessing, but the deck reproduces two published sources without crediting them, carries no reference list at all, has no link to AI data governance, and is roughly an hour short of its 180 minutes with the planned 45-minute visualisation block resting on a single text slide.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

Sound, well-organised coverage of data quality and preprocessing, but the deck reproduces two published sources without crediting them, carries no reference list at all, has no link to AI data governance, and is roughly an hour short of its 180 minutes with the planned 45-minute visualisation block resting on a single text slide.

What already works

The data quality section (slides 22 to 31) is the strongest part of the deck. Eight factors, each broken into named sub-dimensions, and it goes beyond what the lesson plan asks for by adding uniqueness (slide 27) and relevance, interpretability and conciseness (slide 31). The value consistency example on slide 25, USA against US, United States and America, is the kind of concrete detail students.
Slide 2 reproduces the five wiki learning outcomes word for word. That sounds trivial but it is often wrong in these decks, and it makes the mapping from lesson plan to material checkable at a glance.
The discussion question on slide 33 is placed correctly. It asks what makes raw data dirty before slide 34 gives the answer, so it works as genuine elicitation rather than a comprehension check after the fact. The independent work assignment on slide 45 on the three normalization techniques is a sensible piece of self-study.
The preprocessing section (slides 35 to 48) is more thorough than the lesson plan promises. Data integration (39 to 41), data reduction (46 to 47) and discretization (48) are all extra. The conflict examples on slide 40, the same attribute under different names and a derived attribute such as annual revenue, are real problems practitioners hit.
What we would change

Slide 9 reproduces published text from two sources without crediting either, and strips the attribution both sources carry. (Slide 9 (EDA definition and purpose))
The first bullet is the lead sentence of the Wikipedia article on exploratory data analysis with only trivial rewording. The second bullet is verbatim from IBM's exploratory data analysis page, including the run 'help look at data before making any assumptions. It can help identify obvious errors, as well as better understand patterns within the data, detect outliers or anomalous events, find interesting relations among the variables'. I fetched both pages and confirmed the.
Suggested fix: Rewrite slide 9 in the author's own words and add a source line. Add one sentence naming Tukey, J.W. (1977), Exploratory Data Analysis, Addison-Wesley, and note that he introduced the box plot in 1970. If the IBM wording is kept, quote it explicitly and cite the page.
The entire data preprocessing taxonomy on slides 35 to 48 is Han, Kamber and Pei's, reproduced without naming them, and the connecting prose appears to come from a further unidentified textbook. (Slides 35 to 48 (data cleaning, integration, transformation, reduction, discretization))
The five-way split of preprocessing into cleaning, integration, transformation, reduction and discretization is Han, Kamber and Pei's structure. So is the five-item transformation list on slide 43 (smoothing, aggregation, generalization, normalization, attribute or feature construction), the phrase 'concept hierarchy climbing' for generalization, the three normalization techniques on slide 45 (min-max, z-score, decimal scaling), the incomplete/noisy/inconsistent triad on.
Suggested fix: Cite Han, J., Kamber, M. and Pei, J. (2011), Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, 3rd edition, Morgan Kaufmann, on the section divider at slide 32 and against slides 43, 45, 46 and 48. The author must also identify and cite the source of the slide 36 to 38 prose, or rewrite those slides.
There is no reference list anywhere in the deck, and the wiki records no references either. (Whole deck; no references slide between slide 58 and the acknowledgements on slide 59. Wiki, Expected preparation section)
Sixty slides carry zero citations. The wiki's Expected preparation fields all read 'None', including 'References and background for students' and 'Recommended for teachers'. A lecturer who did not write this deck gets no reading to prepare from and no way to check any claim in it. This is what makes the two attribution findings above possible, and the reviewer checklist asks specifically about traceability of claims, frameworks and figures.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide before slide 59 covering Tukey (1977), Han, Kamber and Pei (2011), whatever source the data quality factors come from, and the source of any figure on slides 14, 19 and 20. Fill in the wiki's 'References and background for students' and 'Recommended for teachers' fields with the same list.
The definition of normalization on slide 43 is garbled and wrong as written. (Slide 43, fourth bullet)
It reads 'Normalization: Scaled to fall within a small, specified range and aggregation.' The trailing 'and aggregation' does not belong. Normalization is not aggregation, and aggregation is already the second bullet on the same slide. This looks like a copy artefact, but students will read it as a definition and it contradicts the slide it sits on.
Suggested fix: Cut 'and aggregation'. The bullet should read 'Normalization: values scaled to fall within a small, specified range.'
The lesson plan allocates 45 minutes to graphic displays, the single largest block in the session, and the deck covers it with one text slide plus two slides that carry no extractable text. (Slides 17 to 20, against the lesson plan block 'Graphic displays of the statistical characteristics of data, 45 min')
Slide 17 is a section divider and slide 18 is a six-item bullet list. Slides 19 and 20 have no title and no body text in the PDF, so they are presumably figures, but a lecturer cannot teach 45 minutes from an unlabelled image. Four chart types the plan names are absent from the deck: dot plot, line graph, bubble chart and mosaic plot. The plan also organises this block by univariate, bivariate and multivariate data, and the deck does not; that organisation only appears much.
Suggested fix: Build this section out to match the plan. Add slides for the four missing chart types, organise the section by univariate, bivariate and multivariate as the plan specifies, and give slides 19 and 20 titles, captions and source credits. If the intent is a worked walkthrough of a single dataset across chart types, say so on a slide so the.
Skewness and kurtosis are required by the lesson plan and by the second learning outcome, but are missing from the statistics section. (Slides 11 to 16, against the lesson plan block 'Basic statistical characteristics of data, 20 min, measures of shape (distribution of the data) - skewness, kurtosis')
The statistics section covers central tendency (slides 12 to 13), variability (15) and position (16). Measures of shape are not covered. The words skewness and kurtosis appear once in the whole deck, in a passing list on slide 52, thirty-six slides later and in a different section, with no definition. The learning outcome 'Students know the basic statistical characteristics of data and their graphic displays' is not delivered for this category.
Suggested fix: Add a shape slide between slides 15 and 16 defining skewness and kurtosis, with a figure showing left-skewed, symmetric and right-skewed distributions. This also connects naturally to the histogram on slide 18.
Slide 34 gives an incorrect example of inconsistency, and the rule it teaches would produce discriminatory data validation. (Slide 34, third bullet (Inconsistent))
The example says that if a Name column 'contains values other than alphabetical letters, or if records do not start with a capital letter, discrepancies are present'. Two problems. First, this is a validity and format problem, not an inconsistency problem; the deck itself defines validity correctly on slide 28, so this bullet contradicts its own later slide. Second, the rule is wrong on the merits. Names legitimately contain non-alphabetic characters (apostrophes and.
Suggested fix: Replace the example with a genuine inconsistency case, for example the same customer recorded with two different country codes across two systems, or dates stored as DD/MM/YYYY in one source and MM/DD/YYYY in another. If a name validation example is wanted, turn it into a short discussion of why naive name rules fail and who they fail.
Nothing in the deck connects data quality or data preparation to AI regulation, bias, or the people the data describes. (Whole deck, most sharply slides 21 to 31 (data quality) and 32 to 48 (preprocessing))
This is the practice gap that matters most from our side. Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is the single closest regulatory hook to this lecture's subject. I checked the text: Article 10(2)(c) covers data preparation operations including annotation, labelling, cleaning and aggregation, which is slides 35 to 43; 10(2)(f) and 10(2)(g) require examination for and mitigation of biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights and non-discrimination; 10(3) requires.
Suggested fix: Add two slides. One after slide 31 mapping the deck's data quality factors onto Article 10(3) and noting that completeness in the statistical sense and representativeness in the regulatory sense are different things. One after slide 38 on bias introduced by preparation choices, using missing data as the example: dropping incomplete.
Also noticed

The biggest finding in this deck, missed entirely. Slides 12 to 16 and slide 18 are near-verbatim copies of HC-172 slides 34 to 43, by the same author, and HC-172 is HC-180's own stated prerequisite. HC-172 slide 34 opens 'The central tendency of data is described by averages, which are the most commonly used characteristics in practice. For example, each company stores data.
HC-178 Introduction to Data Types and Data Formats (Part 2), by Kalinka Kaloyanova, duplicates HC-180 slides 34 to 38. HC-178's plan has a 30-minute block 'Data preprocessing: incomplete, noisy, inconsistent data; cleaning, handling missing data, data wrangling' and a learning outcome 'Students can apply basic data preprocessing techniques'. Its material carries the same.
Internal inconsistency inside the data quality section the review calls the deck's strongest part. Validity is a sub-dimension of accuracy on slide 23 and a top-level factor on slide 28. Non-redundancy sits under completeness on slide 24 while uniqueness is its own factor on slide 27 with duplicate detection. The same double-listing is in the wiki plan (accuracy with.
Smaller points

Slide 18, box plot bullet. It says box plots 'Display the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and identify outliers'. Those two claims conflict. In a standard Tukey box plot the whiskers extend to the most extreme observation within 1.5 times the IQR, not to.
Slide 15, variance bullet. 'The average of the squared differences from the mean' is the population variance. At master's level the n against n-1 distinction should be stated, since students will meet both in pandas (which defaults to n-1) and numpy (which defaults to n) and get.
Slide 37, missing data. The strategies listed (ignore the record, fill with a global constant, imputation, inference-based methods) are given with no guidance on when each is defensible. The missingness mechanism decides that, and MCAR, MAR and MNAR are not mentioned anywhere..
Slides 14, 19 and 20 have no title and no body text in the PDF export. If they are figures, give each a title, a caption and a source credit. If any is an empty placeholder, remove it. I can only see the text layer, so the author should confirm which.
I cannot see any speaker notes in the PDF export. The guidelines require lecturer notes sufficient for someone who did not write the deck. Please confirm the source PPTX carries them, particularly for slides 19 and 20 and for the 45-minute visualisation block.
Only two interactive elements across 180 minutes (slides 33 and 45), and both sit inside the preprocessing section. Nothing in the first 32 slides and nothing in the last 15. Add one early, for example asking students on slide 12 which measure of central tendency they would use.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 12 items. The notable results:

IBM 'What is exploratory data analysis?' page, fetched. Confirmed it contains verbatim the wording on slide 9: 'help look at data before making any assumptions. It can help identify obvious errors, as well as better understand patterns within the data, detect outliers or anomalous events, find.
Wikipedia 'Exploratory data analysis', fetched. Lead reads 'an approach of analyzing data sets to summarize their main characteristics, often using statistical graphics and other data visualization methods'. Slide 9 bullet 1 is this sentence with 'statistical graphics and other' removed. Confirmed.
Wikipedia 'Box plot', fetched. Confirmed the whiskers of a Tukey box plot extend to the most extreme observation within 1.5 times the IQR, not to the minimum and maximum, and that points beyond are drawn as outliers. This confirms the internal contradiction in slide 18. Also confirmed Tukey.
Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, verified via Wikipedia's Jiawei Han entry. Authors Jiawei Han, Micheline Kamber, Jian Pei; Morgan Kaufmann; 3rd edition 2011, ISBN 1-55860-901-6. These are the details the author should cite. I confirmed the book is the source of the.
Source of the slide 36 to 38 prose on data munging: NOT verified. This session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could run the phrase searches, and the fallback search engine returned a CAPTCHA which I did not attempt to bypass. I am reporting that the prose is not the author's own.
Plan against material
["They agree on structure and disagree on depth, and the disagreement runs in both directions. Section for section: Introduction (plan 10 min) maps to slides 4 to 7. Nature and goals of EDA (15 min) maps to slides 8 to 10. Data quality (20 min) maps to slides 21 to 31 and the material exceeds the plan, adding uniqueness and three additional factors; the plan should be updated to match. Wrap up (10 min) maps to slides 56 to 58. Those four blocks are fine.", "Three blocks do not agree. Basic statistical characteristics (plan 20 min) explicitly lists measures of shape, skewness and kurtosis, and slides 11 to 16 do not cover them. The plan is right here and the material must change. Graphic displays (plan 45 min) lists dot plot, line graph, bubble chart and mosaic plot, and organises the block by univariate, bivariate and multivariate; slide 18 has none of that structure and four of the.

Coverage
["It does not fill 180 minutes. Of 60 slides, five are front and back matter (title, objectives, agenda, acknowledgements, disclaimer), eight are section dividers, and three (14, 19, 20) carry no text. That leaves about 44 content slides, most of them short definition lists, for three hours. Delivered at a normal lecturing pace with both interactive elements run properly, I would expect this to come in around 100 to 110 minutes. The gap is roughly an hour.", "Two things make the gap worse than the slide count suggests. First, slides 50 to 54 largely restate material already given: the EDA characteristics on slides 50 to 53 repeat the goals on slides 9 to 10, and the technique list on slide.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.heading: Correction from RealAI: our duration comment, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 180 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 60 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.33. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

entries.title: HC-183 Data Exploration and Preparation (Part 2)
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: The lecture content is accurate and the tool choices are sound for 2026, but the learning event ships two third-party PDFs whose licences conflict with the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 notice on the wiki, misattributes one of them and links students to an unauthorised copy, and reduces the 60-minute hands-on block that carries the third learning outcome to a single instruction sentence on slide 32.

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

The lecture content is accurate and the tool choices are sound for 2026, but the learning event ships two third-party PDFs whose licences conflict with the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 notice on the wiki, misattributes one of them and links students to an unauthorised copy, and reduces the 60-minute hands-on block that carries the third learning outcome to a single instruction sentence on slide 32.

What already works

Slides 17 to 26 name Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, PySpark, OpenRefine, Tableau, Power BI, Jupyter, D3.js and RStudio/ggplot2. Every one is still actively maintained and still used in practice in 2026 (I checked OpenRefine 3.10.1, released March 2026, and Orange 3.40.0, December 2025). There is no dead or abandoned tool on the list, which is unusual for a tool survey slide set and worth saying.
Slide 38 includes data leakage prevention as a preprocessing concern. Most introductory preparation lessons leave this out and it is the single most common way a student pipeline produces an inflated score. Including it at this level is the right call.
Slide 36 lists bias detection as a purpose of data exploration, and ties it to unfair or discriminatory model behaviour. That is the correct place to introduce it, at the point where the student is looking at the data rather than at the model.
Choosing Orange for the hands-on part is well judged for a mixed-background master cohort. It is free, GPL-licensed, cross-platform and needs no coding, so the session does not become a Python debugging clinic. The three links on slide 31 (homepage, downloads, documentation) all resolve.
What we would change

The wiki states that the materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but two of the three files are third-party works under incompatible terms. HC-183-Orange Hands-on Course.pdf is a verbatim. (Wiki, Lesson materials section; files HC-183-Orange Hands-on Course.pdf and HC-183_Orange Canvas Tutorial.pdf)
CC BY-NC-SA invites downstream partners to remix and redistribute. ND forbids distributing adaptations, and a work with no declared licence cannot be redistributed at all without the author's permission. These decks get copied onward across the consortium, so a blanket CC BY-NC-SA notice over an ND work exports the problem to every partner who picks it up.
Suggested fix: Do not bundle either PDF. Replace the Zupan and Demsar file with a link to the authoritative free copy at https://file.biolab.si/notes/2018-05-intro-to-datamining-notes.pdf and state its CC BY-NC-ND terms. Replace the Al-Qatawna file with a link to its DOI (10.13140/RG.2.2.34612.94089/1), or obtain and record written permission from the.
Reference [2] on slide 33 reads 'Zupan, D. Introduction to Data Mining with Orange - Lesson Notes' and links to a studocu.vn page. The author initial is wrong (it is Blaz Zupan, not D.), the co-author Janez Demsar is. (Slide 33 (References), and the filename of HC-183-Orange Hands-on Course.pdf)
The material the students open is a named, dated, licensed work by two identifiable authors, and the deck neither names them correctly nor points to the legitimate source. Sending students to a pirated copy while the free official copy sits on the authors' own server is not defensible in a deck that ships under a Creative Commons licence.
Suggested fix: Correct reference [2] to: Zupan, B. and Demsar, J. Introduction to Data Mining: Working notes for the hands-on course with Orange Data Mining. University of Ljubljana, May 2018. CC BY-NC-ND. Available at https://file.biolab.si/notes/2018-05-intro-to-datamining-notes.pdf. Remove the studocu.vn link. Add the same entry to the reference.
The entire independent exercise is slide 32, two bullets: install an appropriate version of Orange, then follow tutorial [1] or [2] to explore a selected dataset and visualize the results. There is no named dataset, no. (Slide 32, and wiki Instructions for teachers, fourth block (60 min))
This block carries 60 of the 180 minutes and is the only place where the third learning outcome ('can independently use a popular free data mining tool') can be met. As written a lecturer cannot run it and a student cannot tell when they are finished. It also fails most of the consortium's own tutorial checklist: required datasets, how the assignment is concluded, expected output format, realistic timing, examples of expected work, sample solutions.
Suggested fix: Specify the exercise. Name one dataset (heart_disease ships with Orange and is used in Lesson 2 of the bundled notes, so it needs no download). State the steps, for example: load the data, inspect it in Data Table, produce one distribution and one scatter plot, use Select Rows to split by a chosen variable, then use the widget Report.
The wiki Instructions for teachers allocates 60 minutes to 'Popular software tools for data preprocessing and data exploration' with four named sub-topics: Python libraries, R packages, Excel / Google Sheets, and. (Wiki Instructions for teachers, third block; deck slides 16 to 27)
A lecturer preparing from the lesson plan will expect to teach four tool families and will find slides for two. Excel and Google Sheets are also the tools most of these students will actually meet first in a workplace, so dropping them removes the most practice-relevant part of the block.
Suggested fix: Either add slides for Excel / Google Sheets (Power Query, pivot tables, the practical row limits and the reproducibility problem) and expand R beyond ggplot2, or amend the wiki Instructions for teachers to list only what the deck covers. The wiki and the deck have to agree; the wiki is currently the more complete of the two, so adding.
Agenda slide 3 lists item 4 as 'Demonstration: data preprocessing and data exploration with Orange'. Section divider slide 28 and the wiki both call the same block 'Independent exercise'. There is also no demonstration. (Slide 3 (agenda) against slide 28 and wiki Instructions for teachers)
A demonstration and an independent exercise are different activities with different room setups, different laptop requirements and different lecturer preparation. A substitute lecturer reading slide 3 will prepare a demo and then find nothing to demonstrate from.
Suggested fix: Decide which it is. If it stays an independent exercise, correct slide 3 to match slide 28 and the wiki. If a short demonstration is wanted first (recommended, given the install and orientation overhead), add three or four screenshots of a File to Data Table to Distributions to Scatter Plot workflow and split the 60 minutes explicitly,.
The wiki Expected preparation section says obligatory preparation for students is 'None', and references and background for students is 'None'. But the session requires Orange to be installed (slide 32) and hands. (Wiki, Expected preparation section)
Installing Orange on a locked-down university laptop is not a five-minute task and it will eat the exercise block if it happens in class. A lecturer reading 'obligatory preparation: None' will not warn students in advance, and the 60 minutes will be spent on installers. Listing the two tutorials as 'None' also leaves them untraceable from the lesson plan.
Suggested fix: Set obligatory preparation to: install Orange (current stable release, https://orangedatamining.com/download/) before the session and confirm it opens. List both tutorials under references and background for students with correct citations. Fill in 'Recommended for teachers' with at least the Zupan and Demsar notes Lessons 1 to 4, which.
Slides 29 and 30 reproduce the feature descriptions from the Orange homepage word for word, presented as body text with no quotation marks and no source line. Slide 29 opens with the site's own wording, 'No coding. (Slides 29 and 30)
This is verbatim third-party text presented as the deck's own in a document that is redistributed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The fix is small but the standard has to hold, because these slides get copied into other partners' decks.
Suggested fix: Put both passages in quotation marks and add 'Source: orangedatamining.com' on each slide. Slide 31 already lists the homepage URL, so this is a two-line change.
Also noticed

The deck makes the same blanket licence claim the review only pins on the wiki. Slide 41 reads 'All materials are made available under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License' and goes on to grant remix and adapt rights. If the third-party PDFs stay in the package, slide 41 needs the same carve-out as the wiki notice. The fix in.
The funding programme question is resolvable and the review left it open. I fetched the EU Funding and Tenders topic record for digital-2023-skills-05-specialedu: programme 'Digital Europe Programme (DIGITAL)', call DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05, topic 'Specialised education programmes in key capacity areas', programme division DIGITAL-1-1. So slide 40 naming the Connecting Europe.
The pedigree of the Al-Qatawna tutorial is the strongest practice argument for dropping it and the review never makes it. The file is a personal MSc course project: cover page carries a private Gmail address, 'PROJECT FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE COURSE', and a closing thank-you to a course supervisor; DataCite lists publisher 'Unpublished'. It is handed to master students as.
Smaller points

Slide 15 carries no title and no body text. If it is meant to be an image (a box plot or an IQR diagram would fit between the outlier bullet on 14 and the section divider on 16) it needs a caption and a source note. If it is a leftover blank, delete it. Either way it reaches the.
Slide 14 says missingness may be 'random or patterned'. The standard practice vocabulary is MCAR, MAR and MNAR (Rubin, D. B., 1976, Inference and missing data, Biometrika 63(3), 581 to 592, verified via Crossref). The mechanism is what decides whether listwise deletion is safe.
Slide 14 lists only z-scores and the IQR method for outlier detection. Orange ships an Outliers widget (Unsupervised category) offering One Class SVM, Covariance Estimator, Local Outlier Factor and Isolation Forest. Naming it connects the lecture bullet to something the student.
Add a sentence on the fairness consequence of outlier handling. Dropping outliers can remove exactly the minority subgroups the programme cares about. This is a one-line addition to slide 14 that would strengthen the human-centred angle at no cost to timing.
For the human-centred orientation, consider the orange3-fairness add-on (version 1.0.3, July 2026), which adds Dataset Bias, Reweighing, Adversarial Debiasing and Equalized Odds Postprocessing widgets. Dataset Bias computes disparate impact and statistical parity difference.
Slide 38's data leakage point has nothing behind it in the hands-on part. The bundled Zupan and Demsar notes cover exactly this in Lessons 9 to 14 (How to Cheat, Cheating Works Even..., How to Correctly...). Pointing students at Lesson 9 and Lesson 14 as optional reading would.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 18 items. The notable results:

DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.34612.94089/1 (slide 33, reference [1]): VERIFIED via the DataCite API. Resolves to Al-Qatawna, Hamza M., 'Orange Canvas "A Machine Learning Toolkit Tutorial"', 2022, type Presentation. Author, year and DOI in the deck are correct. However the record shows publisher.
Bundled file HC-183-Orange Hands-on Course.pdf: VERIFIED as a verbatim copy of Zupan, B. and Demsar, J., 'Introduction to Data Mining: Working notes for the hands-on course with Orange Data Mining', University of Ljubljana, May 2018. I downloaded the official copy from.
Whether a newer edition of those notes exists: CHECKED and none found. The file.biolab.si/notes/ directory listing shows the May 2018 general edition is the most recent under that title; later files are workshop-specific (2019 Pavia, 2019 Ostrava, 2020 Bressanone, 2020 Ljubljana). So the 2018 date.
Reference [2] attribution 'Zupan, D.' (slide 33): CONFIRMED WRONG. The notes are by Blaz Zupan and Janez Demsar, per the running header on all 72 pages of the work itself and the front matter. The initial is wrong and the co-author is missing. The studocu.vn URL returns HTTP 403 to an.
Orange: Data Mining Toolbox in Python (cited without authors in the Al-Qatawna tutorial's reference list): VERIFIED on jmlr.org. Demsar, J. et al. (16 authors, ending Blaz Zupan), Journal of Machine Learning Research 14, pages 2349 to 2353, 2013.
Plan against material
"They agree on shape and disagree on content in four places. The five-block structure and the timings in the wiki Instructions for teachers (15 + 30 + 60 + 60 + 15 = 180) map cleanly onto the deck's five sections, and the three learning outcomes on the wiki are reproduced word for word on slide 2, so the skeleton matches. The disagreements: first, the wiki's tools block names Python libraries, R packages, Excel / Google Sheets and Orange, but the deck has no Excel or Google Sheets content and only one R slide, so the wiki is right and the deck is short. Second, the wiki and slide 28 call block four an independent exercise while agenda slide 3 calls it a demonstration; the wiki is right and slide 3 is wrong. Third, the wiki says obligatory student preparation is None, but slide 32 requires Orange to be installed, so the wiki is wrong and needs an install instruction. Fourth, the wiki.

Coverage
"It fills the 180 minutes on paper but not in practice, and it delivers two of the three learning outcomes. Outcomes 1 and 2 ('aware of the basic techniques', 'aware of a range of tools') are met by slides 6 to 27. Outcome 3 ('can independently use a popular free data mining tool') is not delivered by the material; it is delegated in full to two third-party PDFs by way of one instruction sentence on slide 32. On timing, the middle block is the weak point: slides 16 to 27 are 12 slides of three bullets each against a 60-minute allocation, which will run 20 to 25 minutes as written, and the review block is two slides against 15 minutes. The basic techniques block (10 slides, 30 minutes) and.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

action_summary.text:
Maria and Greg, this is the short, actionable version of our early feedback of 9 September 2026; the full text stays above as the record. RealAI also keeps a longer, more instructional version of our review on file in our PANORAIMA dashboard; ask us if you would like a copy.

Verdict: early feedback only, not yet a formal review (status is still "Learning materials: development"); the lecture content is sound, the hands-on block and licensing are not.

Please do next:
# Specify the exercise on slide 32 and in Instructions for teachers: name a dataset (heart_disease), the steps, the expected output, the finish point.
# Remove both third-party PDFs from the package; link the official biolab.si notes and the Al-Qatawna DOI instead.
# Correct reference [2] on slide 33 to Zupan, B. and Demsar, J., and delete the studocu.vn link.
# Add a third-party licence carve-out to the wiki Lesson materials notice and to slide 41.
# Align the wiki tools block with slides 16 to 27: add Excel / Google Sheets and more R, or shorten the wiki list.
# Change agenda slide 3 from "Demonstration" to "Independent exercise", matching slide 28 and the wiki.
# Quote the Orange homepage text on slides 29 and 30 and add "Source: orangedatamining.com".

Wiki page (to complete before sign-off):
* Expected preparation: all four fields say "None", yet students must install Orange beforehand; list the tutorials as references.
* Acknowledgements: grant number still reads "???", and it names Connecting Europe while the call is Digital Europe (DIGITAL-2023-SKILLS-05); slide 40 repeats this.

A short summary is not a lower bar: a complete wiki page and the best teaching material we can offer remain our conditions for sign-off.

When the items are done, tell us on the Discussion page and email the review inbox, and we will re-review.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 14 October 2026, 20:54 CEST
