entries.title: HC-186 Synthetic Data
entries.author: SU · Maria Nisheva
entries.review_note: HC-186 follows its lesson plan closely and closes with a genuinely good section on what goes wrong with synthetic data, but it reproduces two published CC BY papers without credit, presents a list of real benchmark datasets as examples of synthetic datasets, tells students that subsampling real records protects privacy, and carries no citations, no tools, no metrics and no interactive elements, so

long_form.heading: Early feedback (RealAI): material in development, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
This is early feedback, not a formal review. This learning event is still marked "Learning materials: development" on the wiki, so the material has not been submitted to us for review and we are not asking for a revision. We read it because RealAI is the assigned reviewer and the material is already in SharePoint, and it seemed more useful to say these things now than after the status moves to review. Please treat everything below as optional. We will do the formal review, on whatever version you submit, once the status changes.

HC-186 follows its lesson plan closely and closes with a genuinely good section on what goes wrong with synthetic data, but it reproduces two published CC BY papers without credit, presents a list of real benchmark datasets as examples of synthetic datasets, tells students that subsampling real records protects privacy, and carries no citations, no tools, no metrics and no interactive elements, so it needs revision before it is taught.

What already works

Slides 45 to 48 are the best part of the deck and show real subject understanding. Model collapse, loss of long-tail cases, bias amplification, memorisation, membership inference and the absence of ground truth for multivariate correlations are the right five things to leave students with. The 'false uniformity' point on slide 46, that over-balancing smooths away authentic demographic variation,.
The worked LLM scenario on slides 34 to 36 is how this is actually done in a regulated setting. It goes schema, then prompt with distributions and an ICD-10 validity constraint, then a validation step with three concrete acceptance criteria including re-identification. Making validation a required step rather than an optional afterthought is the correct professional framing.
Slide 11 puts the caveat before the enthusiasm. Distribution shift, bias amplification and model collapse are named on the same slide that introduces synthetic data as the solution, not 30 slides later. That ordering choice is deliberate and it is the right one.
The section structure matches the wiki 'Instructions for teachers' section for section and minute for minute, including the three named sub-topics under machine learning. A lecturer picking this up cold can map the deck to the plan without guessing, which is exactly what the consortium checklist asks for and is rarer than it should be.
What we would change

Slides 16 to 27 and slides 38 to 40 reproduce text and dataset lists from two published papers with no attribution. (Slides 16-27 (programmatic, statistical and ML method sections) and slides 38-40 (dataset lists))
Both source papers are CC BY 4.0. That licence permits the reuse but requires credit. The deck ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with no reference to either paper, so it breaches the attribution term of the licence it depends on and puts NonCommercial and ShareAlike restrictions onto other authors' CC BY work. These decks are designed to be copied onward, so the defect propagates with every reuse.
Suggested fix: Add source lines on the affected slides plus a references slide. The methods prose traces to Goyal, M. and Mahmoud, Q.H. (2024), 'A Systematic Review of Synthetic Data Generation Techniques Using Generative AI', Electronics 13(17):3509, DOI 10.3390/electronics13173509, CC BY 4.0. The dataset lists trace to Zulfiqar, A., Daudpota, S.M.,.
The section titled 'Examples of existing synthetic datasets' is a list of real, human-collected datasets. (Slides 37-40)
CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST, SVHN, mini ImageNet, Omniglot, MS-COCO, Oxford-102 Flowers, Caltech-UCSD Birds, Stanford Cars, CelebA and CelebA-HQ are all collected from the real world. FFHQ is 70,000 real photographs scraped from Flickr. The source paper even labels one entry 'Real face dataset (AffectNET)' and the deck copies that label verbatim under a heading saying these are synthetic. A student who takes this slide at face value goes looking for synthetic data and.
Suggested fix: Retitle these slides to something like 'Benchmark datasets used in generative image research', which is what the source list actually is. Then add a short slide of datasets that genuinely are synthetic and downloadable today: Synthea synthetic patient records (Walonoski et al., JAMIA 2018, 25(3):230-238, DOI 10.1093/jamia/ocx079), the.
Slide 18 says random sampling creates synthetic data by selecting observations from an existing dataset, and that this avoids disclosing sensitive information. (Slide 18)
Both halves are wrong. Rows drawn from a real dataset are real records, not synthetic ones. Sampling them discloses those individuals exactly, in full. This is the single sentence in the deck most likely to cause harm if a student acts on it, because it tells them a subsample is a privacy control. In a human-centred AI programme that cannot ship.
Suggested fix: Rewrite to describe sampling from a fitted distribution rather than sampling rows, which is what the programmatic and statistical approaches actually do. If the intent was to cover resampling and class balancing (SMOTE and similar), say so explicitly and state plainly that resampled real records carry the same disclosure risk as the.
There are no citations anywhere in 50 slides, including for the data crisis claims and for two named frameworks. (Slides 9-11, 29, 31 and 45; there is no references slide)
The empirical claims that motivate the entire lecture are unsourced, and GANs and VAEs are presented without their authors. A lecturer teaching this cold has nothing to point students at, and the wiki compounds it by listing 'References and background for students: None'. The consortium checklist asks explicitly for traceability of claims and figures.
Suggested fix: Add a references slide and inline sources. All of these are verified: Villalobos, P. et al., 'Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data', arXiv:2211.04325 (ICML 2024), for the exhaustion projection behind slide 9. Longpre, S. et al., 'Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons',.
Diffusion models are missing from the method taxonomy. (Slide 14, and the whole of section 5 (slides 24-36))
Slide 14 offers GANs, VAEs and LLMs as the deep learning options. Diffusion has been the default image and video generator since roughly 2022 and is what a student joining a team in 2026 will meet first. The deck names diffusion exactly once, on slide 47, as a memorisation hazard, so students encounter it as a risk before they ever encounter it as a method. The learning outcome about the main types of generation methods is not met without it.
Suggested fix: Add diffusion to slide 14 and give it a block in section 5 alongside GANs and VAEs: why it displaced GANs for images (training stability, mode coverage) and what it costs (sampling time). Keep GANs, but frame them as the historical route and as still current for tabular work through CTGAN.
No named tools, no named evaluation metrics, no differential privacy, and no reference to the EU AI Act. (Slides 41-43 (evaluation), section 5 (methods), and the deck as a whole)
This is the practice layer and it is absent. Slides 42 and 43 name five aspects of quality but not one metric, threshold or library, so the learning outcome about assessing synthetic data quality gives students nothing they can act on. No generator a practitioner would actually run is named anywhere. Differential privacy, which is the accepted answer to the memorisation and inference risks slide 47 raises, never appears. The only legal reference in 50 slides is the word GDPR.
Suggested fix: On evaluation, name the working methods: train on synthetic and test on real for utility, propensity score pMSE for distinguishability, distance to closest record and membership inference AUC for privacy, and point at the SDMetrics library. Name at least one generator students can run, for example SDV with CTGAN (Xu, L., Skoularidou, M.,.
The deck does not fill 120 minutes and contains no interactive elements. (Whole deck, measured against 'Instructions for teachers' on the wiki)
There are roughly 40 content slides, all continuous bullets, with no exercise, no poll, no discussion question and no worked example students touch. Slides 38 to 40 are 60 dataset names that cannot carry the 10 minutes the plan allocates. Delivered at normal pace this runs 60 to 75 minutes against a 120 minute slot. The consortium format scan asks for 2 to 4 clearly indicated interactive elements and for lecturer notes, and the file we received has neither. The sixth.
Suggested fix: Add 2 to 4 interactive elements at the section boundaries: a poll after slide 11 on whether students would accept a synthetic dataset for a credit scoring model, a 10 minute paired exercise after slide 36 where students write the schema and constraints for a synthetic dataset in their own domain, and a discussion after slide 47 on when.
Also noticed

The attribution range is understated. Slides 25, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 31 are also verbatim Goyal and Mahmoud, from the same paper's section 4.4. Slide 25 is 'Machine learning-based techniques have transformed the production of synthetic data, providing a robust and versatile approach that outperforms previous methods in many ways'. Slide 29 is 'GANs are an excellent example of.
The differential privacy gap has a much sharper form than the one they used. Goyal's paper runs 4.1 programmatic, 4.2 statistical, 4.3 Differential Privacy Approach, 4.4 machine learning. The deck reproduces 4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 and skips 4.3 entirely. The author was copying from a source that had the differential privacy section right there and left it out. That is a concrete,.
The privacy misconception is a pattern across the deck, not one slide. Slide 18 says subsampling avoids direct disclosure. Slide 19 goes further and says random sampling is 'especially useful in situations where privacy considerations prevent the direct use of original datasets'. Slide 27 says ML-generated synthetic data can be used 'to share insights and improve models while.
Smaller points

Slide 43 says privacy evaluation 'ensures that the synthetic data does not reveal sensitive information about individuals'. Slide 47 then correctly says generative models memorise records and that membership inference and reconstruction attacks recover originals. Students hear.
Slide 45 presents model collapse as an automatic compounding cycle. The condition matters and changes the practical advice: Gerstgrasser et al., arXiv:2404.01413 (2024), show that accumulating synthetic data alongside real data avoids collapse, while replacing real data with.
Slides 11 and 13 carry the same definition sentence word for word ('Synthetic Data refers to data that is artificially generated rather than directly collected from real-world events or annotations'). Drop one.
Slide 38 misspells Flickr-Faces-HQ as 'Flicker-Faces-HQ'. On slide 39 the Radboud Faces Database appears twice under two spellings, 'RAFD' under face recognition and 'Redboud Faces dataset' under object detection. Both errors are inherited from the source paper and disappear if.
Slide 30 is an image with no caption and no source, presumably the GAN architecture diagram. If it came from a third party it needs crediting; if the author drew it, say so on the slide.
Slides 32 and 33 treat LLM generation as though prompting alone produces a usable dataset. Add a line on the cost side: token cost at scale, near-duplicate detection, and the fact that the ICD-10 validity requirement stated in the prompt on slide 35 has to be enforced by a.
What we checked against sources
We verified the citations, statistics and named frameworks in this material, 14 items. The notable results:

Source of slides 16 to 27. Confirmed. The sentence 'Rule-based systems create synthetic data by complying with a set of established rules and logical constructs that mimic the features and relationships of real data' and the non-parametric models passage both match Goyal, M. and Mahmoud, Q.H..
Source of slides 38 to 40. Confirmed. The dataset lists match Zulfiqar, A., Daudpota, S.M., Imran, A.S., Kastrati, Z., Ullah, M. and Sadhwani, S. (2024), 'Synthetic Image Generation Using Deep Learning: A Systematic Literature Review', Computational Intelligence 40(5):e70002. Verified authors,.
Villalobos, P., Ho, A., Sevilla, J. et al., 'Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data', arXiv:2211.04325. Verified via the arXiv API: exact title, authors, first submitted 26 October 2022, and it does forecast exhaustion of public human-generated text between.
Shumailov, I., Shumaylov, Z., Zhao, Y., Papernot, N., Anderson, R. and Gal, Y., 'AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data'. Verified via Crossref: Nature, volume 631, issue 8022, pages 755-759, 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y. Title, all six authors, volume and pagination.
Gerstgrasser, M., Schaeffer, R., Dey, A. et al., 'Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data', arXiv:2404.01413, submitted 1 April 2024. Verified. Finding confirmed: accumulating successive generations of synthetic data alongside the.
Plan against material
They agree on structure, and that part is done well. The learning objectives on slides 2 and 3 reproduce the wiki's six outcomes verbatim, and the eight sections of the deck map one to one onto the eight timed blocks in 'Instructions for teachers', including the three named sub-topics under machine learning. Where they disagree the wiki is right in one case and wrong in two others. (1) Slide 14 calls the category 'Deep learning-based models' while slide 24 and the wiki both say 'Machine learning-based models'. Follow the wiki and slide 24, and fix slide 14. (2) The wiki lists 'References and background for students: None'. That is wrong now and will be more wrong once the references slide required above exists; three or four of those citations belong here as student reading. (3) The wiki's acknowledgement says 'Under Grant No ???' while slide 49 gives call.

Coverage
It does not fill 120 minutes and it does not deliver all six outcomes. Around 40 content slides of unbroken bullet text, with zero interactive elements and no exercise, realistically runs 60 to 75 minutes. Section by section against the plan: Introduction has six content slides for 20 minutes, which a lecturer can stretch; 'Examples of existing synthetic datasets' has three slides of dataset names for 10 minutes, which cannot be stretched and which are wrong anyway; Evaluation has two content slides for 10 minutes, and that is the thinnest part of the deck relative to its importance. On outcomes: 1 (data crisis) is covered but unsourced. 2 (nature and forms of synthetic data) is covered,.

Nothing here needs a reply. If it is easier to discuss any of it, we are happy to.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026

long_form.heading: Correction from RealAI: our duration comment, 9 September 2026
long_form.text:
Correction to our own review, not a request to the author.

We reviewed all 25 Horizontal learning events and then looked at them as a set. That second pass showed
that our comment about this event not filling its 120 minutes was unfair, and we want that on the record
before anyone acts on it.

The consortium format guidance gives two rules in the same paragraph: approximately one slide per minute of
teaching time, and typically 30 to 60 slides for a lecture. Below an hour those agree. Above an hour they
contradict each other, and the guidance never says which one wins. This event carries about 50 slides,
which is inside the stated 30 to 60 range, so the author followed the written rule.

The pattern is not about any one author. Across the 25 events, slides per declared minute fall into two
bands with no overlap: 0.50 to 1.18 for the nine events of 90 minutes or less, and 0.15 to 0.43 for the
fifteen slide-based events of 120 minutes or more. This event sits at about 0.42. The split follows
duration, not partner or institution, and the one long event that does fill its slot is a notebook
practical rather than a slide deck. The same per-event framing explains why interactive elements fall from
about 3.3 per hour at 60 minutes to about 0.9 per hour at 120 minutes and above, and why no plan of 120
minutes or more in the whole set schedules a break.

So: please read our volume comment as a finding about the guidance, not about your work. We have raised the
guidance problem with WP4 separately. Everything else in our review stands as written.

RealAI (Tarry Singh), 9 September 2026
